units.la: QVis fieri posse credidisset, ut in iis ipsis qui se profiten-tur, abiecta omni Idololatria, Christum adorare, com-perirentur, qui Deitate illum spoliaret, & θεάνθρωπον in θεῖον ἄνθρωπον transformarent? Nam certe amentis est hominis & prorsus ἀναίσθητος[?], Idololatram se negare, & tamen eum verum ac natura Deum esse inficiari, quem invocandum, omni-busque diuinis honoribus afficiendum prædices. Reperta sunt tamen iam olim eiusmodi hominum monstra, quæ propterea Antichristos Orthodoxi vocant, vt Cherinthus & Hebion, ipsis etiam Apostolo-rum temporibus: quorum blasphemiam interpolarunt postea Theo-dotus Byzantinus, & execrandus ille Samosatenus, eius Ecclesiæ conspurcator, in qua primi sunt Christiani nominati. Istis porrò de-bellatis mostris, ecce tandem Arius, rabida illa furia, ex abysso pro-diit, minimè quidem ille Christum φιλὸν ἄνθρωπον[?] statuens illorum exemplo: sed qui τὸν λόγον asserēret creatum quiddam esse, idque in tempore, ac proinde illum vera Deitate privaret, quum vera Deitas nullo modo possit inter res creatas censeri, sed Diuinitas potius, id est qualitas quædam seu præstantia, ex Deitatis virtute & efficacia promanas, quo modo dixit Petrus nos fieri θείας φύσεως κοινωνούς. Sic enim nos docet hæreticorum vafrities Deitatem à Diuinitate distinguere, sicut & ipse Paulus non θεότητος, sed θεότητος[?] plenitudi-nem Christo attribuit. Sed & Græci ipsi prophani scriptores, quam-uis τὸ θεῖον appellent quod Latini Numen, tamē suos illos siue maio-rū siue minorum Gentium Deos, θεοὺς potius quā θεὰς vocant: vnde & istos dicuntur ἐνθεῶσαι[?], id est ex Diuinis, quales eos antea habebant, Deos effecisse, ut Idololatriam excusare nullo modo possint: quoniam (ut adversus illos à nostris copiosè disputatum est) nec religiosè quicquam praeter verum Deum adorari, nec quicquam creatum verus Deus haberi, sine maximo flagitio, potest. Recte igitur adversus Arium universalis illa celeberrima Synodus Nicaena, quam omnes postea tum universales tum provinciales Orthodoxi Synodi perpetuo consensu confirmarunt: recte, inquam, illa, quum & ex ipso communi sensu, quantumuis corrupto, & multo magis ex manifestissimo Dei verbo refelli omnem ἀπολυδρίαν videret, & tamen in scripturis Patrem, Filium, & Spiritum sanctum, extra quos nullus est verus Deus, manifeste inter se distingui, animadverso inter οὐσίαν (id est communem essentiam sive naturam) & ὑπόστασιν, quam postea ὑπόστασιν, id est personam vocarunt, discrimine: decreuit τὸν λόγον esse Filium Patri ὁμοούσιον, id est coessentialem. Hoc autem nomine commodissimè ac plane necessariò ad refellendas illas blasphemias usurpato, duo significavit: nempe sic unam esse Patris & Filij essentiam ac naturam, id est Deitatem, ut sint etiam ὑπόστατοι[?], id est in unica illa ac singularissima Deitate subsistentes, distincti videlicet suis proprietatibus, non autem in duas numero essentias separati: quoniam & unica (ut dixi) & simplicissima, ac proinde insecabilis, cademque in ipsis singulis tota est Deitas, in qua subsistunt. Ipsi verò Ariomanitæ pervicaces, qui & ἑτεροούσιοι dicti sunt, quòd τὸν λόγον facerent natura & essentia diversum à Patre, & ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων creatum dicerent, postea in duas minimum factiones divisi sunt, nempe in ὁμοιουσίας (quasi æquiessentiales dicas) & ἀνομοίους, id est dissimiles. Necenim deerant versuti simul & stolidi homines, qui, quum unicam tantum literulam interponerent, id est ὁμοούσιον in ὁμοιούσιον transformarent, latere posse suum Arianismum sperarent: quùm tamen crassius etiam quam ipse Arius, manifeste ἰτι-[?] ἐπιρρούσιῳ[?], hallucinarentur, nisi vox illa ὁμοιουσίᾳ[?] (sicut de Dionysio Corinthio Basilius ad fratrem scribit) commoda quadam interpretatione, sed plane, ut mihi videtur, violenta leniatur. Nam certè in una eademque prorsus essentia nullus est neque æqualitati neque inæqualitati locus, ut pote quæ minimum in duobus cernantur: ac proinde in hypostasibus, non in essentia, spectari æqualitatè necesse est. Ἀνόμοιοι vero, quamuis & ipsi dogma suum quibus possent coloribus fucarent, tamen vel manifeste se Arianos prodebant, ut qui Filium Patri facerent dissimilem: vel omnino stolidos se præbebant, quum in simplicissima & singularissima natura, nempe Deitate, maius & minus quiddam imaginaretur. Cum his igitur monstris ubi diu multumque luctata est Ecclesia, & quidem eo sæpe redactis rebus, ut nulla re magis quam precibus & innumerabilium Martyrum sanguine restinctum illud incendium videatur: ecce mox ex eiusdem abyssi puteo emergit Nestorius, qui novo quodam artificio idem quod Arius moliretur, ut qui Filium Mariæ secundum carnem, negaret secundum divinam naturam esse Dei filium, ut una eademque persona sit verus Deus & verus homo. Affirmabat enim τὸν λόγον illi carni ex Maria prognatæ, nonnisi ἐνεργητικὴ[?] παρουσίᾳ[?] adfuisse. quod certè nihil aliud erat, quam diuisa Christi Mediatoris persona, illum, ex homine Deo divinissimum quendam hominem statuere. Inde verò quum illud ipsum consequatur, quod per illos priores diuersis cuniculis tentauit Diabolus, nempe ut unicum illum nostrum Seruatorem adorantes, Idololatræ deprehenderemur: quis ita cæcus est, ut non animaduertat quam rabie Sathan aduersus humanum genus feratur, & qua vafritie mutatis subinde coloribus, caligantibus nostris oculis illudat? Detectum igitur tandem & profligatum Cyrilli potissimum opera & virtute fuit monstrum illud in Ephesina Synodo, nō illa λεπρινὴ[?], sed vera & Orthodoxa: quum illic ex verbo Dei decretum esset, Christum vnicam esse personam ex duabus diuersis prorsus naturis, in vnum tamen ὑφιστάμενον[?] incomprehensibili quadam ratione vnitis, vna videlicet diuina assumente, altera vero nempe humana assumpta, con-stantem: quod nisi firmum & inconcussum mancat, ruere sit necesse nostrae salutis basin & fundamentum. Ecce vero statim alterum huic oppositum monstrum parit Sathan, nempe Eutychen illum infelicissimum hominem, qui sic assentiri veritati contra Nestorium videretur, vt tamen reipsa & Arium & Nestorium supergressus, Deum vtraque natura spoliatum prorsus in vanissimum phantasma transformaret, & in eo verissimum esse deprehenderetur, quod inquit Flaccus, Dum vitant stulti vitia, in contraria currunt.
units.tr: Who would have believed it possible that among those who profess to have abandoned all idolatry and to worship Christ, there would be found men who strip him of his deity and transform the God-man into a divine man? For surely it is the mark of a madman, and utterly senseless [ἀναίσθητος], to deny that he is an idolater while denying that he is true and natural God, when you urge that he be called upon and honoured with every divine honour. Yet monsters of this kind were found long ago, which for that reason the orthodox call Antichrists, such as Cerinthus and Ebion, even in the days of the apostles themselves. Their blasphemy was later furbished up by Theodotus of Byzantium and that accursed Samosatenus, the polluter of that Church in which Christians were first named. With these monsters beaten down, behold, at last Arius, that raging fury, came forth from the abyss. He did not, indeed, make Christ a mere man after the example of those others, but he asserted that the Word was something created, and that in time, and so he stripped him of true deity. True deity cannot in any way be reckoned among created things, but rather divinity, that is a quality or excellence which flows from the power and efficacy of deity, in the way Peter said that we become partakers of the divine nature [θείας φύσεως κοινωνούς]. For the cunning of heretics teaches us in this way to distinguish deity from divinity, just as Paul himself ascribes to Christ not deity [θεότης] but the fullness of deity [θεότητος πλήρωμα]. But the Greek profane writers too, although they call what the Latins call numen "to theion," still call those gods of theirs, whether of the greater or lesser nations, "theoi" rather than "theai." Hence they are said to have made those they formerly regarded as gods [ἐνθεῶσαι], that is, divine beings, so that they can in no way excuse their idolatry. For (as has been disputed at length against them by our people) nothing other than the true God can be worshipped with religious devotion, and nothing created can be held to be the true God without the greatest wickedness. Rightly, therefore, against Arius, that most famous universal Synod of Nicaea, which all the later orthodox synods, both universal and provincial, have confirmed by perpetual consensus, rightly, I say, did it decide, since it saw that all such unsound notions were refuted both by common sense, however corrupted, and much more by the most manifest Word of God, and since in the Scriptures the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, outside whom there is no true God, are plainly distinguished from one another, and since it noted the difference between ousia (that is, common essence or nature) and hypostasis, which they afterwards called hypostasis, that is person: it decreed that the Word is homoousios, that is coessential, with the Father. Now by employing this term most conveniently, and altogether necessarily, to refute those blasphemies, it signified two things: namely, that the essence and nature of the Father and the Son is one, that is Deity, in such a way that they are also hypostases, that is subsisting in that single and most singular Deity, distinguished of course by their own properties, but not separated into two essences in number. For that Deity is one (as I have said) and most simple, and therefore indivisible, and in each of them the whole Deity is the same in which they subsist. As for the stubborn Arians themselves, who were also called heteroousians, because they made the Word different in nature and essence from the Father and said he was created out of nothing, they afterwards divided into at least two factions, namely the homoiousians (as if you should say "of like essence") and the anomoians, that is the unlike. For there were not lacking cunning and at the same time foolish men who, by inserting a single little letter, that is by changing homoousios into homoiousios, hoped that their Arianism could lie hidden, although they were deluding themselves even more crudely than Arius himself, unless that word homoiousios (as Basil writes to his brother concerning Dionysius of Corinth) is softened by some convenient but, as it seems to me, plainly forced interpretation. For certainly in one and the same essence there is no place either for equality or inequality, since these are seen only between two things; and therefore equality must necessarily be considered in the hypostases, not in the essence. The anomoians, however, although they too dressed up their doctrine in whatever colours they could, either plainly betrayed themselves as Arians, since they made the Son unlike the Father, or showed themselves utterly foolish, since they imagined something greater and less in the most simple and singular nature, namely the Deity. With these monsters the Church struggled long and hard, and at times things were so reduced that that fire seemed to be quenched by nothing so much as by prayers and the blood of countless martyrs. Then straightway from the well of the same abyss there emerged Nestorius, who by a novel device sought to accomplish what Arius had sought, namely by denying that the Son of Mary according to the flesh is the Son of God according to the divine nature, so that one and the same person might be true God and true man. For he affirmed that the Word had been present to that flesh born of Mary only by an energetic presence [ἐνεργητικὴ παρουσία]. This was surely nothing other than a divided person of Christ the Mediator, making him a most divine man, a man made God. Hence, since that very thing follows which the Devil earlier attempted by various tunnels, namely that we, adoring that unique Saviour of ours, should be caught as idolaters, who is so blind as not to notice with what rage Satan rushes against the human race, and with what cunning, changing his colours from time to time, he mocks our dimmed eyes? That monster was therefore at last exposed and overthrown, principally by the work and power of Cyril, not in that robber council [λῃστρικὴ], but in the true and orthodox Synod of Ephesus, since it was decreed there from the Word of God that Christ is one person from two utterly different natures, united in one hypostasis by some incomprehensible manner: namely the one divine nature assuming, the other, that is the human, being assumed. Unless this stands firm and unshaken, the foundation and basis of our salvation must necessarily collapse. But behold, straightway Satan brings forth another monster opposed to this one, namely that most unhappy man Eutyches, who seemed to agree with the truth against Nestorius, yet in fact surpassed both Arius and Nestorius, transforming God, stripped of both natures, into a most empty phantom; and in him it was shown to be most true what Flaccus says: "While fools avoid vices, they run into the contrary ones."

units.la: Aiebat enim monachus ille delirus, natura à persona non distinguēs, nec vnionem ab vnitate, Christum esse ex Diuinitate & humanitate permixtis coflatum. Quasi vero vel Diuina natura transformari, vel humana in diuinam mutari possit, siue substantias ipsas, siue οὐσιώδεις illarum proprietates considerens. Itaque quum hoc genus vnionis, quod permixtione fit, hoc proprium habeat, vt quod ex vtroque est compo-sitū, neutrum sit per se: sicut videre est in mulso, quod quum ex melle & aqua constet, tamen nec aqua est nec mel, sed ex vtrisque confusis vnum: consequebatur Christum, stante Eutychis dogmate, nec Deum esse nec hominem, nedum vt Deus sit & homo, qualem esse tamen ne-cesse est, vt vere sit Immanuel. Haec porro qui non intelligunt a qui-bus initijs profecta sint, nec quorsum tendant Sathanae conatus, alij quidem per imperitiam, alij vero morositate, & quodam non cogni-tarum controuersiarum taedio, quidam denique audacissima temeri-tate vsi, veteres illos & doctrina & pietate praestantissimos Patres, quorum inexhaustis laboribus detectas haereticorum fraudes & con-seruatam in Ecclesia secundum Deum veritatem debemus, ausi sunt (proh indignum facinus!) quasi extra Dei verbum vagantes, & ve-rum rum Christianismum partim nouis quibusdam vocabulis & formu-lis, partim spinosis & superuacaneis quaestionibus abolétes, accusa-re. Nec sane existimo optimos & integerrimos illos homines durio-ra cum quoquâ certamina sustinuisse, quàm cum iis qui in ipso Eccle-siae sinu versantes, nec regere alios norant, in istis praesertim tem-pestatibus, nec regi sese à peritioribus patiebantur: quae indignitas procul-dubio vocem illam, qua Synodi semel omnes damnari viden-tur, Nazianzeno extorsit. Sed de his alias. Nunc ad rem redeo. Exercuit Ecclesiam crassissimum illud Eutychis delirium annos plus minus trecentos, subinde interpolatis & nouo quodam fuco oblitis er-roribus renascens. Quid plura? toties depulsus Sathan, resumptis vi-ribus, quosdam in Peripateticorum schola eruditos excitat, qui ὁμοού-σιον, toties tantoque consensu explosum monstrum, rursus in theatrum orbis terrarum produceret: sed noua quadam arte transformatum, ut statim à quibusuis dignosci non posset. Ii, quantum ex Nicephoro licet colligere, Deitatis essentiam ut creatas species considerantes, in tria indiuidua sic illam non distinguebant, sed dissecabant, ut sicut homo homine, sic Deus Deum propagasse diceretur. Quod quidem dogma, quanuis omnium sit crassissimum, tamen suos astipulatores inuenit, donec ista Tritheitarum factio in totidem partes dissecta, in quot ipsi prius Deitatem lacerarant, sua sponte concidit. Postea externis po-tissimum bellis, & fatalibus Regnorum mutationibus, vastato O-rientis & Occidentis imperio, barbaries potius maxima quam haere-ses Ecclesiam inuasit, minimè tamè desinente Sathana intus illam af-fligere, sed diuersa prorsus arte ac ratione. Visum enim illi est, omisso, quod toties malè successerat aduersus Christi personam certamine, controuersia potius de Christi officio, in qua iam olim fuerat à Pau-lo potissimum profligatus, rursum tot seculis intermissam mouere: cuius etiam belli semina paulatim, non sentientibus etiam optimis Episcopis, desumpto ex Philosophorum scholis ἀντιξεσίῳ[?], & excitato in Occidente Pelagio, jecerat. Multa hic vero sceleratos ipsius conatus adjuverunt. Primùm duorum Episcoporum, Constantinopolitani nimirum & Romani dissidia, non de regundis Christianæ religionis finibus, sed de dividenda Romani imperij præda: reliquis Episcopis plerisque partim ignorantia, partim stultitia, partim etiam malitia suum quibusque Tyrannum defendentibus. Nulla tum erat linguarum peritia, ut ex fontibus diiudicari possent controversiæ. Optimarum artium studia, quanuis à Carolo magno multis locis excitata, tamen paulatim magis ac magis elanguescebant, ut artificiosæ potius cuiusdam inscitiæ, quàm ullius veræ scientiæ scholæ extarent. Mutatis linguis, manebat nihilominus Latinè scriptæ Liturgiæ, nec alia quàm vulgata illa utriusque Testamenti versio extabat. & quamuis non adessent interpretes, tamen contra Pauli commonefactionem peregrina lingua, auctoritate potissimum Romani Episcopi Tyrannidem suam, quoquo modo posset, stabilientis, retinebatur, adeo ut ne nunc quidem ex Christianorum templis extrudi possit. Hinc factum est, ut paulatim obsolesceret quotidiana Divini verbi prædicatio:de quo etiam Gregorius coqueritur: & quum in hominum manibus nec Apostolorum nec Prophetarum scripta versarentur, Pseudoprophetis impunè quiduis credendum vel faciendum obtrudere liceret. Hinc necessariò sequuta est fœdissima Sacramentorum prophanatio, quum nemo quid illic ageretur intelligeret. Ita etiam factum, ut totus Dei cultus in vanissimas, ac tandem etiam plane blasphemas cæremonias degeneraret, depravatis veteribus, quæ decori tantùm gratia (quanuis interdum non satis prudenter) institutæ fuerant, & nouis certatim introductis ritibus, quorum nullus neque numerus neque modus fuit, quum nullis æquè rebus ac externo illo cultu superstitiosi capiantur, & his potissimum artibus nunquam non consueuerint astuti hypohypocritæ simplicium animis insidiari. Manebat tantum in quibusdam scholis inanissima Theologiæ species, in qua digladiantes sophistæ vel de suis insomniis rabiosissimè debaccharentur, vel si quod verum dogma tractarent, vanissimis plerunque ac futilissimis suis speculationibus vera Theologiam, qualis ex verbo Dei tradita, & doctissimorum Patrum scriptis explicata fuerat, in inanissimam ματαιολογίαν transformarent. Denique eò res deuenit, ut illo perditionis filio in templo Dei sedente, & regibus etiam ipsis pro suo arbitrio dominante, succederet, extincta scientiæ salutis luce, obscurissima ignorantiæ caligo: & doctrina ipsa Christiana, partim sepulta delitesceret, partim placitis ex diametro repugnantibus corrupta iaceret: & quod ad Ecclesiasticum ipsum ordinem attinet, manentibus tantum inanibus nominibus, veluti Episcoporum, presbyterorum, diaconorum, clericorum, quasi ruderibus quibusdam, ab ipsis fundamentis totus convelleretur. Quid interim misera Dei Ecclesia? nempe hæc tum erat ipsius conditio, quæ olim in Israele temporibus Eliæ, delitescentibus in spelunca fidelibus Dei Prophetis: & qualis tum erat, quum euersò Dei templo, & iugi cessante sacrificio, captiua in Babylone tenebatur. Seruabat tamen Dominus renasciturì suo tempore populi semen. Manebat saluus in Papatu Baptismus in Patris, Filij & Spiritus sancti nomen, quanuis peregrinæ linguæ vsu & multis aliis modis conspurcatus. Manebat frustra toties sicuti diximus, oppugnatum vnitatis essentiæ, & Trinitatis personarum fundamentum. Manebat doctrina de duabus Christi naturis, quanuis realis in Cœna Domini præsentiæ carnis & sanguinis Christi dogma, ex necessario consequenti tum Marcionis tum Eutychis delirium ex inferis revocaret. Denique nullo seculo defuerunt, qui vel in ipsis inferorum antris, sese tenebrarum regno tum voce tum scriptis opponerent: cuius rei monimenta Deus opt.max. ab iis ipsis conseruari voluit, in quorum perniciem quotidie in lucem prodeunt. Quid, quod pictores etiā qui scri bere nō norant, fecerunt vt parietes ipsi (quod prædixerat Domi-nus) loquerentur, & illum perditionis filiu spectatoribus omnibus proderent? Ecquod enim templu est cuius pictura & scripturae non sint ipsius Papatus opprobriis refertae? Quaedam tātum ex infinitis commemorabo, quae nunc forte in mente veniunt. Extat in augustissimo patriae meae templo, quod monasterium fuit ipsa pene urbe maius, vi-trea fenestra vetustissima, quod ipsa etiā pictura admodu rudis & Goticis, quas vocant, literis insignis demonstrat. Ibi variis anfractibus depicta est historia Monachi in adulterio deprehensi: obscoena quidem plus satis, sed tamen non temere depicta, & omnium oculis expositá. In Argetoratensis turris primis fere sculptis lapidibus, lupus ministrate vulpe, si bene memini, missam canit. Ibidem in summa templi testudine, nisi me valde fallit memoria, pictus est, qui digito Canonicorum subiecta subsellia demonstrans, his Esaiae verbis incusat, Populus hic labiis me honorat, cor autem eorum longe abest a me. Tubingae in aula Coenobii, quod nunc illustrissimus Princeps VVir-tembergensis otiosis asinis ademptu, studiosis alendis hominibus con secrauit, vetusta extat pictura pone ipsas fores, totum Monachismum accuratissime ob oculos proponens. Monstrū est cucullatum, per gradus veluti sese praecipitas, altero pede ceruino, si bene memini, ut ve loces esse illius pedes ad male agendum intelligas. Alterius pedis vicem gerit inuersa lucerna, ut Monachismi ortum & progressum mera doctrinae lucis euersione niti scirent spectatores. Manus habet aduncas & rapaces: quarum una impositum humeris saccum retinet, orphanorum nimirum & viduarum facultates: altera circulum gestat ex precatoriis illis globulis mirabiliter confertum: si quidem pro minoribus illis, quos AVE MARIA vocat, sunt abaci tabulae orbiculatae: & pro denis illis maioribus, quos PATER NOSTER appellat boni isti patres, singuli sunt taxilli, pulchrè cum tabulis illis cohærentes. Sinum habet oppletum lusorijs chartarum folijs: cucullam à tergo, plenā illis novem metis pyramidalibus, unà cum globo, quo ad illas deijciendas vulgò utuntur, ut qua in re vitam illi consumere solerent longarum precum prætextu, domos etiam regum exhaurientes, nullus ignoraret. Collum est oblongū & asininum, ut bestiarū more ventri deditos esse nemo nesciat. Menti vicem præbet quædā cyathi forma satis conveniens. Nasum facit canis caudam attollentis species, cuius caput latranti simile præstat etiam ipsi monacho capitis vicem, optimè sanè monachorū latratus simul & ingluviem inexplebilem referens. Denique à tergo definit dorsi spina in contortum lituum, ex quo cum fumo quodā extrusus monachus, rapacibus pedū & manuū unguibus, ad mensam quādam assidens, numerata pecunia indulgentias una manu, altera verò κυβώτιον, quod barbare cyborium appellat, in quo illorum fatale crustum continetur, porrigit. Biturigibus, in tabella[?] quadam vetustissima, quo loco vænibant indulgentiæ, reperti sunt nostra memoria multi versiculi in totam illam fœdissimam nundinationem scripti, in quibus & istos fuisse memini,
units.tr: For that deranged monk, failing to distinguish nature from person, or union from unity, taught that Christ was compounded of divinity and humanity mixed together. As if the divine nature could be changed, or the human changed into the divine, whether one considers the substances themselves or their essential properties. Since this kind of union, which comes about by mixture, has this property, that what is composed of both is neither one by itself, as can be seen in mead: though it consists of honey and water, it is neither water nor honey but one thing made from both confused together. It followed that, with Eutyches' doctrine standing, Christ was neither God nor man, much less God and man, which he must be if he is truly Immanuel. Those who do not understand from what beginnings these errors proceeded, or to what end Satan's attempts tend, some do so through inexperience, others through obstinacy and a certain weariness of controversies they do not understand, and some finally, using the most audacious rashness, have dared (what a shameful deed!) to accuse those ancient Fathers, most outstanding in both doctrine and piety, through whose tireless labours we owe the uncovering of the heretics' frauds and the preservation of the truth in the Church according to God. They accuse them as if they were wandering outside the Word of God, while they undermine the Christian religion partly with new vocabularies and formulas, partly with thorny and superfluous questions. Nor do I think those best and most upright men had harder contests with anyone than with those who, living in the very bosom of the Church, neither knew how to rule others, especially in such storms, nor allowed themselves to be ruled by the more skilled. That indignity doubtless drew from Nazianzen that cry by which the Synods seem all to be condemned once for all. But of these things elsewhere. Now I return to my subject. That thick-headed delirium of Eutyches troubled the Church for roughly three hundred years, reviving again and again with errors now and then interpolated and smeared with some new paint. What more? Satan, though repeatedly driven off, regaining his strength, stirred up certain men learned in the school of the Peripatetics, who would bring back onto the stage of the world that monster, so often and so universally exploded, the homoousion itself, but transformed by some new art so that it could not be recognised at once by anyone. These men, as far as one may gather from Nicephorus, considered the essence of the Godhead as they consider created species, and did not distinguish the three individuals in it but cut it apart, so that just as one man begets another man, so God was said to have begotten God. This dogma, though it is the thickest of all, nevertheless found its supporters, until this faction of Tritheites, cut into as many parts as they had first torn the Godhead into, fell apart of its own accord. Afterwards, chiefly through external wars and the fatal changes of kingdoms, when the empire of East and West was laid waste, a monstrous barbarism rather than heresy invaded the Church. Yet Satan did not cease to afflict it from within, but by a quite different art and method. For it seemed good to him to drop the contest over the person of Christ, which so often had gone badly for him, and instead to stir up again, after so many centuries of neglect, the controversy about Christ's office, in which he had already been chiefly routed long before by Paul. He had sown the seeds of this war gradually, taken from the schools of the philosophers (the antixesis?), and with Pelagius roused in the West, even while the best bishops did not notice. Many things helped his wicked efforts. First, the quarrels of two bishops, namely of Constantinople and of Rome, were not about settling the boundaries of the Christian religion but about dividing the plunder of the Roman empire. Most of the other bishops, partly through ignorance, partly through folly, partly also through malice, defended each his own tyrant. There was then no skill in languages by which controversies could be judged from the sources. The study of the good arts, though stirred up in many places by Charlemagne, nevertheless gradually grew more and more feeble, so that there existed schools of a kind of artful ignorance rather than of any true learning. Though languages changed, the liturgy continued to be written in Latin, and there was no other version of either Testament than that common Vulgate. And although there were no interpreters, nevertheless, against Paul's admonition, a foreign tongue was kept, chiefly by the authority of the Roman bishop, who by whatever means he could was establishing his tyranny, so that even now it cannot be driven out of Christian churches. Hence it came about that the daily preaching of the divine Word gradually fell into disuse, a complaint Gregory also makes. And since the writings of neither the Apostles nor the Prophets were in people's hands, false prophets could freely impose on them whatever they wished them to believe or do. From this there necessarily followed the most foul profanation of the sacraments, since no one understood what was going on there. It also came about that the whole worship of God degenerated into most vain and at last even plainly blasphemous ceremonies, the old ones being corrupted, though they had been instituted only for the sake of decorum (somewhat imprudently at times), and new rites were introduced eagerly, of which there was neither number nor measure, since superstitious people are caught by nothing more than external worship, and crafty hypocrites have always, by these very arts, laid snares for the minds of simple people. In some schools there remained only a most empty appearance of theology, in which sophists, fighting with one another, raged furiously either about their own dreams or, if they treated some true doctrine, mostly by their most vain and frivolous speculations turned true theology, as handed down from God's Word and explained in the writings of the most learned Fathers, into the most empty matalogia. At last things came to such a point that, with that son of perdition sitting in the temple of God and dominating even kings at his own pleasure, the light of the knowledge of salvation was extinguished and a most obscure darkness of ignorance succeeded. Christian doctrine itself either lay buried and hidden, or lay corrupted by opinions diametrically opposed to it. As for the ecclesiastical order itself, only its empty names remained, such as bishops, presbyters, deacons and clergy, like certain ruins, and the whole of it was torn up from its very foundations. What meanwhile of the wretched Church of God? Her condition was then such as it was in Israel in the times of Elijah, when the faithful prophets of God hid in a cave, and such as it was when, the temple of God being overthrown and the continual sacrifice ceased, she was held captive in Babylon. Yet the Lord preserved a seed of his people, to be reborn in its time. Baptism remained safe in the Papacy, in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, though polluted by the use of a foreign tongue and in many other ways. The foundation of the unity of the essence and the Trinity of persons, though attacked, as we have said, so often in vain, remained. The doctrine of the two natures of Christ remained, although the dogma of the real presence of the flesh and blood of Christ in the Lord's Supper, by a necessary consequence, would call back from the dead the delirium of Marcion and of Eutyches. Finally, in no age have there been lacking those who, even in the very caves of the underworld, opposed themselves with voice and writings to the kingdom of darkness; God the best and greatest willed that the monuments of this be preserved by the very men to whose ruin they daily come to light. What of the fact that painters, even those who did not know how to write, made the walls themselves speak, as the Lord had foretold, and exposed that son of perdition to all onlookers? For what temple is there whose paintings and inscriptions are not stuffed with the disgraces of the Papacy itself? I will recall only a few of the countless things that now perhaps come to mind. In the most venerable temple of my homeland, which was a monastery almost larger than the city itself, there is an ancient glass window which, even in its very rough painting and its letters called Gothic, shows the story of a monk caught in adultery. It is depicted in various episodes, obscene indeed more than enough, but not carelessly drawn, and displayed to everyone's eyes. On the tower at Strasbourg, among the first carved stones almost, a wolf, if I remember rightly, sings Mass while a fox serves him. In the same place, under the very top of the church vault, unless my memory deceives me greatly, there is a painting of a man who, pointing with his finger at the benches set under the canons, accuses them with these words of Isaiah: "This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me." At Tübingen, in the hall of the monastery, which the most illustrious Prince of Württemberg, having taken it from idle asses, dedicated to the support of studious men, there is an old painting behind the very doors which sets the whole of monkery most accurately before the eyes. It is a hooded monster, falling headlong step by step, with one foot of a deer, if I remember rightly, so that you may understand his feet are swift to do evil. In place of the other foot is an upturned lamp, so that onlookers may know that the origin and progress of monkery rest on the sheer overturning of the light of doctrine. It has hooked and rapacious hands: one of them holds on its shoulder a bag, namely the goods of orphans and widows; the other carries a circle wonderfully packed with those prayer beads; for the smaller beads, which they call "Ave Maria," are round tablets on a counting frame, and for the ten larger ones, which those good fathers call "Our Father," they are single counters, neatly fitted to those tablets. It has its bosom stuffed with playing cards, and at its back a hood full of those nine pyramidal dice, together with the ball which they commonly use to throw them, so that everyone knows in what business they used to spend their lives under the pretext of long prayers, draining even the houses of kings. Its neck is long and asinine, so that no one fails to know that they are given over to the belly like beasts. A certain form of a cup, quite fitting, serves as its mind. The nose is made like a dog lifting its tail, whose head, resembling a barking dog, takes the place of the monk's head; this rightly represents at once the barking of monks and their insatiable gluttony. Finally, at the back the spine of the back ends in a twisted horn, out of which, with some smoke, a monk is pushed, sitting at a table with his feet and hands armed with rapacious claws; with one hand he hands out indulgences for counted money, and with the other a kybotion, which he barbarously calls a "ciborium," in which that fatal crust is contained. At Bourges, on some very old tablet in the place where indulgences were sold, many little verses were found in our time, written against that most foul trade, among which I remember these as well:

units.la: Hic datur exponi Paradisus venditioni, Hic pro mercede Christo dices, Mihi cede.
units.tr: Here Paradise is put up for sale; here, for a reward, you say to Christ: "Give it to me."

units.la: In hac Genevensi civitate pictura inerat, in ipso pene Augustinianorum vestibulo palam omnibus apparēs, addito etiā Iaphredi cuiusdam Taurinensis pictoris nomine, hydra septicipitem suspenso in aere throno insidente referēs, substrata nudi Papæ Romani triplici diademate exornati specie, ex pube infulas, peda Espicopalia, bullas, Pontifices deniq; ipsos, fœdissima sanè stercora, quibus jam plus satis exaturatum esse mundū oportuit, egerentem, subiecta fornace, quæ utrinq; à demonibus eundem illum thronum circunstantibus accensa, miseros illos decidentes excipiat. Hi tum erant igitur Dei opt. max. perfidiam hominum iustis pœnis ulciscentis concionatores, donec nostra memoria idem pro incredibili sua bonitate, post præmissos aliquos, qui mundi veternum utcunque excuterent, magnos illos heroas Spiritu sancto circundatos prodire iuberet, quales inter cæteros fuerunt in Saxonia D. Martinus Lutherus, excellens Dei organum: in Heluetia vero, D. Henricus Zuinglius, uterque eodem tempore, idem opus summa vi moliens: & quidem, quod mirum est, alter alteri ignotus. Quos præstantissimos homines nisi mundi peccata disiunxissent, aut ego vehementer fallor, aut iampridem Antichristus Romanus pro-stratus iaceret. Quid tum igitur Sathan? Primùm sophistarum agmi-na ex suis lustris excitauit, sed frustrà: quum illorum plerique vel in otio vel in futilissimis tantùm nugis tractandis sese exercuissent, ac proinde paucos admodum haberet in tàto numero, ad hoc admini-strandum bellum satis idoneos. Placuit igitur illi cum illo plumbeo sophistarum gladio, edicta Cæsarum, Regum, Principum, Magi-stratuum, denique ipsorum quoque populorum rabiem coniungere. Sed quum neque omnes principes satis ad hanc lanienam paratos in-ueniret, & re ipsa expertus esset Martyrum sanguine rigatâ Eccle-siam fœcudiorem reddi: placuit etiam illi veteres illas artes tentare, id est domesticis hostibus Ecclesiam lacessere. Hinc illa Anabaptista-rum & Catabaptistarum agmina, quos suo enthusiasmo inflatos ni-hil prorsus puderet. Hinc quoque Schuuenckfeldius authoritatem diuini verbi pro viribus eleuans, & Eutychis simul errores pro vi-ribus interpolans. Excitauit altera ex parte Mænonem, in quo relatus est Hebion: Dauidem Georgiũ, qui monstra ipsis Valentini AEo-nibus portentosiora, & ipsis Carpocratianis obscœniora in medium proponeret. Omitto Postellum, monstrum ex omnibus omnium sæculorum hæresibus conflatum, quo nunc etiam quantumuis recutito, bona Sorbona delectatur. Omitto etiam Antinomos à D. Luthero præferpræsertim refutatos. Omitto quoque Libertinorũ agmina, quoniam infinitus est pene isthiusmodi monstrorum numerus. Nec enim hæc omnia mihi propositum nunc est recensere: sed hoc demum agere, de quo nunc proprie laboramus. Dico igitur Sathanam, vt Ecclesiæ instaurationem nostro seculo cœptã impediret, seipsum plane superasse: ita tamen vt nemo nisi volens decipi potuerit, aut nunc etiam possit. Primùm enim ecce in vnico Serueto reuocati sunt ab inferis Samosatenus, Arius, & Eutyches. Quînam hoc tandem, dicet aliquis? Attendat igitur. Negabat Samosatenus æternam τὲ̃ λόγῳ[?] hypostasin, quem duntaxat in mente & decreto Patris ante conceptionem carnis in vtero Mariæ extitisse volebat: docebat Seruetus Filium ex Deo fuisse, non reipsa sed figurativè: quia in eo Deus futurum hominem geniturus erat, mulierem expectans, ex qua eum gigneret. Sentiebat Arius τὸν λόγον esse creatum quiddam, ordine & tempore res cæteras creatas antecedens: sentiebat Seruetus τὸν λόγον tum cœpisse existere, quum mundus creatus est, ac etiam ideam quandam fuisse ex tribus increatis elementis compositam. Negabat Eutyches Christum ex duabus distinctis naturis constare, quòd diceret τὸν λόγον transformatum esse in carnem, quæ postea glorificata, in Deum conversa fuit: affirmabat Seruetus conceptum fuisse Filium in vtero virginis ex ipsa Verbi essentia in carnem transeunte, quæ postea in Deitatem fuerit absorpta. Addere autem etiam istis licet delirium Marcionis & Apollinaris insaniæ proximum, adeò portentum illud fuit errorum omnium fœcundum. Aiebat enim Marcion Filium δοκήσει[?], id est opinione tantum, non autem reipsa carnem induisse. Apollinaris autem Diuinitatem volebat carni assumptæ loco animæ fuisse. Quid autem Seruetus? Certe non verum, sed imaginarium corpus Christo tribuebat, quum illud negaret ex semine Abrahæ simpliciter fuisse genitum, sed partim etiam ex tribus illis elementis conflatum, & substantiali quadam Dei facie, quæ ab initio sanctis Patribus visa fuisset: animam vero Christi sane re ipsa exinanicbat[?], quum illam diceret partim ex humano, partim ex Diuino spiritu fuisse compositam. Hæ sunt igitur Serueti blasphemiæ, quæ & initio à D. Ioanne OEcolampadio, & à D. Philippo Melanchthone postea grauissimè refutatum: ac nouissimè tandem à magno illo Ioanne Caluino quàm potentissimè gladio Dei verbi prostratum: deniq; ob triginta annorum blasphemias execrabiles & indomitam peruicaciam ex Senatus Genevensis sententia iustissimo supplicio affectu, quis non tandem, nisi planè furiosus & excors abominetur? Prodierunt tamen ex illo, tanquam ex ludo quopiam discipuli nō pauci, sui etiam ducis & insaniæ & impietatem pene superates. Hi initio fuerunt apud nos, Paulus quidam Alciatus Mediolanensis, homo iam antea planè phreneticus & verti-ginosus: Valentinus Getilis, cuius qui mores, quæ dogmata, quis deniq; fuerit exitus, ex iis scriptis liquidò cognosci potest, in quæ nunc præfamur. Istis adiungendus est Georgius quidà Blandrata, professione medicus, Gentili quidem indoctior, sed multò etiâ impudentior & sceleratior. Fuit quoq; in hac cohorte pene veteranus Gribaldus Iurisconsultus, homo sanè improbus, vt cui nulla religio fuerit, dogma quod corde retineret, manifesto periurio abnegare. Fuit etiam illis, sed nimiù sero detectus[?], Bernardinus ille Ochinus, impurissimus hypocrita. Fuit quoq; Lælius Sozinus Senensis, incredibiliter ad cōtradicendū, & varios nectendos[?] nodos cōparatus, nec nisi post mortem cognitus huiusmodi perniciosissimis hæresibus laborare. Isti igitur quū neq; Serueti blasphemias, neq; veritatis mysterii, neq; adeò seipsos nossent, prurirent autè incredibili nouitatis studio, cœperunt & ipsi in receptà Trinitatis opinionem inquirere: quibus id statim cōrigit, quod temerè in mari scopuloso nauigantibus solet, nēpe vt nauem alius ad alium scopulū impinges, naufragiū faceret. Facti sunt autem illorum plerique initio Tritheitæ, de quibus paulò ante diximus, non quidē verbo, sed reipsa, vt qui tres personas in totidē οὐσίας transfor-ment: hæc interea cū Ario habentes comunia, quòd Patrem voluit ante Filiū extitisse, quòd vnius veri Dei appellatione ad Patrem restrin-gunt, quòd in Deitate imparitatem imaginantur: sed in eo certe ipso quoq; Ario impudentiores, quòd malebat ille τὸν λόγον ἑτερούσιον[?], atq; adeò ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων[?] creatū docere, quàm eò vsq; insanire, vt simplicissimam & singularissimā essentiam numero multiplicaret. Isti cōtrà, ne videatur Christū sua dignitate spoliare, istud quàm illud affirmare malunt. De duarum autem naturarū vnione, idem prorsus, quod post Eutychē Seruetus, sublata ἰδιωμάτων κοινωνία, docent. Ochinus callidior dubitare de singulis, Academicorū more, videtur maluisse, quàm quicquam definire. Lælius in Samosateni partes clàm transiit, verbo Dei, vt ex quodā eius scripto nunc liquet, adeò veteratorie & plane versute depravato, ac præsertim primo Euangelij Ioānis capite, vt mihi quidē videatur omnes eius corruptores longè superasse. Cæterum ex illis tribus quos primos nominaui, quiq; in hac Ecclesia tum versabantur, primus Valentinus Gentilis in iudicium à Senatu Geneuēsi vocatus, simulata pœnitētia, nō sine insigni periurio profugit. Sequutus est Paulus Alciatus, aut etiā præcessit, solo malæ cōscientiæ vulnere adactus. Bladrata aliquanto post, quū sibi à D. Caluino satisfactū diu simulasset, tādem vanissimo timore à semetipso expauefactus, quasi à Magistratu quæreretur, repetē & ipse ex vrbe in vicinā ditione refugit. Quid plura? post varias deliberationes, ita fors tulit, vt Bladrata, qui Medicinā diu in Polonia primum, deinde in Trassyluania apud Reginas fecerat, eò reuerteretur: vbi nimium facilè illi aditus ad nostros patuit, quantùuis à D. Ioāne Caluino diligeter[?] præmonitos: illū præsertim in illustriß. & præstātiß. alioqui Principis cuiusdā gratiā insinuate Lismanino quodā Corcyrensi, magnæ tum apud Polonicas omnes Ecclesias authoritatis viro. Tum autem forte Francisci Stan-chari Mantuani, petulantissimi hominis, importunitate (ut sane fatalis esse videtur Polonis Italia) scissae erat Polonicae Ecclesiae recens admodum ex Papismo emergentes: quum ille Christum esse Mediatorem secundum humanam naturam: alii vero, pro quibus Germanicae & Helveticae Ecclesiae postea iudicarunt, Mediatoris officium totius esse personae, & quidem diverso utriusque naturae respectu, affirmarent. Obiiciebat autem hoc in primis Stancharus, Mediato-rem non posse dici Christum secundum Divinam naturam, quin Patre minor cum Arianis statuatur. In hoc nodo explicando, quanuis non ita difficili, quum nutare quodammodo nostros videret Calui-nus, non modo argumentum ipse dissoluit, verumetiam fratres sedu-lo monuit, ne, dum vitare Nestorii praecipitium volunt, in Arii vel Tritheitarum abyssum ruerent. Sed vana apud plerosque admoni-tio fuit, animis eorum a Blandrata, qui Gentilem etiam ad se euo-carat, ita iam fascinatis, ut soli Deo medicabilis esset morbus. Hinc illud incendium, quod iam tota vastata Polonia, in Transylvaniam quoque una cum Blandrata, persuasit, Gregorio quodam Paulo impurissimis libellis suis, infinitas blasphemias spargente, & Petro quodam Statorio, iuvene alioqui bono ingenio nec contemnenda doctrina praedito, operam omnem suam fucandis Barbarissimi scriptoris Blandratae commentis navate: nihil denique praetermittentibus Tritheitis, ut paulo ante coeptum aedificium non tantum impedirent, sed etiam prorsus everterent. Nostri interea non cessare, & tum ex Dei verbo, tum ex perpetuo Catholicae Ecclesiae consensu, & certae apud omnes fidei synodis, blasphemias illas refellere: quinetiam a remotissimis quoque Ecclesiis opem, & subsidiu flagitare, feliciter id quidem, non tamen eo, qui sperari potuerat, successu. Quid inter-ea bonus ille Hosius Cardinalis cum suis Catholicis? nempe ridere suauiter, & quasi ista nihil ad ipsos pertineret, aliud quiduis agere: imo etiam nostros undique ad extinguendum hoc incendium accurrentes probrosis libellis lacessere: Regiam denique Maiestatem de coercendis istis blasphemiis cogitantem, a rectis consiliis pro viribus auocare. ac merito quidem. Quorsum enim Satan aduersus seipsum depugnaret? Itaque iam illic res Christiana in extremo discrimine versari videbatur, nisi repente Dominus remedium laborantibus attulisset. quod quidem duplex uno eodemque tempore adhibuit. Praeterquam enim quod Regiae Maiestati suggessit, ut solenni edicto omnes aduenas regni sui turbatores semel proscriberet, illorum etiam haereticorum linguas duisit[?]. Statim ergo non tantum alius alio diffugere, sed etiam nescio quid priori sententiae vel detrahere vel adducere coepit. Ac Gentilis quidem Deo omnem illi metem adimete, in has regiones, id est in Bernensem ditione, ad iustum supplicium infamiae & horroris plenum vltro recurrit: qui quum de Paulo Alciato sodali suo rogaretur, Factus est, inquit, Mahumetanus, nec mihi cum illo iampridem vllum commercium fuit. Idem de Blandrata rogatus, Periit etiam, inquit, ut qui in Sabellij & Samosateni delirium inciderit. Quid commemorem animosi illius Gregorii Pauli, insalutato suo grege, fugam? Quid ab eodem excitata contra Pædobaptismum certamina cum ipso etiam Statorio suscepta? Quid Ochini senis infelicissimi cum illis concertationes? Quid obiurgatum a Blandrata Gregorium, quod minime opportuno tempore controuersiam de Pædobaptismo mouerit? Extat enim apud me ipsius Blandratae Epistola, (non tamen scripta sine Theseo, si Blandratam bene noui:) in qua Gregorium suo quodam iure non tantum de illa Pædobaptismi controuersia non satis opportune mota increpat, verum etiam aperte illum a Tritheismo ad Samosateni dogma reuocare nititur. Incidit enim Blandrata in Transsyluaniam rediens, in quendam paulo magis quàm superiores illi, ut aiunt, prouidum: qui quū nimium cras-sam esse illam Tritheitarum blasphemiam simpliciter propositam ani-maduertisset, maluit omnia involuere permixtis omnium pene hac in re hæreseôn commentis, quàm simpliciter suam sententiam profiteri.
units.tr: In this city of Geneva there was a painting, set almost at the very entrance of the Augustinians' house, where it was plainly visible to everyone. It bore the name of a certain painter from Turin, Jaffredo, and showed a seven-headed hydra sitting on a throne suspended in the air. Beneath it was a naked figure of the Roman Pope, adorned with a triple crown, and from his groin he was dropping mitres, episcopal staffs, bulls, and finally the Pontiffs themselves, most foul dung, of which the world should have had more than enough. A furnace was placed below, lit by demons standing round that same throne, to receive those wretches as they fell. These, then, were the preachers who proclaimed the just punishment of God, the best and greatest, upon the faithlessness of men, until in our own time the same God, in his incredible goodness, after sending some men who might shake off somewhat the lethargy of the world, bade those great heroes come forth, surrounded by the Holy Spirit. Among the others there were, in Saxony, Dr Martin Luther, an excellent instrument of God, and, in Helvetia, Dr Henry Zwingli, both at the same time, both labouring with great force at the same work, and, what is remarkable, each unknown to the other. If the sins of the world had not kept these most outstanding men apart, either I am greatly mistaken or the Roman Antichrist would have been laid low long ago. What then did Satan do? First he roused the troops of the sophists from their dens, but in vain. Most of them had spent their time in idleness or in handling the most trivial trifles, and so he had very few in so great a number who were fit for this war. He therefore decided to join the leaden sword of the sophists with the edicts of Caesars, kings, princes, and magistrates, and finally with the rage of the peoples themselves. But since he did not find all the princes ready enough for this slaughter, and had learned from experience that the Church, watered by the blood of the martyrs, grew more fruitful, he decided also to try those old arts, that is, to assail the Church with enemies from within. Hence those hosts of Anabaptists and Catabaptists, who were puffed up with their enthusiasm and were not in the least ashamed. Hence also Schwenckfeld, who raised up the authority of the divine Word as far as he could, and at the same time mingled in the errors of Eutyches as far as he could. On the other side he stirred up Menno, in whom Hebion was revived, and David George, who put forward monsters more portentous than the Aeons of Valentinus and more obscene than the Carpocratians. I pass over Postel, a monster compounded of the heresies of all the ages, in whom the good Sorbonne still delights, however often he is reprinted. I pass over also the Antinomians, whom Luther had refuted particularly, and I pass over the troops of the Libertines, since the number of such monsters is almost endless. For I do not now intend to list all of them, but to do the thing that we are now concerned with. I say, then, that Satan, in his attempt to hinder the restoration of the Church begun in our age, has plainly surpassed himself, yet in such a way that no one could be deceived unless he willed it, nor can be now. For first, lo, in Servetus alone Samosatenus, Arius, and Eutyches have been called back from the dead. What does this mean, someone will say? Let him attend. Samosatenus denied that the eternal Word was a hypostasis [ὑπόστασις], whom he wanted to have existed only in the mind and decree of the Father before the conception of the flesh in the womb of Mary. Servetus taught that the Son was from God not in reality but figuratively, because in him God was going to beget a man, waiting for a woman from whom he would beget him. Arius held that the Word [λόγος] was something created, preceding other created things in order and time. Servetus held that the Word began to exist when the world was created, and was also a certain idea composed of three uncreated elements. Eutyches denied that Christ consisted of two distinct natures, because he said that the Word had been changed into flesh, which afterwards was glorified and converted into God. Servetus affirmed that the Son was conceived in the womb of the virgin from the very essence of the Word passing into flesh, which afterwards was swallowed up into the Deity. One may add to these also the madness of Marcion and the insanity of Apollinaris, so fruitful was that monstrous thing in all errors. For Marcion said that the Son put on flesh only in appearance [δοκήσει], that is, in opinion only, and not in reality. Apollinaris wanted the Deity to take the place of the soul in the assumed flesh. But what of Servetus? Certainly he ascribed to Christ not a true but an imaginary body, since he denied that it was simply begotten from the seed of Abraham, but said that it was partly formed also from those three elements, and [had] a certain substantial face of God, which had been seen by the holy Fathers from the beginning. And the soul of Christ he truly emptied out, since he said it was composed partly of human and partly of divine spirit. These, then, are the blasphemies of Servetus, which were first most gravely refuted by Dr John Oecolampadius, and afterwards by Dr Philip Melanchthon, and most recently were overthrown as powerfully as possible with the sword of the Word of God by that great John Calvin. Finally, for his thirty years of execrable blasphemies and his untamed obstinacy, he was subjected to a most just punishment by the sentence of the Senate of Geneva. Who, unless utterly mad and foolish, does not at last abominate him? Nevertheless, from him, as from some school, there came forth not a few disciples who even surpassed their leader in madness and impiety. Of these, the first among us were Paul Alciati of Milan, a man already before this utterly frenzied and giddy, and Valentine Gentile, whose morals, doctrines, and finally whose end can be clearly known from those writings which we now preface. To these must be added a certain Georgius Blandrata, a physician by profession, less learned than Gentile but much more shameless and wicked. In this band there was also, almost a veteran, Gribaldi the jurist, a thoroughly dishonest man, for whom there was no religion, since he denied with manifest perjury whatever doctrine he held in his heart. There was also, though detected too late, that Bernardino Ochino, a most impure hypocrite. There was also Lelio Sozzini of Siena, incredibly suited to contradict and to tie together various knots, and not known to be troubled by such most pernicious heresies until after his death. These men, since they knew neither the blasphemies of Servetus, nor the mystery of the truth, nor even themselves, but were itching with an incredible eagerness for novelty, began also themselves to inquire into the accepted opinion of the Trinity. And to them there happened immediately what usually happens to those who sail carelessly in a rocky sea: one ship strikes against one rock, another against another, and they make a shipwreck. Most of them became at first Tritheists, of whom we spoke a little earlier, not indeed in word but in fact, since they transform three persons into as many essences. In this they had in common with Arius that they wanted the Father to have existed before the Son, that they restrict the Father to the name of the one true God, and that they imagine inequality in the Deity. But in this very point they were more shameless even than Arius, since he preferred to teach that the Word was of another essence [ἑτερούσιον], and so created out of nothing [ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων], rather than to rave to such a degree as to multiply the most simple and singular essence in number. These men, on the other hand, lest they seem to strip Christ of his dignity, prefer to affirm the one rather than the other. Concerning the union of the two natures they teach exactly what Servetus taught after Eutyches, namely, that the communion of properties [ἰδιωμάτων κοινωνία] is removed. Ochino, more cunning, seems to have preferred to doubt about individual points, in the manner of the Academics, rather than to define anything. Lelio went over secretly to the side of Samosatenus, the word of God being depraved by him, as now appears from a certain writing of his, so craftily and plainly cunningly, and especially in the first chapter of John's Gospel, that to me he seems to have far surpassed all its corrupters. Moreover, of those three whom I named first, and who were then living in this Church, the first, Valentine Gentile, was summoned to judgment by the Senate of Geneva, and fled with feigned repentance and not without notable perjury. Paul Alciati followed, or even went before, driven only by the wound of an evil conscience. Blandrata some time later, after he had long pretended that he had been satisfied by Dr Calvin, at last, terrified by a most vain fear, as if he were being sought by the magistrate, fled from the city again to a neighbouring territory. What more? After various deliberations it so happened that Blandrata, who had practised medicine for a time first in Poland and then in Transylvania at the court of the queens, returned there. There he found an all too easy entry to our people, although he had been carefully forewarned by Dr John Calvin, especially since he had insinuated himself, through the favour of a certain most illustrious and most excellent prince, into Lismanino of Corfu, a man then of great authority in all the Polish churches. At that time, by the importunity of Francesco Stancari of Mantua, a most impudent man, (for Italy seems fatal to the Poles,) the Polish Church, which had only lately emerged from Papism, was divided. He affirmed that Christ is Mediator according to his human nature, while others, whose judgment the German and Helvetic Churches later followed, affirmed that the office of Mediator belongs to the whole person, with a different respect to each nature. Stancari objected especially that Christ cannot be called Mediator according to the divine nature without being set down, with the Arians, as less than the Father. In untying this knot, although it was not very difficult, Calvin, seeing that our people were in some way wavering, not only solved the argument himself, but also earnestly warned the brethren that in trying to avoid the precipice of Nestorius they should not fall into the abyss of Arius or of the Tritheists. But the warning was in vain with most people, since their minds had already been so bewitched by Blandrata, who had also invited Gentile to himself, that the disease could be cured by God alone. Hence came that fire which, after all Poland had been laid waste, persuaded Transylvania as well, together with Blandrata, while Gregory Paul, a most impure man, spread endless blasphemies in his most filthy little books, and a certain Peter Statorius, a young man otherwise of good talent and not to be despised in learning, devoted all his effort to painting over the inventions of the most barbarous writer Blandrata. Finally the Tritheists left nothing undone, so that they would not only hinder the building begun a little earlier, but would utterly overthrow it. Meanwhile our people did not cease, and refuted those blasphemies both from the Word of God and from the perpetual consent of the Catholic Church and from the creeds of certain faith accepted by all, and indeed they sought help and support even from the most distant Churches. They succeeded in this happily, though not with the success that might have been hoped for. What meanwhile did that good Cardinal Hosius and his Catholics do? Namely, they laughed sweetly, and, as if these things did not concern them at all, they did anything else whatever. Indeed they even assailed our people, who ran from every side to extinguish this fire, with shameful little books; and finally they drew the royal majesty, who was thinking of restraining these blasphemies, away from right counsels as far as they could. And rightly so. For why would Satan fight against himself? And so the Christian cause there already seemed to be in the greatest peril, unless the Lord had suddenly brought a remedy to those who were struggling. And this he applied in a twofold way at one and the same time. For besides suggesting to the royal majesty that by a solemn edict it should once for all banish all the foreigners who were disturbers of the kingdom, he also restrained the tongues of those heretics. Immediately therefore not only did they flee each from the other, but they also began to take away from or add to their former opinions, I know not what. And Gentile, God having taken away all his courage, of his own accord returned to these regions, that is, to the territory of Bern, to a just punishment full of infamy and horror. When he was asked about his companion Paul Alciati, he said: "He has become a Mahometan, and I have had no dealings with him for a long time." Asked the same about Blandrata, he said: "He too has perished, since he has fallen into the delirium of Sabellius and Samosatenus." What shall I mention of the flight of that bold Gregory Paul, leaving his flock without a greeting? What of the controversies against infant baptism stirred up by him, which he undertook even with Statorius himself? What of the disputes of the most unhappy old Ochino with them? What of Gregory being rebuked by Blandrata because he raised the controversy about infant baptism at a most inopportune time? For there is in my possession a letter of Blandrata himself, (not, however, written without Theseus, if I know Blandrata well,) in which he rebukes Gregory with a certain right of his own, not only for raising that controversy about infant baptism too inopportunely, but also tries openly to call him back from Tritheism to the doctrine of Samosatenus. For Blandrata, on returning to Transylvania, fell in with a man somewhat more prudent, as they say, than those earlier ones, who, when he noticed that the Tritheist blasphemy, simply put forward, was too crude, preferred to wrap up everything with a mixture of almost all the heresies on this matter, rather than to profess his opinion plainly.

units.la: Certè in illis thesibus, quæ illi, cuius nunc nomini libes parco, tribuu-tur, ausim dicere & profiteri omniū[?] hæreseôn, quibus unquā Christi personam Satan oppugnauit, semina contineri: ac proinde hominem illum, quem alioquin eximiis multis dotibus ornatum esse audio, ob-testor ego minimus in Ecclesia Dei, sed tamen Dei causam agens pro virilitum[?] ut à Blandrata, selecto Satanæ organo, sibi caueat, cuius veneno jam eum afflatum esse nemo non iudicat aliquo in his rebus iudicio præditus: tum ut aduersus illum ambitionis spiritum, quo præstantissimi quique homines in primis à Satana decipiuntur, no-ctes & dies decertet: denique (quod utinam initio fecisset) nouitios istos prophetas, toti semel Ecclesiæ omnium sine exceptione seculorū testimonio comprobatæ palam repugnantes, & ipsam Christianæ fi-dei basim conuellentes, ex fructibus saltem prius discernat, quàm au-res illis ulterius præbeat. Sed quorsum hæc ad te? dicet aliquis: & quæ tibi in alienas Ecclesias auctoritas? Nulla profecto, fratres. & si forte aliter cogitarem, omnium hominum maximè insanirem. Sed quicunque sunt Christiani, & per Dei misericordiam ad veritatem illius asserendam, & oppugnanda mendacia vocati: minimè, ni fallor, vocationis suæ fines transiliunt, si, salua manente unicuique sua διορθώσει[?], alii alios solentur, doceant, arguant, ac etiam, si sit opus, in-crepent, modò id scienter & rite faciant. Vos igitur Transsyluanos, frater fratres compello, vos Domini seruos vester σύνδουλος per eius nomen obtestor, cuius gloriæ inseruimus, an quis sit Blandrata, quos in Polonia motus excitarit, quot Ecclesias nascentes euerterit, quot animas pessundederit, quas illic in Filium Dei blasphemias sit eiacu-latus, latus, quid nuper ad Gregorium suum de æterna, vt ipse vult, τοῦ λόγου[?] generatione scripserit ignorare potestis? At enim, dicet aliquis, iam apud nos agnouit Vnius Dei appellatione Filium quoque significari. Rectius hoc quidem quam antea, vt qui Gregorium & cæteros Tritheitas, ne ipse quidem inficiari possit nihil in contrariam sententiam, nisi ipso auctore, fautore, adiutore scripsisse, vel dixisse. Sed, obsecro, an putatis lubricam anguillam tam facile teneri? an creditis dealbari, tam citò præsertim, posse AEthiopē? an ignoratis quibus olim artibus, Arius, Apolinaris, Eunomius, Pelagius, etiam conuicti & damnati, Orthodoxis illuserint? an istos ad impediendum opus Dei manifestissimè, vt tot iam ruinæ testantur, ab ipso Satana subornatos, credere potestis alio spiritu regi? Imò liceat etiam mihi aliquid amplius, fratres, bona cum vestra pace loqui. Quanti vobis illa Blandratæ vocula constiterit, an nondum animaduertitis? an non, inquam, sentitis quū hoc à vobis in vestro cathechismo sit extortū, vt non modò symbola reliqua præter illud quod apostolicū vocant, superuacanea nisi ad contradicendum scriberetis, sed etiā Essentiæ, hypostaseos, homoousij, cæteráque id genus vocabula, vt sophistica repudiaretis, ita illos esse vestra simplicitate abusos, vt vos cum tota vetere orthodoxa Ecclesia, atque adeo cum omnibus Ecclesijs, quæ vnquam veræ à temporibus Apostolorum fuerunt, commiserit? An non verò dum ista nonnulli à vobis peterent, in mentem vobis veniebat amplissimus ille Nicenæ, Ephesinæ, Chalcedonensis Synodi confessus, quo nihil vnquam sanctius, nihil augustius ab Apostolorum excessu Sol vnquam aspexit? non adfuit vnus saltem ex multis, qui tam indigno decreto intercedens, maximos illos & præstantissimos angelos Dei, Sophistas fuisse negaret? Nam, vt in ipsis nævi aliqui fuerint, qui putat fundamentum omnis religionis, id est veram veri Dei cognitionem illos non tenuisse, sanè indignus est qui in Ecclesia Dei censcatur[?].Hoccine est, quæso, grata saltem memoria prosequi tot sanctissimorum & eruditissimorum virorum inexhaustos pro hac defendenda & ad nos transmittenda veritate labores, vigilias, la-chrymas, gemitus, exilia, martyria? Non pendemus, inquiunt nonnul-li, a patribus, sed a Dei verbo. Quosdam vero etiam non pudet ista, ut loquuntur, Dialectica, potius quam Theologica aspernari. Atqui miror an unquam isti scripta illorum perlegerint, quibus ut Sophi-stis convincantur. Nam si legerunt, qua fronte tandem audent illos opponere Dei verbo, quos constat uno Dei verbo (ipsis etiam Synodis omissis, quoties ita postularunt illarum, idest veritatis ad-versarij) nixos fuisse? Sin vero vel non legerunt prorsus, vel oscitan-ter legerunt: quis hic pudor est discipulos sedere suorum magistrorum: etiam non auditorum iudices? Ista vero putida obiectio, voces illas in scripturis non inveniri, quoties obiecta, audita, repulsa, damnata est omnium bonorum & doctorum iudicio? Certe si nullis aliis voca-bulis utendum est, nisi quæ totidem literis in sacris libris reperiun-tur: & qui verbi divini διανοίας explicandæ gratia, proprias & accommodatas aliquas voces adhibent, sophistæ censendi sunt, in quas tandem angustias redigemur? imo quid tandem agent illi i-psi quum ad sua defendenda venerint, qui nunc verbi Dei prae-textu, hoc unum moliuntur, ut vos exarmatos opprimant? Nam ego quidem sic statuo, etsi non pendet aliunde rerum sacrarum veritas, quam ab unico Dei verbo, & sedulo vitanda nobis est omnis κενοφωνία: tamen sublato essentiæ, & hypostaseon discrimine (quibuscunque tandem verbis) utaris, & abrogato ὁμοουσίῳ, vix ac ne vix quidem istorum blasphemorum fraudes detegi, & errores satis perspicuè coargui posse. Nego quoque sublatis vocabulis, Naturæ, proprieta-tis, hypostaticæ unionis, ἰδιωμάτων κοινωνίας, posse Nestorij & Euty-chis blasphemias commodè a quoquam refelli: qua in re si forte hal-lucinor. lucinor,hoc age nobis demonstret qui potest, & nos illum coronabi-mus. Illud tamen minimè inficior, quàm simplicissimè proponendam esse Christianæ religionis doctrinam, in Catechismis præsertim: vi-tandas apud populum abstrusas controuersias: τὸ ὅτι explicandum semper, τὸ διότι nunquam nisi sobriè & prudenter attingendum: de-nique hac ætate nobis de hominibus ad emendationem vitæ adducen-dis potiùs laborandum videri, quàm de difficillimis istis quæstioni-bus subtiliter & enucleatè explicandis. Hæc, inquam, omnia minimè inficior. Sed an simplicitatis prætextu damnari vt sophistica opor-tuit, quæ ab ipso sancto Spiritu dictata fuisse, veritas ipsa clamat, & rerum exitus ostendit? an abstrusas controuersias mouet, qui rudi etiam populo, sed iam ab hæreticis fascinato, errores in quibus ver-satur patefacit, pseudoprophetarum fraudes & mendacia firmis & solidis rationibus, nusquam tamen à verbo Dei deflectens, refutat? an τὸ ὅτι simpliciter tractat Paulus ad Galatas scribens? an idè frustrà requirit in Episcopo, vt sit nō tantum διδασκαλος, sed etiam ἀλεγκτος[?]? an quia vitanda est omnis curiositas, idcirco nulla est habenda neces-sitatis ratio? Isti verò qui per summam imperitiam somniant dialecticà Theologicis opponi, cōmiseratione sanè potiùs digni sunt, quàm vllo responso. Primùm enim putare posse quenquàm absque ratiocinãdo ra-tiocinari, siue id ex arte, siue ex sola natura facias, hominis est pror-sus amentis, & qui se hominẽ esse plane sit oblitus. Deinde videntur isti ignorare, Dialecticen non esse ex earum disciplinarum genere, quæ materiam ipsam, de qua agitur, suppeditet: sed id demum osten-dere, quomodo materia à quibusuis sumpta, ita sit vtendum, vt quid cuisit consentaneum vel minùs, quid ex quo consequatur vel non consequatur ostendat, ne falsis ratiocinationibus decepti, pro veri-tate mendacium sequamur. Quod quum ita se habeat, necesse est pro-festò vt isti de rebus sacris vel nullo prorsus modo, vel sine vlla ra-tiocinatione quæri ac disceptari velint: quod vtrunque vel ex eo prorsus absurdum & ineptum esse conuincitur, quòd ne ipsi quidem huius diuinissimæ artis hostes illam possunt nisi ratiocinando oppu-gnare. Illud autem homines imperitos fallit, quòd rationibus agere nullum putet, nisi qui ex suo cerebro rationes petat. ac proinde quum humana ratione Theologia minimè nitatur, excludi quoque Diale-cticen [?] arbitrantur: quod figmentū rursus nullam refutatione mere-tur. Quis enim non videt aliud esse rationem, aliud ratiocinationem? Illam ceu materia sua cuique ars subministrat: hanc natura docet, ars expolit, quæ Dialectice vocata est, quoniam homines de quouis aliu-de subministrato, aptè & ad veritatem appositè loqui docet. Hoc do-num, quod est manifestum imaginis Dei in hominibus vestigium, qui aspernantur, necesse est, vel damnent quod non intelligunt (quod non est certè sapientis:) vel ex eorum sint genere, qui videri volunt cum ra-tione insanire. Nunc superest ut oblata ista occasione, studiosos omnes veritatis in re omnium longè maxima, id est in religione, retinendæ cohorter, ut quo loco res sint, & quid sui sit muneris diligentissimè circunspiciant. Constat de iuris nostri tabulis. Si de interpretatione quæritur, liquet etiam quibus & quot modis illas corrumpere ab initio conatus sit capitalis ille noster hostis: quibus itè rationibus à summis ducibus malæ illius artes (nā de vi manifesta nunc non ago) detectæ fuerint, & veritas fortiter defensa. Hoc autè non ita fuerit difficile nunc quoque intelligere, & in usum nostrum transferre, quum eò sit redactus Satan, ut veluti exhausto illo mendaciorum omniū fœcundissimo pectore, planè cogatur μαγγανεύειν [?], & vetera illa interpolata, sicut paulò ante ostendimus, reponere. Nititur, fateor, Veritas Dei verbo, & cum iudicio legēdi sunt Patres. Sed quis nullam adhuc Ecclesiam fuisse, (ut certè nulla fuit, si isti vera dicunt) concesserit? nisi forte Ecclesia est, quæ quis sit verus Deus ignorat. Deinde si aliunde quoque libet quinam isti [illegible, ~9 letters] sint æstimare, nempe ex manifestis Dei iudicijs, quibus blasphemias in Filiū suum eiacueiaculatas in oculis omnium vindicavit, quid est isto quoque judicio apertius? Servetus vstulata blasphema lingua æternitatem, id est Deitatem Christi negans mortuus est, in medijs ignibus illas æternas flammas velut oculis spectatorum non sine magno omnium horrore subijciens. Gribaldus peste correptus, fugientibus illum omnibus, vix à quo sepeliretur inuenit. Lismaninus à quo introductus fuit Blandrata, seipsum in puteum abiecit. Vir ille istorum perditorum hospes, quod tandem mortis spectaculum præbuit? Ochinus apostata quam miserabiliter obierit cum suis, tota Polonia nouit. Illum quinō ita pridem in Transsyluania Christo postridie maledicturus erat, quid ab extremo corporis & animæ exilio, ruete repente domo, præter longam illam Dei μακροθυμίαν[?] eripuit? Gentilis qua tandem morte anno superiore infelicem vitam finiit? Etsi autem ista non sunt prorsus ἀποδεικτικά[?]: tamen qui priora cum posterioribus comparârit, & propius omnia inspexerit, inueniet profecto in istis tam manifesta diuini furoris testimonia, vt mihi quidè, vel sola sufficere merito posse videantur, tu istis quos adhuc expectat Dei patientia ad metem meliorem reuocandis, tum etiam cæteris expergefaciendis, ne vltrò sese cum istis perditos velint. Tuum autem est in primis, Augustissime Rex fortissimæ Polonorum Gentis, in eo quod tam feliciter cœpisti, constantissimè pergere, neque pati vt qui Filio Dei maledicit (quis autem apertius ei maledicit, quam qui siue vnum siue verum Dei nomen, (nec enim plures veri natura dij esse possunt) ad solum Patrem restringunt, vel illum in creaturam transformant?) regnum tibi à Filio Dei commissum eiusmodi blasphemijs reddat iræ Dei omnipotentis obnoxium. Tuum quoque est, Serenissime Transsyluaniæ Rex, quem penè in sinu imprudens foveas circunspicere, ne ex eo regno quod tibi mirabiliter Dominus tot jam annos conseruat, & nuper etiam sibi incepit consecrare, quispiam ipso Mahumete nihilo melior, authoritate regij tui nominis abutens, in vniuersum Christianum orbem, impetum faciat, magis certè nociturus animis, quàm si vel Moschus vel Tartarus, vel Turca insigni aliqua victoria potiretur. Neque verò difficile vobis fuerit, Augustissimi reges, istorum malo-rum architectos dignoscere, si in hanc rem serio incubueritis, quum istae controversiae tam saepe tamque multipliciter ab ipsis Apostolo-rum temporibus agitatae, tamque feliciter expositae perpetuo doctorum bonorumq; omnium consensu fuerint, ut de istis ne ambigere quidem nunc bona conscientia quisquam, vel mediocriter in verbo Dei & Eccle-siasticis libris versatus, posse videatur. Vos autem Illustres & generosi Domini, quos Dominus ille Dominorum vera sui cognitione in utroq; illo regno dignatus est, osculamini Filium, nec committite ut qui sua illum Deitate spoliat, apud eos consistat, quos in primis oportet ipsius gloriae ac dignitatis vindices & assertores se praebere. Vos vero fra-tres observandi, quibus pascendos suos greges Dominus comisit, an obsecro, vel unicam ouiculam patiemini vestro silentio vobis ab immanibus istis lupis eripi?Te Threci, te Lasici, te Sarnici (quos ego in tanto doctorum & piorum numero, ut mihi de nomine notos cōpello) vos deniq; reliqui Ecclesiarum pastores, ac doctores, obsecro, & ob-testor in Domino, ut totis animis istum toties victū, toties prostratū hostem aggrediamini, nec prius coquiescatis, quàm exerto illo verbi Dei gladio ἀμφιδέξιῳ[?] freti, vel istos nunc perditos rursum Domino lucrifaciatis, vel saltem ab illorum luporum incursibus tutos vestros greges praestetis. En autem vobis συναγωνιστὰς[?] summittimus homines ex praecipuis Christianarum academiarū doctoribus selectos, quorum vel solo nomine vos recreatū iri speramus.Nos vero corporibus quidem absentes, spiritu vero praesentes, vobiscū scitote in summi illius nostri agonothetetae oculis decertare, communis victoriae fru-ctum breui, fauente Deo, vobiscum perceptu-ros.
units.tr: Certainly I would dare to say and declare that in those theses which are attributed to that man, whose name I now spare, are contained the seeds of all the heresies with which Satan has ever assailed the person of Christ. Accordingly, I, the least in the Church of God but still acting in God's cause as far as I am able, beseech that man, whom I hear to be endowed with many outstanding gifts, to beware of Blandrata, that chosen instrument of Satan, by whose poison everyone who has any judgment in these matters agrees he has been breathed upon. I beseech him also to strive day and night against that spirit of ambition by which the most distinguished men are especially deceived by Satan. Finally (and would that he had done this at the start), he should first test these novel prophets by their fruits, since they openly oppose the whole Church, which has been approved by the testimony of all ages without exception, and undermine the very foundation of the Christian faith, before he lends them any further ear. But, someone will say, what has this to do with you? What authority do you have over foreign churches? None at all, brothers; and if I thought otherwise I would be the most insane of men. Yet whoever are Christians, and who by God's mercy have been called to defend the truth and to oppose lies, do not, unless I am mistaken, overstep the limits of their calling when they console, teach, admonish and, if need be, rebuke one another, provided that each keeps his own correction intact [διορθώσει] and that they do so knowingly and properly. I therefore address you, Transylvanians, as brother to brothers, and I call upon you, fellow servants [σύνδουλος] of the Lord, by the name of him whose glory we serve. Can you be ignorant of who Blandrata is, what disturbances he stirred up in Poland, how many newborn churches he overturned, how many souls he destroyed, and what blasphemies against the Son of God he hurled there? Can you be ignorant of what he lately wrote to his Gregory about the eternal generation, as he himself calls it, of the Word [τοῦ λόγου]? But, someone will say, he has already acknowledged among us that the Son is also signified by the name of the One God. That is indeed more correct than before, since he cannot himself deny that Gregory and the other Tritheists wrote or said nothing to the contrary except with him as author, patron and helper. But I ask you: do you think that a slippery eel is so easily held? Or do you believe that an Ethiopian can be whitened, and so quickly? Or do you not know by what arts Arius, Apollinaris, Eunomius and Pelagius, though convicted and condemned, mocked the orthodox? Can you believe that these men, who so manifestly, as so many ruins testify, are instigated by Satan himself to hinder the work of God, are ruled by another spirit? Indeed, brothers, with your good leave, let me say something more. Do you not yet realise what that little word of Blandrata has cost you? Do you not feel, I say, that since this has been wrung from you in your catechism, you have not only written the other creeds besides the one they call Apostolic, superfluously and only for the sake of contradiction, but have also rejected the words essence, hypostasis, homoousios and others of that kind as sophistical, and have been so abused by them in your simplicity that you have broken faith with the whole ancient orthodox Church, and indeed with all the churches that have ever been true since the times of the Apostles? When some people asked this of you, did it not come into your minds that famous confession of the Synods of Nicaea, Ephesus and Chalcedon, than which the sun has never seen anything holier or more venerable since the death of the Apostles? Was there not at least one of the many present to intercede against so unworthy a decree and to deny that those great and most outstanding angels of God were sophists? For even if there were some blemishes in them, whoever thinks that they did not hold the foundation of all religion, that is, the true knowledge of the true God, is certainly unworthy to be counted in the Church of God. Is this, I ask, the way to show at least grateful remembrance of the untiring labours, vigils, tears, groans, exiles and martyrdoms of so many most holy and learned men, who defended this truth and handed it down to us? Some say: "We depend not on the Fathers but on the Word of God." Some are not ashamed to despise what they call dialectic rather than theology. Yet I wonder whether these men have ever read the writings of those whom they are to be convicted of being sophists by. For if they have read them, with what face do they dare to set them against the Word of God, when it is clear that they relied on the one Word of God (even leaving aside the Synods, whenever the adversaries of that truth demanded it)?
