Adhuc si personam Patris expungis e Trinitate: in quo a Filio & Spiritu differret, nisi quia solus est ipse Deus? Fateris Christum esse Deum, fateris a Patre differre: vicissim notam aliquam discretionis esse oportet, ne Pater sit Filius. Tu quum in Essentia eam ponis, nonne manifeste in nihilum redigis veram Christi Deitatem, quae sine Essentia esse non potest, & quidem tota?
units.tr: That other error, no less detestable, that the Essence is in the Father alone, also collapses. For if the name Jehovah is attributed to the one who is named in the passages just cited, it follows that the Son of God is of himself, with respect to the Deity alone. For if he is Jehovah, it cannot be denied that he is the same God who elsewhere cries out through Isaiah, "I, I am he, and there is no God besides me." It would also be useful for you to weigh what that saying of Jeremiah means: "The gods that have not made heaven and earth shall perish from the earth under heaven." Unless you openly wish to curse the Son of God, you will have to confess that he is the one whose Deity is so often proved in Isaiah from the creation of the world. But how will the Creator, who gives being to all things, not be of himself, and borrow his Essence from elsewhere, as if by favour? Nor is there any point in your trying to cast a smokescreen here by subscribing to us on the eternal generation of the Son. For when you say that he is essentiated by the Father, you deny that he is of himself. The Holy Spirit cries out in opposition, naming him Jehovah. Now, if the whole Essence is in the Father alone, either you imagine it as divisible for us, or you will snatch it away from the Son. However often you may now concede that he is the true God, stripped of his Essence he will be God in name only. Here consider again whether you do not either take the Divine Essence from the Son, or dream of a derivation of a part from the whole, whoever substitutes the Essence in the Father in place of the person. According to you, the Essence of God belongs to the Father alone, inasmuch as he alone is, and he is the Essentiator of the Son. Where will the Deity of the Son be, if he is something abstracted from the Essence of God? And what will you say of the Holy Spirit? For if the Father alone is the Essentiator, the Spirit will not be common to the Father and the Son. You want the person of the Spirit to be nothing other than a derivation from the first Essence, which belongs to the Father alone. From this it will be wrung from you that the Spirit is from the Father alone, and that Paul wrongly calls him the Spirit of Christ (Rom. 8). Do you see how your delusions, like manifold snares, entangle you and so strangle you? Furthermore, if you erase the person of the Father from the Trinity, in what would he differ from the Son and the Spirit, unless because he alone is God himself? You confess that Christ is God, you confess that he differs from the Father; in turn there must be some mark of distinction, lest the Father be the Son. When you place this distinction in the Essence, do you not plainly reduce to nothing the true Deity of Christ, which cannot exist without the Essence, and indeed the whole of it?

units.la: Nisi te prorsus excaecauit superbia & furor, disce aliquando Patrem a Filio non distingui, nisi proprium aliquid habeat in se, quod Filio commune non sit. Quid iam reperies in quo Patrem a Filio distinguas? Non erit certe Essentia. Nam si eam communicauit cum Filio, vel in solidum vel ex parte communicauit. Si ex parte, dimidium nobis Deum fabricas. Quomodo enim plena constabit Deitas, nisi in tota & perfecta Essentia? Hoc erit, scilicet, suum honorem dare Filio Dei, Deum partialem fingere. Adde quòd hoc modo nimis scelesta: ac fœdè laceratur Dei Essentia. Restat ut dicas Essentiam perfectè & solidè communem esse Patris & Filij. Quod si verum est, iam certè quoad ipsam nulla erit alterius ab altero discretio. Si respondeas, Patrem essentiando manere nihilominus unicum Deum, penes quem sit Essentia: Christus ergo figuratiuus erit Deus, ac specie tantùm vel nomine, non reipsa: quia Deo nihil magis proprium est quàm Esse: iuxta illud, Qui est, misit me ad vos.
units.tr: Unless pride and fury have utterly blinded you, learn at last that the Father is not distinguished from the Son unless he has something proper in himself that is not common to the Son. What will you now find by which you distinguish the Father from the Son? It will certainly not be the Essence. For if he has shared it with the Son, he has shared it either wholly or in part. If in part, you fabricate for us a half-God. For how will the Deity be complete unless it is in the whole and perfect Essence? This would be, of course, to give the Son of God his honour by feigning a partial God. Add that in this way the Essence of God is too wickedly and foully torn apart. It remains that you say the Essence is perfectly and solidly common to the Father and the Son. But if that is true, then certainly there will be no distinction of one from the other as regards the Essence. If you reply that the Father, by essentiating, nonetheless remains the only God, in whom the Essence resides, then Christ will be God only figuratively, and in appearance or name only, not in reality, because nothing is more proper to God than to Be, according to that saying, "He who is has sent me to you."

units.la: Quòd ratiocinaris, Si Pater esset indiuiduum in Essentia, nō fore solum Patrem atque ingenitū: in eo crassè hallucinaris, quòd indiuidua tibi somnias, quorum singula partem Essentiæ obtineant. Atqui docemus ex Scripturis Deum Essentialiter unum esse: ideóque Essentiam tam Filij quàm Spiritus esse ingenitam. Sed quatenus Pater ordine primus est, atque ex se genuit suam Sapientiam: merito censetur principium & fons totius Diuinitatis. Ita Deus indefinitè est ingenitus, & Pater etiam personæ respectu ingenitus. Quòd autem ex nostra sententia colligere te putas Quaternitatem, hoc est cerebri tui commentum. Gloriaris quidem cœlesti reuelatione errore tibi esse traditum. Quasi verò ignotæ sint nobis naniæ magistri vestri Gribaldi, quas tuus condiscipulus Georgius sedulò huc illuc curauit spargendas. Nam ubi pinxit figuram, in qua Patrem facit Deificatorem Filij & Spiritus, alteram nobis falsò & perfidè adscribit, quasi deriuatiuè fingamus prodire ex una Essentia tres personas: quum tamen certo certius sit, non abstrahere nos personas ab Essentia: sed quanuis in ea resideat, distinctionem interponere. Hoc sensu indiuiduos Tertullianus vocat Patrem & Filiü: non autem (ut tu stultè imaginaris) indiuidua, quæ sub specie comprehendantur. Tibi paralogismus iste tuus arridet, Essentia in semetipsa est verus Deus: Quælibet persona Essentialiter est Deus: Ergo est Quaternitas non Trinitas. Quasi verò fabricemus tres Deos conflatos ex massa Essentiæ, ita ut quæque persona partem aliquam faciat. Nos verò Filium Essentialiter Deum esse asserimus, quia unicus est ille Deus, cuius simplex est Essentia: præterea autem respectu personæ à Patre genitus est. Si separatæ essent ab Essentia personæ, probabilis esset tua argumentatio: sed quum in uno Deo docemus esse tres personas, sequitur Patrem esse Deum, & deinde Filium esse eundem Deum. Præstigiis autem tuis Filium Dei fabricas Essentiatum, & simul tamen absque Essentia, nisi quòd Pater suam Diuinitatem in eü transfudit. Atqui, si ex parte, iam lacera erit diuinitas, & ex transfusione sequetur diminutio. Si in totum, ergo Diuinitas quæ ante fuerat penes Patrem, in Filiü conuersa, in ipso Patre euanuit. Quid obstrepas in contrariam partem, suisque déque nobis est: quia agnoscent sani omnes & integri Lectores, cõsequentiam hæc certa esse & solidam.
units.tr: As for your argument that, if the Father were an individual in Essence, he would not be only Father and unbegotten: in this you grossly err, because you dream of individuals each of which holds a part of the Essence. And yet we teach from the Scriptures that God is essentially one; therefore the Essence of the Son as well as of the Spirit is unbegotten. But inasmuch as the Father is first in order, and begot his own Wisdom from himself, he is rightly reckoned the principle and fount of the whole Deity. Thus God is unbegotten without qualification, and the Father is unbegotten also with respect to the person. As for your thinking that we infer a Quaternity from our view, this is the invention of your own brain. You glory indeed that the error was handed down to you by heavenly revelation. As if the follies of your master Gribaldi were unknown to us, which your fellow-student George has zealously taken care to scatter here and there. For when he drew a figure in which the Father makes the Son and the Spirit divine, he falsely and treacherously ascribes to us another, as if we derivatively imagined three persons to come forth from one Essence; yet it is more certain than certain that we do not abstract the persons from the Essence, but, although they reside in it, we place a distinction between them. In this sense Tertullian calls the Father and the Son individuals, not, as you foolishly imagine, individuals that are comprehended under a species. This paralogism of yours delights you: the Essence in itself is the true God; each person is essentially God; therefore there is a Quaternity, not a Trinity. As if we were fabricating three Gods fused from a mass of Essence, so that each person made up some part. But we assert that the Son is essentially God, because he is the one God whose Essence is simple; moreover, with respect to the person he is begotten of the Father. If the persons were separated from the Essence, your argument would be plausible; but since we teach that there are three persons in the one God, it follows that the Father is God, and then that the Son is the same God. By your sleight of hand, however, you make the Son of God essentiated, and at the same time without Essence, except that the Father has poured his Deity into him. But if this is in part, the Deity is already torn, and the transfusion will bring diminution. If it is in whole, then the Deity which before was with the Father, converted into the Son, has vanished in the Father himself. Why do you strain in the opposite direction? It is all one to us; for all sound and upright readers will recognise that this consequence is certain and solid.

units.la: Hinc soluitur futilis tua quæstio: Vtrum Essentia cōcurrat in Trinitatem, necne. Satis enim liquet, quum tota sit in singulis personis, non concurrere. Quòd inde infers Trinitatem fore sine Deo, imò vanam & nullam, ex eadem insul-sitate sensus tui nascitur: quia etsi non concurrit ad distinguendas personas, sed absque distinctione unica est ac simplex, nō tamen persona sine ipsa vel extra ipsam: quia ideò Pater est Pater, quia Deus: & Filius est Filius, quia Deus. Deum enim esse oportet Sapientiam illam æternam, quæ genita ex Deo. Deitatem absolutè ex seipsa quidem esse dicimus: unde & Filium, quatenus Deus, sublato personæ respectu, ex seipso esse fatemur: quatenus verò Filius est, dici-mus esse ex Patre. Ita essentia eius principio caret: persona autem principium est ipse Deus. Hoc ut ad tuam Quaternitatem arripere desinas, exuere discas commentum illud, Personas esse abstracta quædam Deitatis. Adde quòd veteres quicunque de Trinitate loquuti sunt, ad personas tantum retulerunt hoc nomen. Et certè non modò absurdus esset error, in Trinitate complecti [?] Essentiam, sed nimis crassa impietas. Quarum, obsecro, rerum dices esse Trinitatem? Respondes tria concurrere, Essentiam, Filium, & Spiritum. Hinc verò plane perspicitur, te essentiam Filij & Spiritus exinanire. Alioqui partes inter se commixta coinciderent, ut loquuntur: quod est in omni distinctione vitiosum. Concurrunt ad naturam & statu hominis anima & corpus. Si anima in corpus transiret, iam cessaret concursus iste. Ita nisi bis cæcus es, clare videre potes cōfusam in Deitate mixturam à te fieri, non secus atque in electro, quoniam unius Patris erit Essentia, Filij & Spiritus Diuinitas, forma erit qualem tu imaginaris, fides autem concipere non potest. Quòd autem de voce Trinitatis tā aperte conuictus, non vis tamen cedere, in re minima prodis maximam impudentiam. Vis enim toto inuito mundo Trinitatem esse Trium unitatem: quasi non idem significet Latinis, quòd Græcis nomen τριάδος. Sed ita de reprobis & desperatis loquitur Deus, Nesciunt erubescere.
units.tr: Hence your idle question is resolved: whether the Essence concurs into the Trinity or not. For it is plain enough that, since it is wholly in each of the persons, it does not concur. That you infer from this that the Trinity would be without God, or indeed empty and nothing, is born of the same silliness of your mind; for although it does not concur to distinguish the persons, but is one and simple without distinction, yet no person is without it or outside it, because the Father is Father because he is God, and the Son is Son because he is God. For we must acknowledge that the eternal Wisdom, begotten from God, is God. We say that the Deity is of itself absolutely; whence we also confess that the Son, inasmuch as he is God, is of himself, the respect to the person being set aside; but inasmuch as he is the Son, we say that he is of the Father. Thus his Essence lacks a principle, but the person has a principle, namely God himself. So that you may cease to seize upon your Quaternity, learn to cast off that fiction that the persons are certain abstractions of the Deity. Add that the ancients who spoke of the Trinity applied this name only to the persons. And indeed it would be not only an absurd error to include the Essence in the Trinity, but an excessively gross impiety. Of what things, I beg you, will you say the Trinity consists? You answer that three concur: the Essence, the Son, and the Spirit. From this it is plainly seen that you empty the Essence of the Son and of the Spirit. Otherwise the parts, mixed together, would coincide, as they say, which is faulty in every distinction. Soul and body concur to constitute the nature and state of man; if the soul passed into the body, that concurrence would now cease. So unless you are blind twice over, you can clearly see that you make a confused mixture in the Deity, not unlike amber; for the Essence will be the Father's alone, the Divinity the Son's and the Spirit's; the form will be what you imagine, but faith cannot conceive it. As for your being so openly convicted about the word Trinity, yet unwilling to yield, you show great impudence in a very small matter. For you want, against the whole world, the Trinity to be the unity of three; as if the Latin word did not mean the same as the Greek word for triad. But God speaks thus of the reprobate and desperate: "They know not how to blush."

units.la: Quòd quæris utrum Essentia, Pater, & unicus ille Deus Israel sint synonyma, quæ possint inter se inuicem supponi & prædicari: iam plus satis responsum est. Si enim essent synonyma, Essentia & Pater, liceret tibi pedibus calcare Christum, quasi umbram: quia nulla esset in ipso Diuinitas. Hæc enim deliræ tuæ speculationis summa est, Si Essentia est Pater, & Pater Essentia: sequitur neque Essentiam esse nisi in Patre, neque Patrem aliud esse quàm Essentiam. Item, Si Pater est unicus Deus Israel, & Deus unicus Israel est Pater: ergo Christus non fuit unquam, neque est Deus Israel. Nos autem docemus Patrem esse unicum Deum Israel, ut interea non excludatur Filius.
units.tr: As for your question whether Essence, the Father and the one God of Israel are synonyms that can be substituted for one another and predicated of one another, enough has already been answered. For if Essence and Father were synonyms, you would be free to trample Christ underfoot as a shadow, since there would be no Deity in him. This is the sum of your crazed speculation: if Essence is the Father and the Father is Essence, it follows that there is Essence only in the Father, and that the Father is nothing other than Essence. Likewise, if the Father is the one God of Israel and the one God of Israel is the Father, then Christ never was and is not God of Israel. We, however, teach that the Father is the one God of Israel in such a way that the Son is not thereby excluded.

units.la: Quòd quæris, An Deus Legis & Prophetarum sit Pater Verbi, improbi & proterui scurræ partes agis. Nec certè hîc nobis tēperare possumus, quin saltem uno verbo excutiamus tibi Thrasonicum hunc fastum. Audésne Cerdonem nobis obiicere nebulo, vt tam claram lucem obscures, quæ te subterfugia omnia captantem vrget? Tu stas ad Tribunal pij Magistratus, reus ob execrandas blasphemias: vt te explices, nos in Cerdonis partes pertrahere conaris.
units.tr: As for your question whether the God of the Law and the Prophets is the Father of the Word, you play the part of a shameless and insolent buffoon. Indeed, here we cannot refrain from shaking off, at least with a single word, this boastful pride of yours. Do you dare, you scoundrel, to throw Cerdo at us, in order to obscure a light so clear, you who, catching at every kind of evasion, are pressed hard? You stand before the tribunal of a godly magistrate, a defendant on account of execrable blasphemies, and to extricate yourself you try to drag us into Cerdo's role.

units.la: Eâdem etiam petulantia erumpit in Archonticis: quasi in hac Ecclesia, vbi sub specie ouis fuisti lupus & vulpes simul, audieris Angelos prædicari mundi creatores.
units.tr: The same wantonness breaks out also in the Archontics, as if in this Church, where under the appearance of a sheep you have been both wolf and fox at once, you had heard angels preached as the creators of the world.

units.la: Eódem etiam redit proxima quæstio, quæ eadem est, An neget Caluinus vnicum Deum Israel esse Patrem Verbi. Tu verò Sycophanta satis superque tenes, quid tibi etiam nuper nobis audiētibus dixerit. pridem verò tenere debueras quid coram toto mundo prædicent eius scripta, & quid apud populum quotidie doceat. Apage ergò cum tuis probationibus. Sed interea, vt scias te hominem esse phreneticum, imò dæmoniacum, memoria repetas quod nuper diximus, Quia synonyma non sunt Pater Christi, &, Deus Israel, sententiam non posse conuerti, vt Filio excluso deitas restringatur ad solum Patrem. Nec verbis digna est illa canina improbitas, quum principium illud sumis, Deum non posse inuocari sine Mediatore. Hoc etiam, nisi plusquam turpiter ingratus esses, debueras acceptum referre Caluino, Deum non exaudire preces nostras nisi per Mediatorem. Quid postulas vt tibi clarè respondeat hac de re, quam toti mundo sonorè testatus est? Nisi te possideret Satan, certè in istam petulantiam non erumperes. Tergiuersationem vocas quod scripserat Caluinus docendi tui causa. Si quæritur ánnon tutior precandi forma sit, dum inuocamus Patrem in nomine Filij: respondemus, sicut iam diximus, hanc esse ordinariam & magis familiarem, quia aptior est ruditati nostræ & vtilior. Sed alias formas, quæ etiam in vsu fuerunt Apostolis, & quas illis Spiritus sanctus dictauit, damnare, sacrilegæ temeritatis esset. Nec valet illa obiectio, Frustra Deum inuocari absque Mediatore: quia etsi fixum est illud principium, Non exaudiri nos nisi per gratiam Mediatoris, non tamen semper in promptu occurrere necesse est. Iam prætereiit annus, ex quo scriptum hoc cum tuis condiscipulis legisti: & adhuc discendi studium simulas, quasi diabolus in Christi schola velit proficere. Hæc nobis extorsit fœtida illa tua eructatio. Iam tibi de re simpliciter respondemus, Mediator fuit Christus, vt Deus manifestatus in carne. Neque enim homo, nisi simul Deus esset, perduceret nos ad Deum. Fatemur quidem humanæ naturæ respectu Christum nobis esse Mediatorem, quatenus aduocatus est noster, & apud Patrem pro nobis intercedit: sed vtranque naturam comprehendi necesse est, vbi de Mediatore agitur. Proinde quòd infers, nefas esse vocare Christum Mediatorem, vt est Deus, prorsus est diabolicum. Maior etiam insulsitas in eo quod proximè sequitur, Si Mediator fuit, quatenus Filius, Deum Israel esse eius Patrem sine personæ respectu. Sed quicquid Thrasonicè iactes, ex hac blasphemia perspicimus te nunquam serio invocasse Deum. Reliqua omnia quæ subiicis, non longa refutatione opus habent. Tu qui iuras neque Theologum, neque philosophum te esse, magistrali supercilio doctrinam tibi incognitam perinde damnas, ac si nuper è cælo delapsus esses, Lucifer. Vide interea vt te implices. Abominaris si quis dicat Christum esse Mediatorem, quatenus Deus est: Mediatorem vero dicis esse, quatenus est Filius. Vbi ergo eius deitas, si in æterna generatione non reperitur? Neque hoc tibi nunc demum per incogitantiam excidit: testes enim sumus, pertinaciter te negasse Christum ea ratione, qua Filius est, debere Deum censeri: unde sequitur alia ratione esse Deum. Ita Trinitas tua, non erit Trium unitas, sed coniunctio unius Dei cum duabus rebus creatis. Sermo ille Christi ad Patrem, Hæc est vita æterna, vt credant te unum verum Deum, & quem misisti Iesum Christum, clarè tibi fuit expositus. Nam illic Christus in Mediatoris persona loquens, medium gradum tenet inter Deum & homines. Neque tamen ideo imminuitur eius Maiestas. Nam etsi seipsum exinanivit, gloriam tamen suam, quæ abscondita fuit coram mundo, non perdidit apud Patrem. Sic Apostolus 2, ad Hebræos cap. quanquam fatetur exiguo tempore fuisse imminutum infra Angelos, non tamen dubitat simul asserere, æternum esse Deum qui fundauit terram. Tenendum igitur est, quoties Christus in persona Mediatoris Patrem compellat, sub hoc nomine Diuinitatem complecti, quæ ipsius quoque est. Sic quum Apostolis diceret, Expedit me ascendere ad Patrem, quia Pater maior me est: non secundam diuinitatem tamen sibi tribuit, vt sit quoad æternam essentiam Patre inferior: sed quia cælesti gloria potitus, fideles colligit in participationem diuinitatis, vocat Patrem maiorem, quatenus differt conspicua splendoris perfectio quæ in cælo apparet, ab ea gloriæ mensura quæ conspecta fuit in ipso carne vestito. Eâdem ratione apud Paulum dicitur, Reddet regnum Deo & Patri, vt sit Deus omnia in omnibus. Quærimus abs te, an Christus quem cogeris Deum fateri, esse desinet. Quòd si perpetuitatem eius deitati concedis, sequitur sub Patris nomine vnicam Dei essentiam, quæ tam Filij est quàm Patris, comprehendi. Et certè ideo ad nos descendit Christus, vt ad Patrem attollendo simul etiam ad seipsum attolleret, quatenus vnum est cum Patre. Quæ postea euomis conuitia, omittimus,ubi Filium Dei quem prædicamus,in diabolum transfigurus:Deum quem colimus,vocas Deum Turcarum, multáque eius generis.Sed vide miser, ne te præcipitauerit tuus furor,ut voces emitteres quæ per iugulum redeant.
units.tr: The next question also comes back to the same point, namely whether Calvin denies that the one God of Israel is the Father of the Word. You, sycophant, know well enough, and more than enough, what he said to you lately in our hearing. Long ago, however, you ought to have known what his writings proclaim before the whole world, and what he teaches the people every day. Away then with your proofs! But meanwhile, so that you may know that you are a frenzied man, or rather a demoniac, call to mind what we said recently: that the Father of Christ and the God of Israel are not synonyms, and that the sentence cannot be reversed so that, with the Son excluded, the deity is restricted to the Father alone. That doglike impudence is not even worth words, when you take up the principle that God cannot be invoked without a Mediator. Unless you were shamefully ungrateful, you ought to have credited Calvin with this too, that God does not hear our prayers except through the Mediator. What do you demand, that he answer you clearly on this matter, when he has testified it to the whole world so loudly? Unless Satan possessed you, you would not burst out into such wantonness. You call it evasion that Calvin wrote this for the sake of teaching you. If it is asked whether it is not a safer form of praying to invoke the Father in the name of the Son, we answer, as we have already said, that this is the ordinary form and the more familiar one, because it is better suited to our rudeness and more useful. But to condemn other forms, which were also in use among the Apostles and which the Holy Spirit dictated to them, would be the act of sacrilegious rashness. Nor does that objection hold, that it is in vain to invoke God without a Mediator: for even if that principle is fixed, that we are not heard except through the grace of the Mediator, it is not necessary that this should always be at hand. A year has now passed since you read this writing with your fellow pupils, and yet you still pretend to be eager to learn, as if the devil wished to make progress in Christ's school. That foul belch of yours has forced this from us. Now we answer you plainly on the matter: Christ was Mediator as God manifested in the flesh. For a man, unless he were at the same time God, could not bring us to God. We do indeed confess that Christ is our Mediator with respect to his human nature, insofar as he is our advocate and intercedes for us with the Father; but when the Mediator is under discussion, both natures must be comprehended. Therefore your inference that it is wicked to call Christ Mediator as he is God is utterly diabolical. Still greater is the silliness in what immediately follows, that if he was Mediator insofar as he is the Son, then the God of Israel is his Father without regard to the person. But whatever you boast in your bombastic way, from this blasphemy we see that you have never seriously invoked God. The rest of what you add needs no lengthy refutation. You, who swear that you are neither a theologian nor a philosopher, condemn with a schoolmaster's arrogance a doctrine unknown to you, just as if you had lately fallen from heaven, Lucifer. Meanwhile see how you entangle yourself. You abhor it if anyone says that Christ is Mediator insofar as he is God, yet you say he is Mediator insofar as he is the Son. Where, then, is his deity, if it is not to be found in the eternal generation? Nor has this slipped from you only now through inadvertence: for we are witnesses that you have obstinately denied that Christ must be regarded as God on the ground that he is the Son, from which it follows that he is God on some other ground. Thus your Trinity will not be a unity of three, but a conjunction of the one God with two created things. Christ's saying to the Father, "This is eternal life, that they may believe you to be the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent" (John 17:3), has been clearly expounded to you. For there Christ, speaking in the person of the Mediator, holds a middle place between God and men. Yet his majesty is not thereby diminished. For although he emptied himself, he did not lose his glory, which was hidden from the world, in the sight of the Father. So the Apostle, in Hebrews chapter 2, though he admits that for a short time he was made lower than the angels, nevertheless does not hesitate at the same time to assert that he is the eternal God who founded the earth. It must therefore be held that whenever Christ, in the person of the Mediator, addresses the Father, under this name is embraced the Deity which is also his. So when he said to the Apostles, "It is expedient for me to go to the Father, for the Father is greater than I" (John 16:7; 14:28), he did not thereby attribute to himself a secondary deity, as if he were inferior to the Father in eternal essence; rather, having obtained heavenly glory, he gathers the faithful into participation in the deity, and calls the Father greater insofar as the conspicuous perfection of splendour which appears in heaven differs from that measure of glory which was seen in him when clothed in flesh. On the same principle it is said by Paul, "He will hand over the kingdom to God and the Father, that God may be all in all" (1 Cor. 15:24, 28). We ask you whether Christ, whom you are compelled to confess as God, will cease to be. But if you grant his deity to be everlasting, it follows that under the name of Father is comprehended the one essence of God, which belongs as much to the Son as to the Father. And surely Christ came down to us for this reason, that by raising us to the Father he might at the same time raise us to himself, insofar as he is one with the Father. As for the reproaches you then vomit forth, we pass over them, where you would turn the Son of God whom we proclaim into the devil, the God whom we worship you call the God of the Turks, and many things of that sort. But see, wretch, lest your fury hurl you headlong so that you utter words which return to cut your own throat.

units.la: Quod quæris, An natura Christum esse Filium Dei putemus: facis pro tuo more, in re extra controuersiam posita, rixandi & pugnandi ansam quærens. Natura dicimus esse Filium Dei, quod tu calumniator minimè ignoras: sed stultè inde infers, non liberè & verè prædicari Dei Filium, nisi personali respectu valere iussò. Nam quanuis Dei nomen etiam Filio commune sit, absurdum tamen negamus κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν [?] Patri interdum adscribi: quia ut alibi dictum est, fons est ac principium Diuinitatis. In hac doctrina nihil Sophisticum, sed mera Scripturæ simplicitas. Quod autem Sophistas esse dicis, qui negant Deum esse Filij Essentiatorem, qua arrogantia id tibi sumis, ut homo nullius pretij tam imperiosè damnare audeas, quicunque prodigioso tuo commento nō subscribunt? Nam ex omnibus hæreticis, quorum magna fuit colluuies, tu primus es inuentus qui mundo hoc portentum Essentiandi obtruderes. Odiosè quidem colligere tibi videris, Si Filius Dei est Christus, non esse Filium personæ. Neque verò ita solemus loqui. sed postquam ingenuè confessi sumus esse Dei Filium, explicandi causa addimus, Non discerpi hoc modo Dei unicam essentiam, neque auferri Christo Deitatem: sed esse Filium Dei Patris, quatenus Sermo est ab ipso ante secula genitus. Tu verò quoties solum Patrem garris esse verum Deum, Filio non nisi fictitiam Deitatem relinquis.
units.tr: As for your question whether we think Christ is the Son of God by nature, you do, as is your custom, seek an occasion for quarrelling and fighting over a matter placed beyond dispute. We say that he is the Son of God by nature, which you, a slanderer, are by no means ignorant of; but you foolishly infer from this that the Son of God is not freely and truly proclaimed unless he is made to stand only in personal relation. For although the name of God is common also to the Son, we deny that it is absurd that it is sometimes ascribed to the Father by pre-eminence [κατ᾽ ἐξοχήν], because, as has been said elsewhere, he is the fount and principle of the Deity. There is nothing sophistical in this doctrine, but the plain simplicity of Scripture itself. As for your saying that those are sophists who deny that God is the begetter of the Son's essence, with what arrogance do you, a man of no worth, dare so imperiously to condemn whoever does not subscribe to your monstrous invention? For of all the heretics, of whom there has been a great flood, you are the first found to thrust upon the world this portent of "essencing." You seem to draw an odious conclusion, that if Christ is the Son of God, he is not the Son of the person. We do not usually speak in that way; rather, after we have frankly confessed that he is the Son of God, we add by way of explanation that the one essence of God is not thus torn apart, nor is the Deity taken away from Christ; but he is the Son of God the Father, insofar as the Word was begotten by him before the ages. You, however, whenever you chatter that the Father alone is the true God, leave to the Son only a fictitious Deity.

units.la: Quòd quæris, An unicus Deus Israel fuerit semper Pater, necne: quære alios quibuscum de hac re litiges. Scis enim quid ferat huius Ecclesiæ doctrina & fides de æterna Verbi generatione. Inde infers, Deum igitur Patrem esse Verbi: quod non inficiamur. Cur autè non progressus fueris ultrà, videmus, Blasphemiæ odium fugitare voluisti, Dei Patris essentiam Verbo nō esse communem.
units.tr: As for your question whether the one God of Israel was always the Father or not, ask others with whom you may dispute that matter. You know what the doctrine and faith of this Church teach about the eternal generation of the Word. From this you infer that God, therefore, is the Father of the Word, which we do not deny. Why you did not go further we can see: you wished to avoid the charge of blasphemy, which would be that the essence of God the Father is not common to the Word.

units.la: Quòd obiicis, Sophisticè tribui Patri personam, si verè dicit Apostolus, Deū misisse Filium suum: iam tibi responsum fuit, non posse Deum esse Filij sui Patrem, nisi personæ respectu: quia alioqui vel partibilis esset Dei essentia, vel Filius ipse Deus non esset. Itaque Deum ipsum Israel audire præstat testantem qualis sit, quàm impurum canem de eius mysteriis proterue blaterantem. Speciosi sunt isti prætextus, te nihil detrahere Christi maiestati, quin sit unus idemque Deus, & eiusdem essentiæ. Sed quam inseris exceptio, fucos illos facilè discutit. Exclusiue enim Patrem vocando solum Deum, & exclusiuè Essentiam illi asserendo, palàm demonstras in Filio neque veram esse Deitatem, neque Essentiam. Neque verò nos latet argutia illa, Christum esse verum Deum, quia essentiatus sit à Patre. Sed hoc modo videmus precariam fieri eius Deita-tem, cui datum est esse. Adde, quòd mutuo conflictu sese prosternunt[?] tua com-menta. Nam si nota discretionis quam statuis, vera est, Residere in solo Patre Essentiam: quomodo stabit illud, Eadem quoque essentiam esse Filij: quæ certè nulla erit, si eam vendicat sibi solus Pater, & eius ratione à Filio suo differt. Si causam tuam probare nobis volebas, non debuisti tam crassis mendacijs ora nobis oblinere.
units.tr: As for your objection that the Apostle speaks truly when he says God sent his Son, and that this makes the Father a person only by sophistry: an answer has already been given you, that God cannot be the Father of his Son except with respect to person, because otherwise either the essence of God would be divisible or the Son himself would not be God. It is better, then, to hear God of Israel himself testifying what he is, than to hear that impure dog shamelessly babbling about his mysteries. Your pretexts are specious, that you take nothing from the majesty of Christ, since he is one and the same God and of the same essence. But the exception you add easily shakes off those disguises. For by calling the Father alone God exclusively, and by asserting essence to him exclusively, you plainly show that in the Son there is neither true deity nor essence. Nor are we unaware of that subtlety, that Christ is true God because he is given essence by the Father. But in this way we see his deity made precarious, since it was given him to be. Add that your comments overthrow themselves in mutual conflict. For if the distinction you set up is true, that essence resides in the Father alone, how will it stand that the same essence belongs also to the Son? That essence will certainly be none, if the Father alone claims it for himself and on that ground differs from his Son. If you wished to prove your case to us, you should not have smeared our mouths with such crass lies.

units.la: Satis iam putamus discussas esse absurditatum nebulas, quibus fidei nostræ lucem obtenebrare frustra tentasti. Tabella tua ubi Verbum Dei fateris esse Deum Israel, ne simplicium oculos perstringat, uno verbo dilui potest hic fucus. Nam quum Patrem solum asserens Deum Israel, Filium semper excludas, non relinquis huic Diuinitatem, nisi secundam & creatam, imo imaginariam: quia secundum te essentia caret, nisi quatenus essentiatur à vero Deo: quem tamen solum vis præditum esse essentia, ut Filius & Spiritus titulares sint personæ. Quantumvis ergo flexuosus sis serpens, tuis istis ambagibus nihil proficies. Itaque propositio quam asseris esse veram, Deus Israel est Pater Verbi: si Ver-bum ipsum excludat, impia est ac sacrilega. Atqui nihil aliud latratu tuo contendis, nisi ut vera Deitate Christum spolians, Patrem statuas solum Deum. Hæc tua est innocentia, nempe diabolica vafrities, qua conaris solem detrahere è cælo: nisi quòd in reprobum sensum coniectus, impudetia Satanam superas.
units.tr: We think the clouds of absurdity, by which you vainly tried to darken the light of our faith, have now been sufficiently dispelled. Your little tablet, in which you confess the Word of God to be God of Israel, lest it dazzle the eyes of simple people, can be refuted in one word: this trick. For while asserting the Father alone to be God of Israel and always excluding the Son, you leave to him no divinity except a secondary and created one, or rather an imaginary one. According to you he lacks essence, except insofar as he is essentiated by the true God, whom you nonetheless want alone to be endowed with essence, so that the Son and the Spirit are merely titular persons. However crooked a serpent you are, you will gain nothing by these circumlocutions. Therefore the proposition you assert to be true, that the God of Israel is the Father of the Word, is impious and sacrilegious if it excludes the Word himself. Yet by your barking you contend for nothing but to strip Christ of true deity and set up the Father alone as God. This is your innocence, namely diabolical craftiness, by which you try to drag the sun from the sky; except that, cast into a reprobate mind, you surpass Satan in impudence.

units.la: Superest ut locos ex Irenæo & Tertulliano citatos, breviter explicemus. Neque enim sigillatim singulos excutere necesse erit, quando una est omnium solutio. Hoc tantum ex Irenæo adducis, Patrem Christi esse solum Deum Israel. Quid tibi erroris causam præbuerit, coniicere licet. Arripuit scilicet tibi nomen Dei Israel, quasi aliquod subesset mysterium. Atqui animadvertere debueras sancto viro negotium & certamen fuisse cum phreneticis, qui Patrem Christi negabant illum esse Deum qui per Mosen & Prophetas olim loquutus fuerat: sed nescio quod spectrū è labe mundi productum. Itaque in hoc totus est, ut ostendat eundem illum Deum, qui per Mosen & Prophetas loquutus est, esse Christi Patrem, & perperam alium Deum excogitari. Non mirum igitur si toties concludat, nō alium fuisse Israelis Deum, quàm qui Pater est Iesu Christi. Sic etiam nunc, ubi tuis blasphemiis resistendum est, vere dicemus Deum qui olim apparuit Patribus, non alium fuisse quàm Christum. Porrò si quis excipiat, fuisse Patrem: in promptu erit responsio, dum pro Filij Diuinita-te pugnamus, nos Patrem minimè excludere. Si ad hoc Irenæi c[?] filium atten-das, cessabit omnis disputatio. Quòd si hæc ratio intemperiem tuam nondum placat, obiicimus tibi caput sextum libri tertij, vbi in hoc vnum insistit pius vir,qui absolutè & indefinitè vocatur in Scriptura Deus,illum esse verè vnicum Deum: Christum verò indefinitè & absolutè Deum vocari. Memineris hunc disceptationis statum fuisse Irenæo,sicuti ex toto progressu patet, ac præsertim libri secundi capite 46, non vocari Patrem ænigmaticè & parabolicè qui verè non sit Deus. Adde nonum caput libri tertij, vbi coniunctim tam Filium quàm Patrem dicit à Prophetis & Apostolis prædicatum fuisse Deum. Duodecimo autem capite libri tertii docet,quomodo Christus, qui Dominus est omnium,& Rex,& Deus,& Iudex,ab eo qui est Deus omnium ,acceperit potestatem,nempe subiectionis respectu: quia humiliatus est vsque ad mortem. Interea capite decimosexto eiusdem libri tertii palàm affirmat, Filium esse opificem cæli & terræ,qui Legem tulit per Mosis manum,& Patribus apparuit. Iam vt centies blateres,solum Patrem esse Deum Israel, regerimus tibi quod idem scriptor capite decimooctauo eiusdem libri dicit, Christum vnum & eundem existere: sicuti & 23 capite ad Christum refert vaticinium Habacuc, Deus ad Austro veniet. Eodè pertinet quod legitur cap. nono quarti libri,Ipse igitur Christus cū Patre viuorū est Deus:sicuti & duodecimo eiusdē libri interpretatur Abrahā credidisse Deo,quia factor cæli & terræ & solus Deus sit Christus. Nam quòd expendi iubes hæc verba,Filium esse in Patre, & habere in se Patrem, nescimus quorsum. Certè fidem nostram optimè confirmant. Cæterùm eådem impudentia arripis illud, Mensuram Patris esse Filium, quia & capit eum:quasi Patrem essentiatorem constituant. Nos verò hinc facilè cognoscimus,te nunquam gustasse in quem finem datus nobis fuerit Christus. Nam quia Dei immensitas in Filio à nobis concipitur, ideo vocatus fuit mensura. Tu autem phreneticè hoc ad originem essentiæ trahis.
units.tr: It remains for us to explain briefly the passages cited from Irenaeus and Tertullian. It will not be necessary to examine each one separately, since one solution serves for all. From Irenaeus you adduce only this: that the Father of Christ is alone God of Israel. One may guess what caused your error. You evidently seized on the name God of Israel as if some mystery lay hidden in it. But you ought to have noticed that the holy man had a contest and struggle with frenzied people who denied that the Father of Christ was the God who once spoke through Moses and the Prophets, claiming instead that he was some phantom produced from the filth of the world. Hence his whole aim is to show that the same God who spoke through Moses and the Prophets is the Father of Christ, and that it is wrong to imagine another God. So it is no wonder that he so often concludes that the God of Israel was none other than the Father of Jesus Christ. So also now, when we must resist your blasphemies, we will truly say that the God who once appeared to the fathers was none other than Christ. Further, if someone objects that he was the Father, the answer is ready: while we fight for the deity of the Son, we by no means exclude the Father. If you attend to this purpose of Irenaeus, all dispute will cease. But if this reasoning does not yet soothe your intemperance, we object to you the sixth chapter of book 3, where the godly man insists on this one point: that he who is absolutely and indefinitely called God in Scripture is truly the only God, and that Christ is likewise called God indefinitely and absolutely. Remember that this was the state of the dispute for Irenaeus, as is clear from the whole course of his argument, and especially from book 2, chapter 46, where it is said that one is not called Father enigmatically and parabolically if he is not truly God. Add chapter 9 of book 3, where he says that both Son and Father were proclaimed as God together by the Prophets and Apostles. In chapter 12 of book 3 he teaches how Christ, who is Lord of all, King, God and Judge, received power from him who is God of all, namely with respect to subjection, because he humbled himself even unto death. Meanwhile, in chapter 16 of the same book 3 he plainly affirms that the Son is the maker of heaven and earth, who gave the Law by the hand of Moses and appeared to the fathers. Now, that you may rave a hundred times that the Father alone is God of Israel, we reply to you that the same writer says in chapter 18 of that book that Christ is one and the same, and, as in chapter 23, he refers to Christ the prophecy of Habakkuk, God shall come from the south. To the same point belongs what is read in chapter 9 of book 4: therefore Christ himself, together with the Father, is God of the living; and likewise in chapter 12 of the same book he explains that Abraham believed God because Christ is the maker of heaven and earth and alone God. As for your bidding us weigh the words that the Son is in the Father and has the Father in himself, we do not know to what purpose this is. Certainly these words strongly confirm our faith. Moreover, with the same impudence you seize on the saying that the Son is the measure of the Father, because he also contains him, as if they made the Father the one who gives essence. But from this we easily recognise that you have never grasped for what end Christ was given to us. For because we conceive the immensity of God in the Son, therefore he was called the measure. But you frenziedly drag this to the origin of essence.

units.la: De Tertulliano primùm sic accipe: quanuis asper ac spinosus interdum sit eius sermo, summam doctrinæ quam tuemur eum non ambiguè tradere: nempe quum vnus sit Deus, dispensatione tamen vel œconomia esse eius Sermonem: vnicum verò esse Deum per substantiæ vnitatem, & nihilominus vnitatem mysterio dispensationis in Trinitate disponi: tres esse non statu, sed gradu: nec substantia, sed forma: nec potestate, sed specie. Porrò quum aduersus Monarchicos disputat, disertè pronuntiat euerti Dei monarchiam, quum alia dominatio quasi æmula superinducitur. Vnde aperte colligitur, vbi Deitatis, summíque imperii, & æternæ essentiæ sit mentio, Filium perperam opponi. Secundum à Patre ergo defendit Tertullianus, non qui alius sit nisi distinctione.
units.tr: As for Tertullian, first take him thus: although his style is sometimes harsh and thorny, he unambiguously hands down the sum of the doctrine we maintain. Namely, since God is one, his Word is nonetheless by dispensation or economy; God is one indeed by unity of substance, yet that unity is arranged in the Trinity by the mystery of the dispensation; the three are not in state but in degree, not in substance but in form, not in power but in aspect. Moreover, when he disputes against the Monarchians, he plainly declares that the monarchy of God is overthrown when another dominion is introduced as though it were a rival. Whence it is openly gathered that where mention is made of deity, supreme rule and eternal essence, the Son is wrongly set over against the Father. Tertullian therefore defends the Son as second from the Father, not as other except by distinction.

units.la: Secundum vero testimonium quod adducis, nisi per cōcessionem sumatur, excusari nullo modo poterit, Quòd scilicet Filius sit totius substantiæ deriuatio, & portio. Atqui toto contextu omnē dubitationē eximit, unicā esse substantiā afferens: præsertim vero ubi addit explicationis causā, Bene est quòd & Dominus alium Paracletum vocans, non diuisionem significat, sed dispositionem: quam sententiam fusius deinde prosequitur. Alioqui Dei essentiam secari in partes absurdissimum foret. Sed hinc quoque deprehendere licet quod antè admonuimus, te sub fictitiæ Deitatis larua impiè obtegere quod proferre non audes.
units.tr: The second testimony you adduce cannot in any way be excused, unless it is taken by way of concession: namely, that the Son is a derivation and portion of the whole substance. Yet the whole context removes all doubt by asserting that the substance is one; especially where he adds by way of explanation: "It is good that the Lord, calling another Paraclete, signifies not a division but a disposition," which opinion he then pursues more fully. Otherwise it would be most absurd to say that the essence of God is cut into parts. But here too one may perceive what we noted before: that you impiously hide under the mask of a fictitious deity what you do not dare to bring forward.

units.la: Tertium quoque testimonium peruersè mutilas. Neque enim illic definit Tertullianus quid sentiat, sed in utramque partem ratiocinatur quomodo inuisibilis sit Pater, Filius autem visibilis. Iam tibi absurdi obiectio fidei confessio visa est. Atqui paulò post tollitur omnis ambiguitas, Filium esse inuisibilem quatenus est Sermo. Disce igitur posthac consideratius singula expendere, ne pauca verba excerpens, aliud subinde pro alio subiicias.
units.tr: A third testimony too you distort by mutilating it. For Tertullian does not there settle what he thinks, but argues on both sides how the Father is invisible and the Son visible. Now the absurd objection seemed to you a confession of faith. Yet a little later all ambiguity is removed: the Son is invisible insofar as he is the Word. Learn therefore from now on to weigh each point more carefully, so that by picking out a few words you do not keep substituting one thing for another.

units.la: Quartum testimonium sic nobis suffragatur, ut non aptior quærenda sit probatio. Dicit enim Patrem determinari sua persona. Quod autem in fine addit, Unū esse Patrē, & absque eo non esse alium, quàm insulse torqueas, ex proximo capite patet: ubi seipsum explicans, Filium negat alium esse à Patre Deum, ideóque non violari monarchiam, personæ distinctione. Ubi nunc tuum illud conuitium, à Trinitate debere expungi Patris personam, quia sit Sophistica, quādo[?] essentiam ubique tribus facit communem, tantùm verò personis discernit, quia Pater Filii facit, & Filius vicissim Patrem: denique concludit Patrem Deum esse solum, nempe à cæteris fictitiis, qui alii sunt?
units.tr: The fourth testimony supports us in such a way that no more apt proof could be sought. For it says that the Father is determined by his person. As for what he adds at the end, that the Father is one and that there is no other apart from him, it is plain from the immediately preceding chapter how foolishly you twist it: there, explaining himself, he denies that the Son is another God apart from the Father, and therefore the monarchy is not violated by the distinction of persons. Where, then, is your reproach that the person of the Father must be struck out of the Trinity because it is sophistical, since he makes the essence common to all three and distinguishes them only by persons, because the Father makes the Son and the Son in turn the Father? Finally he concludes that the Father alone is God, namely in contrast to those others who are not real but fictitious?

units.la: Sed apud te parum proficiemus, donec ad perpetuum scriptoris consilium attendas. Contendit enim aduersus Praxeam, quamuis in tres personas distinctus sit unus Deus, non tamen fieri plures Deos, neque discerpi unitatem: & quia secundum Praxeæ commentum Christus non poterat Deus esse, quin esset Pater, ideo tantopere de distinctione laborat. Quod verò & Filium & Spiritum portionem totius vocat, etsi dura est locutio, blasphemiam tamen quam attingis minimè continet: quia nō ad substantiā hoc refertur, sed dispositionē & œconomiā tantùm notat, quæ solis personis conuenit: sicuti clarè sæpius testatur. Inde etiam pendet illud, Quot personæ tibi videntur, peruersissime Praxea, nisi quot sunt voces? Vides ut Patris nomine nō simpliciter essentiā, sed personam velit designari. Sic etiam paulò post, Ut credant Patrem & Filium in suis quenque nominibus & personis. Ubi autem essentiæ fit mentio, Sermonem docet nihil aliud esse quàm Deum. Quare Tertullianum, qui totus noster est, committere nobiscum in certamen volens, non minus tuam impudentiam quàm insciitiam prodis.
units.tr: But we shall make little progress with you until you attend to the author's constant purpose. For he contends against Praxeas that, although one God is distinguished into three persons, there are not thereby made to be several gods, nor is the unity torn apart; and because on Praxeas' fabrication Christ could not be God without being the Father, he labours so hard on the distinction. As for his calling both the Son and the Spirit a portion of the whole, although the expression is harsh, it does not in the least contain the blasphemy you attach to it, because this is not referred to the substance but merely signifies disposition and economy, which belongs only to the persons, as he often testifies clearly. From the same source comes that saying: "How many persons seem to you, most perverse Praxeas, except as many as there are voices?" You see how by the name of Father he wishes not the essence simply but the person to be designated. So too shortly afterwards: "That they may believe the Father and the Son in their own names and persons." But where he mentions the essence, he teaches that the Word is nothing other than God. Wherefore, in wishing to contend with us over Tertullian, who is wholly ours, you reveal no less your impudence than your ignorance.

units.la: Simplicior quidem confessio & docendi forma nos oblectaret: sed quia ad crepandas horribiles blasphemias te impulit Satan, nos officij ratio ad hanc sanae doctrinae defensionem impulit ac coegit. Dominus ambitione & superbia te purget, subigat tuam cotumaciam, prauam curiositatem corrigat: quo te mansuetum & docilem veris monitionibus incipias praebere: alioqui te compescat.
units.tr: A simpler confession and manner of teaching would have pleased us more; but since Satan has driven you to rattle off horrible blasphemies, the duty of our office has driven and compelled us to this defence of sound doctrine. May the Lord cleanse you of ambition and pride, subdue your obstinacy, and correct your depraved curiosity, so that you may begin to show yourself gentle and teachable toward true admonitions; otherwise may he restrain you.

units.la: Hoc responso accepto, etsi in eadem qua coeperat petulantia audacter ad dies aliquot perrexit, sicuti ex eius conuitiis apparet: vbi tamen secum propius expendit, se intemperanter furendo nihil aliud quàm Iudicum animos magis exasperare, repentè exterritus, depòsita priore fiducia ad preces se conuertit, ac poenitentiae simulationem: quemadmodum ex subiecta narratione patet.
units.tr: Having received this answer, although he went on for some days boldly in the same wantonness he had begun with, as is evident from his abuse, yet when he weighed matters more closely with himself, seeing that by raging intemperately he was accomplishing nothing but making the minds of the judges more exasperated, he was suddenly terrified; abandoning his former confidence, he turned to entreaties and to a pretence of repentance, as is clear from the account set out below.

units.la: BREVIS SENTENTIA VALENTINI GENTILIS ANTE ADMISSAM CONFESSIONEM Domini Caluini de Trinitate.
units.tr: A brief statement by Valentinus Gentilis, before the admission of Master Calvin's confession concerning the Trinity.

units.la: Quidem putabam primam personam Patris in vnica Essentia esse Sophisticam, atque ideò hoc sensu excludendam à mysterio Trinitatis. Nam si Pater esset indiuiduum in Essentia simile Verbo, non diceretur verè neque solus Pater, neque ingenitus, neque principium totius Trinitatis. Praeterea eiusmodi sententia Quaternitatem potius, quàm Trinitatem videretur constituere. Quod sic probari potest:
units.tr: I used to think that the first person, the Father, in the one Essence was sophistical, and that in this sense he should be excluded from the mystery of the Trinity. For if the Father were an individual in the Essence, like the Word, he could not truly be called the Father alone, or unbegotten, or the principle of the whole Trinity. Moreover, such an opinion would seem to establish a Quaternity rather than a Trinity. This can be proved as follows:

units.la: Vnica illa Essentia, quum absque consideratione personarum sit ex semetipsa verus Deus: & vnaquaeque trium personarum sit essentialiter Deus. sequitur ergo Quaternitas non Trinitas. Quamobrem existimabam Patrem esse ipsam vnicam Essentiam, Verbum autem splendorem gloriae Dei, & impressam imaginem subsistentiae illius, hac ratione à Patre distinctum, quòd Pater (vt ait Christus) est solus verus Deus & essentialiter, id est informator indiuiduorum: Verbum verò, Filius simul & verus Deus. nequo duo diy tamen: sed vnus Deus. Haec erat summa sententiae meae de vero Patre, veróque Filio. Nam de Spiritu sancto nulla erat quaestio, & tamen confessioni domini Caluini subscripsi. Valentinus Gentilis manu propria.
units.tr: That one Essence, since without consideration of the persons it is of itself the true God, and since each of the three persons is essentially God, it follows that there is a Quaternity and not a Trinity. Therefore I held that the Father is the one Essence itself, and the Word the splendour of God's glory and the impressed image of his subsistence, distinguished from the Father by this: that the Father, as Christ says, is the only true God and essentially so, that is, the informer of individuals, whereas the Word is the Son and also true God. Yet they are not two gods, but one God. This was the sum of my opinion concerning the true Father and the true Son. For there was no question at all about the Holy Spirit, and yet I subscribed to Master Calvin's confession. Valentinus Gentilis, in his own hand.

units.la: Illustrissimi ac verè pÿ domini, Si vos legistis illam meam cõfes-sionem, quam iussu vestro nudiusquartus extemplo exaraui: non dubitò quin ex ea facilè intellexeritis, me satis disertis verbis ostendisse, sententiam D. Caluini Quaternitatem statuere, non Trinitatem. Quum verò nudiustertius ipsius D. Caluini præcipuæ partes essent, se tam execrabili errore expurgare, sciens se malâ causam apud hoc sanctissimum Dei Tribunal minimè posse sustinere (vt vos probè nostis) ne verbum quidem fecit, sed totum tempus terens in conuitiis, & nescio quibus nugis Serueti, artificiosè quidem, sed parum honestè elusit. Equidem bis coepi rem (vt dicitur) acu attingere: sed ille sua mordacitate & conuitiis me semper deterruit. Insuper, (vt vos ipsi audire potuistis) minatus est hoc in caput meum esse vertendum. Quapropter quum satis aperte declararit se esse animo in me nimis infenso, peto à vobis, Illustrissimi domini, ne potentia & volubilitate linguae hominis mea innocentia opprimatur, vt mihi Patronũ & Aduocatum concedatis, qui meam optimam causam, vt par est, tueatur. Nam ingenuè fateor me non posse tuta conscientia Quaternitatem domini Caluini admittere. Exhibeat ille, vt tatum[?] Dei Ministrum decet, veram Trinitatem, & nulla erit inter nos controuersia. Siquidem eo sum natus ingenio, vt veritatem pröptam in frõte[?] geram. Vt enim ipsam Quaternitatem pernego, sic veram Trinitatem & unitatem toto pectore amplector. Praeterea vos oratos etiam atque etiam velim, me, quò possim extra carcerem meam causam tueri, sub idonea cautione liberari. Meam enim innocentiam & integritatem spero adeo cunctis Ecclesiis notam facere, & quasi manibus tractandam præbere, vt ipsi etiam aduersarij fateantur me boni ac pij viri munere functum fuisse. Haec pauca visum est, Illustrissimi domini, à vobis perquàm humiliter postulare, certò sciens, qua estis sanctitate ac pietate præditi, vos quod rectum est executuros, præterea nihil: præsertim quùm me esse peregrinum hominem, imperitum linguae vestrae, ac prorsus ignarum rerum Curialiū probè intelligatis. Sic vnicus ille Deus Israel verus ac naturalis Pater Verbi, cuius causa nunc agitur, huic sanctissimo Tribunali sua virtute perpetuò assistat, vósque omnes, & hanc vrbem vestram in dies magis magisque suis donis augeat, exornétque. Dixi.
units.tr: Most illustrious and truly pious lords, if you have read that confession of mine which I drew up at once on your orders four days ago, I do not doubt that you have readily understood from it that I showed, in quite plain words, that the opinion of Master Calvin establishes a Quaternity and not a Trinity. But when, the day before yesterday, Master Calvin himself had the chief part, to clear himself of so execrable an error, knowing that he could not defend a bad cause before this most holy tribunal of God (as you well know), he did not say a word on the matter, but spent the whole time in insults and in I know not what trifles of Servetus, skilfully yet rather dishonestly evading the issue. Indeed, twice I began to touch the matter (as they say) with a needle, but he always deterred me with his biting tongue and insults. Moreover (as you yourselves could hear) he threatened that this should be turned against my head. Therefore, since he has declared quite openly that he is too hostile to me in spirit, I beg you, most illustrious lords, that my innocence not be overwhelmed by the power and glibness of a man's tongue, and that you grant me a patron and advocate who may defend my very good cause, as is fitting. For I frankly confess that I cannot, with a safe conscience, admit the Quaternity of Master Calvin. Let him set forth, as becomes a minister of God, the true Trinity, and there will be no controversy between us. For I was born with such a disposition that I carry a truth ready to hand. Just as I deny the Quaternity itself, so I embrace the true Trinity and unity with my whole heart. Furthermore, I would ask you again and again, that I may be released from prison under suitable security, so that I may plead my cause outside. For I hope to make my innocence and integrity so known to all the Churches, and to put them, as it were, into people's hands to handle, that even my adversaries will admit that I have discharged the office of a good and pious man. These few things seemed right to request of you, most illustrious lords, most humbly, knowing for certain that, endowed as you are with holiness and piety, you will carry out what is right and nothing else, especially since you well understand that I am a stranger, unskilled in your language and wholly ignorant of courtly affairs. So may that one God of Israel, the true and natural Father of the Word, whose cause is now being pleaded, always assist this most holy tribunal by his power, and may he increase and adorn you all, and this your city, more and more day by day with his gifts. I have spoken.

units.la: Inutilis Christi seruus, Valentinus Gentilis Cosentinus.
units.tr: A useless servant of Christ, Valentinus Gentilis of Cosenza.

units.la: Illustrissimi ac clementissimi domini: Nisi causam meam vobis magis, quàm mihi ipsi notam esse plane intelligerem, pluribus equidem vobiscum agerem. Sed quia rem omnem probè tenetis, paucis me expediam. Principio nostis me iussu vestro confessionem edidisse. Illa autem edita, meas partes esse duxi, quicquid ad eam rem pertineret, sine fuco Ecclesiæ proponere, eaque ratione conscientiam meam omni scrupulo liberare. Quod etsi à me liberius fortasse, quàm oportuit, factum est: gaudeo tamen hoc nomine, quòd amplissimi Consistorii conscientiæ ac judicio me penitus submiserim. Nunc verò quum tot sapientissimi viri, quorum opera Deus manifestè utitur in colligenda Ecclesia sua, luculentissimo scripto meam opinionem uno ore erroneam testentur, visum est potius ipsis vel somnianti-bus, quàm mihi vigilanti credere. Itaque ut pollicitus sum, eorum conscientiæ, ac sententiæ libenter acquiesco, eamque (ut debeo) toto pectore amplector. Quamobrem si quid in ipsa actione mihi imprudenter exciderit, quod ipsos dominos Ministros, ac vos quoque, Illustrissimi domini, offenderit, supplex peto, ut simplicitati meæ ignoscatur. Nunc enim primum ante Tribunal stetr[?]: atque difficile est in rebus novis hominem ita se gerere, ut aliqua in re non labatur. Sed de his hactenus. omnia enim bona de clementia vestra & spero & mihi polliceor. Venio ad dominum Calvinum. Absit ut tantum Doctorem in numero Sophistarum unquam habuerim. Ingenuè fateor, impius nedum iniquus essem, si de tam incomparabili viro, ac de Republica Christiana optimè merito talia sentirem. Soleo equidem Sorbonistas, cæterosque Magistros Papistarum Sophistas appellare. De eius doctrina nihil me tale suspicari, religio est dicere.
units.tr: Most illustrious and most merciful lords: Unless I clearly understood that my cause is better known to you than to myself, I would indeed speak with you at greater length. But since you hold the whole matter well in hand, I shall explain myself in a few words. First, you know that I published the confession at your command. Once it was published, I thought it my part to set before the Church, without pretence, whatever pertained to that matter, and by this means to free my conscience from every scruple. Although this was perhaps done by me more freely than it ought to have been, I rejoice nonetheless on this account, that I have wholly submitted myself to the conscience and judgement of the most distinguished Consistory. But now, since so many most wise men, through whose work God manifestly makes use in gathering his Church, testify with a most lucid writing with one voice that my opinion is erroneous, it seemed better to believe them, even though they were dreaming, rather than myself, who was awake. Therefore, as I promised, I gladly yield to their conscience and judgement, and embrace it (as I ought) with my whole heart. Wherefore, if anything in the very proceedings has slipped from me imprudently, which may have offended the gentlemen ministers, and you too, most illustrious lords, I humbly beg that my simplicity be pardoned. For now I first stand before the tribunal, and it is difficult for a man in new circumstances to conduct himself so as not to stumble in some respect. But enough of these things. For I both hope for and promise myself all good things from your clemency. I come to Master Calvin. Far be it from me that I should ever have counted so great a teacher among the sophists. Frankly I confess that I would be impious, and not merely unjust, if I thought such things of so incomparable a man, who has deserved so well of the Christian commonwealth. I am accustomed, to be sure, to call the Sorbonists and the other masters of the Papists sophists. That I should suspect any such thing of his doctrine is a sin even to say.

units.la: Quare vos etiam atque etiam oratos velim, ne mihi hæc nota inuratur, ut illa mea verba quasi in sanctissimam Ecclesiam vestram dicta detorqueantur. Te-stis est mihi Dominus, me nunquam tale quicquam cogitasse: quin potius hanc Genevensem Ecclesiam cæteris omnibus puriorem ac mundiorem & habui & semper prædicavi. Facessant igitur vanæ suspiciones, & nuda regnet simplicitas. Si quid tamen extat in meis scriptis, quod dominum Calvinum urgeret: id non lædendi sui causa à me dictum esse, mihi velim credatis, sed defendendi mei. Quapropter si quid à me minus reverenter in ipsum dictum est, non modò ab eo veniam peto, verùm etiam (quæ viri est charitas & pietas) oro, ut me totum amplectatur & foveat, inque eorum numero habeat, qui sui nominis sunt perquam studiosi. Quod si in tot meis miseriis mihi contigerit, mune-re videbor donatus immortali. Equidem quod ad me attinet, dabo operam ut tum dictis vestris exequendis, tum illius pietate colenda me omnes fidelem ac constantem prædicent. Si Deus, &c.
units.tr: Therefore I beg you again and again that this mark may not be branded upon me, that those words of mine be twisted as though spoken against your most holy Church. The Lord is my witness that I never thought any such thing; rather, I both held and always proclaimed this Genevan Church to be purer and cleaner than all others. Let idle suspicions therefore depart, and let plain sincerity reign. If there is anything in my writings which might trouble Master Calvin, I would have you believe that it was said by me not to injure him, but to defend myself. Wherefore, if anything was said by me somewhat less reverently against him, I not only ask his pardon, but also (as is the charity and piety of a good man) beg that he embrace and cherish me entirely, and count me among those who are most zealous of his name. If in so many of my miseries this should fall to me, I shall seem to have been given an immortal gift. As for me, I shall take care that, both in carrying out your commands and in cultivating his piety, everyone may proclaim me faithful and steadfast. If God wills, etc.

units.la: Magnifici domini, Certum est quo tempore ex vestro mandato meam illam confessionem vobis obtuli, me tanto zelo fuisse per-citum, ut fuerim paratus quoduis supplicium subire, eius defendendæ causa: verum simulatque perlegi & attentè expendi so-lidam illam & veris rationibus suffultam Consistorii responsionem ad omnes meas obiectiones, visum est Patri misericordiarum, qui me passus erat ad tem-pus evagari, ita me afficere, ut errorem meum cognoscerem, qui quidem tribus præcipuè fundamentis salsissimis nitebatur. Primùm igitur in eo peccavi, quòd quum affirmarem unicum illum Deum Israelis esse Patrem Jesu Christi, non animadverti Filii divinitatem excludi per illas antitheses Unius Dei Patris, & Christi. Secundò, quum Essentiam considerarem extra personas, inde eliciebam Quaternitatem: quod temerè feci, quoniam Essentia non est alibi quàm in ipsis tribus Personis consideranda: quarum unaquæque est integrè tota illa Essentia. Tertium peccatum fuit, quòd affirmarem personam Patris esse Sophisticam: quod ipsum quoque salsissimum est, ut est mihi perspicuè demonstratum. In summa, putribus istis ruinis superstructæ sunt multæ falsæ consequutiones, quas ego abominor & detestor, profiteórque me nòn aliter hæc intelligere, quàm Consistorium in illo suo scripto mihi explanavit. Itaque, Magnifici domini, putavi vos mihi esse præcados [?] unà cum Ministris, totáque adeo Ecclesia, ut graue & enorme istud facinus mihi condonetis: sicuti non dubito quin Deus, ille cordium scrutator, id mihi condonarit, ut qui effecerit ut meũ errorem summo cum animi dolore agnoscerem. Etsi enim dum recordor quantum offendiculum to-ti Ecclesiæ obiecerim, præsertim quum eximio Dei ministro & summo Theo-logo Joh. Caluino tam incōsideratè respondi, idem ille Deus, adeo graviter con-scientiam meam vulnerat, ut non facilè inveniat in quo acquiescat: confido tamen fore ut mea ista perturbatio in meipso gignat veræ pœnitentiæ fructus, adeo ut futura mea vita omnem istius offendiculi labem in posterum abster-gat. Quoniam autem mihi constat tantam esse horum sanctorum Ministrorum clementiam ac bonitatem, ut miseram hanc pecudem, quæ quum antea aberrarit, nunc in viam redit, non modò intra Ecclesiæ gremium & omnium gregem sint recepturi, sed etiā exultaturi de mea conversione. nihil aliud habeo quod dicam, praeter hoc vnum, Magnifici domini, quod à vobis magnopere peto, nempe vt quemadmodum summam operam adhibuistis in curando animi mei morbo, ita etiam nunc habeatis eius ægrotationis & inopiæ rationem, in qua nunc sum constitutus, vt qui abhinc sesquimensem in vestro carcere retinear paupertate simul & morbo pressus: vt illud Christi merito positis vsurpare, Nos totum hominem seruauimus. Hoc certè factu praeterquam quod conuenit principibus verè Christianis, pro singulari beneficio ducam, Si Deus, &c.
units.tr: Magnificent lords, it is certain that at the time when I presented that confession of mine to you by your command, I was so possessed with zeal that I was ready to undergo any punishment in defence of it. But as soon as I had read through and carefully weighed the solid response of the Consistory, supported by true arguments, to all my objections, it seemed good to the Father of mercies, who had allowed me to wander for a time, so to affect me that I recognised my error, which indeed rested upon three most unsound foundations. First, then, I sinned in this, that when I affirmed that the one God of Israel is the Father of Jesus Christ, I did not notice that the divinity of the Son was excluded by those antitheses of the one God the Father and Christ. Second, when I considered the Essence apart from the persons, I drew from this a Quaternity, which I did rashly, since the Essence is to be considered nowhere else than in the three persons themselves, each of whom is wholly that Essence entire. The third sin was that I affirmed the person of the Father to be sophistical, which also is most unsound, as has been clearly demonstrated to me. In sum, many false consequences have been built upon these rotten ruins, which I abominate and detest, and I profess that I understand these things in no other way than the Consistory explained to me in its writing. Therefore, Magnificent lords, I thought that you, together with the ministers and indeed the whole Church, would pardon me this grave and monstrous crime, just as I do not doubt that God, that searcher of hearts, has pardoned it, since he has brought it about that I acknowledge my error with the deepest grief of mind. For although, whenever I recall how great a stumbling block I have placed before the whole Church, especially in answering so thoughtlessly the distinguished minister of God and most eminent theologian John Calvin, that same God so grievously wounds my conscience that it does not easily find rest in anything, I nevertheless trust that this disturbance of mine will bring forth in me the fruits of true repentance, so that my future life will wipe away every stain of that stumbling block. Since, moreover, I am assured that these holy ministers are so merciful and good that they will not only receive into the bosom of the Church and the flock of all this wretched sheep, which, having formerly gone astray, now returns to the way, but will even rejoice at my conversion, I have nothing else to say, except this one thing, Magnificent lords, which I earnestly ask of you: that just as you applied the greatest care in curing the sickness of my mind, so now too you may take account of the illness and want in which I am now placed, since for a month and a half I have been kept in your prison, weighed down at once by poverty and sickness; so that I may rightly use those words of Christ, We have saved the whole man. Indeed, to do this would befit truly Christian princes, and I shall count it a singular kindness. If God wills, etc.

units.la: Humillimus vester seruus, Valentinus Gentilis.
units.tr: Your most humble servant, Valentinus Gentilis.

units.la: ABIVRATIO VALENTINI GENTILIS COSENTINI IPSIVS MANV SPONTE SCRIPTA, & ad Senatum Geneuensem missa.
units.tr: Abjuration of Valentino Gentile of Cosenza, written of his own accord by his own hand, and sent to the Senate of Geneva.

units.la: C[?]onfiteor Patrem, Filium, & Spiritum sanctum, esse vnum Deum, id est, tres personas distinctas in vna essentia. Pater non est Filius, nec Filius est Spiritus sanctus, sed vnaquaeque illarum personarum est integra illa Essentia. Item, Filius & Spiritus sanctus, quantum ad diuinam naturam, sunt vnus Deus cum Patre, cui sunt coaequales & coaeterni. Hoc illud est quod ego sentio, & corde simul ac ore profiteor, & confido fore per Dei gratiam vt in hac confessione viuam & moriar. Omnes autem haereses huic sanctissimæ veritati contrarias damno & detestor, & quidem nominatim blasphemias illas quas ipse mea manu descripsi: quibus inter cæteros errores Quaternitatem asserebam, & Christum statuebam vnius Israelitici Dei Filium, ita vt æterna sua diuinitate spoliaretur. Denique, quoniam ex falsis istis fundamentis multæ salsissimæ consequutiones oriuntur, omnes illas damno & execror, & palàm profiteor me in omnibus & per omnia assentiri sanctæ huius Ecclesiæ doctrinæ, & quidem in primis ac diserte in hoc sanctissimæ Trinitatis articulo: in quo agnosco me tam grauiter tantaque cum blasphemia peccasse, vt libenter velim iam olim interiisse, ne tantum scelus admitterem. Hoc illud est quod sentio in corde meo: & infinitam Dei misericordiam precor, vt in posterum me afficiat tanto istarum rerum sensu, vt aliqua ex parte possint verae meae pœnitentiæ fructus ab omnibus cognosci. 29 Augusti, M. D. LVIII.
units.tr: I confess the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit to be one God, that is, three distinct persons in one essence. The Father is not the Son, nor is the Son the Holy Spirit, but each of those persons is that whole essence. Likewise, the Son and the Holy Spirit, as to the divine nature, are one God with the Father, to whom they are coequal and coeternal. This is what I think, and what I profess with heart and mouth alike, and I trust that by the grace of God I shall live and die in this confession. I condemn and detest all heresies contrary to this most holy truth, and in particular those blasphemies which I wrote out with my own hand, in which, among other errors, I asserted a quaternity and maintained that Christ was the Son of the one God of Israel, so that he was stripped of his eternal divinity. Finally, since many most false consequences arise from those false foundations, I condemn and curse all of them, and I openly profess that I agree in all things and throughout with the doctrine of this holy Church, and especially and expressly in this article of the most holy Trinity. In this I acknowledge that I have sinned so gravely and with such blasphemy that I would gladly have perished long ago rather than commit so great a crime. This is what I feel in my heart, and I pray for the infinite mercy of God that in future he may so affect me with a sense of these things that the fruits of my true repentance may be recognised by all in some measure. 29 August 1558.

units.la: Ioh. Valentinus Gentilis, manu propria.
units.tr: John Valentine Gentile, with his own hand.

units.la: SIC tum ille. Etsi autem minimè nos latebat, simul ac elapsus esset, fore iterum sui similem, nec quicquam synceri ab homine sal-lacissimo lacissimo expectandum esse: iudicum tamen clementiae non inter-cessimus, nobisque quiescentibus lata sententia est, recitata prius ex more, actionis summa. Hoc totū crasso rudique stylo interpretari maluimus, quàm vel tantillum à verbis discedere.
units.tr: So he spoke. Although it was by no means hidden from us that, as soon as he was set free, he would be again like himself, and that nothing sincere was to be expected from a most deceitful man, nevertheless we did not intervene on behalf of the clemency of the judges, and, while we kept silent, sentence was pronounced, after the summary of the proceedings had first been read aloud according to custom. We preferred to render all this in a rough and unpolished style rather than depart from the words even slightly.

units.la: PROCESSVS CRIMINALIS FORMATVS CORAM MAGNIFICIS DOMINIS NOSTRIS Syndicis, instante Iurisprœfecto, aduersus Valentinum filium Francisci Gentilis Neapolitanum.
units.tr: PROCESS CRIMINAL, DRAWN UP BEFORE OUR MAGNIFICENT LORDS THE SYNDICS, AT THE INSTANCE OF THE PRAEFECT OF JUSTICE, AGAINST VALENTINUS GENTILIS, SON OF FRANCIS, OF NAPLES.

units.la: Adductus in carcerem, confessus est se cum aliis complicibus vulgasse opiniones de sancta Trinitate prorsus falsas & erroneas. Atque hac causa Seniores Ecclesiae Italicae coactos fuisse puram confessionem edere, quam se amplecti testatus est, & observaturū promisit, ac iurauit sub poena periurii. Quod subscripsit propria manu.
units.tr: Brought into prison, he confessed that he had, together with other accomplices, spread opinions about the Holy Trinity that were utterly false and erroneous. For this reason the elders of the Italian Church had been compelled to set out a pure confession, which he testified that he embraced and promised to observe, and he swore to this under penalty of perjury. This he signed with his own hand.

units.la: Sponte tamen confessus est, ex quo ita se obligauerat, reuersum fuisse ad pristinos errores, & eos disseminasse, ut quoscunque posset, alliceret: idque eo praetextu, quòd Sophisticum commentum esset, attribuere Patri propriam personam in essentia Deitatis.
units.tr: Yet he freely confessed that, after he had thus bound himself, he had returned to his former errors and spread them abroad, so that he might win over as many as he could, and this under the pretext that it was a sophistical invention to ascribe a proper personhood to the Father within the essence of the Godhead.

units.la: Praeterea quum in carcere admonitus fuerit tam a Dominis nostris, quàm a Verbi ministris, aliisque doctis hominibus, atque etiam abunde conuiciis Scripturae testimoniis: noluit tamen per aliquod tempus culpam agnoscere. imo perstitit tā sermone quàm scriptis obstinatè & impudenter impietatem suam afferere, conuitia etiam & blasphemias addendo, nos fingere quaternitatem, duos Patres, & deum Turcarum. Ita arroganter ausus est tam huic Ecclesiae, quàm omnibus aliis piis & orthodoxis maledicere, turbandae Ecclesiae, & excitandi schismatis consilio.
