units.tr: Moreover, although while in prison he was admonished both by our Lords and by ministers of the Word and other learned men, and indeed was abundantly convicted by the testimonies of Scripture, he nevertheless for some time refused to acknowledge his fault. Rather, he persisted, both in speech and in writing, obstinately and shamelessly in asserting his impiety, adding also reproaches and blasphemies, claiming that we invent a quaternity, two Fathers, and the God of the Turks. So arrogantly did he dare to revile this Church no less than all other pious and orthodox churches, with the aim of disturbing the Church and stirring up schism.

units.la: Tandem sponte confessus est se in his rebus graviter peccasse, & Ecclesiam haeretica impietate offendisse, ac se poenitentia tangi, seque fateri haereticum: nec sermone modò, sed etiam scripto abiurauit suos errores, & agnouit in hac Ecclesia puram & orthodoxam fidem doceri.
units.tr: At length he freely confessed that he had sinned grievously in these matters, and had offended the Church by heretical impiety, and that he was moved to repentance, and acknowledged himself a heretic; and not only by speech but also in writing he abjured his errors, and admitted that in this Church the pure and orthodox faith is taught.

units.la: SENTENTIA.
units.tr: SENTENCE.

units.la: Os Syndici, iudices causarum criminalium in hac vrbe, visoprocessu criminali coram nobis formato, ad instantiam & prosecutionem Iurisprœfecti, contra te Valentinum Gentilem, ex quo & voluntariis tuis confessionibus inter manus nostras saepius iteratis,certò constat & liquet te aggressum esse & conatum spargere haeretica & falsam doctrinà & blasphemiis plenam contra sacrum mysterium Trinitatis: idque contra datam fidem & iusiurandum, tam ubi pollicitus es te fore nobis obsequentem, quàm ubi expresse abiurasti tuâ haeresin. Nihilominus summa impudentia & arrogatia conatus es coram nobis impugnare rectâ fidem pro tua temeritate & impietate. Atque hoc modo nõ solum periurio te implicasti, sed te declarasti apertum hostem & aduersarium Dei & Ecclesiæ: quod crimen detestabile, & graui pœna corporali dignũ pronũtiamus. His iustis causis & aliis adductis, sedentes pro Tribunali, loco maiorũ nostrorũ, ac secundũ antiquum morem, participato cum ciuibus nostris consilio, post inuocatum Dei nomen, ut der nobis rectè iudicare, Deum & sacras Scripturas præ oculis habentes, cum præfatione consueta, In nomine Patris, & Filii, & Spiritus sancti, Amen.
units.tr: We, the Syndics, judges of criminal causes in this city, having seen the criminal process drawn up before us, at the instance and prosecution of the Praefect of Justice, against you, Valentinus Gentilis, from which, and from your voluntary confessions repeatedly made before our hands, it is clearly and manifestly established that you have undertaken and attempted to spread heretical and false doctrine, full of blasphemies, against the sacred mystery of the Trinity; and this against the faith you pledged and your oath, both when you promised that you would be obedient to us and when you expressly abjured your heresy. Nevertheless, with the greatest impudence and arrogance you have attempted to assail before us the right faith, out of your recklessness and impiety. And in this way you have not only involved yourself in perjury, but have declared yourself an open enemy and adversary of God and the Church; which detestable crime we pronounce worthy of severe corporal punishment. For these just causes and others adduced, sitting on the tribunal in place of our ancestors, and according to the ancient custom, with the counsel of our fellow citizens taken, after invoking the name of God, that he might grant us to judge rightly, keeping God and the holy Scriptures before our eyes, with the customary preface, In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, Amen.

units.la: Quanuis malitia & prauitas qua usus es, merita sit ut exterminetis[?] è numero hominũ tanquam seductor, haereticus & schismaticus: tamen habita ratione pœnitentiæ & conuersionis tuæ, de qua apud nos protestatus es, simul ad misericordiâ magis quàm ad rigorem propensi, hac nostra definitiva sententia, quam ex scripto recitamus & edimus, te Valentinũ Gentilem adiudicamus huic pœnæ, ut exutus usque ad camisiam, pedibus nudis, & capite discooperto, facem accensam manu tenens, genibus in terram flexis, veniam à nobis & iustitia depreceris, fatendo te impie & scelerate sparsisse falsam & haereticam doctrinà, & scripta tua in eius defensionem detesteris, eaque propriis manibus tuis in ignem hic accensum coiicias, donec in cineres redigantur, tanquam perniciosis mendaciis referta. Et quo amplior sit reparatio, ut ad clangorem tubæ ducaris per omnia urbis compita in hoc habitu, cum prohibitione egrediendi ex urbe. Sit igitur hæc pœna in exemplum aliis qui tale crimen imitari vellent.
units.tr: Although the malice and perversity you have shown deserve that you be cast out from the number of men as a seducer, heretic and schismatic, nevertheless, having regard to the repentance and conversion of yours which you have professed before us, and being inclined to mercy rather than to rigour, by this our definitive sentence, which we read out and publish from a written text, we adjudge you, Valentinus Gentilis, to this punishment: that stripped to your shirt, with bare feet and bare head, holding a lighted torch in your hand, on bended knees you beg pardon from us and from justice, confessing that you have impiously and wickedly spread false and heretical doctrine, and that you detest your writings in its defence; and that you cast those writings with your own hands into the fire lit here, until they are reduced to ashes, as being full of pernicious lies. And so that the reparation may be the fuller, you are to be led through all the crossroads of the city to the sound of the trumpet, in this garb, with a prohibition on leaving the city. Let this punishment therefore serve as an example to others who might wish to imitate such a crime.

units.la: Hæc igitur ita ut iudicatum erat, executioni sunt mandata, 2. Septembris, 1558. & ille qui exemplaria suorum scriptorum, sicuti iussus erat, nõ sine rara pœnitetiæ simulatione & fallaci detestatione manu sua palàm cõbussit: postea nudus per urbẽ fuit circudu-ctus, ut omnes haberet tum anteacti sceleris, tum etiam consequutæ, ut omnes quidem arbitrabantur, pœnitentiæ testes. Aliquot verò post diebus idem hunc libellum Senatui obtulit.
units.tr: These things were therefore carried out just as judgement had been given, on 2 September 1558; and he, who had been ordered to burn his own writings by hand, did so openly, not without a rare simulation of repentance and a deceitful detestation; afterwards he was led naked through the city, so that all might have witnesses both of his past crime and of his subsequent repentance, as everyone indeed supposed. A few days later, however, the same man offered this little book to the Senate.

units.la: Magnifici domini, pauper ac miserabilis Valentinus, humilis vester seruus, tanto iam tempore in vestris carceribus versatus, supplex vestrae magnificentiae significat, quum ipse ex vestro Senatusconsulto, & quidem addita vestrae indignationis poena, sub interdicto vrbe exire, nisi impetrata a vobis venia, se paratum vobis parere, & omnibus vestris mandatis alacriter obsequi, atque in vrbe vestra comorari quamdiu vestrae Magnificentiae visum fuerit. Caeterum quod a me petiit Commentariensis vt vadem nanciscerer, praestari a me nulla ratione potest, praesertim quum hic habitè prorsus inops, extraneus, solus, absque vllis conterraneis, cognatis, vel aliis quibusuis qui vice mea comiserentur. Itaque supplex peto vt Magnificentia vestra habeat huius miseriae & inopiae meae rationem, quum tantos sumptus ferre non possim quatis [?] hic est opus: sed quod vnis persoluam, sicut hactenus feci aliqua ex parte, cogar ab aliis emendicare. Denique, cupio vestrae Magnificentiae totique adeo Ecclesiae satisfacere, & eius rei praestandae rationem mihi preberi quotidie a Domino peto. Sed vt satis noftis, nemo ad id tenetur quod praestare nullo modo possit. Si hoc mihi concesseritis, feceritis quod est iuri cosentaneum, & singulari beneficio me vobis obstrictum putabo. 5. Septembris 1558. Valentinus Gentilis, vester seruus.
units.tr: Magnificent lords, Valentinus, poor and wretched, your humble servant, who has now for so long a time dwelt in your prisons, supplicantly makes known to your Magnificence that, since by your decree of the Senate, with the added penalty of your displeasure, he is forbidden to leave the city unless he has obtained pardon from you, he is ready to obey you and to comply cheerfully with all your commands, and to stay in your city for as long as it shall seem good to your Magnificence. Moreover, as to what the Commissary asked of me, that I find a surety, this can by no means be done by me, especially since I am here utterly destitute, a stranger, alone, without any fellow countrymen, kinsmen, or any others who might stand surety in my place. Therefore I humbly ask that your Magnificence take account of this my wretchedness and poverty, since I cannot bear such great expenses as are needed here, but what I pay out, as I have done hitherto in some measure, I shall be forced to beg from others. Finally, I desire to satisfy your Magnificence and the whole Church, and each day I ask the Lord to furnish me with the means of doing so. But as you well know, no one is bound to do what he can in no way accomplish. If you grant me this, you will have done what is consonant with justice, and I shall consider myself bound to you by a singular benefit. 5 September 1558. Valentinus Gentilis, your servant.

units.la: Hac accepta supplicatione, placuit clementissimo Senatui ne resipiscens Valentinus teneretur vadem praestare. Ipse vero praesens cum iureiurando promisit ex Senatusconsulti formula, se dominorum iniussu vrbe non exiturum: quo impetrato, quum nemo ei molestiam faceret, pro solita sua perfidia clam aufugit ad hominem sui similem, Matthaeum Gribaldum, turbulenti prauíque ingenii, & fatuis speculationibus deditum: qui domo sua profugus, in quoddam latibulum se abdiderat, vbi petulantius quam vnquam bacchari coepit, sed apud capras & boues, quia locus fere desertus erat. Inde quomodo a D.Cayeli praefecto in carcerem coniectus, simulata rursum probitate euaserit, & mox Lugdunum se proripiens, blasphemum illum aduersus Athanasii symbolum libellum ediderit: postea quomodo ibidem captus, odio in Caluinum fuerit dimissus, caeteraque eiusmodi, alius dabitur narrandi locus.
units.tr: This supplication having been received, it pleased the most merciful Senate that Valentinus, now repentant, should not be obliged to give surety. He himself, present, promised with an oath, in the form of the Senate's decree, that he would not leave the city without the consent of the lords; and this having been obtained, since no one gave him any trouble, he, true to his customary faithlessness, secretly fled to a man like himself, Matthaeus Gribaldus, a man of turbulent and perverse temper, given to foolish speculations; who, having fled from his own home, had hidden himself in a certain hiding-place, where he began to rage more wantonly than ever, but among goats and oxen, since the place was almost deserted. Thence, how he was thrown into prison by the praefect of D. Cayelus, and by feigned honesty again escaped, and how, hurrying soon afterwards to Lyon, he published that blasphemous little book against the Athanasian creed; afterwards how, being seized there and dismissed out of hatred for Calvin, and other things of this kind, shall be told in another place.

units.la: S[?]Ut verbis hominibus perinde est, modò dulci nouitatis illecebra curiosos inescando, acumen, quod sæpe nullum est, fallaci spe-cie ostentent: itaque quo magis prodigiosa commenta illis in mentem venerint, eo cupidius arripiant, & audacius insultent, quàm ampliorem laudis materiam nacti. Porro tàta plerosque titillat vagarum speculationum cupido, tantáque leuitas circumagit, ut facile sit impostoribus, quanuis nec ingenio, nec doctrina, nec dexteritate polleant, tales sibi discipulos momento acquirere. Ita Valentinus Gentilis, homo nihili, fæcem ex deliriis Serueti haustam propinans, insipidis palatis persuasit suauem esse potû. Quàm absurdum sit quod sibi fabricauit dogma, sanis hominibus ex breui relatu per-spicuum fiet. Falli nos dicit, quòd in una Dei essentia tres personas statuimus. Ita enim quaternitatem fingi, acsi Personæ nomen aliquid ab essentia abstra-ctum notaret. Ipse verò nimis crasse hallucinatur, dum tres in Deo proprietates non distinguit, quæ in ipsa essentia resideant, non autem ab ea separetur. Prin-cipium illud Scripturæ tenemus, Unicum esse Deum. Jam dum eadem Scriptu-ra in medium nobis profert Patrem, Filium, & Spiritum sanctum, quid aliud restat, quàm in una simplicíque Deitate tres agnoscere personas, quæ tamen non efficiant plures deos, nec essentiæ unitatem lacerent, aut dissipent? Ubi au-tem quaternitas reperietur, si unus Deus tres in se proprietates contineat? Nunc quàm scitè nostram sententiam corrigat, videre operæpretium est. Comminiscitur essentiam Dei in solo Patre: itaque illum prædicat solum esse verum Deum. Filio deinde concedit Dei nomen, sed quasi precarium: quia scilicet essentiatus sit à Patre. Ergo personam Patris non aliud esse affir-mat, quàm essentiam. Filii vero personam, deificationem esse blaterat. Ubi ad Spiritum sanctum venitur, omnia permiscet: quia iam antea Filium eundem cum Spiritu asseruit. Atqui si proprie in Patrem competit essentia, sicuti quod uni personæ peculiare est cum altera non communicatur, Filius certè Deus non erit. Quid ergo fiet tot Scripturæ locis, quibus docemur Christum esse il-lum Jehouam, qui per Mosen dixit, Ego sum qui sum? Vidit Jesaias Jehouam Deum exercituum sedentem in solio: Johannes interpretatur visam à Pro-pheta fuisse gloriam Christi. Plena est eiusmodi testimoniis Scriptura, quibus nouum hoc portentum essentiationis plus quàm liquido refellitur. In principio erat Sermo, inquit Iohānes. Quodnam intelligit principium? Haud dubiè æternitatis: quia non de mundi creatione verba facit, sed qualis in se semper fuerit Deus, explicat. Sermo itaque semper fuit Deus. Unde sequitur non ei fuisse datum ut esset. Similiter quum pronuntiat Christus ipse, Antequam fieret Abraham, ego sum: sibi profecto essentiam absque principio vendicat. Si Valentini placito standum esset, perperam loquutus esset Christus: quia ut membra inter se quadrarent, sic loqui debuit, Antequam Abraham fieret, ego sum essentiatus. Logè autem aliud est, Perpetuum esse, quam Essentiatio. Adde, quod tempus verbi, æternum statum designat. Si dixisset præterito tempore, Fui, cauillari non destitisset Gentilis. Loquutio autem quam usurpat, omnes tergiversandi ansas præcidit. Iam quid est essentiare, nisi creare? Actus enim essentiandi necessario id secum trahit, ut qui ante non erat, inceperit esse. Unde sequitur, Christum non alio iure Deum censeri, nisi quod dono accepit quod non habebat. Nec verò disputatione opus est in re clara: quia iam ostendimus, nisi Filius sit Pater, cum divina essentia spoliari a Valentino. Rudius loquar, ut apertius quod volo exprimam. Persona Patris est Valent. essentia. Atqui persona Patris non convenit Filio, nec in eum transferri potest. Ergo nulla in eo est deitatis essentia, sed tantum creata Diuinitas, quæ ab hoc nebulone vocatur essentiatio: acsi per apotheosin Christus in hunc honoris gradum receptus foret. Et sanè, quum Deus generaliter essentiam inspiret omnibus creaturis, longè excellentius est deificari quàm essentiari. Præclarè verò & liberaliter agit Valentinus cum Christo, dum privilegio eum dignatur, ut suum Esse dono acceperit. Nec verò priuatam causam agimus, acsi nos seorsum aggressus esset, quando totam vetustatem nobiscum simul oppugnat. Anni iam elapsi sunt mille & trecenti, ex quo in synodo Nicæna damnatus fuit Arius. Huius synodi authoritatem verbo se amplecti simulans, Athanasium, qui præfuit, quibuscunque potest conuitiis spurcissimè flagellat. Sophisticam vocat eius fidem, quæ quartū quendam nouum deum inducat: falsitatis passim eum damnare non dubitat: Sabellio coniungit: exprobrat ei triperfonatum Deum: infamat tanquam præstigiatorem: subinde eum stultitiæ & incogitantiæ insimulat: inuehitur in eius ineptias: denique onerat crimine atrocissimo sacrilegij, quod soluat Christum. Tanta verò arrogantia & fastu crepat suos latratus, ut dicas è cælo tonare. Scio equidem non esse ipsum authorem, sed unum aliquem ex Epicureorum caterua repertum esse, qui ad maledicendum esset aliquantum disertus. Nisi forte credibile est eum, qui nomen Christi scribere non potest, Græcas voculas [?]aspergere ad fucandum sermonem. Sed quoniam multi hodie ex turbis ac dissd[?] is, veraeque doctrinae labefactatione delicias sibi faciunt, nihil mirum si Lugduni garrulus quispiam ex antro viruletiam suam euomuerit. Quinetiam exortus est poeta, qui Valentini theologiam suis carminibus ornaret. Inter alia non dubitat praeclarum illud axioma obtrudere, Numero Deus impare gaudet. Quid vero, si tibi vicissim obiiciam nugator, Ter tria multiplica, quam multos deos scaturire necesse erit? Nec me latet vos deorum myriadas audacter fateri. Sed quosnam putas tuo tinnitu sic fascinatum iri, ut poritetis[?] tuis capiantur, nisi tui forte similes? Atque ut nulla illis religio est licentiose mentiri, inscribitur Valentini Confessio ad Praefectum Gaiensem, coram quo seruiliter abiurauit quicquid tradiderat: nec aliter elapsus est, quam aperta omnium quae nunc tam superbe obtrudit, abnegatione. Porrò ne quis scrupulus haereat, petulantissimi canis petulantiam paucis detegam. Arium & Sabellium plenis buccis damnans, ab Ecclesia pridem damnatos esse adiungit. Quid, phrenetice? Quum Ecclesiae nomen Athanasio eiusque collegis tribuas, unde mox, nisi ex ore impurissimo, tanta eos insectandi erupit audacia? Quum tibi instar oraculi sit Nicaena confessio, cuius frontis est, eum a quo profecta est, tam contumeliose proscindere? Certè ut es omnis liberalis doctrinae ignarus, nunquam didicisti tam Nicaenae si rem spectes, quam Alexandrinae synodo praefuisse Athanasium, atque eius decreto damnatos fuisse haereticos, quorum erroribus socius & suffragatorem te adiungis. Quid hac impudentia foedius? Atque hac una furendi causa, quod Athanasius Filium facit αὐτόθεον. Unde perspicuum fit hoc esse causae statum, quod contendit Valentinus Christum aliunde esse Deum, qui ab alio mutuatus sit id quod est. Valde enim logodaedalus, qui eius personam sumpsit, delectant istae voces, Unum esse Deum Patrem, qui & sit αὐτόθεος, & solus αὐτουσίαν[?] in se habeat: quod si recipitur, cocident quaecunque Scripturae testimonia in hanc rem citatur ab Apostolis. Clamat Getulus, solius esse hoc Patris elogium, nec Christo commune, Ego sum Deus, & praeter me non est alius. Paulus autem, Sistemur omnes ad tribunal Christi: quia scriptum est, Viuo ego, dicit Dominus, mihi flectetur omne genu. Videmus ut ad Christi personam accommodet quicquid apud Iesaiam gloriae & imperij sibi vedicat[?] Deus. Quid magis proprium est Deo, quam viuere? aut quid aliud est αὐτουσία? Hac gloriam Paulus Christo cum Patre communem facit. Dicitur in Psalmo, Caeli peribunt: tu autem idem es semper Deus. Hoc Christo Valentinus pugnaciter eripit: Apostolus autem de eo dictum esse interpretatur. Quid plures locos cogerere attinet, quorum passim copia occurrit? Sed verba Cocilij Nicaeni sonant, Deum esse de Deo. Dura loquutio, fateor, sed ad cuius tolledam[?] ambiguitatem nemo potest esse magis idoneus interpres, quàm Athanasius, qui eam dictauit. Et certè nō aliud fuit Patrum consilium, nisi manere originē quam ducit à Patre Filius, persona respectu, nec obstare quominus eadē sit vtriusque essentia & deitas: atque ita, quoad essentiam, Sermonem esse Deum absque principio: in persona autem Filij habere principiū à Patre. Desinat ergo latrare Valentinus, Scripturam nō nisi vni Patri essentialem deitatē tribuere. Nam quoties vel apud Moysem, vel apud Prophetas loquitur Deus, non cōparat se Filio, acsi huc ernando, ipsum minueremus, sed idolis se opponit: quae nisi in nihilum redigantur, nō obtinet ipse in solidum quod suum est. Longius progrediar. Si Valentino creditur, epitheton Creatoris in solum Patrem copetit. Nam inter alia quae Deus pronuntiat apud Iesaiam sibi propria esse, subinde repetitur, Ego sum cuius manus fundauit terram, & expandit caelos. Solus ergo Pater, Filij & Spiritus essentiator, censebitur opifex caeli & terrae. Interea Christum esse Deum, verbo non negat. Nunc attendamus ad verba Ieremiae, Dij qui non fecerunt caelum & terram, pereant è mundo. An Filio Dei maledixit Propheta? Atqui dira imprecatio interitus ad eum pertinet, nisi Creator sit. Hoc uno verbo discutiuntur omnes Valentini nebulae de vnius Patris essentia. Cur ergo Creator dicitur Pater, & hoc titulo seorsum ornatur? Nempe ratione ordinis, dum respicitur ad personas. Vnde etiam aperte conuincitur erroris Valentinus, qui non putat saluam Patri fore suā deitatem, si Christus eiusdem essentiae sit particeps. Nam certè vno consensu fatemur Christum impropriè vocari Creatorem caeli & terrae, quoad personae distinctionem. Neque enim dubium est quin Scriptura Patri nomen Creatoris vendicans, personas distinguat. Si verè Creator est Christus, neque id personae respectu: sequitur necessariò referri hoc ad essentiam, qua eum Valentinus spoliat. Et audet obscoenus canis, Arij & Mahometis nos facere socios, quia Christum essentialiter Deum credimus. Deridet etiam argumentum quod non refellit: Vnus est Deus, Filius est Deus, & Spiritus sanctus Deus sicut Pater: ergo Pater, Filius, & Spiritus, sunt vnus Deus. Notandum erat vitium in syllogismo. Nullum deprehendit: vult tamen vitiosum esse. En quàm imperiosi sint paedagogi in Italia! Sed contrarium syllogismum opponit: Vnus est Deus absque vllo principio, & vniuersitatis author: Solus Pater originem nescit, & ab eo sunt omnia: Ergo solus Pater, vnus est ille Deus. Quasi futilitas assumptionis longa refutatione indigeat. Ludit in voce Originis: cuius dū experiet facit Patrem, libenter assentiar: quia & Deus est qui principiū nescit, quoad essentiam, & origo est ac principiū Filij, quoad ordinem personae. Filiu itaque concedimus originem habere à Patre, quatenus Filius est: originem vero non temporis, neque essentiæ, quorum vtrunque absurdissimum est, sed ordinis duntaxat. Sic omnia dicuntur esse à Patre, quatenus fert personalis relatio. Quis inde, nisi ter & quater vesanus, colliget Patrem solum esse Deum? Præcipuum vero telum Valentini ad nos confodiendos, hoc est, Pugnare inter se, nec posse conciliari, eundem esse Dei Filium, & αὐτόθεον: nempe, si idem esset persona quod essentia. Nam si dicas Deum in sua essentia esse Dei Filium, absurditas repugnantiæ mnnifesta erit. Si autem in essentia Dei primum locum Patri assignes, secundum Filio, rectè convenient æqualitas Filij cum Patre, imò identitas essentiæ & generationis origo. Plenis buccis detonat Valentinus eminentiam Patris & authoritatem, quia alterum sibi Deum adoptauerit. Quid ergo sibi vult illud Pauli, Non rapinam arbitratus esset, Deo æqualem esse? Respondeat Valentinus, de Patre ne primario Deo, an de secundo & essentiato hoc debeat intelligi? Certè nimis insipidum esset, Christum dicere iure suo fuisse facturum, si se pro se tulisset æqualem sibi. Nec sanè dubium est quin referat Paulus ad Patrem, de quo etiam mox subiicit, Ideo exaltauit illum, &c. Porro ne fucum faciat hic nebulo imperitis, monendi sunt lectores, vbi Filius Dei vocatur Christus, non tam ad Filij personam, quæ fuit ante mundi creationem, quàm Mediatoris hoc speculare. Vbi autem nobis offertur Mediator Christus, quia medius esse non potest, nisi Deo sit inferior, Patri integra datur deitatis gloria. Nec mirum: quia sponte ad nos descendit, vt sursum nos ad Deum attolleret. Iam sicuti eos repudiamus, qui nimis subtiliter rapiuntur ad speculādam Christi deitatem, vt in Mediatoris persona Deum simpliciter quærant: ita merito abhorremus à Valentini delirio, dum Filij Dei nomen instar umbræ obtendit ad occultandam eius deitatem. Christus Dei Filius est, quatenus Sermo est Dei ante secula à Patre genitus, tandem manifestatus in carne. In Sermone æterno tantùm distinctio personalis notetur: ita relatiuè Dei Filius erit, & sine relatione simul Deus. Quatenus vero formam serui induit, Filius est Dei, vt Patri obediat, atque ita noua sit eius conditio, & à priore diuersa. Hoc etiam modo diluitur quicquid ex Tertulliano non minus stultè & insulsè quàm improbè Valentinus profert. Confessus sum in aliis scriptis pium illum virum sæpe durius loqui. Sed quicquid de persona Mediatoris disserit, ad Christi deitatem torquere, nulla ratio patitur. Eius testimonio abutitur Valentinus, vt probet Filium Dei propriam essentiam non habere. Atqui sententiam suam Tertullianus Christi dicto confirmat, Pater maior me est: quod nemo verecundus audebit de sola deitate accipere. Hoc vnum quisquis prudenter observabit, mirabitur, & simul securè contemnet cuffam Valentini hallucinationem. Quòd si Tertulliani authoritate pugnandum est, præter multos insignes locos, quibus Serueti errorem refutauit, quid hoc sibi vult? Alium à Patre Filium profiteri, personæ non substantiæ nomine, quia vbique tenet vnam substantiam in tribus cohærentibus? Si excipiat Valentini larua, vnam vocari substantiam, quia essentiatus sit Filius à Patre, nihil proficiet, quando diserte negat Tertullianus differre Filium à Patre substantia. Possetne apertius doctrinæ nostræ suffragari, quàm substantiam, id est essentiam à personis distinguendo? Eodem sensu paulò post subiicit, Ratione reddidimus, qua non duo dicantur dii, sed qua Pater & Filius duo: & hoc non ex separatione substantiæ, sed dispositione. Irascitur Valentinus simulac audit aliquam esse Filio essentiam, maximè verò vnam & eandem cum Patre. Tertullianus verò non alibi quàm in dispositione personæ discrimen statuit, eundem substantia Filium cum Patre nominans. Eodem libro relatio quam asserimus clarè tradita est, dum ita scribit Tertullianus: Sine Filio nominatur, quum principaliter determinatur, vt prima persona, quæ ante Filii nomen erat præponenda: quia Pater ante cognoscitur, & post Patrem Filius nominatur. Cæterùm alius non est Filius à Patre. Ex Christi dicto, Ego & Pater vnum sumus, putat Valentinus posse elici non eundem esse cum Patre Deum. Quid autem Tertullianus? Ad substantiam, inquit, vnitatem hoc pertinet, non ad numeri singularitatem. Videmus vt numerum ad personas restringens, essentiam, quæ vna est, seorsum relinquat. Quia nolo actum agere, cognoscent Lectores, si volent, ex refutatione Serueti quàm stolidè Irenæum in suas partes trahere conetur fœtidus hic impostor. Eadem est Iustini ratio, quo nullus doctrinæ nostræ luculentior patronus nobis optandus est. Ac miror Serueti stultitiam ausum fuisse imitari, qui quum sancti Martyris nomine ferociter gloriaretur, prolato volumine obmutuit. Nænias quæ sub Ignatii nomine feruntur, omitto: qua tamen in parte iterum vel nequitia, vel insania eiusdem Valentini conuincitur, dum magnificè iactat Ignatium loquutum esse cum Virgine Maria, & eius nomine epistolam venditat pudendis monachorum deliriis refertam. Plenior tamen danda est Filii definitio, quæ omnes nodos melius expediat. Fatetur Valentinus consubstantialem esse Patri secundum diuinitatem, nobis verò secundum humanitatem. Diceres hominem orthodoxæ fidei loqui: nisi quod recte ex aliis sumpsit, mox ex furioso suo sensu corrumperet. Indiuiduum, inquit, non compositum ex partibus vt homo, sed naturaliter regenitum. Ac paulò post, Non recte dicitur, Christum constare ex λόγω & homine, sicut Alexander constat ex corpore & animo: quia λόγος ita per incarnationis mysterium Immanuel est, ut non mutata Dei substantia hominis formā sumpserit, utque ambarū naturarū attributa & proprietates sint propriæ & naturales unius eiusdemque subiecti. Unde nō minus Dei sanguinem & carnem, quàm divinitatem hominis Iesu absque ullo tro-po, proprie dicimus & confitemur. Nisi enim sanguis & caro Christi verè & proprie Dei sanguis & caro essent, neque hæc verè expiatrix hostia dicere-tur, neque ille purgaret nos à peccatis: quemadmodū etiam nec homo Iesus po-testatem haberet remittendi peccata, nisi homo-deus esset. Certè nunquam nisi ex vertiginoso spiritu prodirent sententiæ adeò inter se pugnantes. Postquam enim duas in Christo naturas agnovit, unitatis prætextu quod singulis proprium est permiscet ac confundit: ut sine ulla figura Deus sit mortalis, & homo per se sit vita. Non insistam Scripturæ testimoniis ad oppugnandum hoc commen-tum: quæram duntaxat quî eum non pudeat in Tertullianum contumeliosè insurgere, cuius verba sunt, Quum duæ naturæ censeantur in Christo, divina & humana: constet autem immortalem esse divinam, mortalem quæ humana sit: apparet quatenus eum mortuum dicat Paulus, id est, quâ carnem & ho-minem & Filium hominis, nō quâ Spiritum, & Sermonem, & Dei Filium. Discant tandem lectores quàm dexter sit interpres Tertuliani, & quàm bo-nus ac fidelis discipulus. Nos verò in Christo Mediatore non impedit personæ unitas, quin sua utrique naturæ distincta proprietas salua maneat, ut Christus sit Deus & homo: vel, sicuti Paulus loquitur, Deus manifestatus in car-ne verè & naturaliter Dei Filius, sed qui ex duabus naturis constet, quia in homine habitavit plenitudo Divinitatis. Et Christus ipse clarè pronuntiat, corpus suum esse templum, quod certè minimè quadraret, nisi esset Deus ipse. Etsi autem Deitatis respectu unum est cum Patre, sicut iam sæpe diximus, quâ tamen Mediator est, quoad dispensationem, quodammodo subsidit infra Deum, qua ratione Patri subiicietur ultimo die, regnúmque[?] quod acce-pit, restituet, ut sit Deus omnia in omnibus. Quisnam Deus? Si ad Patrem restringas, certè Filii deitas erit temporalis, quo nihil absurdius. Quare alias machinas excogitet Valentinus oportet, quibus convellat orthodoxam fidem: quando ingenuè prædicamus unicum esse Deū, à quo missus est Chri-stus, & unicum esse Dei Filium, qui sponte se exinanivit, ut nos in societa-tem suæ gloriæ ascisceret. Frivola autem calumnia est, nos Christum discerpe-re, imò i..[?] alium Christiū qui non est, transformare, dū nunc ut Deum, nunc ut Dei Filium, nunc ut natum ex Virgine consideramus. Quanquā suo se gladio iugulat hic phreneticus, qui hominē[?] factum ex muliere, missum in plenitudi-ne ne temporum, seorsum considerari non sustinet ab æterno illo Sermone, qui ante sæcula genitus fuit. Diuinam verò essentiam quàm rectè considerari nolit, iam ex pluribus testimoniis palàm fecimus, & ex Malachia dicere promptum est, Donec veniat, inquit, Dominator ad templum suum. Certè non aliis insignibus magis gloriam suam illustrauit Deus, quàm legali cultu, sacrificiis, & templi imperio. Vbi ergo palàm asserit Propheta, Christum, qui venturus est, illum esse Deum qui semper in templo adoratus fuerit, omnem controuersiam diremptam esse existimo. Eat nunc Valentinus, & neget colendum esse Christum, quia Patrem nobis colendum proposuit.
units.tr: <i>As for empty words, people are always the same: they catch the curious with the sweet allure of novelty and show off a cleverness that is often nonexistent under a deceptive appearance. So the more monstrous the inventions that come into their heads, the more eagerly people seize them and the more boldly they insult others, once they have found a larger matter for praise. Moreover, such a strong desire for wandering speculations tickles most people, and such levity drives them around, that impostors, however unremarkable in talent, learning or skill, can easily win such disciples in a moment. So Valentinus Gentilis, a man of no account, offering a cup drawn from the ravings of Servetus, has persuaded insipid palates that it is a pleasant drink. How absurd the doctrine he has fabricated is will be clear at once to sensible people from a brief account. He says we are wrong because we posit three persons in the one essence of God. For in this way, he says, a quaternity is invented, as if the word "person" signified something abstracted from the essence. But he himself is grossly mistaken, since he does not distinguish the three properties in God, which reside in the essence itself and are not separated from it. We hold that principle of Scripture, that God is one. Since the same Scripture sets before us the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, what remains but to acknowledge in the one simple Deity three persons, which nevertheless do not make several gods, nor rend or dissipate the unity of the essence? But where would a quaternity be found, if one God contains three properties in himself? Now it is worth seeing how cleverly he corrects our view. He invents that the essence of God is in the Father alone, and so he proclaims that the Father alone is the true God. Then he grants the name of God to the Son, but as something held on sufferance, because, of course, he has been essentiated by the Father. So he affirms that the person of the Father is nothing other than the essence; but the person of the Son he babbles to be deification. When it comes to the Holy Spirit, he confuses everything, because already before he asserted that the Son is the same as the Spirit. And yet if essence belongs properly to the Father, as what is peculiar to one person is not shared with another, then the Son will certainly not be God. What then will happen to so many passages of Scripture, by which we are taught that Christ is that Jehovah who spoke through Moses: "I am who I am"? Isaiah saw Jehovah, the God of hosts, sitting on a throne; John interprets that the glory seen by the prophet was the glory of Christ. Scripture is full of testimonies of this kind, by which this new monstrosity of essentiation is refuted more than clearly. "In the beginning," says John, "was the Word." What beginning does he mean? Undoubtedly that of eternity: for he is not speaking of the creation of the world, but explains what God was always in himself. Therefore the Word was always God. From this it follows that it was not given to him to be. Likewise when Christ himself says, "Before Abraham was, I am," he certainly claims for himself an essence without beginning. If Valentinus's pleasure were to be followed, Christ would have spoken improperly; for in order that the parts should fit together, he ought to have said, "Before Abraham was made, I am essentiated." But it is one thing to be perpetual, another to be essentiated. Add that the tense of the verb designates an eternal state. Had he said in the past tense, "I was," Gentilis would not have stopped quibbling. But the form of speech he uses cuts off every opening for evasion. Now what is to essentiate, if not to create? For the act of essentiating necessarily carries with it that what did not exist before has begun to be. From this it follows that Christ is considered God by no other right than that which he received as a gift, which he did not have. Nor is argument needed in a clear matter: for we have already shown that, unless the Son is the Father, Valentinus strips him of the divine essence. I will speak more bluntly, to express what I mean more openly. The person of the Father is, according to Valentinus, the essence. But the person of the Father does not belong to the Son, nor can it be transferred to him. Therefore there is in him no essence of deity, but only a created divinity, which this scoundrel calls essentiation, as if Christ had been received into this rank of honour through apotheosis. And indeed, since God generally breathes essence into all creatures, to be deified is far more excellent than to be essentiated. Valentinus deals most splendidly and generously with Christ, when he deigns to grant him the privilege of having received his being as a gift. Nor are we pleading a private cause, as if he had attacked us alone, when he assails all antiquity together with us. It is now one thousand three hundred years since Arius was condemned at the Synod of Nicaea. Pretending to embrace the authority of that synod in word, he most filthily lashes Athanasius, who presided over it, with whatever abuse he can. He calls his faith sophistical, which introduces a certain fourth new god; he does not hesitate to condemn him everywhere as false; he joins him with Sabellius; he reproaches him with a triperson God; he defames him as a juggler; from time to time he accuses him of folly and lack of thought; he rails against his silliness; finally he burdens him with the most atrocious crime of sacrilege, that he dissolves Christ. And with such arrogance and haughtiness he rattles off his barking that you would say he was thundering from heaven. I certainly know that he is not himself the author, but that some one has been found from the troop of the Epicureans who was rather skilled at slander. Unless perhaps it is credible that he, who cannot write the name of Christ, sprinkles Greek words to adorn his speech. But since many today make their pleasures out of disturbances and the undermining of true doctrine, it is no wonder if some chatterer has vomited his venom from a cave in Lyons. Moreover a poet has arisen who adorns Valentinus's theology with his verses. Among other things he does not hesitate to thrust forward that splendid axiom, "God delights in an odd number." But what if, in turn, I, a trifler, should object to you: "Multiply three by three: how many gods will necessarily gush forth?" I am not unaware that you boldly confess myriads of gods. But whom do you think will be so bewitched by your tinkling that they will be caught by your snares, except perhaps those like you? And since there is for these men no scruple against lying freely, there is a "Confession" of Valentinus addressed to the Prefect of Gex, before whom he slavishly recanted whatever he had handed down; and he escaped in no other way than by an open denial of all the things that he now so proudly thrusts upon us. Moreover, lest any scruple should cling to anyone, I will briefly expose the impudence of this most impudent dog. Condemning Arius and Sabellius with full cheeks, he adds that they were long ago condemned by the Church. What, madman? Since you attribute the name of the Church to Athanasius and his colleagues, whence, if not from your most impure mouth, has such boldness of attacking them burst out? Since the Nicene confession is for you like an oracle, is it so insolent to tear apart him from whom it came? Certainly, since you are ignorant of all liberal learning, you never learned, if you look at the matter, that Athanasius presided not so much at the Nicene as at the Alexandrian synod, and that by its decree the heretics were condemned, whose errors you join yourself to as companion and supporter. What is more shameful than this impudence? And this is the one reason for his raving: that Athanasius makes the Son autotheos [αὐτόθεον]. From which it is plain that this is the point at issue, that Valentinus contends that Christ is God from another source, having borrowed from another what he is. For that sophist who has taken on his persona delights greatly in these words: "that God the Father is one, who is both autotheos [αὐτόθεος] and alone has autousia [αὐτουσία] in himself"; and if this is received, all the testimonies of Scripture that the Apostles cite for this matter will collapse. Getulus cries that this declaration, "I am God, and besides me there is no other," is the praise of the Father alone and not common to Christ. But Paul says, "We shall all be set before the judgment seat of Christ, because it is written, 'As I live, saith the Lord, every knee shall bow to me.'" We see how he applies to the person of Christ whatever Isaiah records God claiming for himself of glory and dominion. What is more proper to God than to live? Or what else is autousia [αὐτουσία]? By this the Apostle makes glory common to Christ and the Father. It is said in the Psalm, "The heavens shall perish, but you are the same God forever." Valentinus stubbornly snatches this from Christ, but the Apostle interprets that it was said of him. Why should I gather more passages, of which there is an abundance everywhere? But the words of the Council of Nicaea sound, "God of God." It is a harsh expression, I grant, but to remove its ambiguity no one can be a better interpreter than Athanasius, who dictated it. And certainly the Fathers' intention was nothing other than that the origin which the Son draws from the Father remains, in respect of person, and does not prevent the essence and deity of both from being the same: and thus, as regards essence, the Word is God without beginning, but in respect of the person of the Son, he has a beginning from the Father. Let Valentinus therefore stop barking that Scripture grants essential deity only to the Father alone. For as often as God speaks, either in Moses or in the Prophets, he does not compare himself with the Son, as if by this he diminished him, but sets himself against idols, which unless they are reduced to nothing, he does not wholly obtain what is his own. I will go further. If Valentinus is believed, the epithet "Creator" belongs to the Father alone. For among other things which God declares to be his own in Isaiah, there is repeatedly stated, "I am he whose hand founded the earth and stretched out the heavens." Therefore the Father alone, the essentiator of Son and Spirit, will be considered the maker of heaven and earth. Meanwhile he does not deny in words that Christ is God. Now let us attend to the words of Jeremiah: "The gods who did not make heaven and earth shall perish from the world." Did the Prophet curse the Son of God? And yet a dreadful curse of destruction applies to him, unless he is Creator. By this one word all of Valentinus's clouds about the essence of the one Father are dispelled. Why then is the Father called Creator, and adorned with this title apart? Surely by reason of order, when regard is had to the persons. Whence Valentinus is also plainly convicted of error, who does not think that the Father's deity would remain safe if Christ were partaker of the same essence. For certainly we all confess with one accord that Christ is improperly called Creator of heaven and earth, with respect to the distinction of persons. Nor is there doubt that Scripture, in attributing the name of Creator to the Father, distinguishes the persons. If Christ is truly Creator, and not with respect to person, it necessarily follows that this is referred to the essence, of which Valentinus strips him. And that obscene dog dares to make us companions of Arius and Muhammad, because we believe Christ to be God in essence. He even mocks an argument which he does not refute: "There is one God; the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God as the Father is: therefore the Father, Son and Spirit are one God." The fault in the syllogism ought to have been pointed out. He detects none; yet he wishes it to be faulty. Behold how imperious the schoolmasters in Italy are! But he opposes a contrary syllogism: "There is one God without any beginning, and the author of the universe; only the Father does not know origin, and all things are from him: therefore only the Father is that one God." As if the falsehood of the assumption needed a long refutation! He plays on the word "origin"; when he makes of it the Father, I will gladly assent: for God is he who does not know a beginning, as regards essence, and origin and beginning belong to the Son, as regards the order of the person. We therefore concede that the Son has his origin from the Father, as far as he is the Son; but origin not of time nor of essence, both of which are most absurd, but of order only. So all things are said to be from the Father, insofar as personal relation bears it. Who from this, unless he is three or four times insane, would gather that the Father alone is God? But the chief weapon of Valentinus for stabbing us, namely that it is impossible to reconcile the two things, that the same one is the Son of God and autotheos [αὐτόθεος], is contradictory: that is, if the person were the same as the essence. For if you say that God in his essence is the Son of God, the absurdity of the contradiction will be manifest. But if you assign the first place in the divine essence to the Father and the second to the Son, the equality of the Son with the Father and even identity of essence and origin of generation agree correctly. Valentinus thunders with full cheeks against the eminence and authority of the Father, because he has adopted for himself another God. What then does that saying of Paul mean, "He did not think it robbery to be equal with God"? Let Valentinus answer whether this ought to be understood of the Father, the primary God, or of the second, essentiated one. Certainly it would be too insipid to say that Christ would have acted by his own right if he had claimed equality with himself. Nor is there any doubt that Paul refers this to the Father, of whom he also adds immediately, "Therefore God exalted him," and so on. Moreover, lest this scoundrel make a smokescreen for the unlearned, readers must be warned that where the Son of God is called Christ, this is to be considered not so much with regard to the person of the Son, who existed before the creation of the world, as to the Mediator. But where Christ is offered to us as Mediator, since he cannot be mediator unless he is inferior to God, the full glory of deity is given to the Father. Nor is this strange: for he descended to us of his own accord, in order to lift us up to God. Now just as we reject those who are too subtly carried away to speculate on the deity of Christ, so that in the person of the Mediator they seek God simply, so we rightly abhor the delirium of Valentinus, who holds up the name of the Son of God like a shadow to hide his deity. Christ is the Son of God, insofar as he is the Word of God, begotten by the Father before the ages, at last manifested in the flesh. In the eternal Word only personal distinction is to be noted: thus he will be the Son of God relatively, and at the same time God without relation. But insofar as he has put on the form of a servant, he is the Son of God so as to obey the Father, and thus his condition is new and different from his former one. By this same method is refuted whatever Valentinus brings forward from Tertullian, no less foolishly and insipidly than wickedly. I have acknowledged in other writings that that pious man often speaks too harshly. But whatever he discusses about the person of the Mediator, to twist it against the deity of Christ is no reasonable thing. Valentinus abuses his testimony to prove that the Son of God has no essence of his own. And yet Tertullian confirms his opinion with the saying of Christ, "The Father is greater than I"; which no modest man will dare to take as referring to deity alone. Whoever prudently observes this one point will marvel, and at the same time will securely despise the crude delirium of Valentinus. But if we must fight with the authority of Tertullian, besides many notable passages by which he refuted the error of Servetus, what does this mean: that he professes the Son to be other than the Father, using the name of person and not of substance, because everywhere he holds one substance in three cohering persons? Even if the mask of Valentinus should object that the Son is called one substance because he is essentiated by the Father, it will avail him nothing, when Tertullian plainly denies that the Son differs from the Father in substance. Could he support our doctrine more clearly than by distinguishing substance, that is, essence, from the persons? In the same sense he adds shortly afterward: "We have given a reason by which two are not called gods, but by which the Father and the Son are two; and this not by separation of substance but by disposition." Valentinus rages as soon as he hears that there is some essence in the Son, and especially one and the same with the Father. But Tertullian sets the distinction nowhere except in the disposition of the person, calling the Son the same as the Father in substance. In the same book the relation which we assert is clearly set out, when Tertullian writes thus: "The Son is named without the Father when he is principally determined as the first person, who was to be placed before the name of Son; for the Father is known before, and after the Father the Son is named. But the Son is not other than the Father." From the saying of Christ, "I and the Father are one," Valentinus thinks it can be drawn that the Son is not God the same as the Father. But what does Tertullian say? "This pertains," he says, "to the unity of substance, not to singularity of number." We see how, while restricting number to the persons, he leaves the essence, which is one, apart. Since I do not wish to make a long business of it, readers will know, if they wish, from the refutation of Servetus how foolishly this stinking impostor tries to draw Irenaeus to his side. The same is the case with Justin, than whom we ought to desire no more luminous patron of our doctrine. And I wonder that Servetus's folly dared to imitate him, who, while fiercely boasting of the name of the holy Martyr, fell silent once the volume was produced. I omit the trifles that are carried under the name of Ignatius; yet in this part too the wickedness or madness of this same Valentinus is convicted, when he magnificently boasts that Ignatius spoke with the Virgin Mary, and under his name sells an epistle stuffed with the shameful ravings of monks. Yet a fuller definition of the Son must be given, which will untie all the knots better. Valentinus confesses that the Son is consubstantial with the Father according to deity, but with us according to humanity. You would say he was speaking as a man of orthodox faith, except that, having rightly taken some things from others, he soon corrupts them by his frenzied sense. "An individual," he says, "not composed of parts as a man is, but naturally reborn." And a little after: "It is not rightly said that Christ consists of logos [λόγος] and man, as Alexander consists of body and soul; because the Logos, through the mystery of the incarnation, is Immanuel in such a way that, the substance of God being unchanged, he took the form of man, and so that the attributes and properties of both natures are proper and natural to one and the same subject. Hence we no less properly and without any trope say and confess the blood and flesh of God, than the deity of the man Jesus. For unless the blood and flesh of Christ were truly and properly the blood and flesh of God, this would not be called a true expiatory victim, nor would he cleanse us from sins: just as also the man Jesus would not have the power of remitting sins, unless he were a God-man." Certainly such sentences, so mutually at war, could only come forth from a giddy spirit. For after acknowledging two natures in Christ, under the pretext of unity he mingles and confounds what is proper to each, so that without any figure God is mortal, and man is by himself life. I will not insist on the testimonies of Scripture to overthrow this fiction. I will only ask how he is not ashamed to rise up insolently against Tertullian, whose words are: "Since two natures are reckoned in Christ, divine and human; but it is agreed that the divine is immortal and the human mortal: it appears that, insofar as Paul says he died, it is as flesh and man and Son of man, not as Spirit and Word and Son of God." Let readers at last learn how skilful an interpreter of Tertullian this man is, and how good and faithful a disciple. But we hold that in Christ the Mediator the unity of the person does not hinder each nature from keeping its distinct property safe, so that Christ is God and man; or, as Paul speaks, "God manifested in the flesh," truly and naturally the Son of God, yet one who consists of two natures, because in the man dwelt the fullness of the Godhead. And Christ himself plainly declares that his body is the temple, which certainly would not fit unless he were God himself. And although with respect to deity he is one with the Father, as we have often said, yet insofar as he is Mediator, in regard to the dispensation, he in some measure stoops below God; for which reason he will be subjected to the Father on the last day, and will restore the kingdom which he received, that God may be all in all. Which God? If you restrict this to the Father, the deity of the Son will certainly be temporal, than which nothing is more absurd. Therefore Valentinus must devise other machines with which to overthrow the orthodox faith, since we openly proclaim that there is one God, by whom Christ was sent, and one Son of God, who of his own accord emptied himself, that he might admit us to the fellowship of his glory. But it is a frivolous calumny that we tear Christ apart, or rather transform him into another Christ who does not exist, while we now consider him as God, now as Son of God, now as born of the Virgin. Yet this frantic man cuts his own throat with his own sword, since he cannot bear that the man made of a woman, sent in the fullness of time, should be considered apart from that eternal Word who was begotten before the ages. How rightly he is unwilling to consider the divine essence we have already made plain from many testimonies; and it is easy to say from Malachi: "Until the Lord, he says, comes to his temple." Certainly God has made his glory illustrious by no other marks more than by legal worship, sacrifices and the rule of the temple. Where then the Prophet plainly asserts that Christ, who is to come, is that God who was always adored in the temple, I think all controversy is settled. Let Valentinus now go, and deny that Christ is to be worshipped, since he has set forth the Father for us to worship.</i>

units.la: PROTHESES VALENTINI GENTILIS, QVAE MERA SOPHISMATA CONTINENT, NE VIDE-
units.tr: THE PROPOSITIONS OF VALENTINUS GENTILIS, WHICH CONTAIN MERE SOPHISMS, LEST I SHOULD SEEM TO

units.la: rer cum umbra certare, an attingerem dubitaui. Quia tamen argutulus sibi visus est earum author, siue Gribaldus, siue alius quispiam similis: malui aliquantulum temporis perdere, quàm non monere simplices quomodo sibi ab insidiis caveant.
units.tr: FIGHT WITH A SHADOW: I hesitated. Yet since their author seemed clever to himself, whether he is Gribaldus or some other man like him, I preferred to spend a little time rather than fail to warn simple readers how to guard themselves against snares.

units.la: PRIMA.
units.tr: FIRST.

units.la: Infinitum, siue interminatū est quicquid nec originem omnino habet, nec finem. Duo autem infinita neque dantur, neque esse possunt.
units.tr: That is infinite, or unbounded, which has neither origin nor end at all. Two infinites neither are given nor can exist.

units.la: Ut hoc totum concedam, quid inde consequitur qui solum Patrem vult habere infinitum? Quasi verò Filium doceamus aliud esse à Patre.
units.tr: Even if I grant all this, what follows from it for one who wants only the Father to be infinite? As if we were teaching that the Son is something other than the Father.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Deus est nomen increatæ substantiæ & Deitatis plenitudinis.
units.tr: God is the name of an uncreated substance and the fullness of Deity.

units.la: Perge verò, & ostende quorsum tendas. Nos verò inde colligimus Sermonem esse verum Deum: quia & increatus est, & postquā in carne manifestatus est, in eo residet plenitudo Divinitatis.
units.tr: Go on, then, and show where you are heading. For our part we conclude from this that the Word is true God, since he is both uncreated and, once manifested in the flesh, in him dwells the fullness of the Godhead.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Ut in æternitate personarum datur principium ordinis, non temporis: sic in earum deitate datur gradus, non distinctio. Est autem persona, substantia intelligens, individua, incommunicabilis.
units.tr: As in the eternity of the persons there is a principle of order, not of time, so in their deity there is a degree, not a distinction. A person, however, is an intelligent, individual, incommunicable substance.

units.la: Quænam ratiocinandi forma, ut si principium ordinis sit in personis, ideò in deitate sit gradus? Hic unus error. Simul observent lectores, istum, quum de æternitate personarum loquitur, Filii seorsum ab humana natura considerare: quod nuper fieri nefas esse clamabat. Secundus error, cui tertius mox accedit, Gradum in Patris & Filii deitate esse,non distinctionem.Quid? An gradus diuer-fi erunt,&nihil differentiae?Certè prodigium est dicere non distin-gui quod inferius est à superiori.In definitione Personae suam in-scitiam turpiter prodit.Nam quum secundùm ipsum essentiatio communis sit Filio & Spiritui, sit autem essentiatio persona, ergo Filii & Spiritus personae erunt communicabiles.
units.tr: What kind of reasoning is this, that if there is a principle of order in the persons, therefore there is a degree in the deity? Here is one error. Let readers also observe that he, when he speaks of the eternity of the persons, considers the Son apart from human nature, which he lately cried out was wicked to do. A second error, to which a third soon joins: that there is a degree, not a distinction, in the deity of the Father and the Son. What? Will there be different degrees and no difference? It is surely monstrous to say that what is lower is not distinguished from what is higher. In his definition of person he shamefully betrays his own ignorance. For since, by his own account, essentiation is common to the Son and the Spirit, and essentiation is a person, then the persons of the Son and the Spirit will be communicable.

units.la: IIII.
units.tr: IIII.

units.la: Vnus, in natura diuina non ad singularitatem subfiantia, sed tantùm ad originem siue αὐτουσίαν refertur.
units.tr: In the divine nature, "one" refers not to singularity of substance but only to origin, or autousia.

units.la: Inani garritu se in crassam repugnantiam implicat.Quid enim aliud est αὐτουσία,quàm essentiae singularitas, vbicumque reperiatur?
units.tr: He entangles himself in a gross contradiction with empty chatter. For what else is autousia [αὐτουσία] than the singularity of the essence, wherever it is found?

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: Vnus Deus naturalem generationem & propagationem admittit: vnicus autem omnino sterilis est,ac solitarius.
units.tr: One God admits natural generation and propagation; but a solitary God is altogether barren and alone.

units.la: Atqui,vnicum Deum non fingunt,qui in eius essentia fatentur Patrem,& Filium,& Spiritum. Tibi autem naturalis generatio noui & secundi Dei,sicut & propagatio tertii,deificatio est.
units.tr: Yet those who confess in his essence the Father, the Son and the Spirit do not invent a solitary God. For you, the natural generation of a new and second God, and likewise the propagation of a third, is deification.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: Pater non est hypostasis,siue persona, in uno Deo:sed teste Apostolo, est vnus ille Deus,à quo omnia.
units.tr: The Father is not a hypostasis or person in the one God; but, as the Apostle witnesses, he is that one God from whom are all things.

units.la: Si Pater non est hypostasis,quomodo Filius character erit hypostaseos eius? nam distinctam ab ipso esse oportet hypostasin cuius est character.Ac inscite huc torquetur Apostoli dictum,Vnum esse Deum à quo omnia.quia elogium hoc nihil aliud est quàm personae eius proprietas. Nec verò nos negamus, dum confertur Filius cum Patre,suum cuique titulum attribui.Adde quòd Christus illic non pro aeterna sua deitate commendatur,sed tantùm locatur in gradu dominii,quod à Patre acceptum,vltimo die redder.
units.tr: If the Father is not a hypostasis, how will the Son be the character of his hypostasis? For the hypostasis of which he is the character must be distinct from him. And the Apostle's saying, that there is one God from whom are all things, is wrongly twisted here, since this formula is nothing other than a property of his person. Nor do we deny that, when the Son is compared with the Father, each is given his own title. Add that Christ is not commended there for his eternal deity, but is merely placed in the rank of lordship, which he received from the Father and will hand back on the last day.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Solus Pater est vnus Deus,id est,sine vllo principio aut origine inuentus.
units.tr: The Father alone is the one God, that is, found without any beginning or origin.

units.la: Quia ludis in vocibus Originis & Principii, falso & perperam infers vnum esse Patrem Deum, quia origine careat.Christi enim origo non nisi personae aptatur.
units.tr: Because you play with the words origin and beginning, you falsely and wrongly infer that the Father alone is God because he lacks origin. For origin is applied to Christ only as to a person.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: Solus Pater est αὐτόθεος, id est,à nullo superiore numine essentiatus,sed à seipso Deus. Ubi probaueris essentiatum esse Filium, de solo Patre extorque-bis quicquid voles. Interea si numen Patris superius est, mentitus est Apostolus, Filium ei æqualem asserens.
units.tr: The Father alone is autotheos [αὐτόθεος], that is, essentiated by no superior divinity, but God from himself. Once you have proved that the Son is essentiated, you may twist whatever you like from the Father alone. Meanwhile, if the divinity of the Father is superior, the Apostle has lied in asserting that the Son is equal to him.

units.la: IX.
units.tr: IX.

units.la: Qui unum Deum in tres proprietates seu personas distinguit, vel sibi præstigias facit, vel necessario unius Dei substantiam diuidit atque dis-cerpit.
units.tr: Whoever distinguishes the one God into three properties or persons either deceives himself by tricks, or necessarily divides and tears apart the substance of the one God.

units.la: Cuius, obsecro, pudoris est, obscurum pædagogum verbulo uno iudicium ferre de cunctis Ecclesiæ scriptoribus? Probet ergo, vel neminem sanum mouebit eius temeritas.
units.tr: I beg you, what shame is it for an obscure schoolmaster to pass judgment in one word on all the writers of the Church? Let him prove it; otherwise his rashness will move no sane person.

units.la: X.
units.tr: X.

units.la: Deus habuit vim generandi ac propagandi, quia voluit: ideoque & λόγον ante secula genuit, & Spiritum propagauit.
units.tr: God had the power of generating and propagating because he willed it; and therefore he begot the logos [λόγον] before the ages, and propagated the Spirit.

units.la: Hac sententia minimè labefactatur nostra fides, quando inge-nuè tradimus καθ' ὑπεροχὴν Dei nomen Patri proprie ascribi.
units.tr: Our faith is in no way shaken by this sentence, when we frankly teach that the name God belongs properly to the Father as kath' hyperochēn [καθ' ὑπεροχὴν], by way of pre-eminence.

units.la: XI.
units.tr: XI.

units.la: Æterna λόγου substantia, principium & originem habet à Deo, quate-nus genita ac distincta sit, nō quatenus sit. Non enim est ex nihilo creata, aut de aliqua non extante materia facta, sed de immensa substantia illius summi Dei genita.
units.tr: The eternal substance of the Word has its principle and origin from God, insofar as it is begotten and distinct, not insofar as it is. For it was not created out of nothing, nor made from some matter not existing, but was begotten from the immense substance of that highest God.

units.la: Si diceres Filii originem esse à Patre, quatenus est genitus, nihil esset controversiæ. Essentiam verò genitam probes, si quem velis tuo commento acquiescere. Interea notemus Christi essentiam, quatenꝰ est, carere origine. Quòd si in Filio est æterna Patris essen-tia, evinco[?] personam esse communicabile. Quod addit de immen-sa substantia Dei summi esse genitâ, non aliter stabit, quàm si con-cedat aut immensitatem essentiæ residere in Christo, aut aliquam eius portionem. Si communis est Filio essentiæ immensitas, seque-tur esse interminatum. Quid ergo fiet primæ prothesi? Atqui substantiam Dei facere partibilem, detestabile sacrilegium est.
units.tr: If you said that the Son's origin is from the Father insofar as he is begotten, there would be no controversy. But prove that the essence is begotten, if you wish anyone to rest satisfied with your invention. Meanwhile let us note that the essence of Christ, insofar as it is, lacks origin. And if the essence of the Father is in the Son, I conclude that the person is communicable. As for what he adds, that the immense substance of the highest God is begotten, this cannot stand except by conceding either that the immensity of the essence resides in Christ, or some portion of it. If the immensity of the essence is common to the Son, it follows that he is unbounded. What then will become of your first proposition? Yet to make the substance of God divisible is a detestable sacrilege.

units.la: XII.
units.tr: XII.

units.la: Qui Filium αὐτόθεον esse contendit, is vel duo afferat principia, vel tur-rim Babel ædificet necesse est.
units.tr: Whoever contends that the Son is autotheos must either posit two principles or necessarily build a tower of Babel.

units.la: Tibi verò non adeò facile erit solo virulentæ tuæ linguæ flatu, totum sanctorum chorum evertere. Sed vide ne putida tua arro-gantia turris sit Babel.
units.tr: For you it will not be so easy, by the mere blast of your venomous tongue, to overthrow the whole choir of the saints. But take care lest your rotten arrogance be the tower of Babel.

units.la: XIII.
units.tr: XIII.

units.la: Vnus Deus qui est Spiritus ἀγέννητος καὶ αὐτόθεος absque vlla sui diminutione ante secula λόγον Spiritum ineffabiliter genuit: non autem sophisticam cogitationem, proprietatem, aut inanem relationem.
units.tr: The one God, who is Spirit, unbegotten and autotheos [ἀγέννητος καὶ αὐτόθεος], without any diminution of himself, ineffably begot the Word and the Spirit before the ages; not however a sophistic thought, a property, or an empty relation.

units.la: Modò facessant calumniæ, nihil in priore membro dicis, nisi ex nostris & Patrum libris sumptum. Quo intolerabilior est tua improbitas, dum nostram doctrinam continuò pòst deformas tuis figmentis.
units.tr: Away with your slanders! In the first member you say nothing that is not taken from our books and the books of the Fathers. All the more intolerable is your wickedness, since immediately afterwards you disfigure our doctrine with your own fictions.

units.la: XIIII.
units.tr: XIV.

units.la: Quicunque illum vnum Deum sine origine ex propria substantia nihil imminuta Filium genuisse negant, tanquam manifeste Iudaizantes ac Mahometizantes, à Christianis mysteriis arcendi sunt.
units.tr: Whoever denies that the Son was begotten from the one God, who is without origin, from his own substance undiminished, is to be excluded from the Christian mysteries as manifestly Judaizing and Mohammedanizing.

units.la: Videtur sibi valdè callidus, qui pulchri coloris obtentu, falsa in-vidia nos grauat. Nos vero ingenuè idem prædicamus, modò ne perperam restringens ad Patrem vnius Dei nomen, Filium à Dei-tate arceas & excludas.
units.tr: He seems to himself very clever, who under the cover of a fair colour burdens us with false odium. We, however, frankly preach the same thing, provided that you do not wrongly restrict the name of the one God to the Father and shut out and exclude the Son from the Deity.

units.la: XV.
units.tr: XV.

units.la: Dominus noster Iesus Christus est verus, proprius & naturalis Filius vnius Altissimi ac viuentis Dei, nec alium habet Patrē, quàm solum Deum, à quo omnia.
units.tr: Our Lord Jesus Christ is the true, proper and natural Son of the one Most High and living God, and he has no other Father than God alone, from whom are all things.

units.la: Exposui quo sensu Scriptura, dum Patrem Christo comparat, eum prædicet vnicum Deum: nempe quia legatione pro ipso Christus fungitur, eiusque virtute & mandato mundum gubernat: sed hæc in persona & statu Mediatoris submissio nihil detrahit ex im-mensa deitatis eius gloria. Ita dicitur Pater Filio dedisse vt habeat vitam in seipso, in quo tamen vita erat ab vltima æternitate. Deni-que Scripturæ tritum est, in Patre, tanquam in speculo, nobis pro-ponere summam deitatis gloriam: non vt quicquam Filio auferat, sed quia Christus ipse inferior factus est Patre, vt ad Patrē nos du-cendo., ad seipsum quoque nos duceret. Vnde Augustinus non minus scitè quàm verè eum nominat Viam qua itur, & Scopum vel Metam quò tenditur.
units.tr: I have explained in what sense Scripture, when it compares the Father with Christ, proclaims him the only God: namely, because Christ acts as his envoy and governs the world by his power and command. But this submission in the person and state of the Mediator takes nothing away from the immense glory of his deity. Thus it is said that the Father gave to the Son to have life in himself, though in him life was from eternity. Finally, it is a commonplace of Scripture that the Father sets before us, as in a mirror, the highest glory of the deity; not that he takes anything from the Son, but because Christ himself, made lower than the Father, led us to the Father and, by leading us to the Father, also led us to himself. Hence Augustine, no less wisely than truly, calls him the Way by which one goes, and the Goal or Mark to which one strives.

units.la: XVI.
units.tr: XVI.

units.la: Christus non ideò Dei Filius est, quia Deus: sed contrà, ideò est Deus, quia Dei Filius.
units.tr: Christ is not the Son of God because he is God; but on the contrary, he is God because he is the Son of God.

units.la: Non sufficeret Christum esse Deum, nisi & genitus esset à Pa-tre. tre.Filius tamen esse non potuit,nisi Deus esset.
units.tr: It would not suffice for Christ to be God unless he were also begotten of the Father. Yet he could not be the Son unless he were God.

units.la: XVII.
units.tr: XVII.

units.la: Aut λόγος ille est Spiritus ab uno Deo in immensa æternitatis latitudine immediatè genitus, aut substantiua res non est.
units.tr: Either that Word is a Spirit begotten immediately from the one God in the immense breadth of eternity, or he is not a substantial thing.

units.la: Si intelligas Spiritū essentiatum, probatio exigitur: nec ante fidem tuis ambagibus facies, donec ex hac latebra egressus fueris.
units.tr: If you understand the Spirit as having substance, proof is required; nor will you give a clear account of your faith with your evasions until you come out of this hiding-place.

units.la: XVIII.
units.tr: XVIII.

units.la: Nisi esset substantialis inter Deum λόγον, & invisibilem Patrem distinctio, nō poterat λόγος in Virginis utero cōcipi, quin simul Pater incarnaretur.
units.tr: Unless there were a substantial distinction between God the Word and the invisible Father, the Word could not be conceived in the Virgin's womb without the Father being incarnate at the same time.

units.la: Tu verò imperitia laberis, qui hypostasin non intelligis vel substantiam vel subsistentiam esse : atque ita Christum, quatenus Deus est, induisse carnem, & tamen non nisi in sua hypostasi.
units.tr: But you stumble through ignorance, not understanding that hypostasis means either substance or subsistence; and so you say that Christ, as far as he is God, put on flesh, and yet only in his own hypostasis.

units.la: XIX.
units.tr: XIX.

units.la: Non est substantialis distinctio, quæ λόγου hypostasin à Dei hypostasi non distinguit.
units.tr: There is no substantial distinction which does not distinguish the hypostasis of the Word from the hypostasis of God.

units.la: Ego verò libenter assentior. Sed non animaduertis longè aliud esse hypostasin quàm οὐσίαν [?], ideòque hypostaticè Christum à Patre distingui, qui vnius est cum ipso essentiæ.
units.tr: I for my part gladly agree. But you do not notice that hypostasis is something quite other than ousia [οὐσία], and that therefore Christ is distinguished hypostatically from the Father, though he is one with him in essence.

units.la: XX.
units.tr: XX.

units.la: Genitus à genitore substantiali numero differt, non potestate, sententia, aut diuersitate naturæ.
units.tr: What is begotten from a begetting substance differs in number of substance, not in power, opinion, or diversity of nature.

units.la: Hic se prodit diabolica impietas, quòd Filiū essentialiter alium à Patre fuisse blaterat. Quid enim aliud est, numero essentiali differre,(quod per substantiam intelligit)quàm essentia duos esse Patrem & Filium?
units.tr: Here his diabolical impiety shows itself, in that he babbles that the Son was essentially other than the Father. For what else is it to differ in essential number (which he understands as substance) than for Father and Son to be two in essence?

units.la: XXI.
units.tr: XXI.

units.la: Unus Deus, & λόγος eius, duæ sunt eiusdem naturæ substantiæ intelligen-tes:id est, duo æterni spiritus consubstantiales, congruo ordine, gradu, & proprie-tate distincti.
units.tr: God and his Word are two intelligent substances of the same nature: that is, two eternal consubstantial spirits, distinguished by a fitting order, rank and property.

units.la: Si quis ad tam tetras blasphemias nō horreat, plusquā stupidus est.Fatetur Filium æternum & consubstantialè Patri:nempe quod Seruetus de hominis anima ac ipso diabolo scripsit. Quis enim est ei congruus ordo, nisi Filium essentiatū esse, ut precariò fit Deus? Præclara scilicet eius æternitas!
units.tr: Anyone who does not shudder at such foul blasphemies is more than stupid. He confesses the Son to be eternal and consubstantial with the Father, just as Servetus wrote about the soul of man and the devil himself. For what fitting order is there, unless the Son is essentiated, as he is precariously made God? Splendid indeed is his eternity!

units.la: XXII.
units.tr: XXII.

units.la: Plures Spiritus immensæ substantiæ esse non possunt. Nos vero spiritualem naturam agnoscimus in ipsa Dei essentia: tu contrà, dum imaginaris Christum numero alium esse Spiritum à Patre, immensa substantia eum palàm spolias.
units.tr: There cannot be several spirits of immense substance. But we acknowledge a spiritual nature in the very essence of God; you, on the contrary, while you imagine Christ to be a Spirit other than the Father in number, openly strip him of immense substance.

units.la: XXIII.
units.tr: XXIII.

units.la: Omnis Spiritus qui sub ascititiam, seu naturalem formam visibilem cadit, circunscriptibilis sit substantiæ necesse est.
units.tr: Every spirit which falls under an assumed or natural visible form must necessarily be of circumscribable substance.

units.la: Si de Christo loqueris, ut eum facias circunscriptibilè, quatenus carne indutus est, totus mundus, me tacente, furorem tuum detestetur. Nec verò coniecturis opus est: quia magis ac magis se præcipitat, ut sequitur.
units.tr: If you speak of Christ so as to make him circumscribable, inasmuch as he was clothed in flesh, the whole world, even without my words, would detest your madness. Nor is conjecture needed, since you hurl yourself headlong more and more, as follows.

units.la: XXIIII.
units.tr: XXIV.

units.la: Solus Pater est Spiritus, ἀγέννητος, universitatis author, immensæque substantiæ: Filius verò Spiritus est ex Deo ineffabiliter generatus, paternæ voluntatis executor, ac pro generationis modulo circunscriptibilis genitus. Ambo tamen sunt unius eiusdemque infinitæ virtutis ac perfectionis.
units.tr: The Father alone is Spirit, unbegotten, author of the universe and of immense substance; the Son, however, is Spirit, ineffably generated from God, executor of the Father's will, and begotten circumscribable according to the measure of his generation. Yet both are of one and the same infinite power and perfection.

units.la: Pronuntiat Iohannes Christum esse verum Deum, & vitam æternam. Hic nebulo essentiam tantum concedit pro modulo generationis circūscriptibilē. Ubi ergo plenitudo deitatis? Ubi essentiæ immensitas, quæ clarè elicitur ex Christi verbis, quibus testatur se in sinu Patris & in cælo fuisse, quo tempore in terris versatus est? Agedum phrenetice, si ineffabilis est generatio, quod toties tibi effluxit, quomodo mensura eam includere non contentus, ignominiosè ad modulum restringis?
units.tr: John proclaims Christ to be the true God and eternal life. This scoundrel concedes essence only as circumscribable according to the measure of generation. Where then is the fullness of deity? Where is the immensity of essence, which is clearly drawn from Christ's words, in which he testifies that he was in the bosom of the Father and in heaven at the time when he was living on earth? Come now, frenzied man: if the generation is ineffable, as you have so often let slip, how is it that you are not content to leave it unmeasured, but shamefully restrict it to a measure?

units.la: XXV.
units.tr: XXV.

units.la: Qui λόγον illum, per quem facta sunt omnia, fuisse in Virginis utero hypo-statice inclusum, & per incarnationis mysterium verum hominem factum negat, is mendaces facit Domini testes veraces, quos propriis oculis eum vi-disse, ac manibus contrectasse Sacræ literæ aperte testantur.
units.tr: He who denies that that Word, through whom all things were made, was hypostatically enclosed in the Virgin's womb, and was made a true man through the mystery of the incarnation, makes the Lord's witnesses liars; the Holy Letters openly testify that they saw him with their own eyes and handled him with their hands.

units.la: Si qua tibi gutta esset sanæ mentis, nobiscum facilè conveniret: sed quia hypostasin perversè confundis cum essentia, & Christi Deitatem localiter restringis in angustias materni uteri, atrocem iniuriam Christi Apostolis inuris, eos in erroris tui societatem trahendo.
units.tr: If you had any drop of sound mind, you would easily agree with us; but because you perversely confuse hypostasis with essence, and narrow Christ's deity locally into the confines of his mother's womb, you inflict an atrocious injury on Christ's apostles, dragging them into the fellowship of your error.

units.la: XXVI.
units.tr: XXVI.

units.la: Quicunque à Virginis partu æternum λόγον à visibili Christo seorsum considerant, duos sibi Filios necessariò constituunt, inuisibilem alterum & imcrimpatibilem[?]. Quam sententiam diuus Irenæus merito homicidiale appellat.
units.tr: Whoever considers the eternal Word apart from the visible Christ after the Virgin's birth necessarily sets up for himself two Sons, one invisible and the other impassible. Blessed Irenaeus rightly calls this opinion homicidal.

units.la: Tantùm ad portenta attendant Lectores: Deum proprie fuisse passibilem & mortuum, tristitiæ, dolori, timori, ignorantiæ quoque obnoxium. Mortuus est Christus: Deum vult mortuum esse hic nebulo. Lachrymatus est, doluit, timuit, denique nesciuit diem resur-rectionis: mauult Valentinus ignorātiæ Deum subiicere, quàm di-stinguere inter duas naturas. Quid vero impudentius, quàm talibus blasphemiis obtendere Irenæi nomen? Omitto quòd prodigiosam vocem Homicidialis sententiæ ex suo cerebro genuit. Disputat Irenæus cōtra Demiurgi fictores, quibus Spiritus sanctus erat Chri-stus. Quum ergo plures fabricarent, ac garrirent etiam Christum in specie columbæ descendisse super Christum: eos quidem Spiritum interimere, alium autem Christum, & alium Iesum docere dicit. Totus autem mundus satis superque nouit quàm remoti simus non tantùm à tali vesania, sed etiam à Nestorii commento, qui Christum duplicem induxit.
