units.tr: Let the readers attend only to these monstrosities: that God was properly passible and mortal, and subject also to sorrow, pain, fear and ignorance. Christ died, and this scoundrel wants God to be dead. He wept, grieved, feared, and finally did not know the day of the resurrection; Valentinus prefers to subject God to ignorance rather than distinguish between the two natures. What could be more shameless than to put Irenaeus' name forward for such blasphemies? I pass over that he invented the monstrous phrase "homicidal opinion" out of his own brain. Irenaeus disputes against the fabricators of the Demiurge, for whom the Holy Spirit was Christ. When many of them prated that Christ descended in the form of a dove upon Christ, he says that they indeed kill the Spirit and teach another Christ and another Jesus. But the whole world knows well enough, and more than enough, how far we are not only from such madness, but also from the invention of Nestorius, who introduced a double Christ.

units.la: XXVII.
units.tr: XXVII.

units.la: Qui contendit Spiritum sanctum, siue tertiam Trinitatis personam, tam re-spectiuè quàm ad se, non esse verè spiritualem substantiam, sed nescio quam fictitiam proprietatem, is manifestè negat Spiritum esse Spiritum, hoc est veritatem esse veritatem.
units.tr: Whoever contends that the Holy Spirit, or third person of the Trinity, is not truly a spiritual substance, both relatively and in himself, but some fictitious property I know not what, plainly denies that the Spirit is Spirit, that is, that truth is truth.

units.la: Non dubiū est quin sibi in puerilibus istis ineptiis valdè placuerit Gribaldus, cuius Valentinus est histrio. Sed quàm ridiculè ine-ptiat, nullo negotio ostendam. Primò fallitur, quòd eodem vbique sensu accipit nomen Spiritus. Nam quum Deus sit Spiritus, frustra distingueretur à Patre Spiritus, atque eius Spiritus vocaretur, nisi diuerso modo & respectu. Videmus ergo vt nebulo rudimentorum expers, omnia conturbet. Iam si proprietate Spiritus personam ab aliis duabus distinguimus, an fictitium quid erit, quia non capitur à Valentino? Nos verò Spiritum in tertia persona asserimus esse Deū, quia spiritualis est essentiæ, & ei nihilominus suam proprietatem seruamus.
units.tr: There is no doubt that Gribaldus, whose stage-player Valentinus is, took great delight in those childish trifles. But how ridiculously he trifles I will show without difficulty. First, he errs in that he takes the name Spirit in the same sense everywhere. For since God is Spirit, the Spirit would be vainly distinguished from the Father and called his Spirit, unless in a different manner and respect. We see, therefore, how this scoundrel, lacking the rudiments, confounds everything. Now if we distinguish the person by the property of Spirit from the other two, will it be something fictitious because Valentinus does not grasp it? But we assert that the Spirit in the third person is God, because he is of spiritual essence, and nevertheless we preserve his own property for him.

units.la: XXVIII.
units.tr: XXVIII.

units.la: Pater & Filius non sunt, vt aiunt, ad aliquid nuda nomina relatiua sine veritate, quæ ad se insolidū ac sigillatim sint summa illa res, siue immensa substantia: sed simpliciter citra illam sophisticam exceptionem nomina sunt rerum sui[?]. substantialium, quæ quarta illam rem Scripturis sacris prorsus incognitam neque admittunt, neque agnoscunt.
units.tr: The Father and the Son are not, as they say, mere relative names without truth, which in themselves and individually are that supreme thing or immense substance; but simply, without that sophistical exception, they are names of substantial things, which neither admit nor acknowledge that fourth thing wholly unknown to the holy Scriptures.

units.la: Quod impugnat, ab vltima vsque vetustate docuerùt orthodoxi omnes Scriptores. Exurgit Valentinus, & suum decretum pro-nūtiat. Nulla ratio, nullum testimonium: imò quod temerè reiicit, à sensu communi dictatur. Filium negat esse nomen ad aliquid: negat relatiuè sumi. Pater ergo in se & ad se Pater erit. Filius itè ad se. Vnde sequetur Patrem esse absque Filio, & Filium absque Patre.
units.tr: What he attacks, all the orthodox writers have taught from the most ancient times. Valentinus rises up and pronounces his own decree: no reasoning, no testimony; indeed what he rashly rejects is dictated by common sense. He denies that Son is a relative name, and denies that it is taken relatively. Therefore the Father will be Father in himself and to himself, and the Son likewise to himself. Whence it will follow that the Father is without the Son, and the Son without the Father.

units.la: XXIX.
units.tr: XXIX.

units.la: Nisi Pater, Filius, & Spiritus tres essent intelligentes substantiæ eiusdem naturæ, falsò consubstantiales dicerentur.
units.tr: Unless Father, Son and Spirit were three intelligent substances of the same nature, they would be falsely called consubstantial.

units.la: Tu vero fallaciter insidias struis in voce ambigua. Scitur quo sensu veteres dixerint Filium Patri consubstantialem, nempe ut essentiæ vnitatem exprimeret. Hic impostor ad essentias numero di-stinctas crassa astutia trahit.
units.tr: But you lay deceitful snares in an ambiguous word. It is known in what sense the ancients called the Son consubstantial with the Father, namely to express the unity of essence. This impostor, with crude cunning, drags in essences distinct in number.

units.la: XXX.
units.tr: XXX.

units.la: Quicquid substantialiter alicunde est, non est idipsum vivens in individuo ex quo est, sed qualis ille est. Unde λόγος Dei non est unus ille αὐτόθεος cuius est λόγος: neque Spiritus Dei est Spiritus ille immensus ac sempiternus, cuius est Spiritus: licet uterque hypostaticè in eo contineatur, sitque cum illo unius eiusdemque divinitatis, plenitudinis ac perfectionis.
units.tr: Whatever is substantially from something else is not the very same living thing in the individual from which it is, but is such as that is. Hence the Word of God is not that one self-God [αὐτόθεος] of whom he is the Word, nor is the Spirit of God that immense and eternal Spirit of whom he is Spirit; although both are contained hypostatically in him, and are with him of one and the same divinity, fullness and perfection.

units.la: Voluit mundum aliquem creare ex duobus elementis, igni & aqua, hoc est rebus pugnantissimis. Verùm ut de repugnantia taceamus, quo iure λόγον infert non esse Deum, asi[?] cōcessum esset aliunde esse Christi essentiam? Ergo quò lōgius texet suo errores, eò maiore labyrintho se implicabit. Immensum verò Spiritū negare, non minus cæci furoris est. Sed quoniam hæc monstra detexisse, vicisse est, satis fuerit monuisse lectores, ut hæc secum placidè expendant.
units.tr: He wanted to create some world out of two elements, fire and water, that is, most opposed things. But to say nothing of the repugnance, by what right does he infer that the Word is not God, as if it had been granted that Christ's essence comes from elsewhere? Therefore the further he weaves his errors, the more deeply he entangles himself in a labyrinth. To deny the immense Spirit is no less the work of blind fury. But since to have uncovered these monsters is to have won the day, it will suffice to have warned the readers to weigh these things calmly for themselves.

units.la: XXXI.
units.tr: XXXI.

units.la: Λόγος ac Spiritus substantialis, generatio & processio Patris eminentiam tuentur, Turcas, Iudæos, hæreticos, sophistasque[?] prosternunt, atque omnes erro-res ab Ecclesia propellunt.
units.tr: The Word [Λόγος] and the Spirit, and the generation and procession of the Father, maintain the Father's pre-eminence, overthrow the Turks, the Jews and heretics and sophists, and drive out all errors from the Church.

units.la: Plausibilis color, quia Filium Dei abnegando, nodū Gordianum abrumpere sibi videtur Valentinus, suum errorem venditare, qui omnibus aliis deterior est. Sicut phreneticus olim quidam nullum melius compendium esse dictitabat ad tollenda Sanctorū patrocinia, superstitiosas pro mortuis preces, purgatorii figmentum, & si-milia, quàm si mortem, interitum esse animarum crederemus. At-qui orthodoxa fides, quam tuemur, hactenus non solùm contra Iu-dæos & Turcas, sed omnes inferorũ munitiones præualuit: atque ita mendacio Valentini non indiget, quin potius tales quisquilias dissipabit.
units.tr: It has a plausible colour, since Valentinus thinks he cuts the Gordian knot by denying the Son of God, and he hawks his error, which is worse than all the others. Just as a certain madman once kept saying that there was no better shortcut to abolish the patronage of the saints, superstitious prayers for the dead, the fiction of purgatory and the like, than to believe that death is the destruction of souls. But the orthodox faith we defend has so far prevailed not only against the Jews and Turks but against all the fortifications of hell. So it has no need of Valentinus's lie; rather, it will scatter such trifles.

units.la: XXXII.
units.tr: XXXII.

units.la: Qui Patrem à Filio, & Spiritum sanctum ab utroque hypostatice, hoc est, substantialiter, distingui negant, in falsa & absurda dogmata incidunt, omniá-que diuina mysteria necessario confundunt.
units.tr: Those who deny that the Father is distinguished from the Son, and the Holy Spirit from both, hypostatically, that is, substantially, fall into false and absurd doctrines and necessarily confuse all the divine mysteries.

units.la: Tolle istud tuum Substantialiter, quod perperam cum essentia confundis, vera erit propositio: quæ nunc salsissima est, quia hypo-stasin bruta inscitia tantundem valere putas atque ὁσίως[?].
units.tr: Remove that "substantially" of yours, which you wrongly confuse with essence, and the proposition will be true. As it is, it is most foolish, because in your brutish ignorance you think "hypostasis" means as much as "essence" [οὐσία].

units.la: XXXIII.
units.tr: XXXIII.

units.la: Confusio trium in unum & eundem numero Spiritum, fundamentum & origo omnium errorum & impietatum fuit.
units.tr: The confusion of three into one and the same numerical Spirit was the foundation and origin of all errors and impieties.

units.la: Nempe, Valétino authore, nisi Deus in tres essentias dividitur, concidit ac periit tota religio. Quid enim sunt tres Spiritus, nisi tripertita essentia?
units.tr: Indeed, on Valentinus's authority, unless God is divided into three essences, the whole religion collapses and perishes. For what are three Spirits, if not a tripartite essence?

units.la: XXXIIII.
units.tr: XXXIV.

units.la: Λόγος & Spiritus sanctus ita ab uno Deo Patre substantialiter distincti sunt, ut ab eius substantia separari non possint.
units.tr: The Word [Λόγος] and the Holy Spirit are so distinguished substantially from the one God the Father that they cannot be separated from his substance.

units.la: Pulchra vero connexio, si Filii substátia cum paterna cohæreat, quia inde abstracta, & ex traduce manauit: sicuti quibusdam visum est animas hominum alias ex aliis originem ducere.
units.tr: A fine connection indeed, if the Son's substance coheres with the Father's, yet is drawn off from it and flowed out by transmission, just as some have thought that the souls of men derive their origin one from another.

units.la: XXXV.
units.tr: XXXV.

units.la: Una Dei essentia non est Deus ipse, sed ipsius Dei natura, sive Deitatis plenitudo.
units.tr: The one essence of God is not God himself, but the nature of God himself, or the fullness of Deity.

units.la: Ergo male Deus apud Mosen à suo Esse cognosci voluit. Nā certè illic Essentia ponitur tanquam Dei definitio. Verum ut obtineat hic phreneticus quod sumit: vel non erit in ChristoDei natura, nec deitatis plenitudo, vel erit essentia Dei, quæ secundũ ipsum est Patris persona. Hoc modo Patris personam in Filium transfundit.
units.tr: Therefore God wrongly wished to be known by Moses from his Being. For certainly there Essence is put forward as the definition of God. But if this madman is to obtain what he assumes, either there will be in Christ no nature of God and no fullness of Deity, or there will be the essence of God, which by his own account is the person of the Father. In this way he transfers the person of the Father into the Son.

units.la: XXXVI.
units.tr: XXXVI.

units.la: Unus ille Iehova non essentia dici debet, sed unus essentiator.
units.tr: That one Jehovah ought to be called not essence but the one who gives essence.

units.la: Si tenuiter gustasses Hebraicæ linguæ elemeta, scires utrunque exprimi verbis Mosis: nempe Deum esse id quod vere est, & quod aliis esse dat. Cæterum si Iehoua est essentiator, ut tu fateris, Christus, quem Apostoli plus decies Iehouam esse affirmant, non fuit essentiatus, ut tu latras.
units.tr: If you had tasted even slightly the elements of the Hebrew language, you would know that both are expressed by the words of Moses: namely, that God is what truly is, and that which gives being to others. But if Jehovah is the giver of essence, as you admit, then Christ, whom the Apostles more than ten times affirm to be Jehovah, was not given essence, as you bark.

units.la: XXXVII.
units.tr: XXXVII.

units.la: Nisi Pater esset Filij ac Spiritus essentiator,id est,suorum attributorum per æternam generationem & processionem naturaliter communicator:neque tres unum essent, neque ulla reliquarum personarum esset plenus & perfectus Deus.
units.tr: Unless the Father were the giver of essence to the Son and the Spirit, that is, the natural communicator of their attributes through eternal generation and procession, the three would not be one, and neither of the remaining persons would be full and perfect God.

units.la: Quid phrenetice? si Christus vere & proprie sit Deus, ut fert no-stra fides, an perfectus nō erit? Perfectio autem erit maior, si tibi de-tur fuisse essentiatum, & aliunde habere ut sit Deus, & deitatem e-ius ex transfusione principium habere? Quid quod ante blaterasti, Pro modulo generationis, finitum esse non immensum?
units.tr: What do you mean, madman? If Christ is truly and properly God, as our faith holds, will he not be perfect? But will perfection be greater if you grant that he was given essence, and has from elsewhere that he is God, and that his deity has its origin from transfusion? What about what you babbled before, that according to the measure of generation he is finite, not immeasurable?

units.la: XXXVIII.
units.tr: XXXVIII.

units.la: Christus est plenus & perfectus Deus: quia integram Patris essentiam, hoc est, deitatis plenitudinem suo modulo metitur & capit.
units.tr: Christ is full and perfect God, because he measures and contains the whole essence of the Father, that is, the fullness of Deity, according to his own measure.

units.la: Eadem ratione quilibet ex Angelis perfectus erit Deus: quando omnes pro suo modulo capiunt Deitatis plenitudinem. En qualis sit Christi deificator hic sceleratus & quater periurus apostata.
units.tr: By the same reasoning, every one of the angels will be perfect God, since all of them take in the fullness of Deity according to their own measure. Behold what sort of deifier of Christ this wicked man is, a four-times perjured apostate.

units.la: XXXIX.
units.tr: XXXIX.

units.la: Calumniosè quidam Christum esse secundum, siue paruulum alium à Patre Deum ex nostris assertionibus imperito vulgo persuadere conatur, quum nos Filium eandem deitatis plenitudinem cum Patre & à Patre habere constanter testamur, firmiter credimus, & diserte confitemur.
units.tr: Some men, slanderously, try to persuade the unskilled crowd from our assertions that Christ is a second God, or a little God other than the Father; whereas we constantly testify, firmly believe and plainly confess that the Son has the same fullness of Deity as the Father, and has it from the Father.

units.la: Quod odiosum, adeoque prorsus intolerabile esse videt, cuperet diluere: sed nuper magis fuit disertus, quàm ut leui fuco impietatem suam obtegat. Nobis verò quicquam persuadere necesse non est: quia eius assertiones sponte impietatem suam produnt.
units.tr: He sees that this charge seems hateful and utterly intolerable, and would like to refute it. But he has lately been more eloquent than fit to cover his impiety with a light veneer. For our part, there is no need to persuade anyone of anything, since his assertions betray his impiety of their own accord.

units.la: XL.
units.tr: XL.

units.la: Unus Iehoua Pater λόγου, & unus ille Deus Israel, synonyma sunt primæ personæ Trinitatis.
units.tr: One Jehovah, the Father of the Word [Λόγος], and that one God of Israel, are synonyms of the first person of the Trinity.

units.la: Quum deitatis definitio, cuius author est ipse Deus, αὐτουσίαν in se contineat, Christus certè desinet esse Deus. Adde quòd si Iehoua unus est Deus, Apostolis, qui hoc nomine Christum ornarunt, potiùs credendum est, quàm cani, qui eorum authoritatem suo vomitu conspurcat. Demonstravi enim Christi personæ aptare quod dicitur apud Iesaiam, Vivo ego, dicit Iehova: Iohannem similiter eiusdem Prophetæ vaticinium, Vidi Iehovam sedentem in solio: alium Apostolum ex Psalmo citare, non de Patre solo, sed de Filio pronuntiatum, Tu Iehova idem semper es. Iam si Pater fuit solus Deus Israel, quomodo Filius in templum suum dicitur ven-turus? Teplum enim nō nisi vni Deo fuisse dicatū probè intellexit Malachias:quod tamen sub Christi ditione esse asserit. Denique, si non fuit Christus Deus Israel, non adorauit Abraham eum in di-vina essentia, quem Angeli exhibitum adorant: sicuti rursum A-postolus prodiisse in orbem terrarum Christum docet cum hoc iure imperii, Adorent eum omnes Angeli. Quid porrò absurdius, quàm Deũ, qui præerat veteri populo, erátque dux eius & custos, non fuisse adoratum à sanctis Patribus: adorari vero cœptum ab Angelis, ex quo factus est homo? Posthac quidem nullus erit color, cur se calumniis gravari queratur: quia ex meris eius verbis iudi-cium de eius impietate ferri postulo. Convitia quibus Deum im-petit, refellere supersedeo pluribus, quia sine horrore attingi ne-queunt, atque, ut tacea, recident in eius caput. Contremiscet ali-quando ad tribunal eius Dei, cuius gloriâ omni probro conspuere pro diabolica sua superbia, cæcóque furore non metuit: imò sen-tiet quàm terribili modò fulminet contra se-curos nominis sui con-temptores.
units.tr: Since the definition of deity, whose author is God himself, contains self-existence [αὐτουσία] in itself, Christ certainly ceases to be God. Add that if Jehovah is the one God, it is more right to believe the Apostles, who honoured Christ with this name, than this dog, who defiles their authority with his vomit. For I have shown that what is said in Isaiah, "As I live, saith Jehovah," applies to the person of Christ; likewise the prophecy of the same prophet, "I saw Jehovah sitting on a throne"; and that another Apostle quotes from a Psalm, declared not of the Father alone but of the Son, "Thou, Jehovah, art the same always." Now if the Father was the sole God of Israel, how is the Son said to be coming to his own temple? For Malachi clearly understood that the temple was dedicated to one God alone, yet he asserts that it is under Christ's dominion. Finally, if Christ was not the God of Israel, Abraham did not adore him in the divine essence, whom the angels, when displayed, worship; and again the Apostle teaches that Christ, when he went forth into the world, was given this right of rule: "Let all the angels of God worship him." What could be more absurd than that God, who presided over the ancient people and was their leader and guardian, was not worshipped by the holy Fathers, but began to be worshipped by the angels only from the time he became man? Henceforth there will be no pretext for his complaining that he is burdened with slanders, since I demand that judgment of his impiety be passed on his own words alone. I refrain from refuting at length the insults with which he assails God, since they cannot be touched without horror, and, to say nothing more, they will fall back on his own head. Someday he will tremble before the tribunal of that God whose glory he, in his diabolical pride and blind fury, is not afraid to spit upon with every insult. Indeed, he will feel with what terrible force God thunders against those who carelessly despise his name.

units.la: AD QUÆSTIONES GEORGII BLANDRATAE, RESPONSUM D. Ioannis Caluini.
units.tr: Reply of Dr. John Calvin to the Questions of George Blandrata

units.la: QUUM dicimus nos credere in unü Deum, sub Dei nomine intelligimus unicam & simplicem essentiam, in qua comprehendimus tres personas vel hypostaseis.
units.tr: When we say that we believe in one God, by the name of God we understand one single and simple essence, in which we comprehend three persons or hypostases.

units.la: Ergo quoties Dei nomen indefinitè ponitur, non minùs Filium & Spiritũ sanctum quàm Patrem designari credimus. Vbi autem adiungitur Filius Patri, tunc in medium venit relatio, atque ita distinguimus inter personas.
units.tr: Therefore, whenever the name God is used without qualification, we believe that the Son and the Holy Spirit are designated no less than the Father. But when the Son is joined to the Father, then relation comes into play, and so we distinguish between the persons.

units.la: Quia verò proprietates in personis ordinem suum ferùt, ut in Patre sit principium & origo, quoties fit mentio Patris & Filii simul, vel Spiritus, nomen Dei peculiariter Patri tribuitur.
units.tr: Since the properties belong to the persons in their own order, so that in the Father there is principle and origin, whenever the Father and the Son or the Spirit are mentioned together, the name God is assigned particularly to the Father.

units.la: Hoc modo retinetur unitas essentiæ, & habetur ratio ordinis: quæ tamen ex Filii & Spiritus unitate nihil minuit.
units.tr: In this way the unity of essence is preserved, and the order is maintained; yet this order takes nothing away from the unity of the Son and the Spirit.

units.la: Quòd unica sit Patris & Filii & Spiritus essentia, ex claris Scripturæ testimoniis constat. Certè unus est Iehova: quod nomen Filio commune est cum Patre.
units.tr: That the essence of Father, Son and Spirit is one is established by clear testimonies of Scripture. Surely there is one Jehovah, and this name is common to the Son with the Father.

units.la: Si quis excipiat, trásferri elogium hoc ad Christum, quia ex Patre ortus sit: facilè refellitur tam frivolum cavillum, quia unus est Iehova.
units.tr: If anyone objects that this title is transferred to Christ because he was born of the Father, such a frivolous quibble is easily refuted, because there is one Jehovah.

units.la: Jam quum Apostoli Filium Dei asserât illū esse, quem Moses & Prophetæ testati sunt esse Iehovam, semper ad unitatem essentiæ venire necesse est.
units.tr: Since the Apostles assert that the Son of God is he whom Moses and the Prophets testified to be Jehovah, we must always come back to the unity of essence.

units.la: Proinde nobis sacrilegium detestabile est, Filium alium Deum vocari à Patre, quia simplex nomen Dei relationem non admittit: nec potest Deus ad seipsum dici, hoc, vel illud esse.
units.tr: Therefore it is a detestable sacrilege to us that the Son should be called another God from the Father, since the simple name God does not admit of relation, nor can God be said to be this or that with respect to himself.

units.la: Nomen verò personæ dum Christo ascribitur, bifariam dici potest. Nam & Sermo ex Patre genitus ante mundi creationem, persona est in æterna essentia Dei. Et quemadmodum unus est Christus Deus in carne manifestatus: ita duæ naturæ sic unitæ personam unam constituunt. Ideóque aliud est loqui de æterna Dei Sapientia antequam indueret carnem, vel de Mediatore ex quo in carne patefactus est.
units.tr: The name of person, however, when it is ascribed to Christ, can be used in two ways. For the Word begotten of the Father before the creation of the world is a person within the eternal essence of God. And just as Christ is one God manifested in the flesh, so two natures united in this way constitute one person. Therefore it is one thing to speak of the eternal Wisdom of God before he put on flesh, and another to speak of the Mediator from the time he was revealed in the flesh.

units.la: In hanc Mediatoris personam proprie competit nomen Domini, quatenus medium gradum statuit inter Deum & nos. Quò pertinet illud Pauli, Unus Deus ex quo omnia, & unus Dominus per quem omnia. Eodem sensu illud accipitur, Pater maior me est: & quæ alia de Mediatore dicitur apud Iohannem. Cæterùm vbi simpliciter Christus vocatur Deus, & non opponitur nomen Patris, solida Dei essentia comprehēditur. Sicuti quùm dicitur Ioh. 1. Sermo ille erat Deus: tenenda est essentiæ vnitas. Similiter vbi Paulus dicit, Deum esse benedictum in secula: non alium Deum fas est imaginari, quàm illum qui per Mosen asseruit, se vnicum & solum esse: & qui per Esaiam iurauit, se non daturum alteri suam gloriam. Ideo Iohannes non contentus Dei nomine, expressius loquitur in fine canonicæ Epist. Hic est verus Deus & vita æterna.
units.tr: To this person of the Mediator the name of Lord properly belongs, insofar as he holds an intermediate place between God and us. To this refers that saying of Paul: "One God, from whom are all things, and one Lord, through whom are all things." In the same sense is to be understood, "The Father is greater than I," and the other things said of the Mediator in John. Moreover, where Christ is simply called God, and the name of the Father is not opposed to him, the whole essence of God is comprehended. Just as when it is said in John 1, "That Word was God," the unity of essence must be held. Similarly, where Paul says that God is blessed forever, it is not right to imagine any other God than he who through Moses asserted that he alone is one and only, and who through Isaiah swore that he would not give his glory to another. Therefore John, not content with the name God, speaks more expressly at the end of his canonical Epistle: "This is the true God and eternal life."

units.la: Quòd nomen Iehouæ indefinitè sumptum, in Christum competat, patet etiam ex Pauli verbis, Propterea ter rogaui Dominum: quia subiicit paulò post, Vt inhabitet in me virtus Christi.
units.tr: That the name Jehovah, taken without qualification, belongs to Christ is also plain from the words of Paul: "Therefore I besought the Lord three times," for he adds shortly after, "that the power of Christ may dwell in me."

units.la: Quòd autem Christus, vbi de Patre loquitur, Dei nomine ipsum insignit, nō mirum est: quia expendere conuenit quam personam sustineat. Quatenus enim Mediator est, officij sui respectu se inferiore gradu locat, vt nos paulatim ad Patrem ducat.
units.tr: That Christ, however, when he speaks of the Father, marks him with the name God is no wonder, for we ought to consider what person he sustains. For insofar as he is Mediator, with respect to his office he places himself in a lower rank, so that he may gradually lead us to the Father.

units.la: Hoc autem respectu Filius ipse subiicitur Patri in futuro seculo, quia ipsa Diuinitatis perfectio tunc nobis erit conspicua, quæ nunc in imagine pro nostro modulo nobis relucet.
units.tr: In this respect, moreover, the Son himself will be subject to the Father in the future age, because the very perfection of the Godhead will then be visible to us, which now shines upon us in an image, according to our measure.

units.la: Et tamē Christus, licet raro, Dei mentionem indefinitam facit, velut quùm dicit Ioh. 4, Deus Spiritus est: quod eius personæ non minùs quàm Patris conuenit. Nec obstat quòd mox exprimit nomen Patris: quia vbi doctrinam generalem tradidit, eandem pro Mediatoris officio confirmat.
units.tr: And yet Christ, though rarely, makes an indefinite mention of God, as when he says in John 4, "God is Spirit," which applies to his person no less than to the Father's. Nor does it stand in the way that he soon expresses the name of the Father, because when he has delivered a general doctrine, he confirms it with reference to the office of the Mediator.

units.la: Hoc modo Christus nō aliū Deum manifestauit quàm Patrem: quia ipsum ad nos descendere necesse fuit, vt fidem nostram ad gloriam Deitatis attolleret. Interea notandum est eius dictum, Creditis in Deum? etiam in me credite. Quo significat illum se esse Deum, in quo acquiescere debet fides.
units.tr: In this way Christ revealed no other God than the Father, because it was necessary for him to come down to us, so that he might raise our faith to the glory of the Deity. Meanwhile it is to be noted what he said: "You believe in God? Believe also in me." By this he signifies that he is the God in whom faith ought to rest.

units.la: Quùm vero Legis summam colligit, nomen Dei indefinitè ponēs, sibi nihil derogat: sed contentus est recepta loquendi forma. Sicuti eius interrogatio illa, Quid me vocas bonum? Vnus Deus bonus est: non eò tendit, vt Deitatis gloriam à seipso reiiciat: quin potiùs se alio modo esse bonum subindicat, quàm intellexerat adolescens, humanæ bonitatis elogio eum honorans.
units.tr: When he gathers up the sum of the Law, using the name God without qualification, he does not detract from himself, but is content with the accepted form of speech. Just as in his question, "Why do you call me good? One God is good," he is not aiming to take away the glory of the Godhead from himself; rather he hints that he is good in another way than the young man had understood, honouring him with a title of human goodness.

units.la: Similiter Iudæis exprobrans, quòd Deum iactarent esse suum Deum: quia tamen eius Filium respuebãt, vanitatē eorum refellit, quòd Mediatorem propinquum non agnoscant, quū fallaci Dei nominis obtentu magnificè transuolent supra nubes.
units.tr: Likewise, rebuking the Jews because they boasted that God was their God, yet rejected his Son, he refutes their vanity, in that they do not acknowledge the Mediator who is near, while under the false pretext of the name of God they magnificently fly above the clouds.

units.la: Paulus 10. prioris ad Cor. tametsi expresso[?] Deum vnum Idolis opponit, non tamen abs re Patrem nominat, ex quo omnia: quia relatiuè continuò post Mediatorem adiungit. Sed alibi vnum Deũ esse docens, sicut vnum Baptisma, certè Iehouam esse intelligit. Et quamuis paulò post diserte Patrem nominat, id facit, quia ad Christum descendere volebat: ideóque adhibenda fuit talis distinctio. Nam vnitatem Dei & Baptismi coniungens, certè Christum nō excludit, in cuius nomine baptisamur. Conueniunt igitur optimè inter se appellatio Dei simplex ac definita, & distinctio Dei Patris à Christo Mediatore.
units.tr: Paul, in 1 Cor. 10, although he sets the one God over against idols, nevertheless names the Father not without reason, "from whom are all things," because immediately after he adds the Mediator in a relative sense. But when elsewhere he teaches that there is one God, just as there is one Baptism, he certainly understands it to be Jehovah. And although shortly afterwards he expressly names the Father, he does so because he wished to come down to Christ, and therefore such a distinction had to be used. For in joining the unity of God and of Baptism, he certainly does not exclude Christ, in whose name we are baptized. Therefore the simple and definite designation of God and the distinction of God the Father from Christ the Mediator agree very well with one another.

units.la: Quòd initio Epistolarum Patrem Deum priore loco statuens, deinde Christum adiungit, ex eadem ratione manat: quia deitatem statuit in Patris nomine, deinde Mediatorem interponit, qui nos ad Deum erigat. Sed in eadem epistola vbi ita loquutus erat, non tamen dubitat Christum vocare Deum in secula benedictum.
units.tr: It follows from the same reasoning that, at the beginning of the Epistles, he places God the Father first and then adds Christ, because he sets the Godhead in the name of the Father, and then interposes the Mediator, who raises us up to God. But in the same Epistle, where he has spoken in this way, he nevertheless does not hesitate to call Christ God blessed forever.

units.la: Hinc sequitur quærendũ esse Deum, in cuius essentia comprehenduntur tres personæ: & tamen vbi in medium prodit Christus, Deum verè & propriè vocari Patrem Iesu Christi, quia tũc Mediatoris gradum obtinet Christus, vt nos ad Deum attollat, & ita ad seipsum.
units.tr: From this it follows that we must seek a God in whose essence the three persons are comprehended; and yet, when Christ comes forward, God is truly and properly called the Father of Jesus Christ, because then Christ holds the rank of Mediator, to raise us up to God, and thus to himself.

units.la: Quòd ad locum illum attinet, Ascendo ad Patrem meum & Patrem vestrum, confirmat & apertius declarat quòd iã dixi, vbi Christus loquitur in Mediatoris persona, quodammodo descendere infra Deum, vt nobis sit propior. Sed hoc non obstat, quo minus ipse quoque verus sit Deus noster. Nam quod dicit Thomas, non aliunde quàm ex eius ore didicerat, Dominus meus & Deus meus.
units.tr: As for that passage, "I ascend to my Father and your Father," it confirms and more plainly declares what I have already said: where Christ speaks in the person of the Mediator, he in some measure descends below God, so as to be nearer to us. But this does not prevent him from being also the true God of us. For what Thomas says, "My Lord and my God," he had learned from no other source than from the mouth of Christ himself.

units.la: De nomine Personæ ita breuiter respondeo, necessitate esse inuectũ ad detegendas eorum fraudes, qui hoc fidei principiũ aflutè subuertere moliebantur. Interea obiicere sententias, vbi se Christus à Patre distinguens, hac voce abstinet, putidũ est cauillum. Neque enim hac loquendi forma in communi sermone vtimur, Persona Patris salutem nobis contulit per Filij personam: sed vbi distinctionem exprimere volumus, quæ est inter Patrem & Filium.
units.tr: Concerning the name of Person I respond briefly thus: it was introduced out of necessity, to expose the frauds of those who were craftily striving to subvert this foundation of faith. Meanwhile, to object to sayings in which Christ, distinguishing himself from the Father, refrains from this word, is a foolish quibble. For we do not use this form of speech in common discourse, as in "the Person of the Father brought us salvation through the person of the Son"; but we use it when we wish to express the distinction that exists between the Father and the Son.

units.la: Quod ad Christi dictum spectat, Hæc est vita æterna, vt credant in te verum Deum, &c. Si eius prætextu restringi debeat vera diuinitas ad vnum Patrem, mentitus esset Iohannes dicendo, Hic est verus Deus & vita æterna.
units.tr: As for the saying of Christ, "This is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, etc.," if the true deity were to be restricted to the Father alone on the pretext of this saying, John would have lied in saying, "This is the true God and eternal life."

units.la: Vnicam verò essentiam in tribus personis nō fuisse à Christo patefactam, salsissimum est. Nam quum voluit nos baptisari in nomine Patris, & Filij, & Spiritus sancti, has certè personas distinctè posuit, quas extra Dei essentiam quærere nefas est.
units.tr: It is most absurd to say that Christ did not reveal the single essence in three persons. When he commanded that we be baptized in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, he certainly set these persons apart as distinct, and it is wrong to look for them outside the essence of God.

units.la: Iam vbi Iohannes dicit, Sermonem ab initio fuisse Deum, certè non lacerat Dei essentiam: sed clarè docet vnum & eundem fuisse Deum cum Patre.Ubi vero statim subiicit, fuisse apud Deum, vel caecis ipsis monstratur distinctio. Item quum Christus ipse postulat manifestari gloriam, quam initio habuit apud Patrem ante creationem mundi: certe personam sibi tribuit peculiarem, & interea eandem sibi essentiam cum Patre vendicat: quia Dei gloria & maiestas separari ab essentia non potuit.
units.tr: When John says that the Word was God from the beginning, he certainly does not tear apart the essence of God, but clearly teaches that the Word was one and the same God with the Father. But when he immediately adds that he was with God, the distinction is shown even to the blind. Likewise, when Christ himself asks that the glory he had with the Father before the creation of the world be made manifest, he certainly claims for himself a peculiar person, and at the same time claims for himself the same essence as the Father, because the glory and majesty of God cannot be separated from his essence.

units.la: Similiter quum Petrus dicit Ananiæ, Cur mentitus es Spiritui sancto? non hominibus mentitus es, sed Deo: non minus Christus ipse & Spiritus, quam Pater comprehenditur. Sicuti quum idem Petrus & Johannes respondent, Deo magis quam hominibus obediendum esse, Christum certe non excludunt: sed quia nomen Dei ponunt indefinite, non minus Deum in carne manifestatum quam Patrem designant.
units.tr: Similarly, when Peter says to Ananias, "Why have you lied to the Holy Spirit? You have not lied to men, but to God," he includes not less Christ and the Spirit than the Father. Likewise, when Peter and John answer that God must be obeyed rather than men, they certainly do not exclude Christ, but because they use the name of God without qualification, they designate God manifested in the flesh no less than the Father.

units.la: Quòd si cui nimis morosò displiceat nomen Personæ, certè Apostolus 1. ad Heb.per hypostasin nihil aliud intelligit, quam quod nos personam vocamus. Atque ita est relatio, de qua litigant cōtentiosi homines, ac si esset humanum commentum.
units.tr: But if the name "person" displeases anyone who is too fastidious, certainly the Apostle in Heb. 1 understands by "hypostasis" nothing other than what we call a person. And so the relation about which contentious men quarrel is in fact just that, as if it were a human invention.

units.la: Quòd ad precandi formam spectat, illa est ordinaria quæ nobis in Euangelio præscribitur, dum ad Patrem verba dirigimus in Christi nomine.
units.tr: As for the form of prayer, that is the ordinary one prescribed to us in the Gospel, when we direct our words to the Father in the name of Christ.

units.la: Cæterùm ubi nulla fit Christi mentio, nō minùs sub Dei nomine ad Filium quàm ad Patrem dirigitur precatio, sicuti dilucidè patet ex loco illo Pauli, Propterea ter rogaui Dominū: & respondit mihi, Sufficit tibi gratia mea: cùm statim subiiciat, Libenter gloriabor super infirmitatibus meis, ut inhabitet in me virtus Christi. Unde sequitur Christum esse Deum illum quem Paulus rogauerat.
units.tr: But where there is no mention of Christ, prayer is directed to the Son under the name of God no less than to the Father, as is clearly evident from that passage of Paul: "Concerning this I besought the Lord three times, and he said to me, 'My grace is sufficient for you'" (2 Cor. 12), since he immediately adds, "I will gladly boast of my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me." From this it follows that Christ is that God whom Paul had besought.

units.la: Porrò vocem Domini restringere ad personam Mediatoris, friuolum est ac puerile, quum passim Apostoli usurpet nomen Domini pro Jehoua. Et ne procul quærendum sit exemplū, nō alio sensu orauit Dominum Paulus, quàm quo citatur locus Johelis à Petro, Quisquis invocauerit nomen Domini, salvus erit.
units.tr: Moreover, to restrict the voice "Lord" to the person of the Mediator is frivolous and childish, since the Apostles everywhere use the name "Lord" for Jehovah. And, lest we seek an example far away, Paul prayed to the Lord in no other sense than that in which Peter quotes the passage of Joel: "Whoever calls on the name of the Lord will be saved."

units.la: Similiter quiu[?] hac forma precantur Discipuli, Tu Domine qui nosti corda omnium, nō seorsum convertunt ad Christum sermonem, quia separatim ei elogium non quadraret: sed fides illorum Dei essentiam simpliciter respicit. Denique ubi nulla est relatio, nomen Dei ad Filiũ & Spiritum sanctũ extenditur.
units.tr: Likewise, when the disciples pray in this form, "You, Lord, who know the hearts of all," they do not turn their speech separately to Christ, because such a title would not fit him separately; but their faith looks simply to the essence of God. Finally, where there is no relation expressed, the name of God extends to the Son and the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Si quæritur, an non tutior precandi forma sit, dum invocamus Patrem in nomine Filij? Respondeo sicut iā dixi, hanc esse ordinariā & magis familiarem, quæ aptior est ruditati nostræ & utilior. Sed alias formas quæ etiam in usu fuerunt Apostolis, & quas illis Spiritus sanctus dictauit damnare, sacrilegæ temeritatis esset. Nec valet illa obiectio, Frustra Deum invocari absque Mediatore : quia etsi fixum est illud principium, Non exaudiri nos nisi per gra-tiam Mediatoris, non semper tamen in promptu occurrere necesse est.
units.tr: If it is asked whether a form of prayer that invokes the Father in the name of the Son is not safer, I answer, as I have said already, that this is the ordinary and more familiar form, which is better suited to our weakness and more useful. But to condemn other forms, which were also in use among the Apostles and which the Holy Spirit dictated to them, would be sacrilegious rashness. Nor does that objection hold, "God is invoked in vain without a Mediator," because although that principle is fixed, that we are not heard except through the grace of the Mediator, it is not necessary that it always be present to mind.

units.la: Quæstio ista, An Patrem rogando, rogemus verum Deum, ex ignorantia principij nascitur. neque enim epithetū Veri Patrem à Filio discernit: quia no-men Dei essentiam illam designat, quæ complectitur tres personas: atque ita nulla est antithesis quod attinet ad unam deitatem.
units.tr: This question, "When we pray to the Father, do we pray to the true God?", arises from ignorance of the principle. For the epithet "true" does not distinguish the Father from the Son, since the name God designates that essence which embraces the three persons; and so there is no contrast as far as the one deity is concerned.

units.la: Ad hæc Patrem rogando, ad Filij quoque Deitatem preces dirigimus, quan-vis medius ipse quoque nobis occurrat. Diversi enim respectus nobis notandi sunt: quia etsi quod Patri proprium est, respicet in eius persona, nec Filio convenit, Deus tamen in sua essentia totus & integer manet. ac proinde hæc inter se non pugnant, rogari Patrem Filij respectu, & Dei in solida (ut ita loquar) essentia: non quia ullo modo sit partibilis, sed quia nihil absurdi est dum conci-pimus deitatem Patri, Filio & Spiritui communem, si intuitus Filij mentes nostras reflectit ad Patris Personam.
units.tr: Moreover, in praying to the Father we direct our prayers also to the deity of the Son, although he too presents himself to us as mediator. For we must observe different respects: because, although what is proper to the Father regards his person and does not belong to the Son, God nevertheless remains whole and entire in his essence. Therefore these things do not contradict one another: that the Father is asked with respect to the Son, and that God is asked in his solid (so to speak) essence; not because it is in any way divisible, but because there is nothing absurd in conceiving of a deity common to the Father, the Son and the Spirit, if the regard for the Son directs our minds to the person of the Father.

units.la: Jam etsi Mediator est Christus quatenus Deus est in carne manifestatus: ideóque secundum utramque naturam: humanæ tamen naturæ ratione & proprie tribuitur intercedendi officium, idque in subsidium nostræ tarditatis. Unde & Paulus eum nobis advocatū proponens, hominem potius quàm Deum vocat. Et certè ut carnem suam offerens victimam, sacerdotis officio functus est in carne: ita & intercedit pro nobis.
units.tr: Now, although Christ is Mediator inasmuch as he is God manifested in the flesh, and so according to both natures, the office of interceding is nevertheless properly ascribed to him in respect of his human nature, and that for our help in our slowness. Hence Paul, when he presents him to us as our advocate, calls him man rather than God. And certainly, as he offered his flesh as the victim, performing the office of priest in the flesh, so also he intercedes for us.

units.la: Dum invocatur Christus ipse, quod Ananias ab omnibus pijs factum esse testatur, & Stephani exēplo ritè sanctéque fieri cōstat: nō homini per se defer-tur hic honor, sive ratione humanitatis: sed æterno Dei Filio, qui ut nobis salutem acquireret carnem nostram induit. Est enim precatio sacrificium, quod sibi uni Deus vendicat. Ideóque ad nudum hominem nihilo magis illud trans-ferre fas est, quàm alias divini cultus partes. Atque ita invocatur Christus ut Deus qui ex seipso author est omnium bonorum: & Stephanus plena Deitatis potentia eum ornat, spiritum suum in eius manus commendans.
units.tr: When Christ himself is invoked, as Ananias testifies was done by all the godly, and as it is established that it is rightly and holily done by the example of Stephen, this honour is not transferred to a mere man on account of his humanity, but to the eternal Son of God, who took on our flesh in order to win salvation for us. For prayer is a sacrifice, which God claims for himself alone. Therefore it is no more lawful to transfer that to a bare man than other parts of divine worship. And so Christ is invoked as God, who is of himself the author of all good things; and Stephen adorns him with the full power of the Deity, when he commends his spirit into his hands.

units.la: Quæstio, An æternus Sermo Dei sit aliquid substantivum & essentiale, ambigua est: ac proinde captiosa esse potest. De nomine Substantiæ, tenendum est non esse proprie substantiam, sed hypostasin. Si tamen aliter accipere li-beat, facile concedo. Itaque Sermo est aliquid hypostaticum. Sed quùm Sermo ipse vere sit Deus, essentiam designat. Sic tamen habendum est, Sermonem es-sentialiter esse Deum, & tamen in hac voce simul esse personæ notationem. Persona autem in ipsa essentia subsistit.
units.tr: The question, "Is the eternal Word of God something substantive and essential?", is ambiguous, and therefore it can be captious. Concerning the name "substance", it must be held that properly speaking he is not substance but hypostasis. If, however, one prefers to take it otherwise, I readily concede it. Thus the Word is something hypostatic. But since the Word is truly God, he designates the essence. Yet it must be held that the Word is essentially God, and that at the same time this term also marks a person. A person, moreover, subsists in the essence itself.

units.la: Ex superioribus colligere promptum est, si quis syncerè & absque fuco vel fallacia credat in Deum Patrem,in Dominum Iesum Christum,& in vnum Spiritum:id sufficere. Sed inde simul elicere licet,fucum facere,qui se in Christum credere profitentur,cuius æterna Deitatem abnegant. Similiter in Spiritum, quem non putant Deum esse, si Pater sit Deus. Tales enim essentiam Dei discerpere palàm est,nec vnitatem retinere,quùm Patris Diuinitatem asserere nequeant,nisi eam detrahant Filio & Spiritui sancto.
units.tr: From what has been said above, it is easy to gather that if anyone believes sincerely and without pretence or deceit in God the Father, in the Lord Jesus Christ, and in the one Spirit, that is sufficient. But from this it can also be inferred that those who profess to believe in Christ, while denying his eternal Deity, are playing a trick. Likewise with the Spirit, whom they do not think to be God if the Father is God. For it is plain that such people tear apart the essence of God, and do not keep its unity, since they cannot assert the divinity of the Father unless they take it away from the Son and the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Qui verò fidem orthodoxam odiosè calumniatur hoc prætextu, quòd speculatio de vnica essentia & tribus personis inutilis sit, improbam malitiam produnt: quia non speculamur vltrà quàm scriptura nos attollit: sed geminum & simplicem eius sensum reddimus. Nemo enim Christum ex animo agnoscet Deum suum,nisi qui in essentiæ vnitate diuersas personas apprehenderit, vt ea deorum pluralitas,quam fingunt nonnulli,execrabile sit delirium.
units.tr: But those who maliciously slander the orthodox faith on this pretext, that speculation about the one essence and three persons is useless, betray a wicked malice; for we do not speculate beyond what Scripture lifts us up to, but render its twofold and simple sense. For no one will acknowledge Christ from his heart as his God unless he has grasped distinct persons in the unity of the essence; otherwise that plurality of gods which some invent would be an execrable delirium.

units.la: Et quibus nimis arguta videtur hæc distinctio, monendi sunt, vt attentius quàm exitialis sit sua ficta simplicitas expendant. Quia vbi Christum professi fuerint esse Deum, nunquam ex Sathanæ laqueis aliter se expedient,quàm ista distinctione quam fugiunt,interposita.
units.tr: And those to whom this distinction seems too subtle are to be warned to weigh more carefully how deadly is their invented simplicity. For when they have professed Christ to be God, they will never extricate themselves from the snares of Satan otherwise than by this distinction, which they flee.

units.la: Huc spectauit Nicænum Concilium, vbi asseruit Christum esse Deum de Deo. Neque enim duos fabricare voluit Deos,sed, quanuis à Patre distinctus sit Filius,veruntamen Deum esse & eundem cum ipso,excepta personæ notatione.
units.tr: To this the Council of Nicaea looked, when it asserted that Christ is God of God. For it did not wish to fashion two gods; but, although the Son is distinct from the Father, he is nevertheless God and the same with him, except for the designation of person.

units.la: Sic quum Athanasius & reliqui veteres dixerunt coessentialem Patri Filium:non aliud cesuerunt[?],quàm eiusdem esse essentiæ,quia vnica sit & indiuidua. Qui autem duos numero faciunt Deos,nunquam ex hoc absurdo elabi poterunt,quin partibilem faciant essentiam Dei.
units.tr: So when Athanasius and the other ancients said that the Son is coessential with the Father, they meant nothing other than that he is of the same essence, because that essence is one and indivisible. But those who make two Gods in number can never escape this absurdity without making the essence of God divisible.

units.la: Ita dixerunt tres coæternos,& tamen Deum vnum æternum:quia non nisi in vno Deo residet æternitas,quæ tamen tribus personis est communis. Atque vt duæ naturæ constituunt vnum Christum,quia idem Deus & homo duabus constat naturis: ita tres personæ constituunt vnicum Deum,quia eius essentia,quæ vna est & simplex,constat tribus personis.
units.tr: So they spoke of three coeternal persons and yet of one eternal God, because eternity resides in the one God alone, though it is common to the three persons. Just as two natures make up the one Christ, since the same person who is God and man consists of two natures, so three persons make up the one God, since his essence, which is one and simple, consists of three persons.

units.la: Vbi de Christo loquitur Scriptura,nunc quæ propria sunt humanæ naturæ,nunc quæ in solam Deitatem competunt,ei tribuit:sæpius verò complectitur vtranque naturam,& Mediatoris personam describit. Itaque prudenter consideranda sunt elogia,quæ nec homini,nec Deo seorsum conueniunt: sed Deo manifestato in carne. qualia ferè sunt quæ leguntur in Euangelio Ioh. à 3. cap.vsque ad 18.
units.tr: Where Scripture speaks of Christ, it sometimes attributes to him what is proper to human nature and sometimes what belongs to the Deity alone; but more often it embraces both natures and describes the person of the Mediator. Therefore the sayings that fit neither man nor God taken separately, but God manifested in the flesh, must be weighed carefully. Such are most of those read in the Gospel of John from chapter 3 to 18.

units.la: Iam quæ prædicantur de Christo,specialem interdum respectum habent ad alterā naturam. Sicuti Christi nomen non tantùm homini, sed Deo in carne manifestato convenit, unctio tamen proprie ad humanitatem refertur. Mediator Deus & homo, verè est Filius Dei secundùm utramque naturam ratione unionis, proprie tamen Divinitatis respectu, quia Sermo est ante secula à Patre genitus. Sermo enim caro factus dicitur, quia carnem induit, ut qui æternus erat Deus, idem homo quoque mortalis esset: nec solùm ut humanitas templum esset deitatis, sed ut naturis duabus in unam personam unitis, ille per quem creati, idem esset & Redemptor noster.
units.tr: Now, what is predicated of Christ sometimes has a special reference to one nature or the other. Thus the name Christ belongs not only to the man but to God manifested in the flesh, yet the anointing is properly referred to the humanity. The Mediator, God and man, is truly the Son of God according to both natures by reason of the union, yet properly with respect to his Divinity, because he is the Word begotten of the Father before all ages. For the Word is said to have become flesh because he put on flesh, so that he who was eternal God might also be a mortal man; and this was not only so that the humanity might be a temple of the Deity, but so that, the two natures being united in one person, he through whom all things were created might also be our Redeemer.

units.la: Omnes loquendi formulas quibus usi sunt veteres excutere, nimis longum foret[?]. Nam & hoc ineffabile mysterium nullis humanis sermonibus proprie & pro dignitate unquam explicabitur: & suum quisque loquendi modum habet, ut in optimo cōsensu aliter tamen hic loquatur quàm ille. Piè & rectè censuerunt Iustinus & Tertullianus, nec utrique propositum fuit docere aliud quàm nos fatemur. Sed quia ille non tam erat exercitatus, hic verò posterior aspero ubique & spinoso loquendi modo utitur: non mirum est si loquutiones alicubi occurrant cavillis obnoxiæ: quarum tamen facilis est excusatio, modò facessat libido rixandi & calumniandi.
units.tr: It would be too long to go through all the forms of speech the ancients used. For this ineffable mystery will never be explained properly and worthily by any human words, and each writer has his own manner of speaking, so that, in the best agreement, one speaks here differently from another. Justin and Tertullian judged piously and rightly, and neither intended to teach anything other than what we confess. But because the former was not so practised, and the latter, who came later, uses a harsh and thorny manner of speaking throughout, it is no wonder if some expressions lie open to quibbles. Yet their excuse is easy to make, provided that the lust for quarrelling and calumny is set aside.

units.la: BREVIS ADMONITIO IOANNIS CALVINI AD FRATRES POLONOS, NE TRIPLICEM in Deo essentiam pro tribus Personis imaginando, tres sibi Deos fabricent.
units.tr: A BRIEF WARNING OF JOHN CALVIN TO THE POLISH BRETHREN, THAT, IMAGINING A THREEFOLD ESSENCE IN God for three Persons, they should not make three Gods for themselves.

units.la: [Fabulam] solidè ac dilucidè refutatum fuit. Nunc fratres nostros, qui paucorum homi-num astu deceptifuerunt, rogabo & hortabor, saltem vt composita mente ad meam admonitionem attendere non grauentur. Quòd si ad resipiscendum do-ciles fuerint, mihi, vt spero, non erit difficile efficere, vt ab impio commento, quod nimis leuiter & inconsideratè amplexi sunt, abhorreant.
units.tr: The fable has been refuted soundly and clearly. Now I will ask and urge our brethren, who have been deceived by the cunning of a few men, at least to be willing to give my warning attention with a calm mind. If they are teachable enough to repent, it will not, I hope, be hard for me to bring it about that they shrink from the impious invention which they embraced too lightly and without consideration.

units.la: Falsum principium est quod in tabula ponitur, Scriptura semper distinctè loqui de Patre, Filio, & Spiritu: quum ex locis compluribus liqueat nunc comparatiuè, nùc absque distinctione fieri Dei mentionem. Si obtineo duplicem esse loquendi modum, mox euanescet tota illa inanis speculatio, Vnum esse verum Deum Patrem Domini nostri. Fateor certè, vbi simul Patris & Filii fit mentio, distinguì Filiũ à Patre: verùm ne sibi placeat tabulæ artifex, distinctionem, vt inscitè iactat, perpetuam esse nego. Incipiam à primo loco, quæ turpiter corrupit. Iehoua Deus tuus, Deus vnus est. Hìc quoniã nulla fit comparatio inter Personas, perperam dico ad Patrem restringi vnius Dei nomen. Nam si Iehoua, qui à seipso habet esse, solus est Pater, sequetur, Filium non esse Iehouam. Quomodo enim quod de solo Patre asseritur, ad Filium licebit transferre? Nunc videndum, sitne Christus Iehoua necne. Vidit Isaias Deum exercituum sedentem in solio. Negari non potest quin fuerit idem ille Iehouah, quem Moses prædicat vnum esse Deum. Quid autem Ioannes? Quum tot signa fecisset coram eis Iesus, non crediderunt in eum, vt sermo Isaiæ compleretur. Deinde recitato loco, Hæc dixit Isaias quando vidit gloriam eius, & loquutus est de eo. Futile cauillum est excipere, ostensam fuisse Prophetæ Christi gloriam, quia est imago Patris. Neque enim nobis excutietur, si de Christo loquutus est Isaias, in ipsum competere quod dicit de Iehoua. Iam Paulus, vt probet oportere nos omnes sisti ad Christi tribunal, alteram Prophetæ sententiam adducit, Viuo ego, coram me flectetur omne genu. Certè apud Prophetam loquitur Deus Israelis, quem vnicum testatus fuerat Moses. Atqui teste Paulo, competit hoc elogium in Christum. Ille ergo idem est qui per vitam suam iurat se gloriam suam alteri nõ daturum. Ac frustra effugere tentabunt, Deum fore iudicem in Christi persona, quia omne iudicium dedit Filio, quando pro confesso sumit Paulus, verè in Christum competere quod de summo Dei imperio dicitur apud Prophetam. Simili ratione ex eodem Isaia probat Christum esse in lapidem scandali Iudæis, quum tamen Propheta id non nisi de vnico Deo pronuntiet. Iam ad Christum perperam accommodaret quod Dauid affirmat de summo Deo, nisi fatemur sub illa Deitate Christum comprehendi. Alloquitur Dauid vnicum Deum his verbis, Ascendisti in altù.Paulus docet id in Christo impletù fuisse. Ad hæc, si quid Dei proprium est, singularibus elogiis insignitur in his verbis, Tu initio Iehoua fundasti cœ-lum & terrâ.Item, Adorate eum omnes Angeli. Atqui Apostolus Christo vendicat: sequitur ergo illic sub Dei nomine totam diuinam essentiam desi-gnari,quæ Christo & Spiritui communis est cum Patre. Ac proinde quoties suas distinctiones mihi obtrudet tabulæ fictor, in promptu erit regerere, vbi confertur Christus cum Patre, merito distinguì Personas: vbi autem simplici-ter nominatur Deus, minimè Filium excludi.Et certè si soli Patri conuenit, esse vitam, falsum erit illud Ioannis, Hic est verus Deus, & vita æterna. Quæro enim an alium verum Deum inducat, quàm qui apud Mosen & Pro-phetas celebratur? Adde etiá, quamuis Malachias peculiariter de Christo loqua-tur, ei tamen ascribere quod transferri fas non est à vero & vnico Deo Israelis. Nã cui dicatum fuit templum in monte Sion? cui oblata fuerunt sacrificia? Certè præter verum Deum illic numen colere, sacrilega fuisset profanatio. Malachias autem de Christo loquens, Veniet, inquit, ad Templum suum Dominator quæ vos quæritis. Nempe quia Iehoua nominatur apud Ieremiâ, coledus semper simul cum Pa-tre fuit. Nam quid valeat nomen Iehouæ, diligenter piáque attentione ex-pendere conuenit in hac causa. Hoc elogio Deus Israelis non tantùm se ab omnibus creaturis separat, sed ostendit non alibi quàm in se vno quærendâ esse essentia. Hoc nomen dum Prophetæ cum Christo communicat, satis clarè demon-strant eũ esse qui apud Mosen sic loquutus est. Alioqui nõ modò Stephanus, vbi Christum precatus est, violasset legitimâ precâdi formam: sed tota quoque Ecclesia eiusdem impietatis rea foret. Deus Israelis, quem tabulæ fictor vult esse solù Patrè, sacrificiis omnibus præfert inuocatione sui nominis, atque hunc sibi honorem vendicat tanquam præcipuum sacrificium. Quid autem Stephanus? precationem suam ad Christum dirigit. Ananias autem apud Lucam dicit pios omnes inuocasse Christi nomen. Quomodo hæc inter se conuenient, Christum ritè inuocari, & tamen non esse illum Deum, qui per Dauidè illud sacrificiu laudis exigit? Euersum est igitur figmentum illud, vbique Scripturam distinctè de Patre & Filio loqui, quum sæpe vnicam vtriusque deitatem com-memoret sub vno Iehouæ nomine. Vbi autem Filius Patri adiungitur, mirum non est suam cuique Personam attribui. Quanquam dum multam congeriem affectat tabularius, locos nonnullos male detorquet. Scio veteres ita exposuisse illud Mosis, Pluit Dominus à Domino : sed cùm nomen Iehouæ in vtroque membro expressum sit, sensus nullo modo quadraret, Patrem à Filio pluis-se. Verùm vt Moses formidabilem Dei vindictam melius demonstret, repetit secundò Dei æterni nomen .Ita vbi dicitur Deus fecisse hominem ad imaginem Dei, stultè quæritur distinctio inter Personas. Quòd ad sententiā ex primo capite Ioannis sumptā, distinguitur quidem Filius à Patre,quòd fuerit apud Deum:sed vbi additur,Sermonē illum fuisse Deum,detestabile sacrilegium est, nouam aut aliam deitatē fingere. Melius etiam abstinuisset à loco illo Psalmi, Verbo Domini cœli firmati sunt, &c.non quòd insectari placeat,si minus aptè Scripturam citet: verùm ne suum acumen tanta insolentia nobis venditet. In illa etiam sententia , quam profert ex priore ad Corinth. Distributiones ministeriorum sunt, idē autē Dominus: non assequutus est mētē Pauli.In multis locis pueriliter argutatur:sed interea venenum suum prodit, Christus non dicit,Ego & Pater vnus sumus,sed vnū: fateor:quia illic propositum nō erat vnum se cū Patre Deū vocare: verùm captiosè inde elicit Christū esse alium à Patre Deū.Similiter quum dicit Ioanes, Hi tres vnum sunt, quia nō disserit ex professo de essentia vel Deitate,sic loquitur. Hic autē vel impostor malitiosè, vel nugator inepte ad nomē Dei trahit quod prorsus in diuersum finem dictum est.V no quidem verbo negat se statuere tres Deos:sed hanc absurditatē effugere nō poterit,quandiu negabit Christum esse vnum cum Patre Deum.Si enim non est idem Deus,& tamen Deus est:ergo alius.Apertius dicam,Si Pater suum esse habet à seipso, Filius suū esse habet à Patre, Spiritus ab vtroque,an non tres essentiæ emerguntatque ita vna discerpitur? Et certè si recipitur eius commentū, nō alia relinquitur Christo essentia, quàm nescio quid abstractū:sicuti iactat Patris essentiā ab initio,ne sterilis esset quæ dat omnibus fœcunditatē,Filium ex se protulisse.Hic vero rursus fratres obtestor,vt sibi ab occultis decipulis prudenter caveant: quia si seorsum locatur Christi Deitas à Patris Deitate, pluralitas deorū inducitur. Et detegitur hæc captio eius verbis,vbi somniū esse dicit, si in vnū conflantur Filius & Pater. Cōflatura enim secundū eū nihil aliud est,quàm simplex essentiæ vnitas. Nec vero meas coniecturas in medium profero.Scitur apud nos in qua officina fabricatº fuerit diabolicus error, quo Poloniā infecit Blandrata.Verè vnū fuerunt ipse,& Matthæus Gribaldus, & Valetinus quidā nomine Getilis. Duos nō puduit palā quod dixi profiteri,Plures numero esse deos.Verum quibuscunque se tegāt fucis, deprehēsa tenebuntur eorū impudētia:quia si idē Deus est Filius cū Patre,sequitur eū semper fuisse Deū Israelis,à quo honoris gradu eū palā excludūt.Porrò quòd in Symbolo Niceno Deº ex Deo vocatur: tametsi dura est loquutio,nō tamē aliò tendit,nisi obstaculo nō esse discrimē inter Personas,quo minº vna sit essentia, Ideo sic resolui debet oratio,quāuis ex Deo sit,est tamen Deus, & quidem verus Deus. Imò verisimile est, quum fraudem metuerent sancti Patres, consultò illud additum curasse, Deû verum de Deo vero. Certè hanc fuisse Concilii mente ex Symbolo Athanasii colligitur, qui illic præfuit, si rem ipsam spectes. Ac valde miror eos qui Symbolû iactant, fastidiosè re-spuere certum & idoneum eius interpretem. Quas ex aliis veteribus Patribus obtendunt sententias iam, non excutio, quia id mihi præstitisse videor in refu-tatione Gentilis.
units.tr: The principle placed at the head of the table is false, namely that Scripture always speaks distinctly of Father, Son and Spirit, since it is clear from many passages that mention of God is sometimes made comparatively and sometimes without distinction. If I show that there is a twofold manner of speaking, that whole empty speculation, "There is one true God, the Father of our Lord," will soon vanish. I certainly admit that where the Father and the Son are mentioned together, the Son is distinguished from the Father. But lest the maker of the table be pleased with himself, I deny that the distinction is perpetual, as he clumsily boasts. I will begin with the first passage, which he has shamefully corrupted: "Jehovah your God, God is one." Here, since no comparison between the Persons is made, I wrongly say that the name of the one God is restricted to the Father. For if Jehovah, who has being from himself, is the Father alone, it will follow that the Son is not Jehovah. How could what is asserted of the Father alone be transferred to the Son? Now we must consider whether Christ is Jehovah or not. Isaiah saw the Lord of hosts sitting on a throne. It cannot be denied that this was the same Jehovah whom Moses proclaims to be the one God. What then of John? When Jesus had done so many signs before them, they did not believe in him, so that the word of Isaiah might be fulfilled. Then, the passage having been recited: "Isaiah said these things when he saw his glory, and spoke of him." It is a futile quibble to object that the glory shown to the prophet was Christ's, because he is the image of the Father. For it will not escape us that if Isaiah spoke of Christ, what he says of Jehovah belongs to him. Next, Paul, to prove that we must all be brought before the judgment seat of Christ, adduces another saying of the prophet: "As I live, every knee shall bow before me." Certainly the God of Israel, whom Moses had attested as the only one, speaks in the prophet, and yet, according to Paul, this praise belongs to Christ. He therefore is the same one who swears by his own life that he will not give his glory to another. And in vain will they try to escape by saying that God will be judge in the person of Christ, because all judgment has been given to the Son, since Paul takes it as granted that what is said of the supreme dominion of God in the prophet truly belongs to Christ. By a similar argument, from the same Isaiah, he proves that Christ is the stone of stumbling to the Jews, although the prophet pronounces this only of the one God. Again, he wrongly applies to Christ what David affirms of the supreme God, unless we confess that Christ is comprehended under that Deity. David addresses the one God in these words, "You have ascended on high," and Paul teaches that this was fulfilled in Christ. Moreover, if anything is proper to God, it is marked with singular praises in these words: "You, Jehovah, in the beginning founded the heavens and the earth." Likewise: "Let all the angels worship him." Yet the Apostle claims these for Christ. It follows that under the name of God the whole divine essence is there designated, which is common to Christ and the Spirit with the Father. Accordingly, whenever the maker of the table forces his distinctions upon me, it will be easy to reply: where Christ is compared with the Father, the Persons are rightly distinguished, but where God is named simply, the Son is by no means excluded. And certainly, if being life belonged to the Father alone, the saying of John would be false: "This is the true God, and eternal life." For I ask whether he introduces another true God than the one celebrated by Moses and the Prophets. Add also that although Malachi speaks peculiarly of Christ, he nevertheless ascribes to him what may not be transferred from the true and only God of Israel. For to whom was the temple on Mount Zion dedicated? To whom were sacrifices offered? Surely, to worship another deity there besides the true God would have been a sacrilegious profanation. But Malachi, speaking of Christ, says: "The Lord whom you seek will come suddenly to his temple." Indeed, because Jehovah is named in Jeremiah, he has always been worshipped together with the Father. For in this matter it is fitting to weigh carefully and with pious attention what the name Jehovah means. By this title the God of Israel not only separates himself from all creatures, but shows that his essence is to be sought nowhere but in himself alone. While the prophets share this name with Christ, they clearly demonstrate that he is the one who spoke thus through Moses. Otherwise not only Stephen, when he called upon Christ, would have violated the lawful form of prayer, but the whole Church would be guilty of the same impiety. The God of Israel, whom the maker of the table wants to be the Father alone, prefers the invocation of his name to all sacrifices, and claims this honour for himself as the chief sacrifice. But what did Stephen do? He directs his prayer to Christ. Ananias, in Luke, also says that all the godly have invoked the name of Christ. How can these agree: that Christ is rightly invoked, and yet is not that God who through David demands that sacrifice of praise? That fiction is therefore overthrown, the fiction that Scripture everywhere speaks distinctly of Father and Son, since it often recalls the single deity of both under the one name Jehovah. Where the Son is joined to the Father, it is no wonder that each is assigned his own Person, although the table-maker, eager for a great heap of proofs, twists some passages badly. I know that the ancients explained that saying of Moses, "The Lord rained from the Lord," in this way. But since the name Jehovah is expressed in both members, the sense does not in any way fit that the Father rained from the Son. Rather, that Moses might better demonstrate the terrible vengeance of God, he repeats the name of the eternal God a second time. So when it is said that God made man in the image of God, it is foolish to seek a distinction between the Persons. As for the sentence taken from the first chapter of John, the Son is indeed distinguished from the Father, in that he was with God. But where it is added that the Word was God, it is a detestable sacrilege to feign a new or different deity. He would have done better to abstain from that passage of the Psalm, "By the word of the Lord the heavens were established," and so on. Not that I wish to attack him if he cites Scripture less aptly, but lest he sell his own cleverness to us with such insolence. In that saying too, which he quotes from the first epistle to the Corinthians, "There are diversities of ministries, but the same Lord," he did not grasp Paul's meaning. In many places he argues in a childish way, but meanwhile he reveals his poison. Christ does not say "I and the Father are one," but "one." I grant it, because there it was not his purpose to call himself one God with the Father. Yet he craftily deduces from this that Christ is a God other than the Father. Similarly, when John says "These three are one," since he does not discuss essence or Deity ex professo, he speaks thus. But this man, either a malicious deceiver or a foolish trifler, drags to the name of God what was said for a completely different purpose. He denies in one word that he sets up three Gods, but he will not escape this absurdity as long as he denies that Christ is one God with the Father. For if he is not the same God, and yet is God, then he is another. To speak more plainly: if the Father has his being from himself, and the Son has his being from the Father, and the Spirit from both, do not three essences emerge, and so the one is torn apart? And certainly, if his fiction is accepted, no essence is left to Christ other than I know not what abstraction, just as he boasts that the Father's essence from the beginning brought forth the Son from itself, lest that which gives fruitfulness to all be barren. Here again I earnestly urge the brethren to guard prudently against these hidden snares. For if Christ's Deity is located apart from the Father's Deity, a plurality of gods is introduced. This trick of his is exposed by his own words, where he says it is a dream if the Son and Father are merged into one. For a merging, according to him, is nothing other than a simple unity of essence. Nor do I bring forward my own conjectures. It is known among us in what workshop the diabolical error was forged with which Blandrata infected Poland. Indeed, he, Matthew Gribaldi and a certain Valentinus named Gentilis were one in this. Two of them were not ashamed to profess openly what I have said, that there are more gods in number. However they hide themselves under whatever pretences, their shamelessness will be caught and held fast. For if the same God is the Son with the Father, it follows that he has always been the God of Israel, from whose rank of honour they openly exclude him. Furthermore, that in the Nicene Creed he is called "God from God": although the expression is harsh, it does not tend anywhere else than to say that there is no distinction between the Persons that would prevent there being one essence. So this statement ought to be resolved thus: although he is from God, he is nevertheless God, and indeed true God. Indeed it is likely that when the holy Fathers feared fraud, they deliberately added it to take care that God is true of true God. Certainly the mind of the Council is gathered to be this from the Athanasian Creed, which presided there, if you look at the matter itself. And I greatly wonder at those who boast of the Creed, scornfully rejecting its certain and suitable interpreter. As for the opinions they put forward from the other ancient Fathers, I do not examine them now, because I seem to have done that in my refutation of Gentilis.

units.la: Nunc venio ad secundum huius quæstionis caput. Christus vbique se à Patre discernit. Fateor, nempe quatenus Mediatoris personam sustinet. Rectè enim alicubi admonui, imò sæpiùs inculcaui, quæ de se Christus prædicat in Euangelio Ioannis, neque in humana neque in Diuina eius natura seorsum competere, sed ad munus à Patre iniunctu referri. Itaque vbi se vnû cum Patre facit, longè aliud consilium eius fuit, quàm nos ad nudam arcanæ suæ essentiæ speculationem euchere: quin potius à fine ratiocinatur, nos fore vnû cum Patre, quia Pater in ipso residet. Itaque nō pigebit referre quod pridem scripsi. Vt ritè comprehendas quomodo Christus & Pater vnum sint, caue ne illum exuas Mediatoris persona, sed potius considera vt est Ecclesiæ caput, & membris suis coniunge: ita optimè stabit contextus, ne irrita sit vel inutilis Filii cum Patre vnitas, eius virtute oportere in totû piorû corpus diffundi. Rursû, vbi Filius Patri subiicitur quasi inferior, curiosius disputare nō attinet quomodo hoc Deo conueniat in carne manifestato: quia sufficere nobis debet admirabile Dei consilium, quod nomine Dispensationis non male expressum fuit. Sententia Christi, Pater maior me est, restricta fuit ad humanam eius naturam: ego verò nō dubito ad totû complexum extendere: quia tametsi Deus sit æternus, quû tamen ad nos descendit, medius esse cœpit inter Deum & nos. Hac ratione vocatur Pater vnus Deus, quia Christus carne circûdatus, sic Ecclesiæ præest, vt Deû habeat caput, quèadmodû Paulus docet. Hoc etiâ modo Deus mediatè nos per manum Filii sui gubernat, donec perducti simus ad solidam gloriæ coniunctionē, in qua Filius subiicitur Patri, vt sit Deus omnia in omnibus. Secûdû hanc Dispensationem orauit Christus ipse in terris, & nûc ipso aduocato freti, in eius nomine Patrem oramus. In hac doctrina nihil coactû, vel spinosum, quia nõ prodit Christus ad nos nisi Mediator, qui à Deo exiuit: habet tamen Deû in se manentem, & in ipso residet omnis plenitudo Deitatis, vt ad Deû nos tandem perducat, dû familiari & immediato, vt loquuntur, Deitatis aspectu, quæ nûc in imagine relucet, solidè fruemur. Clamet nunc Stacarus nos esse Arianos, statim euanescet huius calumniæ futilitas, quãdo fatemur nõ cadere in Diuinam naturam, quod tamen personæ Mediatoris restè[?] aptatur. Vbi autem in vna Dei essentia tres agnoscimus distinctas hypostases, vt Christi respectu vnus sit Deus eius Pater, ipse vero sit imago Dei inuisibilis, nihil in hac doctrina est affine Sabellij errori. Viderint autem quos tantopere oblectat perpetua distinctio, ne omnia misceant ac confundant: quia Deitatis nomen vbique ad Patris nomen restringendo, mox lacerant in partes, vbi Filij & Spiritus commune esse nolunt. Porro hallucinandi causa illis est, quòd nihil observant discriminis inter duas notitiæ species, vbi indefinitè nobis describitur Dei maiestas: deinde in tribus personis se patefacit. Ac vsqueadeò vera est ea quam asserimus vnitas, vt dum seorsum Deus vocatur Christus, simul comprehendatur Patris Deitas. Nam vbi exclamat Thomas, Dominus meus, & Deus meus, Mediatore agnito, altius transcendit. Paulus etiam quum pronuntiat Christum esse Deum in secula benedictum, non secundam vel productâ Diuinitatem imaginatur, sed quæ vna est, in Christum competere intelligit. Neque tamen dum sub Dei nomine continentur Filius & Spiritus, obducitur caligo, quin tres Personæ refulgeant, & sua cuique constet proprietas.
units.tr: Now I come to the second point of this question. Christ everywhere distinguishes himself from the Father. I admit this, insofar as he bears the person of the Mediator. For I have rightly pointed out elsewhere, and indeed often insisted, that what Christ says of himself in John's Gospel belongs neither to his human nor to his divine nature taken separately, but is referred to the office enjoined on him by the Father. Therefore, when he makes himself one with the Father, his purpose was far different from drawing us into a bare speculation on his hidden essence. Rather, he reasons from the end: that we shall be one with the Father because the Father dwells in him. So I will not hesitate to repeat what I wrote before. To grasp properly how Christ and the Father are one, beware of stripping him of the person of the Mediator. Rather, consider him as he is, the head of the Church, joined to his members. The context then stands well, and the unity of the Son with the Father is not empty or useless, since by his power it must be poured out into the whole body of the faithful. Again, where the Son is subjected to the Father as inferior, it is not worth inquiring too closely how this agrees with God made manifest in the flesh. The wonderful counsel of God should suffice for us, which is not badly expressed by the name of Dispensation. Christ's saying, "The Father is greater than I," was restricted to his human nature; but I do not doubt that it extends to the whole complex of his person. For although God is eternal, yet when he came down to us he began to be a mediator between God and us. In this way the Father is called the one God, because Christ, clothed in flesh, so presides over the Church that he has God as his head, as Paul teaches. Also in this way God governs us mediately by the hand of his Son, until we are brought to the solid union of glory, in which the Son is subjected to the Father, so that God may be all in all.
