According to this Dispensation Christ himself prayed on earth, and now, relying on him as our advocate, we pray to the Father in his name. In this doctrine there is nothing forced or thorny, because Christ comes to us only as Mediator, who went forth from God. Yet he has God dwelling in him, and in him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead, so that he may at last lead us to God, while we solidly enjoy the familiar and immediate, as they say, sight of the Deity, which now shines forth in the image. Let Stancarus now cry out that we are Arians; the futility of this slander will at once vanish, since we confess that this does not fall upon the divine nature, but properly applies to the person of the Mediator. But where, within the one essence of God, we acknowledge three distinct hypostases, so that with respect to Christ the one God is his Father, and he himself is the image of the invisible God, nothing in this doctrine is akin to the error of Sabellius. Let those look to it who take such delight in a perpetual distinction, lest they mix and confuse everything. For by always restricting the name of Deity to the name of the Father, they at once tear it into parts, refusing that it be common to the Son and the Spirit. Moreover, the cause of their error is that they observe no difference between the two kinds of knowledge: the one where the majesty of God is described to us indefinitely, and the other where he reveals himself in three persons. So true is the unity we assert that when God is called Christ alone, the Father's Deity is comprehended at the same time. For when Thomas exclaims, "My Lord and my God," he, having acknowledged the Mediator, rises higher. Likewise Paul, when he pronounces that Christ is God blessed for ever, does not imagine a second or derived Deity, but understands that the one Deity belongs to Christ. Yet while the Son and the Spirit are included under the name of God, no darkness is cast over things, so that the three Persons do not shine forth and each keep its own property.

units.la: Vtinam hæc qua decet modestia & sobrietate secum probè reputent fratres Polonici! & qui nunc commenti nouitate tanquam musto inebriati exultant, gustare de-integro nō grauentur doctrinâ bene defæcatam & concoctam.
units.tr: Would that the Polish brethren would weigh these things in their own minds with the modesty and sobriety that befit them! And let those who now exult in the novelty of their invention, as if drunk on new wine, not be reluctant to taste again, from the beginning, a doctrine well clarified and digested.

units.la: EPISTOLA IOANNIS Caluini, qua fidem Admonitionis ab eo nuper edita apud Polonos confirmat.
units.tr: EPISTLE of John Calvin, in which he confirms the faith of the Admonition lately published by him among the Poles.

units.la: GENEROSIS ET NOBILIBVS DOMINIS, PROCERIBVS MINORIS POLONIAE, ET ornatissimis viris ciuibus inclytæ vrbis Cracouiæ, qui orthodoxam fidem constanter sequuntur, Ioannes Caluinus.
units.tr: TO THE NOBLE AND GENEROUS LORDS, THE NOBLES OF LESSER POLAND, AND THE DISTINGUISHED CITIZENS OF THE FAMOUS CITY OF KRAKOW, WHO CONSTANTLY FOLLOW THE ORTHODOX FAITH: John Calvin.

units.la: S.
units.tr: S.

units.la: Generosi, nobiles, præstantissimi viri, & Domini, quum ante quatuor menses allatus esset tristis nuncius de multorum leuitate, qui apud vos à recta & syncera fide ad impium & detestabile figmentum defecerant, imò ab ipsis vulgata esset Tabula, quæ veram Christi Deitatem abolere tentabant: statim breuem admonitionem conscripsi, qua sobrij, dociles, & modesti homines ad cauendas insidias instructi, in sana pietatis doctrina retinerentur. Postea ex optimo fratre nostro Domino Christophoro Trecio cognoui, à prudetibus & cordatis viris deprehensas fuisse eorum fraudes, qui fidei principiu de tribus in Deo personis labefactare conati fuerat. Idem mihi scripserut fideles Christi serui D.D.Stanislaus Sarnicius, & Iacobus Syluius. Imprimis vero latatus sum, vestra diligentia & virtute iterum colligi apud vos Ecclesiam, cuius timenda erat misera dissipatio. Interea tamen didici, quia vobis negocium est cum hominibus superbis & praefractis, duris & assiduis certaminibus vos exerceri: ac proinde non inutile vobis fore, si quod à piis fratribus ad vos confirmados oblatum esset subsidium. Ego autem cum in eorum numero censeri cupiam, partibus meis deesse nolui.
units.tr: Noble, generous, and most excellent gentlemen and lords: four months ago a sad report reached me that many among you had fallen away from the straight and sincere faith into an impious and detestable fiction. Indeed, a pamphlet had been published by those very men, which tried to overthrow the true divinity of Christ. I therefore at once wrote a short admonition, so that sober, teachable, and modest people, forewarned against the snares, might be kept in the sound doctrine of piety. Afterwards I learned from our excellent brother, the Lord Christopher Trecius, that prudent and judicious men had detected the frauds of those who had tried to shake the foundation of the faith concerning the three persons in God. The faithful servants of Christ, the Lords Stanislaus Sarnicius and James Sylvius, wrote the same to me. I was especially glad that, through your diligence and courage, the Church, whose wretched dispersal had been feared, is being gathered together again among you. Meanwhile, however, I have learned that you have to contend with proud and obstinate men, and that you are exercised by harsh and constant disputes. Therefore, it will not be useless for you if some help is offered by the godly brethren to strengthen you. For my part, since I wish to be counted among their number, I have not wanted to be lacking in my share.

units.la: Porro teterrimus hic error, qui apud vos grassatur, fauorem obtinuit ex immodico contentionis feruore. Nam quum Stancarus insulsus Sophista, & rabula improbissimus commenta sua ingereret, Christum Mediatorem duntaxat esse, quatenus homo est, ideoque apud totam Trinitatem intercederet optimum compendium quidam esse duxerunt, si responderent solum Patrem vere & proprie esse Deum. Ita effugium illud nimis cupide multi arripuerunt, quod ita putaret nullo negocio refutari Stancari ineptias. Sic ut veteri proverbio dicitur, nimium altercando veritas amissa fuit. Equidem non dubito quosdam inscitia, vel inconsiderata facilitate lapsos esse: verum coniicere simul licet, nonnullos astute captasse occasionem, ut execrabile delirium, quod plausibile fore sperabant, simplicibus impune obtruderent. Sunt enim apud vos impuri nebulones Georgius Blandrata, Valetinus Gentilis, Ioannes Paulus Alciatus, & similes, quos furiosa libido novadi & turbandi praecipites agit. Verum illis omissis, summam ipsius quaestionis perstringere expediet.
units.tr: Moreover, this most abominable error, which is spreading among you, has gained favour from an immoderate heat of controversy. For when Stancarus, that foolish sophist and most shameless wrangler, pressed his fancies, saying that Christ is Mediator only in so far as he is man, and therefore intercedes before the whole Trinity, some thought it the best shortcut simply to answer that only the Father is truly and properly God. Many eagerly seized upon that escape, supposing that the absurdities of Stancarus could be refuted without any trouble. Thus, as the old proverb says, through too much wrangling the truth was lost. Certainly I do not doubt that some have slipped through ignorance or thoughtless readiness; yet one may also suspect that some have cunningly seized the occasion, so that they could foist this execrable delirium, which they hoped would be plausible, upon simple people with impunity. For among you there are impure scoundrels, Georgius Blandrata, Valentinus Gentilis, Giovanni Paolo Alciati, and their like, whom a mad lust for novelty and disturbance drives headlong. But setting those aside, it will be helpful to lay bare the sum of the question itself.

units.la: Volunt quoties occurrit nomen Dei in Scriptura, restringi ad solum Patrem. Atqui postquam Spiritus sanctus unum esse Deum pronuntiauit, aperte docet Christum fuisse illum Deum. Nec vero aliter staret testimonium Ioan-nis, Hic est verus Deus & vita aeterna, nisi esset idem cum Patre Deus. Iam vbi Dei nomen indefinite usurpat Paulus apud Lucam, non nisi de Filio id po-test intelligi, quado diserte exprimit sanguine Dei redemptam esse Ecclesiam. Verum satis superque nobis esse debet, quod tradunt Prophetae de unico & aeterno Deo, Apostolos aptare ad Christi personam. Luculentas eius rei probationes suggeret vobis mea admonitio. Quod obstrepunt, Deum passim vocari Patrem Christi: in promptu solutio est, Quoties inter se comparatur duae Personae, Dei nomē[?] peculiariter ascribi Patri, quia Deitatis principium est: sed ubi nulla fit coparatio, Filium comprehedi sub Dei nomine. Et sane si admittitur relatio in ipsa Dei essentia, iam non una, nec simplex erit, sed lacerabitur. Paulo clarius id explicabo. Si essentiae respectu confertur Filius cum Patre, multiplex inde emerget Deitas, quo nihil absurdius est. Et tamen non pudet illum ter perfidum apostatam Gentilem blasphemiā hanc euomere, Christum esse à Patre essen-tiatum: ubi agnoscitis diabolico figmento excogitatam esse prodigiosam vocem. Denique sicut olim Manichæi fabulati sunt animam hominis ex Dei traduce originem ducere: ita hic praestigiator fingit Dei Filium esse nescio quod abstra-ctum à vera Deitate. Atqui si essentiatus est Christus, non est ille Iehoua, qui olim Prophetis apparuit: quod tamen Apostoli testantur. Hoc quidem effugere nequeunt, quin discerpant essentiam Dei, nisi concedant Christum essentialiter unum esse Deum. Detegitur etiā alter eorum furor: quia nisi idem sit Fi-lius cum Patre Deus, plures deos inducī[?] necesse est. Tergiuersando nihil prosi-ciunt, quia planè elicitur ex eorum commentis, Christū alium esse à Patre Deum. Quod obiiciunt, alium vocari, sicuti & Spiritus vocatur alius ab ipso consolator, nullo negocio diluitur. Neque enim usquam Scriptura ubi Personas distinguit, Deum ipsum secat in partes vel frusta, ac si secum eius essentia cōfligeret[?]. Alius ergo Filius est à Patre, sed non alius Deus. Quare distinctio non potest nisi ad Personas accommodari. Hoc autem modo nō habemus Deum conflatum, ut odiosè, simulque futiliter garriunt: quia tametsi unus est nobis Deus, ubi tamen in medium prodit Filius, suum gradum obtinet Pater, ut discrimen eminēat[?].
units.tr: They want that whenever the name of God occurs in Scripture, it be restricted to the Father alone. Yet after the Holy Spirit has declared that there is one God, he plainly teaches that Christ was that God. Nor would the testimony of John stand otherwise: "This is the true God and eternal life," unless he were God together with the Father. Again, where Paul in Luke uses the name of God without qualification, it can be understood of the Son only, since he expressly says that the Church was redeemed by the blood of God. But it ought to be enough for us, and more than enough, that the Prophets hand down concerning the one and eternal God, and that the Apostles apply it to the person of Christ. My admonition will supply you with clear proofs of this matter. As for their clamour that God is everywhere called the Father of Christ, the answer is ready: whenever two persons are compared with each other, the name of God is ascribed in particular to the Father, because he is the source of the Deity; but where no comparison is made, the Son is included under the name of God. And indeed, if a relation is admitted in the very essence of God, then God will no longer be one, nor simple, but will be torn apart. I will explain this a little more clearly. If the Son is compared with the Father with respect to the essence, a manifold Deity will emerge from this, and nothing is more absurd. And yet that thrice-faithless Gentile apostate is not ashamed to vomit forth this blasphemy, that Christ has been essentiated from the Father, where you recognise that the monstrous word was devised by a diabolical fiction. Finally, just as the Manichaeans once fabled that the soul of man derives its origin from the transmission of God, so this trickster pretends that the Son of God is I know not what abstraction from true Deity. Yet if Christ has been essentiated, then he is not that Jehovah who once appeared to the Prophets, which nevertheless the Apostles testify. They cannot escape this, that they tear apart the essence of God, unless they concede that Christ is essentially one God. Their second madness is also laid bare: unless the Son is the same God as the Father, it is necessary to introduce several gods. By evasions they gain nothing, because it is plainly drawn out of their fictions that Christ is a God other than the Father. The objection that he is called "another," just as the Spirit is called another Comforter besides him, is refuted without any trouble. For nowhere does Scripture, when it distinguishes the Persons, cut God himself into parts or pieces, as if his essence were thereby torn apart. Therefore the Son is another from the Father, but not another God. Hence the distinction can only apply to the Persons. In this way we do not have a God put together from parts, as they wrangle in their hateful and at the same time futile way; for although we have one God, yet when the Son comes forward, the Father keeps his own rank, so that the distinction stands out.

units.la: Tenenda quoque est loquendi ratio Scripturæ trita, dum Christus quatenus Mediator est, inferior Patre statuitur (de toto complexu loquor, hoc est, Deo manifestato in carne) quia nunc Pater caput est, donec Christus acceptum ab eo imperium restituat, ut sit Deus omnia in omnibus. Nec est cur Stancarus hic insultet, ac si Christus fieret Patre minor, quando hic non de natura Deitatis agitur, sed notatur tantum œconomia vel dispensatio admirabilis consilij Dei, quæ nihil derogat æternæ Christi gloriæ. Hinc elicitur pura fidei synceritas, in-uno Deo ita esse tres Personas, ut Filius nō sit Pater, sed differat à Patre, ut una sit utriusque essentia. Unde sequitur, quamuis nō comparatiuè, tamen inde-finitè unum esse Deum. Quidquid blaterent virulentæ linguæ, in hac fide ac-quiescere semper tutū erit: sicuti utile quoq; spinosis multis quæstionibus ansam præcidere, simulque supersedere à formulis loquendi vel nimium asperis, vel à Scripturæ usu remotis. Precatio vulgò trita, Sancta Trinitas unus Deus miserere-re nostri, mihi nō placet, ac omnino barbariem sapit. Nolim igitur vos de rebus superuacuis litigare, modò illibatum maneat quod dixi de tribus in vna essen-tia Personis. Quid blateret Stancarus nihil moror, nec verò æquum est, puram & genuinam pietatis doctrinam, cui nihil affine habet, eius commentis obscurari. Quod ergo ab eo dicitur, Vnus Deus & vnus Mediator, id est Trinitas: item, Vt cognoscant te vnum Deum, id est, Trinitatem: Creditis in Deum, id est, in Trinitatem: Quidquid petieritis à Patre, id est, à Trinitate: non modò tanquam insipidum, sed profanum quoque repudiamus. Facessant igitur perversæ illæ speculationes, quæ inuidiam conflare possent sanæ doctrinæ apud imperitos, & ab improbis nebulonibus in hunc finem captiosè obtenduntur. Vbicunque enim occurrit Filij mentio, Dei nomen distinctè in Patrem competit. Sed interea minimè ferendum est, vt artifices isti Blandrata, & Valentinus indignè corrumpat Scripturæ locos, vbi Christus simpliciter Deus vocatur. De solo Christo volunt esse dictum, Sermo erat Deus: item, Sanguine Dei acquisita est Ecclesia: item, Qui est Deus benedictus in secula: item, Hic est verus Deus & vita æterna. Fateor quidem hoc de solo Christo prædicari, modò ne Deum secundum comminiscatur: quod facere ipsos liquet. Quo enim sensu hæc elogia ad solum Christum restringunt, nisi quia aliter Christus quàm Pater vocatur Deus? Ego au-tem contendo Deum vocari, quia vnus est cum Patre Deus, & vna est vtriusque essentia. Nam si Christus Patrem vocando solum verum Deum, se nō excludit, certè non attingit suam essentiam, sed tantum dispensationem respicit, & personam Mediatoris.
units.tr: The customary manner of speaking of Scripture must also be maintained, namely that Christ, in so far as he is Mediator, is set below the Father (I am speaking of the whole complex, that is, God manifested in the flesh), because now the Father is head, until Christ restores the authority received from him, so that God may be all in all. Nor is there any reason for Stancarus to insult us here, as if Christ became less than the Father; for this is not a question of the nature of the Deity, but only the economy or dispensation of the wonderful counsel of God is noted, which takes nothing away from the eternal glory of Christ. From this is drawn the pure sincerity of faith: that in the one God there are three Persons, so that the Son is not the Father but differs from the Father, and yet the essence of both is one. Hence it follows that, although not comparatively, nevertheless absolutely, God is one. Whatever the venomous tongues babble, it will always be safe to rest in this faith; just as it is also useful to cut off the occasion of many thorny questions, and at the same time to refrain from forms of speech either too harsh or remote from the usage of Scripture. The prayer commonly repeated, "Holy Trinity, one God, have mercy on us," does not please me, and smacks altogether of barbarism. I would not therefore have you quarrel about superfluous matters, provided that what I have said about the three Persons in one essence remains unimpaired. I pay no heed to what Stancarus babbles, nor is it right that the pure and genuine doctrine of piety, which has nothing akin to it, should be obscured by his fictions. Therefore we reject, not only as insipid but also as profane, what he says: "one God and one Mediator," that is, the Trinity; likewise, "that they may know you, the one God," that is, the Trinity; "you believe in God," that is, in the Trinity; "whatever you ask of the Father," that is, of the Trinity. Let those perverse speculations depart, which could stir up hatred of sound doctrine among the unlearned, and which are craftily put forward by wicked scoundrels to this end. For wherever mention of the Son occurs, the name of God properly belongs to the Father distinctly. But meanwhile it is by no means to be tolerated that those artful men, Blandrata and Valentinus, should shamefully corrupt the passages of Scripture where Christ is simply called God. They want it said of Christ alone: "the Word was God"; likewise, "the Church was obtained by the blood of God"; likewise, "who is God blessed for ever"; likewise, "this is the true God and eternal life." I grant indeed that this is said of Christ alone, provided they do not invent a God apart from him, which they plainly do. For in what sense do they restrict these attributions to Christ alone, unless because Christ is otherwise called God than the Father is? But I maintain that he is called God because he is one God together with the Father, and the essence of both is one. For if Christ, in calling the Father "the only true God," does not exclude himself, then certainly he does not touch his essence, but looks only to the dispensation and the person of the Mediator.

units.la: Patrum testimonia non minus inscitè depravant. Neque tamen miror tam audacter hincinde arripere quæ facere putant ad suam causam. Homines sunt indocti, nec exercitati in scriptis veterum. Iam dum turbulento impetu ferun-tur ad captanda patrocinia, promiscuè arripiunt quæcunque videntur à recepto vsu paulùm remota esse. Luculentum eius rei specimen est, quòd superbè iactât Tertulliani verba, ac si nobis aduersarentur. Quid autem verba illa continent? Si natus fuisset innatus, comparatus cum eo qui esset innatus, æquatione in utroque duos faceret innatos, si nō genitus esset, collatus cum eo qui genitus non est. Atqui non aliud tradit pius vir, quàm quod subinde inculco, Filium tunc de-mum à Patre discerni, vbi in comparationem veniunt Personæ. Quid enim significant participia, Comparatus & Collatus, nisi ex relatione vnius Personæ ad alteram existere discrimen? Relatio autem ad essentiam vno veterum omnium consensu damnatur. Quæ verò falsarij isti ad stabiliendum suum errorem detorquent, plusquā friuola sunt. Pater & Filius, teste Hilario, non est vnus, nempe Persona: quando pius ille doctor non definit singulis ferè paginis vnam & simplicem Patris & Filij essentiam asserere, vt Filius idem sit cum Patre Patre Deus, & tamen Personæ respectu differat. Quàm verecundè autem Basilium, & Athanasium, & similes nobis obtrudunt? quorum testimoniis millies confoditur detestabilis ista impietas. Cæterùm, quia in refutatione Serueti, & Gentilis, hanc partem satis probè explicuisse mihi videor, quæ inde sumere licet repetendo, molestiam & tædium vobis non afferam.
units.tr: They distort the testimonies of the Fathers no less ignorantly. Yet I am not surprised that they snatch so boldly here and there whatever they think serves their cause. They are unlearned men, untrained in the writings of the ancients. Since they are carried along in a turbulent rush to seize on patrons, they grab indiscriminately whatever seems to be somewhat remote from the accepted usage. A striking example of this is that they proudly boast of Tertullian's words, as if they were against us. But what do those words actually say? If the Son had been born unbegotten, compared with one who is unbegotten, he would make two unbegotten beings by equality in each; if he were not begotten, compared with one who is not begotten. Yet the godly man teaches nothing other than what I keep repeating: that the Son is distinguished from the Father only when Persons are brought into comparison. For what do the participles "compared" and "collated" mean, unless a distinction arises from the relation of one Person to the other? But relation to the essence is condemned by the unanimous consent of all the ancients. And the things these forgers twist to establish their error are more than frivolous. "The Father and the Son are not one," according to Hilary, namely one Person: whereas that godly teacher hardly ever fails, on nearly every page, to assert one and the same essence of Father and Son, so that the Son is the same as the Father, God of God, and yet differs in respect of Person. But how shamelessly they thrust Basil, and Athanasius, and others like them upon us! By whose testimonies this detestable impiety is refuted a thousand times. Moreover, since I seem to have sufficiently explained this part in my refutation of Servetus and Gentilis, I will not trouble or weary you by repeating what may be drawn from there.

units.la: Superest nunc, Generosi, Nobiles ac præstantissimi viri, vt in huius causæ defensione infatigato studio pergatis. Res est non leuis momenti, tenere Christum esse vnicum Deum, à quo vita & salus petenda est, & in quo gloriari fas est. Id vobis eripere conantur sacrilegi isti errones. Quare non aliter vobis certandum, quàm si ad Deum fictitium vos abducerent. Pluribus vos hortarer, nisi sponte satis animatos esse considerem. Valete igitur, Nobiles & Generosi Domini, & præstantissimi viri. Dominus vos Spiritu prudentiæ semper gubernet, inuicta virtute sustineat vsque ad extremum. Geneuæ, pridie Calend. Maij, M. D. LXIII.
units.tr: It remains now, noble, distinguished and most excellent gentlemen, that you continue in the defence of this cause with untiring zeal. It is a matter of no small importance to hold that Christ is the only God, from whom life and salvation are to be sought, and in whom it is right to glory. These sacrilegious deceivers try to snatch this from you. Therefore you must contend no otherwise than if they were leading you away to a fictitious God. I would urge you further, were I not sure that you are already sufficiently spirited of your own accord. Farewell, then, noble and generous lords, and most excellent men. May the Lord always guide you by the Spirit of wisdom, and sustain you with unconquered courage to the end. Geneva, the day before the Calends of May, 1563.

units.la: MAGNIFICIS, GENEROSIS ET NOBILIBVS DOMINIS AC PIIS ET FIDELIBUS Ecclesiarum ministris in Polonia & Russia, dominis & fratribus suis charis & honorandis, Iosias Simlerus Gratiam & pacem à Deo precatur.
units.tr: To the magnificent, generous and noble lords, and to the pious and faithful ministers of the Churches in Poland and Russia, their dear and honourable lords and brothers: Josias Simler wishes grace and peace from God.

units.la: CHristiana[?] Charitas, qua omnes qui eandem religionem profitemur inter nos coniunctli sumus, & meus erga vos omnes amor singularis ex admiratione-vestræ fidei & pietatis ortus, fecit vt ego homo peregrinus & vobis ignotus auderem ad vos de rebus maximis & grauissimis scribere. Nihil enim existimo in humanis rebus cognitione Dei maius esse, nullisque controuersias graviores quàm quæ sunt de rebus diuinis, in quibus vniuersa ratio salutis nostræ posita est. Quare postquam superioribus annis audiuimus Ecclesias vestras, arrogantium quorundam & contentiosorum hominum improbitate laceratas & turbatas esse, magnum & incredibilem ea de re omnes boni dolorem accepimus. Facilè e-nim videbamus semel motis nouis quæstionibus, alias quoque nouas controuersias quotidie oriturás[?], dum quisque semel conceptam opinionem pertinaciter tuetur: ex quo deinde sequitur multorum offensio & abalienatio, & studium piæ Christianæque disciplinæ in tanto rixandi studio negligitur. Huic malo nos omnes qui Tiguri Christum praedicamus, mederi voluisse, & literis priuatim ac publicè scriptis pacis & concordiæ authores fuisse, vos ipsi optimi testes estis. Quinetiam quum nuper apud vos Franciscus Stancarus, libro in publicum edito omnibus probris & conuiciis nos consectatus esset: non tamen his ad respondendum quisquam nostrum commotus fuisset, nisi statuissemus aliquam ex hac responsione utilitatem ad vos posse redire. Ideóque ego fratrum consilio has respondendi partes suscepi, si forte controuersia hac exactè discussa in concordiam pristinam ecclesiæ reduci possint, cuius rei nodum prorsus omnem spem ex animo meo depositi. Non quòd existimem Stancarum ipsum, hominem natura contentiosum & maledicum, posse vllam moderationem huius controuersiæ admittere: sed quòd videam sequi eius partes homines doctos quoque & moderatos, cum quibus, si perspicuè exponantur aliqua quæ in hac controuersia ambiguè dicuntur, non difficulter aliqua concordiæ ratio inuri[?] poterit.
units.tr: Christian charity, by which all of us who profess the same religion are joined together, and my singular love for all of you, which arose from my admiration for your faith and piety, have made me, a foreigner and unknown to you, bold enough to write to you about the greatest and most serious matters. For I think there is nothing greater in human affairs than the knowledge of God, and no disputes more serious than those about divine things, on which the whole account of our salvation depends. So when in recent years we heard that your Churches had been torn and disturbed by the wickedness of certain arrogant and quarrelsome men, all good people felt great and unbelievable grief over it. For we could easily see that once new questions had been stirred up, other new controversies would arise every day, as long as each man stubbornly defends the opinion he has once formed. From this follows the offence and estrangement of many, and while the zeal for a godly and Christian discipline is neglected, the zeal for quarrelling grows. To this evil, all of us who preach Christ at Zurich have wished to bring a remedy, and in private and public letters have been authors of peace and concord; you yourselves are the best witnesses of this. Indeed, when recently Franciscus Stancarus attacked us with every kind of insult and abuse in a book published among you, none of us would have been moved to answer him, unless we had judged that some benefit could come back to you from such an answer. So I have, at the wish of my brothers, taken up the part of replying, in case perhaps this controversy, once carefully examined, might be brought back to the former harmony of the Church. I have altogether given up all hope of this in my own mind. Not that I think Stancarus himself, a man contentious and abusive by nature, can admit any moderation into this controversy; but I see that men learned and moderate also follow his side, and with them, if certain things said ambiguously in this controversy are clearly set out, some way of concord should not be hard to find.

units.la: Nam si primum inter partes conueniat de fide sanctæ Trinitatis & incarnationis Domini nostri Iesu Christi, ita ut dilucidè & perspicuè Sabellij, Arij, Nestorij atque Eutychetis errores excludantur, & deinde explicetur quid sub mediationis nomine & officio comprehendatur, & quid sit Christum facere aliquid, aut esse secundum diuinam aut humanam naturam, ita ut de harum loquutionum sensu partes inter se conueniant, existimo deinceps non fore difficilem & obscuram de Mediatore controuersiam.
units.tr: For if first the parties agree about the faith in the holy Trinity and the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, in such a way that the errors of Sabellius, Arius, Nestorius and Eutyches are clearly and plainly excluded; and then it is explained what is comprehended under the name and office of mediation, and what it is for Christ to do something according to the divine or the human nature, so that the parties agree among themselves on the sense of these expressions, I think that afterwards there will be no difficult or obscure controversy about the Mediator.

units.la: Quapropter etiam Sabelliani non sumus: quanuis. n. unum Deum unamque essentiam credimus, non facimus tamen unum Deum trium nominum, sed personas distinctas conseruamus, ita ut Pater non sit Filius, & Filius non sit Pater: & libenter admittimus ut dicatur aliud esse Patrem, & alium esse Filium, & alium esse Spiritum sanctum, non tamen addatur aliud Deum esse Patrem, & alium Deum esse Filium aut Spiritum sanctum: nomen enim Dei cum essentiam significet, ex æquo ut essentia omnibus personis idem est, neque relatione patitur. Itaque falsum est quod auctor tabulæ scribit, Quoties nomen Dei absolute ponitur, de solo Patre intelligendum esse: ut quum dicitur, Audi Israel, Dominus Deus tuus unus est. Nam hunc unum Deum Israelis lex ab eo data adorare iubet. Christus etiam inquit, Dominum Deum tuum adorabis, & illi soli seruies: & per Prophetam Deus inquit sibi flectendum esse omne genu: igitur si Dei nomen hic solum Patrem significat, peccamus adorates Filium: & male Apostolus ad Filium transtulit, illi flectendum esse omne genu. Deus qui unus est, creauit cælum & terram, omnemque hanc rerum universitatem, & hoc elogio se per Prophetas ornat, & a falsis diis distinguit: atqui Apostolus ad Colossenses & ad Hebræos hoc Christo tribuit, quod per ipsum omnia condita sint & consistant. Israelitæ in deserto tentarunt Dominum Deum suum, qui eos ex Ægypto eduxit, & se unum ac solum Deum ipsorum esse testatus est. Apostolus autem hoc interpretatur de Christo, quæ Israelitæ in deserto tentarunt. Unus ille Deus Israelitarum peculiariter sibi hoc nomen Iehova vendicat, & tamen Apostoli ea quæ in Prophetis de hoc uno Iehova dicuntur, ad Christum accommodant, quòd ipse sit hic Iehova. Tribuitur quidem aliquando Deitas Patri, ut quum Apostolus precatur Gratiam & pacem à Deo Patre & Domino Iesu Christo: item quùm meminit agnitionis, conspectus, gratiæ & pacis Dei & Domini Iesu Christi: verùm hic Patri non ita tribuitur Deitas, ut non eadem etiam sit Deitas Filij: sed quia Mediatoris Domini nostri Iesu Christi mentio fit, per quem nobis ad Deum accessus est, ideò Christus medius quasi inter Deum Patrem & nos interponitur, nō quod essentia, sed persona & officio alius sit:at quum essentiam respiciunt Apostoli Chri-stum Deum super omnia benedictum, & magnum Deum, ac verum Deum nominat. Itaque quū Apostolus ad Timotheū inquit, Unus Deus, unus Mediator Dei & hominum homo Christus Iesus, nō negamus unius Dei nomine posse Patrem intelligi: sed tamen contendimus Filium esse etiam unum Deum cum Patre, si essentiam spectemus: id quod communi consensu Patrum doctissimi in huius loci interpretatione docent. Videtur quibusdam Paulus Patris & Filii Deitate distinguere, quum inquit, Tamē nobis est unus Deus qui est Pater, à quo sunt omnia & nos in eo: & unus Dominus Iesus Chri-stus per quem omnia & nos per ipsum. Sed Apostolus hoc loco Deum verum à falsis diis distinguit: inquit enim, Nam etiamsi sint qui dicantur dij, & in cælo & in terra (sicut sunt dij multi & domini multi) nobis tamen unus est Deus Pater ille à quo omnia. Itaq; si Pater ita est unus, ut Filius alius ab eo sit Deus, necessario Filius falsis diis adnumerandus erit: nā præter unum Deum non alios Deos agnoscit Apostolus, nisi eos qui dicuntur dii, & ut alibi inquit, Natura dii non sunt. Distinguit, fateor, Patre à Filio, Patrique tribuit quòd ab ipso sint omnia, quia ab ipso est origo: in personarum distinctione, ipse solus est ingenitus: quod Patri proprium est ratione personæ, non autem in essentia discrimen facit. nam & Filii essentia est ingenita, unde Basilius inquit ἀγέννητος ἐστὶ ἡ [?]ἁπλωσις τῆς ὑπάρξεος οὐ τῆς οὐσίας. Neque ideò Filius non est Deus à quo omnia, quia dicitur per ipsum omnia: nā harū præpositionū discrimen nullum in scripturis servatur, quandoquidē Apostolus ad Romanos, Ex eo inquit, & per eum, & in ipsum sunt omnia: hoc sive de Patre sive de Filio intelligamus, sive Deo simpliciter attribuamus Patri Filio & Spiritui sancto, corruit illa ab Arianis conficta distinctio: qui diversitate istarum præpositionum probare volunt, diversam aut distinctam esse Patris & Filii essentiam. Afferuntur præterea multa alia ex Paulo, quo probetur Patris & Filii eiusmodi distinctio, ut non sint unus Deus: quæ omnia commemorare longum esset, cùm in omnibus nō essentia Filii à Patre distinguatur, sed Christus ut Mediator Patri conferatur: quod etsi ante dictum est non temere repeto. Ne ta-men videar ea velle subterfugere aliqua apponā. Colossenses tertio: Vita no-stra, inquit, abscondita est cum Christo in Deo. loquitur hic Apostolus de Chri-sto ut Mediatore, qui à mortuis resurrexerit, & ad dextram Dei sedeat: num ergo essentiam ideò distinguit, aut propter dispensationem veram Deitatem soli Patri tribuit? Gratias ibidem iubet agere Deo & Patri per Christum, haud dubiè ut per Mediatorem. Ad Timoth. scribit Apostolus, Denuntio tibi coram Deo qui vivificat omnia,&Iesu Christo, qui testatu fecit cora[?] Pontio Pilato bonam professionem. An obscurum est Christum hic ut Mediatorem à Patre distinguì? Quod si Deus qui vivificat omnia, ita de Patre dicitur ut non sit Filio proprium, quare ergo Apostolus Christum vitam nostram nominat? quare Filius se dicit vivificare quos velit? quare Spiritus vivificare dicitur? Ad Thessalonicenses scribitur poenam daturos eos qui non nouerunt Deum, neque auscultant Euangelio Domini nostri Iesu Christi. An nō aute[?] Deus hic quem illi ignorarunt, is Deus est cui illic Apostolus tribuit iustū iudicium, regnum pro quo fideles patiuntur, cuius sunt ecclesiæ quas Dei ecclesias nominat: quæro igitur an hæc solius Patris sint, & non etiā Filii? Ad Philippenses Pax, ait, Dei quæ superat omne intellectum, præsidio erit cordibus vestris, & mentibus vestris in Christo Iesu. Sed si hæc pax Patris tantū est, aliáne erit ab ea in quā vocati sumus, ab ea pace quā Christus suā vocat, & se eam fidelibus dare & relinquere inquit: si pax hæc nō etiā Christi est, frustra propheta Esaias ipsum Principem pacis nominauit, & quidē eius pacis cuius non erit finis. Ad Thessalonicenses, Ut glorificetur, inquit, nomen Domini nostri Iesu Christi in vobis, & vos in eo, ex gratia Dei nostri, & Domini Iesu Christi. Sed quomodo glorificamur in Christo? Quòd potentiam & robur ab ipso accipimus, ut malis non cedamus. de hac enim glorificatione in persecutionibus hoc loco Apostolus loquitur. Si hæc gratia solius Patris est, quare in eadem epistola Paulus precatur, ut Dominus noster Iesus Christus, & Deus ac Pater consoletur corda fidelium ac stabiliat? cur item inquit, Fidelis est Dominus qui stabiliet vos & tuebitur à malo? Si gratia Dei Patris tantum est, quare in fine epistolarum Paulus non Patris aut Dei, sed gratiam Domini nostri Iesu Christi fidelibus optat? In Apocalypsi optat Ioannes pacem ab eo qui Est, qui Erat, qui Venturus est, & à Iesu Christo, qui fidus est ille testis, primogenitus ille ex mortuis. Quæro an non Christus reuelarit hæc Ioanni? utique. Nam ideo Apocalypsis Iesu Christi nominatur. Is autem qui Ioannem alloquitur, inquit, Ego sum A & Ω primus ille & ultimus. Et hæc dicere inquit Ioannes eum qui Est, Erat, & Venturus est. Quæro hic qui Venturus est, an non potius de Filio esset intelligendum, etiamsi Ioannes hoc non explicaret? Hæc tamen omnia non ideo adduximus, ut negemus Filium à Patre distinctum esse: sed ut ostendamus ita esse distinctum ut una eademque sit utriusque Deitas, ita ut quæ Deo simpliciter tribuantur in scripturis, non ita uni Deo Patri tribuantur, ut non etiam Filius Dei nomine intelligatur, etsi ut Mediator à Deo Patre distinguitur. Quòd si omninò ita unus nus Deus est Pater, ut Filius non sit idem Deus: ergo quum Christum unum Dominū appellat apostolus, Pater non erit Dominus. at qualis Deus erit abs-que dominio? Si igitur ubique in sacris literis quū Dei nomē absque adiunc̄o aliquo Filii autverbi nomine ponitur, solus Pater significatur, quid dicemus de dicto Christi, Nemo est bonus nisi unus Deus? negabimusne Christum bonū esse? num etiam negabimus eum esse æternum, immortale, invisibilem, sapien-tem? quandoquidem hæc soli Deo tribuit apostolus ad Tim. Respondent Filium hæc omnia habere, sed depēdenter: Patrē vero independenter. Nā Patrem esse ingenitum & αὐτόθεον[?], Filium à Patre essentiatum esse, itaque habere eum æternitatē, immortalitatem, bonitatem & reliqua à Patre. Et hæc quidē exponunt verbis paucis, erroribus multis. Cūm.n. Filium à Patre essentiatum esse dicunt, videntur præsupponere prius Patrem fuisse, & deinde ex eo Filium natum esse, ac ita suam essentiam accepisse à Patre, quemadmodum fit in generatione humana. Filium item faciunt Patre minorem: si.n. Pater omnia habet à seipso, nihil autem à seipso Filius habet, ingens inter ipsos discrimen & tale statuitur quod vix ullam comparationem admittit. Ponunt essentiam generare & generari, cùm tamen in his rebus inferioribus & imperfectis non essentia generet, sed res subsistens. Nō negamus Filium habere essentiam à Deo Patre, sed essentiam genitam negamus. Et quum dicimus Filium essentiam à Patre habere, credimus illum, & eandem & totam à Patre habere, atque hoc ab æterno. Si enim non habet essentiam Patris, est diversus Deus, imò non est Deus. Sin eam habet totam & æqualis est Patri, tum eadem erit utriusque essentia: nam æqualitas in essentia est identitas. si autem non habet totam, non est Deus, aut esset Deus cum defectu: id enim non haberet quod illi deest, & in Patre est: deinde statuceretur hac ratione essentiam Dei, quæ simplicissima est, in partes posse dividi: quod est salsissimum. Sin verò dixerint illum non habere essentiam Dei, sed esse ex essentia Dei (hoc enim cauillo u-tuntur) generationem eius tollunt: in rebus enim naturalibus omne quod generatur non tantùm fit ex essentia aut substantia alterius, sed eam in se habet non totam sed ex parte, ob harum rerum imperfectionem: in diuinis autem non pars, sed tota essentia generantis communicatur. Verùm de his nunc dis-putare non est mei propositi, quandoquidem jam dudum hos errores diligen-ter confutarunt cùm alii, tum præsertim quem honoris causa nomino Ioan-nes Caluinus ecclesiæ Dei decus, qui primùm Serueti & postea Valentini quoque Gentilis blasphemias doctissimè confutauit, & nuper breui ad vos honorandi fratres admonitione conscripta, paucis multa complexus est, quæ ad hanc causam faciunt. Equidem meliora spero de tabulæ auctore, quis-quis is tandem fuerit: neque enim in eas blasphemias erumpit quas Gentilis e-ructauit, & quidam alij clanculum susurrare solent. Sed tamen ea semina ia-cit, ex quibus deinde magna impietatis messis oritur. Nam si voluerimus in Trinitate talem distinctionem consectari, quæ essentiam Patris à Filii essen-tia distinguat, ita ut in Patre tantùm vera deitas remaneat, statim hinc conficietur, Patrem & Filium duos esse Deos, & quidem admodum ine-quales. Hoc autem asserere adeo impium & à ratione alienum est, ut ipse Arius huius impietatis patronus, maluerit Filium Dei creaturam dice-re, quàm duos Deos fateri. Posito autem semel hoc fundamento, aliam esse essentiâ Patris quàm Filii, quum deinde incarnatio Filii explicanda est, bone Deus quæ portenta comminiscuntur nonnulli: quantam confusionem introdu-cunt, dum ea quæ humanæ naturæ sunt, omnia ipsi deitati tribuunt, omniá-que quæ de Christo dicta sunt in sacris literis, simpliciter & absque o-mni tropo intelligi debere contendunt. Quæ cùm ita sint, Fratres honorandi, vestræ pietatis & prudentiæ erit vigilare, & cauere ne impium hoc semen sa-tan in ecclesiis vestris serat: nam si radices egerit, nunquam poterit nisi cum magno motu & turbatione ecclesiarum denuo extirpari. Quas enim turbas o-lim in ecclesia excitarit Arius, cuius errores nunc alio nomine & titulo re-nouātur, omnes historiæ testantur. Quanuis autem pii principes Synodis mul-tis malum hoc compescere conati sint, semper tamen aliqui fuerunt, qui illud aliis verbis, quasi alia ac nova quadam veste tectum & ornatum in publicum producerent: donec tandem omnis hæc impietas, in Mahometanismum quasi quandam omnium hæresecon sententiam confluxit. Est scilicet humanis inge-niis insita quædam curiositas, quæ cùm in aliis rebus sæpe pernitiosa est, tum maximè ubi se ad Diuinam maiestatem scrutandam contulerit: cuius gloria a-cies humanæ mentis quantumuis perspicax opprimitur. Quare illi rectissimè consulere videtur, qui iubent huiusmodi curiosas quæstiones omni studio vita-re, & acquiescere simplici doctrinæ, quam nobis tradunt sacræ litere. Multa quidem præclarè à Patribus de Trinitate scripta sunt, postquam Arius hac de re controuersiam mouit: & legibus quoque Imperatoriis prohibitum est, ne quis puram hanc & catholicam Patrum doctrinam è scripturis desumptam impugnet. verùm ab his hominibus & hic Patrum consensus spernitur, & leges ab ipsis Leguleis qui sunt ex hac factione negliguntur: tantùm quæ ob-scurius dicta sunt à vetustoribus antequam vlla hac de re controuersia esset, col-ligunt. Itaque ego nunc neque ad Patres, neque ad leges, sed ad scripturas, de quiquibus gloriatur eos provoco. Illa igitur & præterea ipsa ratio docet nos Deum esse ens summum & unicum, atque ut Tertullianus loquitur, summum magnum, & forma & ratione & vi & potestate: itaque quum Deus nominatur, omnes animo concipimus Deum esse summū quid, quo nihil melius, nihil maius & præstatius esse possit. Rursus eadem Scriptura prædicat nobis Patrem, Filium & Spiritum sanctum, & Patrem verum Deum, & Filium verum Deum, & Spiritum sanctū verum Deū esse testatur. Hæc tamen quum audimus, nō dicimus tres esse Deos: quia unum Deum Scriptura prædicat, & Deus si nō est unicus non est Deus, quia nō est summus: quare etsi tres nominari audimus, unum tamen Deum credimus, unā scilicet naturam seu essentiā omnibus tribus communem: & rursus, quia certis propriisque notionibus eadem Scriptura Patre a Filio & Spiritu sancto distinguit, rursus illi fidem habemus esse hanc distinctionem veram, quæ re non tantum nomine distinguatur. Ratio quidem hic hæret quomodo Deus sit trinus & unus: & ideo plerique acuti homines hac doctrinam impugnant, quod eam non possunt ratione comprehendere: sed in hac quæstione, ut bene monet Athanasius, etiam si te non explices, non est ideo diffidendum sacris Scripturis, quoniam melius est hæsitabūdos ignorata causa tacere & credere, quam ideo nō credere quia hæsites. In hac fidei simplicitate scimus multa cavillari homines sciolos, qui in his rebus acumen suum volunt ostendere: sed eorum sophismata facile retundere & cavere poteritis, si Scripturarū lumine adhibito non tantum obiter initia & semina[?] huius adversæ doctrinæ considerave-ritis, sed flores & fructus impiorum dogmatum qui ex his oriuntur. Qua in re observanda studium & diligentia adhibenda est, propterea quod huius erroris patroni suam impietatem non statim produnt, sed initio in paucis ab usitata doctrina recedunt, donec se in animos hominum penitus insinuarint: tum enim demum libere suam impietatem effundunt. Itaque quidam huius factionis princeps inter suos aperte docet duos esse Deos, & multa impie de incarnatione Dei nugantur, quæ eius discipuli apud vos forte adhuc vix musitare nunc audent: verum si locum nacti fuerint & tempus idoneum, tum demum aperte Arianismum eos prædicare videbitis. Turbavit aliquandiu Ecclesias vestras Stancarus, sed mihi credite, plus est periculi ab his qui se amicos nobis in eo impugnādo simulat, quam ab eius aperta maledicētia. Non sumo mihi tantum, ut existimem me affirmare posse, quo animo quisque doceat: sed tamen nisi me multa & graves coniectura fallunt, plerique ex his qui novas has de Trinitate quæstiones movent, non tam Christi quam suam gloriam quærunt: & non ecclesiæ utilitati, sed suo commodo student, atque vestra bonitate abutuntur. Nam ut olim pseudoapostoli Corinthios, sic nonnulli horum vos quoque conantur in seruitutem redigere, extollunt sese vt vos excedant, & à vobis accipiant. Quare, Magnifici Domini & Fratres honorandi, euigilate, & in tempore horum insidiis occurrite: ac vos quidem, quibus docendi munus commissum est, non patiamini vos seduci horum hominum astutiis, vt aliquid nouitatis studio à veritate simplicis doctrinæ recedatis: vos etiam, Magnifici domini patroni ecclesiarum, ne faciatis ecclesias vestras asylum ambitiosorum & contentiosorum hominum, qui religionis titulo non tantùm optimè institutas ecclesias, verùm etiam ipsam Christi gloriam, quam nos defendimus, impugnant: nolite quaeso pati vt illi diutius pios illudant, & ita turpiter vestra bonitate & libertate abutantur. Agnosco quidem in me non esse authoritatem aut doctrinam tantam, vt vos admonere aut vobis consilium dare possim: veruntamen ardore quodam & studio vestri accensus, non potui quin Stancaro respondissem, vos non alterius periculi admonere, quod mihi priore grauius esse videtur: cupio autem, Fratres, hæc accipi eo animo quo à me scripta sunt, vt hæc omnia ad Dei gloriam, pacem & salutem ecclesiarum faciant, id quod vnice hæc scribendo spectaui. Deus gubernet vos Spiritu suo, errores eorumque auctores confundat, & exoptatam ecclesiis pacem restituat. Amen.
units.tr: Nor, for that reason, are we Sabellians. Although we believe in one God and one essence, we do not make one God of three names. We maintain distinct persons, so that the Father is not the Son and the Son is not the Father. We willingly grant that the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another. But we do not add that the Father is one God and the Son or the Holy Spirit another God, since the name of God signifies the essence, which is equally the same in all the persons, and it does not admit relation. So the author of the table is wrong to write that whenever the name of God is used absolutely it must be understood of the Father alone, as when it is said, "Hear, O Israel, the Lord thy God is one" (Deut. 6:4). For the law given by him commands Israel to worship this one God. Christ also says, "Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve" (Matt. 4:10), and through the Prophet God says that every knee must bow to him (Isa. 45:23). If, then, the name of God here signifies the Father only, we sin by worshipping the Son, and the Apostle wrongly applied to the Son that every knee must bow to him (Phil. 2:10). The God who is one created heaven and earth and this whole universe of things, and he adorns himself with this title through the Prophets and distinguishes himself from false gods. Yet the Apostle to the Colossians and to the Hebrews ascribes this to Christ, that all things were made and hold together through him (Col. 1:16–17; Heb. 1:2). The Israelites in the desert tempted the Lord their God, who led them out of Egypt and declared himself the one and only God of them. The Apostle, however, interprets what the Israelites tempted in the desert as referring to Christ (1 Cor. 10:9). That one God of Israel claims this name Jehovah for himself in a peculiar way, and yet the Apostles apply to Christ what is said of this one Jehovah in the Prophets, because he himself is this Jehovah. Indeed, Deity is sometimes ascribed to the Father, as when the Apostle prays for "grace and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ," and likewise when he speaks of the knowledge, the appearing, the grace and the peace of God and the Lord Jesus Christ. But here Deity is not ascribed to the Father in such a way that the same Deity is not also the Son's. Rather, because mention is made of our Mediator, the Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have access to God, Christ is placed as it were in the middle between God the Father and us. This is not because he differs in essence, but in person and office. When the Apostles regard the essence, they call Christ "God over all, blessed for ever" (Rom. 9:5), "the great God" and "the true God." So when the Apostle says to Timothy, "There is one God and one Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus" (1 Tim. 2:5), we do not deny that the Father may be understood by the name of the one God. Yet we contend that the Son is also one God with the Father, if we consider the essence. The most learned of the Fathers, by common consent, teach this in their interpretation of this passage. To some it seems that Paul distinguishes the Deity of the Father and of the Son when he says, "Yet to us there is one God, the Father, of whom are all things, and we in him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, by whom are all things, and we by him" (1 Cor. 8:6). But the Apostle here distinguishes the true God from false gods. For he says, "For even if there are those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth (as there are many gods and many lords), yet to us there is one God, the Father, of whom are all things" (1 Cor. 8:5–6). So if the Father is one in such a way that the Son is another God apart from him, the Son would necessarily have to be counted among the false gods. For apart from the one God the Apostle acknowledges no other gods except those who are called gods, and, as he says elsewhere, "those which by nature are not gods" (Gal. 4:8). I grant that he distinguishes the Father from the Son, and ascribes to the Father that all things are from him, because the origin is from him. In the distinction of persons he alone is unbegotten, which is proper to the Father by reason of his person, but this does not make a difference in essence. For the essence of the Son is also unbegotten. Hence Basil says, "Unbegottenness is the simplicity of the existence, not of the essence" [ἀγέννητος ἐστὶ ἡ ἁπλωσις τῆς ὑπάρξεος οὐ τῆς οὐσίας]. Nor, because all things are said to be through the Son, is he therefore not the God from whom all things are, for no difference between these prepositions is kept in the Scriptures. The Apostle to the Romans says, "For from him, and through him, and to him are all things" (Rom. 11:36). Whether we understand this of the Father or of the Son, or ascribe it simply to God, to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, that distinction devised by the Arians falls to the ground. They wish to prove by the difference of these prepositions that the essence of the Father and of the Son is different or distinct. Many other passages from Paul are also cited to prove such a distinction between Father and Son that they are not one God. It would be tedious to recount them all, since in all of them it is not the essence of the Son that is distinguished from the Father, but Christ is set over against the Father as Mediator. I do not repeat this carelessly, although I have said it before. Yet, so that I may not seem to wish to evade these passages, I will add some of them. "Our life," says the Apostle in Colossians 3, "is hid with Christ in God." Here the Apostle speaks of Christ as Mediator, who rose from the dead and sits at the right hand of God. Does he therefore distinguish the essence, or does he ascribe true Deity to the Father alone on account of the economy? In the same place he bids them give thanks to God and the Father through Christ, undoubtedly as through the Mediator. The Apostle writes to Timothy, "I charge thee before God, who quickeneth all things, and before Jesus Christ, who before Pontius Pilate witnessed a good confession" (1 Tim. 6:13). Is it unclear that Christ is here distinguished from the Father as Mediator? But if "God who quickeneth all things" is said of the Father in such a way that it is not proper to the Son as well, why then does the Apostle call Christ our life (Col. 3:4)? Why does the Son say that he quickens whom he will (John 5:21)? Why is the Spirit said to quicken (John 6:63; Rom. 8:11)? To the Thessalonians it is written that those who do not know God, and do not obey the gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ, shall be punished (2 Thess. 1:8). Is not this God whom they did not know the God to whom the Apostle there ascribes the righteous judgment and the kingdom for which the faithful suffer, and whose churches he calls the churches of God? I ask, then, whether these belong to the Father alone and not also to the Son. To the Philippians he says, "The peace of God, which passes all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds in Christ Jesus" (Phil. 4:7). But if this peace belongs only to the Father, how will it differ from that peace into which we are called, the peace which Christ calls his own and says he gives and leaves to the faithful (John 14:27)? If this peace is not also Christ's, the prophet Isaiah called him the Prince of Peace in vain (Isa. 9:6), and indeed of that peace there shall be no end. To the Thessalonians he says, "That the name of our Lord Jesus Christ may be glorified in you, and you in him, according to the grace of our God and the Lord Jesus Christ" (2 Thess. 1:12). But how are we glorified in Christ? In that we receive power and strength from him, so that we do not yield to evils. For the Apostle speaks in this place of this glorification in persecutions. If this grace belongs only to the Father, why does Paul in the same letter pray that our Lord Jesus Christ and God and Father may comfort and establish the hearts of the faithful (2 Thess. 2:16–17)? Likewise he says, "The Lord is faithful, who shall establish you and keep you from evil" (2 Thess. 3:3). If the grace of God the Father is only the Father's, why at the end of his letters does Paul wish the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ to the faithful, and not the grace of the Father or of God? In the Apocalypse John wishes peace from him who is, who was, and who is to come, and from Jesus Christ, who is the faithful witness, the firstborn from the dead (Rev. 1:4–5). I ask whether Christ did not reveal these things to John? Certainly he did, for the Apocalypse is therefore called the revelation of Jesus Christ. And he who speaks to John says, "I am the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last" (Rev. 1:8, 17). And John says that these things are said by him who is, who was, and who is to come. I ask here whether "who is to come" ought not rather to be understood of the Son, even though John does not explain this. Yet we have not brought forward all these things to deny that the Son is distinct from the Father, but to show that he is distinct in such a way that the Deity of both is one and the same. What is ascribed to God simply in the Scriptures is not so ascribed to the one God the Father that the Son is not also understood by the name of God, even though as Mediator he is distinguished from God the Father. If indeed the one God is the Father in such a way that the Son is not the same God, then, when the Apostle calls Christ "one Lord," the Father will not be Lord. But what sort of God would he be without dominion? So if everywhere in the sacred letters, when the name of God is used without any addition of the name of the Son or of the Word, the Father alone is signified, what shall we say of the saying of Christ, "None is good but one, that is God" (Mark 10:18)? Shall we deny that Christ is good? Shall we also deny that he is eternal, immortal, invisible, wise? Yet the Apostle ascribes these things to God alone (1 Tim. 1:17). They answer that the Son has all these things, but dependently, whereas the Father has them independently. For they say the Father is unbegotten and self-God [αὐτόθεον], while the Son has his essence from the Father, and so has eternity, immortality, goodness and the rest from the Father. These they set forth in a few words, but with many errors. For when they say that the Son has his essence from the Father, they seem to presuppose that the Father existed first, and then the Son was born from him and so received his essence from the Father, as happens in human generation. They also make the Son less than the Father. For if the Father has all things from himself, and the Son has nothing from himself, a vast difference is set up between them, and such that it hardly admits any comparison. They posit that essence begets and is begotten, whereas in these lower and imperfect things it is not the essence that begets but the subsisting thing. We do not deny that the Son has his essence from God the Father, but we deny that the essence is begotten. And when we say that the Son has his essence from the Father, we believe that he has it from the Father wholly and identically, and this from eternity. For if he does not have the essence of the Father, he is a different God, indeed he is not God. But if he has it wholly and is equal to the Father, then the essence of both will be the same, for equality in essence is identity. If, however, he does not have it wholly, he is not God, or he would be God with a deficiency. For he would not have what is lacking to him and is in the Father. Further, by this reasoning the essence of God, which is most simple, could be divided into parts, and that is most false. But if they say that he does not have the essence of God but is from the essence of God (for they use this quibble), they take away his generation. For in natural things whatever is generated is not only from the essence or substance of another, but has that essence in itself not wholly but in part, because of the imperfection of these things. In divine things, however, not a part but the whole essence of the begetter is communicated. But it is not my purpose now to dispute these things, since long ago they have been carefully refuted, both by others and especially by one whom I name out of respect, John Calvin, the glory of the Church of God, who first most learnedly refuted the blasphemies of Servetus and afterwards also those of Valentinus Gentilis. Recently, in a brief admonition written to you, honoured brothers, he has embraced in few words many things that bear on this cause. Indeed, I hope better things of the author of the table, whoever he may be, for he does not break out into those blasphemies which Gentilis belched forth and which some others are accustomed to whisper secretly. Yet he sows those seeds from which a great harvest of impiety then springs up. For if we should wish to pursue in the Trinity such a distinction as separates the essence of the Father from the essence of the Son, so that true Deity remains only in the Father, it will at once follow that the Father and the Son are two Gods, and indeed very unequal ones. To assert this is so impious and so foreign to reason that Arius himself, the patron of this impiety, preferred to say that the Son of God was a creature rather than confess two Gods. Once this foundation is laid, that the essence of the Father is other than that of the Son, then when the incarnation of the Son is to be explained, good God, what monstrosities some devise! What great confusion they introduce, while they ascribe to the Deity itself all that belongs to human nature, and contend that all things said of Christ in the sacred letters must be understood simply and without any trope! Since these things are so, honoured brothers, it will be your task in godliness and prudence to be watchful and to take care that Satan does not sow this impious seed in your churches. For if it takes root, it can never be uprooted again except with great upheaval and disturbance of the churches. All histories bear witness to the tumults that Arius once stirred up in the Church, whose errors are now renewed under another name and title. Although godly princes have tried to check this evil by many synods, there have always been some who brought it forward again in public in other words, as if covered and adorned with some new and different garment, until at last all this impiety flowed together into Mohammedanism, as into a kind of summary of all heresies. Of course there is an innate curiosity in human minds which, while it is often pernicious in other matters, is especially so when it sets itself to scrutinize the divine majesty. Under its weight the keenest sight of the human mind, however sharp, is crushed. Therefore he seems to counsel most rightly who bids us avoid such curious questions with all care and acquiesce in the simple doctrine which the sacred letters deliver to us. Many excellent things have indeed been written by the Fathers about the Trinity since Arius stirred up controversy on this matter. By imperial laws it has also been forbidden that anyone should impugn this pure and catholic doctrine of the Fathers, drawn from the Scriptures. But these men scorn both the consensus of the Fathers and the laws, and the very lawyers who belong to this faction neglect the laws. They gather only what has been said more obscurely by the older writers, before any controversy on this matter arose. Therefore I now challenge them, not to the Fathers nor to the laws, but to the Scriptures, on which they glory. Those Scriptures, and reason itself besides, teach us that God is the supreme and unique being, and, as Tertullian says, "great in form, reason, power and might." So when God is named, we all conceive in our minds that God is something supreme, than which nothing better, nothing greater and more excellent can be. Again, the same Scripture proclaims to us the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and testifies that the Father is the true God, the Son is the true God, and the Holy Spirit is the true God. Yet when we hear these things we do not say that there are three Gods, because Scripture proclaims one God, and if God is not unique he is not God, because he is not supreme. So although we hear three named, we nevertheless believe in one God, namely one nature or essence common to all three. And again, because Scripture distinguishes the Father from the Son and the Holy Spirit by certain and proper notions, we in turn hold that this distinction is true, and is a distinction not only in name but in reality. Reason indeed sticks here at how God is three and one, and therefore many keen men attack this doctrine because they cannot grasp it by reason. But in this question, as Athanasius rightly reminds us, even if you cannot explain it, one should not therefore distrust the sacred Scriptures, since it is better to be silent and believe when hesitating about a cause unknown, than not to believe because one hesitates. In this simplicity of faith we know that smatterers, who wish to show off their cleverness in these matters, cavil at many things. But you will be able to easily repel and guard against their sophisms if, with the light of the Scriptures brought to bear, you consider not only in passing the beginnings and seeds of this contrary doctrine, but also the flowers and fruits of the impious dogmas that spring from them. In this matter zeal and diligence must be applied, because the patrons of this error do not at once betray their impiety, but at first depart in a few points from the accepted doctrine, until they have insinuated themselves deeply into men's minds. Only then do they freely pour out their impiety. So a certain leader of this faction openly teaches among his own that there are two Gods, and talks impiously in many ways about the incarnation of God. His disciples perhaps hardly dare to mutter these things among you as yet. But if they find an opportunity and a fitting time, then at last you will see them openly proclaiming Arianism. Stancarus disturbed your churches for a while. But believe me, there is more danger from those who pretend to be our friends in attacking him than from his open abuse. I do not claim so much for myself as to think I can affirm with what intention each man teaches. Yet, unless my many and grave conjectures deceive me, most of those who stir up these new questions about the Trinity seek not so much the glory of Christ as their own, and they study not the benefit of the Church but their own advantage, and abuse your goodness. For as the false apostles once tried to bring the Corinthians into bondage, so some of these try to do with you too. They exalt themselves so as to surpass you, and to receive from you. Therefore, honoured Lords and brothers, be watchful, and in time meet their snares. You, to whom the office of teaching has been committed, do not allow yourselves to be seduced by the cunning of these men, so that through a zeal for novelty you depart from the truth of the simple doctrine. You also, honoured lords and patrons of the churches, do not make your churches a refuge for ambitious and contentious men who, under the title of religion, assail not only well-ordered churches but even the glory of Christ itself, which we defend. I beg you, do not suffer them to mock the godly any longer, and so shamefully abuse your goodness and liberty. I acknowledge that in myself there is not such authority or learning that I can admonish you or give you counsel. Nevertheless, kindled by a certain ardour and zeal for you, I could not but answer Stancarus, and warn you of a danger which seems to me heavier than the former. I wish, brothers, that these things be received in the spirit in which I have written them, so that all of them may serve the glory of God, the peace and salvation of the churches, which alone I have aimed at in writing. May God govern you by his Spirit, confound the errors and their authors, and restore to the churches the peace they long for. Amen.

units.la: THESES THEOLOGICÆ D. IOH. HYPERII DE TRINITATE, QVOD FILIVS Patri coessentialis, coæternus, & per omnia coæqualis sit, propositæ à doctore Andrea Hyperio, in Academia Marpurgensi, 28 Augusti, M. D. LXIIII.
units.tr: THESES THEOLOGICAE OF DR JOHANN HYPERIUS CONCERNING THE TRINITY, THAT THE SON IS CO-ESSENTIAL AND CO-ETERNAL WITH THE FATHER AND IN ALL THINGS EQUAL TO HIM, PROPOSED BY DOCTOR ANDREAS HYPERIUS IN THE ACADEMY AT MARBURG, 28 AUGUST 1564.

units.la: BAsilius lib. 1. contra apologiam Eunomij, testis est, hæreticum Eunomium citò quàm plurimos seduxisse, quòd callidè fingeret, se cum orthodoxis plane idem de Filio Dei sentire: quum revera quamuis iisdem uteretur verbis, sententiam tamen tueretur longè diuersissimam. Idem faciunt nunc quidam noui Ariani, vel potiùs Eunomiani, qui simulant se nobiscum confiteri Filium Dei verum Deum, de Deo vero: cogerunt interim undecunque possunt arma & argumenta, quibus Patre inferiorem, & nullo modo æqualem demonstrent.
units.tr: Basil, in Book 1, against the Apology of Eunomius, bears witness that the heretic Eunomius quickly led very many astray, because he cunningly pretended that he thought exactly the same as the orthodox about the Son of God. In truth, although he used the same words, he defended a view very far different. Some new Arians, or rather Eunomians, do the same today. They pretend that they confess with us that the Son of God is true God, of true God; meanwhile they gather from every quarter whatever weapons and arguments they can to demonstrate that he is inferior to the Father and in no way equal.

units.la: 2 Atqui obsistunt eis plures Scripturarum loci, apertissimè testantes, Filium Dei verum & perfectum Deum, Patri cum essentia, tum potentia ac dignitate per omnia parem, & aequalem existere.
units.tr: 2 Yet several passages of Scripture stand against them, testifying most openly that the Son of God is true and perfect God, who exists as equal to the Father in every respect, both in essence and in power and dignity.

units.la: 3 Ante omnia verum esse oportet, quod genitum[?] & simpliciter de Filio dicitur, Quum in forma Dei esset, non rapinam arbitratus est, ut esset aequalis Deo, Philipp. 2. Quum etiam ubicunque Filius se appellat Filium Dei, & suum Patrem Deum, ibi se Deo Patri aequalem asseuerat, ut Ioan. 5.
units.tr: 3 Above all, what is said simply of the Son must be true: "Being in the form of God, he did not think it robbery to be equal with God" (Phil. 2). Also, wherever the Son calls himself the Son of God and calls the Father his God, there he asserts that he is equal to God the Father (John 5).

units.la: 4 Quod autem Filius sit Patri ὁμοούσιος, suis ipse confirmat verbis, dicens, Ego & Pater unum sumus, Ioan. 10. Mea omnia tua sunt, & tua mea sunt, Ioan. 17. Qui videt me, videt & Patrem. Credite mihi, quod ego in Patre sum, & Pater in me, Ioan. 14.
units.tr: 4 That the Son is consubstantial [ὁμοούσιος] with the Father he confirms himself in his own words: "I and the Father are one" (John 10); "All my things are yours, and yours are mine" (John 17); "He who sees me sees the Father also"; "Believe me that I am in the Father and the Father in me" (John 14).

units.la: 5 De Patris & Filij in potentia aequalitate. Sicut Pater meus ad hoc usque tempus operatur, & ego operor. Et quaecunque Pater fecerit, haec itidem & Filius facit. Item, Sicut Pater suscitat mortuos & viuificat, sic & Filius quos vult viuificat. Neque enim Pater iudicat quenquam, sed omne iudicium dedit Filio, ut omnes honorent Filium, sicut honorat Patrem. Ioan. 5. Iterum, Vos dicitis me blasphemare, quia dixerim, Filius Dei sum: si non facio opera Patris mei, nolite credere mihi: sin vero facio, & si mihi non creditis, operibus credite, ut cognoscatis & credatis quod Pater in me est, & ego in eo.
units.tr: 5 Of the equality of Father and Son in power. "My Father works even until now, and I work" (John 5). "Whatever the Father does, these things the Son also does likewise." Again: "As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so the Son also gives life to whom he wills. For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, that all may honour the Son just as they honour the Father" (John 5). Again: "You say that I blaspheme, because I said, I am the Son of God. If I do not do the works of my Father, do not believe me; but if I do them, even if you do not believe me, believe the works, that you may know and believe that the Father is in me and I in him" (John 10).

units.la: 6 Ad haec, ratione principij, ordinis, sive gradus, vel quocunque alio modo non esse Patre inferiorem, ex his colligitur. In principio erat Verbum, & Verbum erat apud Deum, Ioann. 1. Ipse est ante omnia, & omnia per illum consistunt: & ipse est caput corporis Ecclesiae, qui est principium, Coloss. 1. Aliquoties Filius ante Patrem collocatur, Ioann. 1. In principio erat Verbum, & Verbum erat apud Deum. Galat. 1. Paulus Apostolus per Iesum Christum, & Deum Patrem. 2. Corinth. 13. Gratia Domini nostri Iesu Christi, & charitas Dei, & communicatio Spiritus sancti sit in omnibus vobis. 2. Thessal. 2. Ipse Dominus noster Iesus Christus & Deus, & Pater noster. Eodem spectant loci, qui significant, Filium sedere aut stare ad dextram Patris, Psalm. 110. Matth. 22. 26. Marc. 16. Luc. 23. Quid, quod Actor. 2. 8. Nomen Christi Iesu in quo baptizabantur credentes, pro nomine Patris & Filij & Spiritus sancti ponitur?
units.tr: 6 Besides, from these passages it follows that in respect of origin, order, or degree, or in any other way, he is not inferior to the Father. "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God" (John 1). He is before all things, and all things consist in him; and he is the head of the body of the Church, who is the beginning (Col. 1). The Son is sometimes placed before the Father: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God" (John 1); "Paul, an apostle, by Jesus Christ and God the Father" (Gal. 1); "The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Spirit be with you all" (2 Cor. 13); "Our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God our Father" (2 Thess. 2). Passages that say the Son sits or stands at the right hand of the Father point the same way (Ps. 110; Matt. 22, 26; Mark 16; Luke 23). What of Acts 2:38, where the name of Jesus Christ, in which believers were baptized, is put in place of the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit?

units.la: 7 Breuiter quaecunque de Patre praedicantur, ad ipsius dignitatem extollendam, eadem exceptis proprietatibus, cuiusmodi sunt, generare, mittere, de Filio quoque recte asseruntur.
units.tr: 7 In short, whatever is predicated of the Father to extol his dignity is rightly asserted of the Son as well, except for the properties, such as to beget and to send.

units.la: 8 Quamuis nec ipsae proprietates ita accipi debent, ceu qui Patrem a Filio essentia, aut dignitate distinguunt, quum tantum personas, & certas actiones vnicuique personae conuenientes, discernant.
units.tr: 8 Nor should these properties themselves be understood as if they distinguished the Father from the Son in essence or dignity, since they distinguish only the persons and the particular actions belonging to each person.

units.la: 9 Hæc autem omnia quum manifesta sint, nihil prodest Eunomianis quod ad minuendam Filij dignitatem, vocabula essentia, coessentialis, persona, relationis, Trinitatis, vnitatis, prorsus reiici cupiant. Causantur ea in Scripturis non haberi, & nuper à scholasticis & pontificijs doctoribus excogitata.
units.tr: 9 Since all these things are plain, it does the Eunomians no good that they wish utterly to reject the words essence, co-essential, person, relation, Trinity, and unity, in order to diminish the dignity of the Son. They allege that these words are not found in Scripture and were recently devised by the scholastic and Papist teachers.

units.la: 10 Neque id patrocinatur ipsorum causæ, quod docere conantur, solum Deum Patrem esse vnum verum Deum ab omnibus adorandum & invocandum.
units.tr: 10 Nor does it help their cause that they try to teach that God the Father alone is the one true God to be worshipped and invoked by all.

units.la: 11 Falsa quoque est, quam obtrudere conatur hypothesis, seu regula: Vbicunque in scriptura Dei nomen absolutè, & absque adiecto ponitur, de solo Patre debere accipi.
units.tr: 11 Equally false is the hypothesis, or rule, which they try to impose: that wherever the name of God stands absolutely in Scripture, without an addition, it must be understood of the Father alone.

units.la: 12 Perœque [?] absurdum est, epitheton Vnius in solum Deum Patrem competere.
units.tr: 12 It is equally absurd to apply the epithet "one" to God the Father alone.

units.la: 13 Sed neque illæ sententiæ idoneæ sunt ad probandum Filium esse inferiorem Patre, in quibus particulæ, Ex, A, De, In, Per, aliquid secundum divinam naturam à Filio minus vel humilius, quàm in Patre, videntur notare.
units.tr: 13 Nor are those sentences suitable for proving that the Son is inferior to the Father, in which the particles "from", "of", "concerning", "in", and "through" seem to indicate something less or lower in the Son than in the Father, with respect to the divine nature.

units.la: 14 Horrenda porro illorum blasphemia est, qui quo soli Patri supremam afferant dignitatem, Filium, vel Spiritum sanctum debere invocari pernegant.
units.tr: 14 Moreover, the blasphemy of those is dreadful who, in order to ascribe supreme dignity to the Father alone, deny that the Son or the Holy Spirit ought to be invoked.

units.la: 15 Facile insuper intelligimus, eodem illa spectare quæ contendunt, Spiritum sanctum non æqualiter ex Patre & Filio, sed tantum ex Patre per Filium procedere.
units.tr: 15 We easily understand that they aim at the same thing when they contend that the Holy Spirit does not proceed equally from the Father and the Son, but only from the Father through the Son.

units.la: 16 Nos proinde secundum locos Scripturarum antè recitatos, & tria symbola, Apostolicum, Nicenum, Athanasianum, tum Scripturis consentientia credimus, & confitemur in vna essentia divina tres esse personas, Patrem, Filium, & Spiritum sanctum, coessentiales, coaeternas, & per omnia æquales.
units.tr: 16 Therefore, in accordance with the passages of Scripture cited above, and with the three creeds, the Apostles', the Nicene, and the Athanasian, which agree with Scripture, we believe and confess that in the one divine essence there are three persons, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, co-essential, co-eternal, and in all things equal.

units.la: 28. Augusti habita disputatio Marpurgi.
units.tr: 28 August: the disputation was held at Marburg.

units.la: DE DEO, CONTRA NOVOS ARIANOS NVPER IN POLONIA EXORTOS, LIBER secundus, eorundem refutationem continens, per D. Ioannem VVigandum.
units.tr: ON GOD, AGAINST THE NEW ARIANS RECENTLY ARISEN IN POLAND, BOOK TWO, CONTAINING THEIR REFUTATION, BY MASTER JOHANN WIGAND.

units.la: IN omnibus hæreticis tres insignes & tetra notæ, quasi stigmata quædam apparere solent. Primum, detestanda perplexitas rerum nouarum. Deinde horribilis blasphemia. Tertiò effrenis maledicentia. Fontes verò præstigiarum illarum sunt, leuis ambitio, & vindictæ cupiditas, interdum etiam crassa & affectata propemodum insci-tia. Sic noui Ariani, qui in Polonia iam recens exorti sunt, & quorum sese caput& ducem profitetur quidam Gregorius Pauli, Minister Cracouiensis, edita monstrosa tabula & Turri Babel, ex putrida ambitione veluti Scarabaei ex asinis mortuis pullulant. Nam Luthero vix minimam partem revelationis & destructionis Antichristi relinquunt, nempe superioris tantum tecti in aedificio Antichristiano denudationem. At sibimetipsis isti spiritus arrogant Antichristi excisionem & extirpationem ab imis usque fundamentis. Gloriantur sibi longè plura a Deo esse data, quàm Luthero aut aliis. In haeresi vero tradenda, tam sunt intricati, obscuri, variabiles, ut magna attentione adhibita, diuinare vix queas quidnam asseuerare conentur. In blasphemiis porro effutiendis, plane effrontes sunt. Maledicta quoque adeo cumulatè & liuidè effundunt, ut existimes eos meris viperinis linguis pungere.
units.tr: Three distinct and foul marks usually appear on all heretics, like certain brands. First, a loathsome tangle of novelties. Second, a horrible blasphemy. Third, an unbridled slander. The sources of these deceits are a shallow ambition, a desire for revenge, and sometimes also a gross and almost deliberate ignorance. So it is with the new Arians, who have only lately arisen in Poland, and whose head and leader is a certain Gregorius Pauli, minister at Kraków. Having published a monstrous tablet and a Tower of Babel, they swarm out of putrid ambition like beetles from dead asses. For they leave Luther barely the smallest part of the revelation and destruction of Antichrist, namely only the stripping away of the upper roof of the Antichristian building.
