But these spirits claim for themselves the cutting out and uprooting of Antichrist from the very foundations. They boast that far more has been given to them by God than to Luther or to others. Indeed, in delivering their heresy they are so tangled, obscure and changeable that, even with the closest attention, you can scarcely guess what they are trying to assert. Moreover, in pouring out their blasphemies they are plainly brazen. Their curses, too, they pour out so abundantly and so spitefully that you would think they were stinging with pure viperous tongues.

units.la: Tres autem habent isti recentes Ariani hypotheses, sicuti ex tabula ipsorum monstrosa, ex Turri Babel, quam conflant, & ex epistola ad Tigurinos scripta, & ex reliquis ipsorum libris, colligitur.
units.tr: Now these recent Arians have three hypotheses, as is gathered from their monstrous tablet, from the Tower of Babel which they put together, from the letter written to the Zurich people, and from their other books.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: Tres esse, Patrem, Filium & Spiritum sanctum, sed non esse tres personas.
units.tr: That there are three: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, but that they are not three persons.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Unam esse Naturam seu Deitatem, communem tribus illis, sed non esse unam Essentiam.
units.tr: That there is one Nature or Deity, common to those three, but that it is not one Essence.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Unum esse Deum, sed tantùm Patrem dici unicum & verum Deum, Filium verò & Spiritum sanctum non dici unicum illum Deum.
units.tr: That there is one God, but that only the Father is called the sole and true God, while the Son and the Holy Spirit are not called that one God.

units.la: Hinc postea nascuntur ipsis & aliae quaedam locutiones. Ersi enim fatentur, Filium Dei esse Deum ex Deo genitum, tamen nusquam dicunt, Unicum illum Deum, esse Patrem & Filium & Spiritum sanctum, & Spiritum sanctum quidem nusquam Deum nominant. Haec non obscure portendunt, quonam isti praestigiatores contendant.
units.tr: From this there arise for them certain further expressions. For although they admit that the Son of God is God begotten of God, yet they nowhere say that that one God is the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and they nowhere actually call the Holy Spirit God. These things clearly foreshadow what those deceivers are aiming at.

units.la: DE PRIMA HYPOTHESI.
units.tr: ON THE FIRST HYPOTHESIS.

units.la: Dicunt esse tres, eosque nominant Patrem, Filium & Spiritum sanctum, sed hosce contendunt non esse personas.
units.tr: They say there are three, and they name them the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, but they maintain that these are not persons.

units.la: RATIO ISTORUM ARIANORUM HAEC EST.
units.tr: THE REASONING OF THESE ARIANS IS THIS.

units.la: Quod scriptura non docet, non est asseuerandum.
units.tr: What Scripture does not teach must not be asserted.

units.la: Sed in sacris literis nusquam leguntur haec verba, esse tres personas: sed tantùm ista, Tres sunt, qui testimonium perhibent, 1.Iohan.5.
units.tr: But in the sacred writings the words "three persons" are nowhere read, only these: "There are three who bear witness" (1 John 5).

units.la: Ergo non sunt tres personae.
units.tr: Therefore there are not three persons.

units.la: Ista quidem prima fronte apparent, quasi ex λογομαχία nascantur, verùm longè vlterius isti Ariani procedunt. Nam cùm ipsum Patrem, vnicum ac verum duntaxat vocent Deum, non item Filium, neque Spiritum sanctum vnà cum Patre: ideo res etiā ipsas, quae de personis istis traduntur, impugnant, sicut paulò pòst annotabimus. Sed ad argumentum respondeo.
units.tr: At first sight these points look as if they arise from a war of words [λογομαχία], but these Arians go much further. For while they call only the Father the sole and true God, and not the Son or the Holy Spirit together with the Father, they therefore also attack the very things that are taught about those persons, as we shall note shortly. But I reply to the argument.

units.la: Maior loquitur de rebus:Minor verò de verbis: Ideo sunt quatuor termini. Adres enim eius doctrinae, quam de sua essentia & voluntate Deus revelauit, nos alligati sumus.Gal.1. Si quis adiud Euangelium docuerit, id est, doctrinam pugnantem cum hoc vnico fundamento, sit Anathema.De verbis verò dicitur, vt sint analoga fidei, Ro.12.Nam ad institutionem rudiorum, & ad confutationem praestigiatorum, licitum est aptis & intelligibilibus verbis ac sententiis vti, modò istae loquutiones non mutent res ipsas in sacris literis praescriptas & traditas.
units.tr: The major premise speaks of things, but the minor speaks of words. So there are four terms. For we are bound to the doctrine that God has revealed concerning his own essence and will (Gal. 1). "If anyone has taught another gospel," that is, a doctrine contrary to this one sole foundation, "let him be anathema." But concerning words it is said that they should be consistent with the faith (Rom. 12). For in instructing the simpler sort, and in refuting deceivers, it is lawful to use apt and intelligible words and phrases, provided these expressions do not alter the very things prescribed and handed down in the sacred writings.

units.la: Ad Minorem: Recte ac verè dicitur, istos tres esse tres personas. Rationes sunt istae:
units.tr: To the minor premise: it is rightly and truly said that these three are three persons. The reasons are these:

units.la: 1. Quia vocabulum Persona, declarat quidnam sint isti tres, nempe non vmbrae, non somnia, aut cogitationes solummodo hominum inanes & euanidae, sed viuae quaedam substantiae. Nam res, est generale vocabulum. Iam verò res dividi oportet in species quasdam suas, id quod etiam ipsa ratio dictat.
units.tr: 1. Because the word "person" declares what these three are: not shadows, not dreams, nor mere empty and vanishing thoughts of men, but living substances. For "thing" is a general word. Now things ought to be divided into their own kinds, as reason itself dictates.

units.la: 2. Quia sacrae literae clarè docent, istos tres, nempe Patrem, Filium, & Spiritum sanctum, esse res vivas, & subsistentes, & distinctas. Nam de Patre simul & de Filio dicitur, Tu es Filius Dei viuentis. Ergo Pater est res viuens ac subsistens: Filius quoque est viuus Filius viuetis[?] Patris. Nam quando Petrus inquit, Tu es Filius Dei, perinde est ac si dixisset, Tu EXISTIS Filius Dei, tu es quiddam ὑφιστάμενον, quod est Filius Dei. Non es vmbra Dei, nō cogitatio euanesces, sed existes Filius Dei. Pater genuit Filium, ergo Pater est quiddam existens. Filius genitus à Patre, non est somnium Patris, sed tale ὑφιστάμενον, quod mittitur in mundum, induit carnem humanam, redimit genus humanum. Spiritus sanctus specie columbae descendit, arguit & docet mundum. Ergo Spiritus sanctus est existens quiddam, viuum & efficax, neque est figmentum quoddam, sine subsistentia quadam.
units.tr: 2. Because the sacred writings clearly teach that these three, namely the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, are living, subsisting and distinct realities. For of the Father and the Son together it is said, "You are the Son of the living God." Therefore the Father is a living and subsisting reality; the Son too is the living Son of the living Father. For when Peter says, "You are the Son of God," it is just as if he had said, "You EXIST as the Son of God; you are something subsisting [ὑφιστάμενον], which is the Son of God. You are not a shadow of God, not a thought that vanishes, but you exist as the Son of God." The Father begot the Son; therefore the Father is something existing. The Son, begotten of the Father, is not a dream of the Father, but a subsisting being of this kind, who is sent into the world, takes on human flesh, and redeems the human race. The Holy Spirit descended in the form of a dove, convicts and teaches the world. Therefore the Holy Spirit is an existing thing, living and effective, and is not some figment without any subsistence.

units.la: Sed Persona in hac doctrina nihil aliud significat, quàm substantiam individuam, intelligentem, incommunicabilem. Pater enim non est Filius, neque Spiritus sanctus: & Filius non est Pater, nec Spiritus sanctus: denique Spiritus sanctus non est Pater nec Filius, sed sunt tres res verè subsistentes. Huc pertinent & reliquae actiones trium istarum personarum, quae idem euincunt. Proinde vocabulum Personæ non mutat rem ipsam, verum cum ipsa re verè ac proprie congruit.
units.tr: But in this doctrine "person" means nothing other than an individual, intelligent, incommunicable substance. For the Father is not the Son, nor the Holy Spirit; the Son is not the Father, nor the Holy Spirit; and finally the Holy Spirit is neither the Father nor the Son, but they are three truly subsisting realities. The other actions of these three persons, which all prove the same, also belong here. Therefore the word "person" does not change the thing itself, but agrees truly and properly with the thing itself.

units.la: 3. Quia propter captum rudiorum, licet uti vocabulis notis & receptis, cum rebus ipsis tamen, uti dictum est, congruentibus, ne homines sibi talia fingant, quæ sunt contra scripturam. Sed vocabulum Personæ vel Substantiæ, notum est hominibus in Ecclesia CHRISTI ex longo & approbato usu, & congruit cum rebus traditis in verbo Dei. Ergo sic recte loquuntur Ecclesiæ Doctores.
units.tr: 3. Because for the sake of the understanding of the simpler sort, it is permissible to use familiar and accepted words, yet ones agreeing with the things themselves, as has been said, so that people do not invent for themselves notions that are contrary to Scripture. But the word "person" or "substance" is familiar to men in the Church of Christ from long and approved usage, and it agrees with the things handed down in the Word of God. Therefore the teachers of the Church speak rightly in this way.

units.la: 4. Quia ad confutandos hæreticos licitum est uti vocabulis, quæ rebus ipsis conueniunt. Ecclesia igitur vocabulum Personæ recepit & usurpauit, quando aduersus Simonianos, Arium, Sabellium, Samosatenum, & similes præstigiatores, confundentes personas, vel alioqui eas abolentes, vera doctrina in verbo Dei tradita, fuit propugnanda. Sicut recte Augustinus inquit: Licuit loquendi & disputandi NECESSITATE dicere, tres esse personas, non quia scriptura dicit, sed quia scriptura non contradicit. Græci dixerunt initio tres esse hypostases, id est, substantias: verum postea imitati sunt Latinos, nihil de rebus ipsis mutantes, licet verba quædam variarent.
units.tr: 4. Because in refuting heretics it is lawful to use words that suit the very things. The Church therefore received and adopted the word "person" when it had to defend the true doctrine handed down in the Word of God against Simonians, Arius, Sabellius, Samosatenus and similar deceivers who confused the persons or otherwise abolished them. As Augustine rightly says: "It was permitted, by the necessity of speaking and disputing, to say that there are three persons, not because Scripture says so, but because Scripture does not contradict it." The Greeks at first spoke of three hypostases [ὑποστάσεις], that is, substances; but afterwards they imitated the Latins, changing nothing in the things themselves, though they varied some of the words.

units.la: Debebant igitur noui Ariani primum ostendere, quod vocabulum Personæ non congrueret rebus isiis[?] diuinis, in verbo Dei traditis, priusquam illud exploderent tanta austeritate & vehementia.
units.tr: The new Arians ought therefore first to have shown that the word "person" does not agree with the divine things handed down in the Word of God, before they rejected it with such severity and vehemence.

units.la: Deinde debebant prius monstrare conuenientius vocabulum, quàm illud quod receptum & vsitatum est in Ecclesia Dei multis iam seculis, abolerent.
units.tr: Next, they ought first to have shown a more suitable word before abolishing that which has been received and used in the Church of God for many centuries.

units.la: Tertiò, si qui scelerate abuterentur vocabulo Personæ, ut Seruetus & alii, non debebat id Ecclesiæ Christi recte loquenti, esse fraudi.
units.tr: Thirdly, if some have wickedly abused the word "person," as Servetus and others did, that should not be made a reproach against the Church of Christ, which speaks rightly.

units.la: Quartò, propter vocabulorum discrepantium, quæ quidem non sunt à rebus ipsis aliena, non est ipsa doctrina funditus convellenda aut condemnanda. Nam isti Ariani negant tres esse personas. Si iam de vocabulo tantùm disceptant, cur doctrinam abiiciunt?
units.tr: Fourthly, because of differing words, which are not in fact alien to the things themselves, the doctrine itself must not be utterly overthrown or condemned. For these Arians deny that there are three persons. If they are now disputing only about the word, why do they reject the doctrine?

units.la: Cùm igitur negent esse tres personas, id est, res subsistentes, vivas, efficaces, non confusas, suum errorem produnt, quòd à doctrina Verbi divini, quam recte profitetur & tuetur Ecclesia Christi, ab Antichristi deliriis repurgata, turpiter & manifestè deficiant. Explicent igitur se clarius, cur negent tres ὑποστάσεις[?] sive personas? Et dicant plane & dilucide, quidnam sint illi tres, cùm personæ non sint? Non enim satis est dicere, quòd hi tres sint Pater, Filius & Spiritus sanctus. Quæritur enim quales sint res, an sint umbrae tantum, vel cogitationes quaedam, an vero substantiae? Ineptum est vociferari, sunt tres & semper tres, nec definire quidnam sint. Si negas personas esse tres, simul nega esse tres res.
units.tr: Since they deny that there are three persons, that is, three subsisting, living, effective realities, and not confused with one another, they reveal their error: they shamefully and openly fall away from the doctrine of the divine Word, which the Church of Christ rightly professes and maintains, cleansed of the delusions of Antichrist. Let them therefore explain themselves more clearly. Why do they deny three hypostases, or persons? Let them say plainly and clearly what those three are, if they are not persons. It is not enough to say that these three are Father, Son and Holy Spirit. The question is what sort of realities they are: are they mere shadows, or some thoughts, or real substances? It is foolish to shout "there are three, and always three" without defining what they are. If you deny that there are three persons, you must at the same time deny that there are three realities.

units.la: Neque nuper adeo hoc vocabulum vsurpari coeptum est in Ecclesia Christi. Nam antiquissimi Ecclesiae doctores, & substantiae & personae nomine vsi sunt. Vt Ignatius ad Magnesianos de Filio inquit, quòd sit οὐσία γεννητὴ [?] SVBSTANTIA genita. Loquitur enim de verbo substantiali. Tertullianus ad Praxeam inquit, Quaecunque substantia sermonis fuit, illam dico PERSONAM, & illi nomen Filii vindico: & dum Filium agnosco, secundum a Patre defendo. Item libro de Trinitate, Filium esse secundam personam post Patrem contendit. Adiicit, inquit, Sumus, non sum, vt ostenderet per hoc quod dixit sumus, & Pater, duas esse personas. Cyprianus inquit, Diuinitas & humanitas in vnam personam conuenerunt. Reliquorum doctorum testimonia in praesentia omitto, quia isti Ariani noui eam ob causam eos repudiant, quia contra Arium, suum parentem, praeclarè & fideliter ex verbo Dei decertarunt, & veritatem vindicarunt: id quod obseruatione dignissimum est.
units.tr: Nor is this word a recent innovation in the Church of Christ. The most ancient teachers of the Church used both the word substance and the word person. Thus Ignatius, writing to the Magnesians about the Son, says that he is an begotten substance [οὐσία γεννητὴ], that is, a begotten SUBSTANCE, for he speaks of the substantial Word. Tertullian, against Praxeas, says: "Whatever substance the Word was, I call it person, and I claim for it the name of Son; and while I acknowledge the Son, I defend him as second to the Father." Likewise, in his book On the Trinity, he maintains that the Son is the second person after the Father. He adds: "We are," not "I am," so that by saying "we are," he might show that there are two persons, the Father and the Son. Cyprian says: "Divinity and humanity came together into one person." I pass over the testimonies of the others for now, because these new Arians reject them for this reason: that these men contended clearly and faithfully against Arius, their own father, from the word of God, and vindicated the truth. This is a matter most worthy of notice.

units.la: DE SECUNDA HYPOTHESI.
units.tr: On the Second Hypothesis.

units.la: Vnam esse NATVRAM seu DEITATEM, communem tribus illis, sed non esse vnam ESSENTIAM illorum trium, inquiunt noui Ariani.
units.tr: The new Arians say that there is one NATURE or DEITY common to those three, but that there is not one ESSENCE of those three.

units.la: Si rationes inquiras istius paradoxi, nullam aliam inuenies, quàm quòd in sacris literis non extant illae syllabae, ESSENTIA vna. Ergo simpliciter & superstitiosè decernunt, id esse Antichristi dogma.
units.tr: If you ask for the reasons for this paradox, you will find none other than that the syllables "one essence" do not occur in the sacred writings. So they decree simply and superstitiously that this is a dogma of Antichrist.

units.la: Sed rectè & verè dicitur, vnam esse diuinam essentiam, propter hasce rationes.
units.tr: But it is rightly and truly said that there is one divine essence, for these reasons.

units.la: I. Quia etiamsi hae literae, ESSENTIA, in sacra Scriptura non inueniuntur, tamen res ipsae, quae hoc vocabulo in Ecclesia Christi exprimuntur, sunt in sacris literis comprehensae & traditae. Nam saepius repetitur haec oratio, Ego sum Deus tuus, Dominus Deus tuus Vnus est, &c. Haec dicta testantur, Deum existere. Ideo res sunt in verbo Dei planae, Deum esse quiddam existens. Existentia autem & Essentia Dei, idem sunt. Mutanda igitur forent ista verba, Deus est, in aliam formam, vt Deus fingitur esse, seu Deus est somnium hominum, est inane nomen, sicut Plinius fere nugatur, &c. si non Essentia quaedam, vt sic dicam, existeret.
units.tr: First, even if the letters ESSENCE are not found in Holy Scripture, the realities themselves, which are expressed in the Church of Christ by this word, are comprehended and handed down in the sacred writings. For this saying is often repeated: "I am your God," "The Lord your God is one," and so on. These sayings testify that God exists. Therefore it is plain in the word of God that God is some existing thing. But the existence and the essence of God are the same. The words "God is" would therefore have to be changed into another form, so that God is imagined to be, or God is a dream of men, an empty name, as Pliny more or less trifles, and so on, if some essence, so to speak, did not exist.

units.la: Sic dicitur Psalmo 93. A seculo tu es. Item, prima Iohann. quarto: Sicut ille est, & nos sumus. 1. Corinth. 8. Scimus, quòd Idolum est NIHIL in mundo, & quòd nullus EST Deus nisi vnus. In hoc dicto opponuntur sibi inuicem, Idola & Deus. Deinde proprietates discernuntur. Idola sunt NIHIL, hoc est, non sunt essentiae quaedam viuae, omnipotentes. Deus vero EST vnus, id est, non est somnium humanum, vt idola, sed vera, viua, existens essentia.
units.tr: So it is said in Psalm 93: "From everlasting you are." Likewise, 1 John 4: "As he is, so are we." 1 Corinthians 8: "We know that an idol is NOTHING in the world, and that there is NO God but one." In this saying, idols and God are set against each other, idols and God. Then their properties are distinguished. Idols are NOTHING, that is, they are not living, omnipotent essences. But God IS one, that is, he is not a human dream, as idols are, but a true, living, existing essence.

units.la: 2. Quia aequipollentes loquutiones, in sacris literis extant. Nam proprium illud Dei nomen Iehoua, quod creaturis, quemadmodum aliae appellationes Dei, nunquam adscribitur, ab esse seu essentia est deductum. Significat igitur Iehoua illum Deum, qui vere existit, seu qui est essentia quaedam aeterna. Neque est figmentum quoddam hominum, vt apud gentes, Fortuna, Pluto, Gratia, &c. Item, Exod. 3. Deus ipsi Mosi suum nomen manifestat, hisce verbis, Sum qui sum. Sic dices ad filios Israel, Sum misit me ad vos. Idem vero est, acsi dixisset, Ipsa essentia, id est, is Deus, qui existit semper, me misit.
units.tr: 2. Second, because equivalent expressions are found in the sacred writings. For the proper name of God, Jehovah, which is never ascribed to creatures, as the other titles of God are, is derived from being or essence. Jehovah therefore signifies that God who truly exists, or who is an eternal essence. It is not a figment of men, as among the nations: Fortune, Pluto, Grace, and so on. Likewise, Exodus 3: God makes his name known to Moses himself in these words: "I am who I am. Thus you shall say to the sons of Israel: 'I am has sent me to you.'" It is indeed the same as if he had said: "The essence itself, that is, the God who always exists, has sent me."

units.la: 3. Quia Ecclesia vetustissima sic est loquuta, vt Tertullianus aduersus Praxeam, vnius substantiae, & vnius status & potestatis, quia vnus est Deus. Autor symboli in Cypriano dicit, Deum quum audis, substantia intellige. Item Martialis ad Burdegalenses, Vnius voluntatis, vnius essentiae. Quando enim de vnitate Dei loquuti sunt veteres, Substantiae & Essentiae vocabulis indifferenter vsi sunt. Reliquorum testimonia no adscribo, quia passim sunt obuia.
units.tr: 3. Third, because the ancient Church spoke thus, as Tertullian against Praxeas does: "of one substance, and of one state and power, because God is one." The author of the creed in Cyprian says: "When you hear God, understand substance." Likewise Martial, to the Burdigalians: "of one will, of one essence." For when the ancients spoke of the unity of God, they used the words substance and essence interchangeably. I do not cite the testimonies of the rest, because they are everywhere to be met with.

units.la: 4. Quia Natura, Deitas & essentia, in hoc quidem loco de Deo, & in hoc cardine nihil differunt. Sic Nazianzenus inquit, Deus, quid tandem in sua Natura & essentia sit, hoc hominum nemo nouerit vnquam, sed quod sit, hoc nemo no inuenerit. Iā [?] quia isti noui Ariani fatentur, vnam esse Naturam seu Deitatem, fateantur simul necesse est, vnam esse essentiam. Si repudiant Essentiae vocabulu, quia in scriptura non sunt istae syllabae, primum eadem ratione repudient & sua vocabula. Nam Naturam esse vnam, de Deo nusquam dicunt sacrae literae, hoc est, syllabas istas non habent, licet res ipsas tradant. Ita suis ipsorum iaculis semetipsos configunt Ariani. Deinde probent vocabulum Essentiae, non convenire ipsis rebus, quas de Deo sacra scriptura profert atque affirmat. Tertiò perspicue & valide demonstrent, Naturae vocabulum esse significantius & intelligibilius, quam Essentiae.
units.tr: 4. Fourth, because Nature, Deity and essence, in this place about God and on this key point, differ in nothing. So Nazianzen says: "What God is in his own nature and essence, no one of men has ever known; but that he is, no one has failed to find." Since these new Arians confess that there is one Nature or Deity, they must at the same time confess that there is one essence. If they reject the word Essence because these syllables are not in Scripture, let them first reject their own words by the same reasoning. For that Nature is one is nowhere said of God in the sacred letters; that is, they do not have those syllables, though they hand down the realities themselves. So the Arians pierce themselves with their own darts. Then let them prove that the word Essence does not suit the realities which Holy Scripture sets forth and affirms concerning God. Thirdly, let them demonstrate clearly and forcefully that the word Nature is more significant and more intelligible than Essence.

units.la: 5. Quia absurdissima sententia ex ipsorum negatione nascitur. Cùm enim noui isti Ariani essentiam Dei negent, necesse est, ipsos Naturam seu deitate absque essentia comminisci & tradere. Quo quidem portento quid portentosius dici potest? Haec autem re ipsa tradunt, verum inuolutè & perplexè, quia vbi se magis euoluerint, monstrum hoc horrendum lucidius apparebit.
units.tr: 5. Fifth, because a most absurd opinion arises from their denial. For since these new Arians deny the essence of God, they must invent and hand down a Nature or Deity without essence. What monstrosity could be called more monstrous than this? Indeed, they hand this down in fact, but obscurely and in a tangled way; for when they unfold themselves further, this horrible monster will appear more clearly.

units.la: DE TERTIA HYPOTHESI
units.tr: ON THE THIRD HYPOTHESIS

units.la: Vnum esse Deum, tali quidem pacto, vt tantùm Pater dicatur vnicus & verus Deus:Filiu vero & Spiritu sanctu:n non dici vnicum & verù Deum
units.tr: That there is one God in such a way that only the Father is called the sole and true God, while the Son and the Holy Spirit are not called the sole and true God.

units.la: Mirum sanè est, quòd hoc relinquunt isti noui Ariani, vnicum nempe esse Deum. Negant enim tres esse personas, negant essentiam vnā esse. Quid igitur de Deo retinent? Vnum Deum faciunt, qui non sit tres personae, hoc est, Pater, Filius, & Spiritus sanctus, neque sit vnica essentia. Interea tamen contendunt esse tres, & esse vnam Naturam seu Deitatem. Nec volunt videri λογομαχίαν quandam, sed necessariam potiùs pugnam de rebus ipsis, ad doctrinam de Deo pertinentibus, suscepisse.
units.tr: It is truly remarkable that these new Arians retain this one thing, namely that God is one. For they deny that there are three persons and they deny that there is one essence. What then do they hold about God? They make God one, who is not three persons, that is, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and who has no single essence. Yet at the same time they insist that there are three and that there is one Nature or Deity. Nor do they want to seem to have engaged in some war of words [λογομαχίαν], but in a necessary contest over the realities themselves that pertain to the doctrine of God.

units.la: Sed non solum Patrem esse vnicum & verum Deum, verum tres istas personas, Patrem, Filium, & Spiritum sanctum, esse vnicum & verum Deum, ex immotis rationibus perspicuum est.
units.tr: But that not only the Father is the sole and true God, but that these three persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, are the sole and true God, is evident from the following arguments.

units.la: 1. Quia hoc proprium, Deum esse, non tantù Patri, sed etiam Filio, & Spiritui sancto, in sacris literis tribuitur. De Patre dicitur, 2.Cor.1. Benedictus Deus & Pater Domini nostri Iesu Christi. De Filio, Iohan.1. Verbum erat Deus. Iohan.20. Domin9 meus & Deus meus. Rom.9. Ex quib9 est Christus secundùm carnē, qui est super omnia Deus benedictus in secula. De Spiritu sancto, I de vero est Deus (loquitur de Spiritu sancto) qui operatur omnia in omnib9.
units.tr: 1. Because this property, to be God, is ascribed in the sacred writings not only to the Father but also to the Son and to the Holy Spirit. Of the Father it is said, 2 Cor. 1: Blessed be God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Of the Son, John 1: The Word was God. John 20: My Lord and my God. Rom. 9: Of whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed for ever. Of the Holy Spirit (he is speaking of the Holy Spirit), 1 Cor. 12: But it is the same God who works all things in all.

units.la: Sed non sunt tres Dij, verum vnicus tantùm & verus Deus. Ergo hi tres Pater, Filius, & Spiritus sanctus, sunt vnicus & verus Deus. Pater cùm sit Deus, non est peculiariter aut solus Deus: Filius cùm sit Deus, non est solus Deus: sic Spiritus sanctus cùm sit Deus, non est solus Deus, sed hi tres sunt vnus Deus. Ratio huius consequentiae est, quia sacra scriptura vtrumque dilucidè asseuerat, primùm Patrem esse Deum, Filium esse Deum, Spiritum sanctum esse Deum: deinde, non tamen tres esse Deos, sed vnicum duntaxat Deum. Haec autem fide accipienda, non ratione humana æstimanda sunt.
units.tr: But there are not three Gods; there is only one God, and he is true. Therefore these three, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, are the one and true God. The Father, since he is God, is not peculiarly or solely God; the Son, since he is God, is not solely God; likewise the Holy Spirit, since he is God, is not solely God, but these three are one God. The reason for this inference is that Holy Scripture clearly affirms both: first that the Father is God, the Son is God, the Holy Spirit is God; then that they are not three Gods, but only one God. These things, moreover, must be received by faith and not judged by human reason.

units.la: 2. Quia in Veteri Testamento, & crebrò etiam in Nouo, non distinctis personis, dicitur Vnum esse Deum: vt Deuter. 6. Audi Israel, Dominus Deus tuus, Deus vnus est. Esa. quadragesimoquarto. Ego sum primus & nouissimus, & praeter me non est Deus. Marci 12. Vnus est Deus, & non est alius praeter eum. 1.Corinth.8. Nullus est Deus, nisi vnus, &c.
units.tr: 2. Because in the Old Testament, and often also in the New, it is said without distinction of persons that there is one God: for example, Deut. 6: Hear, O Israel, the Lord your God, the Lord is one. Isa. 44: I am the first and the last, and besides me there is no God. Mark 12: There is one God, and there is none other but he. 1 Cor. 8: There is no God but one, etc.

units.la: In hisce sententiis verus Deus designatur, sicuti se patefecit. Sed patefecit se in tribus personis, Patre, Filio, & Spiritu sancto.
units.tr: In these sayings the true God is designated as he has revealed himself. But he has revealed himself in three persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

units.la: Ergo istæ loquutiones de vno Deo, synecdochicè includunt tres illas quas dixi personas. Ille est, inquâ, vnicus Deus, qui est Pater, Filius & Spiritus sanctus. Maxima enim impietas est asseuerare, Filium vel Spiritum sanctum non includi in hoc dicto, Deus tuus Vnus est. Deut.6.
units.tr: Therefore these statements about the one God include those three persons I have mentioned, by synecdoche. That, I say, is the one God who is Father, Son and Holy Spirit. For it is the greatest impiety to assert that the Son or the Holy Spirit is not included in this saying, "The Lord your God is one," Deut. 6.

units.la: 3. Quia Iohannes clarißimè inquit 1.Epist.cap.5. Ethi tres VNVM sunt.Tres quidem numerat, Patrem,λογον[?] & Spiritum sanctum. Vnum vero esse pronunciat. Porrò vnum esse, & vnum Deum esse,in hoc quidè articulo nihil differunt,quia scriptura docet vnicum esse Deum.
units.tr: 3. Because John states most clearly, 1 John, ch. 5: And these three are one. He counts three, the Father, the Word [λόγος] and the Holy Spirit, yet he declares that they are one. Moreover, to be one and to be one God do not differ in this article, because Scripture teaches that God is one.

units.la: 4. Quia Christus inquit, Ego & Pater vnum sumus, Iohan.10.Personas quidem distinguit, quando inquit Sumus: sed quum inquit, Vnum sumus, se cum Patre vnicum esse Deum affirmat. Neque verò Spiritus sanctus excluditur, quia in præsenti loco Christus hunc scopum sibi præfixum habebat,vt declararet quid ipsemet esset. Sic Iohan.14.inquit,sese in Patre esse, id est,coessentialem esse Patri.
units.tr: 4. Because Christ says, "I and the Father are one," John 10. He distinguishes the persons when he says "we are," but when he says "we are one," he affirms that he is, together with the Father, the one God. Nor is the Holy Spirit excluded, since in the present passage Christ had set before himself the aim of declaring what he himself was. So in John 14 he says that he is in the Father, that is, that he is co-essential with the Father.

units.la: 5. Quia non tantum in vno opere omnium amplißimo, nempe in regeneratione hominis,coiunguntur Pater,Filius,& Spiritus sanctus,tanquam coomnipotente: sed etiam ibi vno nomine copulantur, sicut inquit Christus Matt.28.Baptisantes eos IN NOMINE Patris, & Filii, & Spiritus sancti.IN Nomine autem, non tantum significat ex præcepto & efficacia communi istorum trium,sed etiam in cognitionem & fidem in hunc vnicũ Deũ, qui in primo decalogi præcepto inquit:Non habebis Deos alienos. Habes igitur hic tres,nimirum Patrem,Filium, & Spiritum sanctum, sed vnicum nomen,in testimonium luculentißimum quòd vnus sit Deus.
units.tr: 5. Because the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are joined together, as co-omnipotent, not only in one work, the greatest of all, namely the regeneration of man, but there too they are linked under one name, as Christ says in Matt. 28: Baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. But in the name signifies not only by the command and common efficacy of these three, but also into the knowledge and faith of this one God, who in the first precept of the Decalogue says, "You shall have no other gods." Here, then, you have three, namely the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, but one name, as a most clear testimony that God is one.

units.la: 6. Quia vnica est Deitas,sicut vnus est Deus,sine omni dubitatione.
units.tr: 6. Because the Deity is one, just as God is one, beyond all doubt.

units.la: Sed isti noui Ariani ipsimet fatentur vnam esse Deitatem, communem istis tribus,Patri,& Filio,& Spiritui sancto.
units.tr: But these new Arians themselves confess that there is one Deity, common to those three: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Ergo non tantum Pater habet illam Deitatem,neque solus Deus est,sed Pater,Filius & Spiritus sanctus, est vnicus & verus ille Deus, quem sacræ literæ proponunt.Suo ipsius igitur gladio sese iugulant isti amentes Ariani.
units.tr: Therefore not only the Father has that Deity, nor is he alone God, but the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are the one and true God whom the sacred writings set forth. These foolish Arians, therefore, cut their own throats with their own sword.

units.la: 7. Quia Filius est genitus à Patre, & eam ob causam coessentialis Patri. Nam Filius,vti dictum est,in sacris etiam literis vocatur & est Deus.
units.tr: 7. Because the Son is begotten of the Father, and for that reason is co-essential with the Father. For the Son, as has been said, is also called and is God in the sacred writings.

units.la: Ergo Filius cum Patre,est vnicus & verus ille Deus.
units.tr: Therefore the Son, together with the Father, is that one and true God.

units.la: 8. Quia Spiritus sanctus procedit à Patre & Filio. Sed Spiritus sanctus nõ ita procedit ex Patre &Filio,tanquâ spiratio ex nostris pectoribus,quæ est tantùm ardens halitus,amorem seu affectus ex corde effundens,&mox iterù euanescens,verùm est Deus, 1.Corin.12.& est coessentialis Patri & Filio.
units.tr: 8. Because the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. But the Holy Spirit does not proceed from the Father and the Son as a breath from our breasts, which is merely a warm exhalation pouring forth love or affection from the heart and soon vanishing again; he is true God, 1 Cor. 12, and is co-essential with the Father and the Son.

units.la: Ergo Spiritus sanctus cũ Patre & Filio,est vnicus & verus ille Deus, de quo inquit Moses Deu.6.Audi Israel,Domin⁹ Deus tuus,Deus v n v s est.
units.tr: Therefore the Holy Spirit, together with the Father and the Son, is that one and true God, of whom Moses says, Deut. 6: Hear, O Israel, the Lord your God, the Lord is one.

units.la: 9. Quia si Filius & Spiritus sanctus, non sunt vnicus Deus cum Patre, tum necesse est plures esse Deos.Nam scriptura vocat Filium Deũ,& eodem modo Spiritum sanctum appellat Deum, quemadmodum etiam opera divina, & omnipotentiæ propria, utrisque atribuuntur. In quascunque igitur species sese vertant isti Chamæleontes, necesse est ipsos tres Deos asserere.
units.tr: 9. Because if the Son and the Holy Spirit are not the one God together with the Father, then it is necessary that there be several Gods. For Scripture calls the Son God, and in the same way it names the Holy Spirit God, just as the divine works and the properties of omnipotence are ascribed to both. In whatever shapes these chameleons turn themselves, they must assert that there are three Gods.

units.la: Vel si Filius & Spiritus sanctus non sunt revera unicus & verus Deus cum Patre, tum necesse est ipsos vocem, Deus, quæ eis adscribitur, aliter interpretari: id quod audiemus & indicabimus ex sacris literis. Sequetur autem, si unicus & verus Deus tantum est Pater, & non Filius & Spiritus sanctus simul, tum Filius non est revera Deus: item Spiritus sanctus non est revera Deus. Hoc pacto novi isti Ariani ad veterem illum Arium recurrunt, ac ve-teres hæreses cum contumelia Filii Dei & Spiritus sancti ressuscitant.
units.tr: Or if the Son and the Holy Spirit are not truly the one and true God together with the Father, then it is necessary that they interpret the word God, which is ascribed to them, in some other way; which we shall hear about and show from the sacred writings. It would follow, however, if the one and true God is the Father only, and not the Son and the Holy Spirit together with him, that the Son is not truly God, and likewise the Holy Spirit is not truly God. In this way these new Arians run back to that old Arius, and revive the old heresies to the reproach of the Son of God and the Holy Spirit.

units.la: FUNDAMENTORUM ARIANORUM CONFUTATIO.
units.tr: REFUTATION OF THE ARIANS' FOUNDATIONS.

units.la: Iactis hisce fundamentis pro doctrina catholica, quòd Pater, Filius & Spi-ritus sanctus, sit Unicus & verus Deus, de quo etiam primum Decalogi præ-ceptum inquit, Non habebis deos alienos: nunc istorum novorum Arianorum fulcra exploremus, quibus stabiliunt hanc suam aulam, seu potius ollam testaceam, quòd non Filius, non Spiritus sanctus, sed solus Pater sit unicus & verus Deus.
units.tr: Having laid these foundations for the catholic doctrine, that the Father, Son and Holy Spirit are the one and true God, of whom the first commandment of the Decalogue also says, "You shall have no other gods," let us now examine the props by which these new Arians prop up their hall, or rather their earthen pot: that not the Son and not the Holy Spirit, but the Father alone, is the one and true God.

units.la: Argumenta, quæ nascuntur ex dictis scripturæ malè detortis.
units.tr: Arguments that arise from passages of Scripture wrongly twisted.

units.la: I
units.tr: I

units.la: Inaudita Prophetis, Christo, & Apostolis asseuerare, impium est.
units.tr: To assert things unheard of by the Prophets, Christ and the Apostles is impious.

units.la: Sed esse unicum Deum, & tamen esse tres personas, est inauditum Prophetis, Christo, & Apostolis.
units.tr: But to hold that God is one and yet that there are three persons is unheard of by the Prophets, Christ and the Apostles.

units.la: Ergo hæc doctrina est impia. In tabula & epistola ad Tigurinos.
units.tr: Therefore this doctrine is impious. In the table and in the epistle to the Tigurines.

units.la: R. Minor est salsissima. Ecquid autem frontis isti Ariani habent? Nam utrumque, uti demonstravimus, sacra scriptura tradit, & Unicum duntaxat esse Deum, Deut. 6. Et, tres esse personas, Patrem, Filium & Spiritum san-ctum, Matt. 28. Liquidissimè etiam Ioannes inquit, Tres sunt in cælo, qui testi-monium perhibent, Pater, λόγους[?] & Spiritus sanctus (Audis tres personas?) & sequitur, Et hi TRES UNUM sunt. Sed exagitant isti Ariani loquutio-nem Ecclesiæ, Unum esse Deum, & tamen trinum: quæ quidem oratio non discrepat à verbis Euangelistæ Iohannis, qui inquit, Hi tres unum sunt.
units.tr: R. The minor premise is most insipid. But what brazenness these Arians have! For Holy Scripture teaches both things, as we have shown: that God is only one, Deut. 6; and that there are three persons, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, Matt. 28. John also says most clearly, "There are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word [λόγος], and the Holy Spirit" (do you hear three persons?), and it follows, "And these three are one." But these Arians harass the Church's way of speaking, that God is one and yet threefold. This expression does not differ from the words of the evangelist John, who says, "These three are one."

units.la: Christus non ita loquitur, quia tantùm invocat Deum Patrem, & nos e-tiam iubet Patrem invocare. Ergo unicus est Deus Pater.
units.tr: Christ does not speak thus, because he only invokes God the Father, and he also bids us invoke the Father. Therefore the one God is the Father alone.

units.la: R. Est fallacia compositionis & divisionis, qua incautis hominibus isti præstigiatores imponunt. Quando enim de aliquo fidei articulo dicendum est, non tantùm una aliqua sententiola excerpenda est ex sacris literis, sed integer contextus, & quasi corpus illius doctrinæ inspici & considerari debet. Constat autem Christum disertè docuisse, unum esse Deum, Matthæi quarto, decimonono, 22. Marci 12. Deinde etiam perspicuè docuisse de tribus personis, Patre, Filio & Spiritu sancto, Matthæi 28.Iohan. 14.15. & alijs in locis. Ergo verum & unicum Deum, non vocat aut docet alium, quàm qui est Pater, Filius & Spiritus sanctus, in cuius nomine omnes sunt baptizandi. Quòd verò Patrem interdum solum nominat Deum, non est exclusiva oratio, quasi Pater solus sit Deus, exclusò Filio & Spiritu sancto. An non legerūt etiā ista, quòd λόγος sit Deus, Iohan. 1. Quòd Christus sit Dominus & Deus, Iohan. 20. Præterea hîc se produnt Ariani, quòd negant Filium esse unum illum Deum, coessentialē & coomnipotentē cum Patre & Spiritu sancto. Item quòd negant Spiritum sanctum esse Deum. Ista monstra isti Spiritus fouent & parturiunt.
units.tr: R. This is a fallacy of composition and division, by which these sleight-of-hand artists impose upon the unwary. For when something must be said about any article of faith, one should not pick out some single little sentence from Holy Scripture, but the whole context, and as it were the body of that doctrine, must be examined and considered. Now it is certain that Christ plainly taught that God is one, Matt. 4, 19, 22; Mark 12. Then also that he clearly taught about three persons, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, Matt. 28; John 14, 15; and in other places. Therefore the true and only God whom he calls upon and teaches is none other than he who is Father, Son and Holy Spirit, into whose name all are to be baptized. But that he sometimes names only the Father as God is not an exclusive expression, as though the Father alone were God, with the Son and Holy Spirit excluded. Have they not also read that the Word is God, John 1. that Christ is Lord and God, John 20. Moreover, here the Arians betray themselves, in that they deny that the Son is that one God, co-essential and co-omnipotent with the Father and the Holy Spirit. Likewise they deny that the Holy Spirit is God. That spirit of theirs nourishes and brings forth these monsters.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: In verbis Baptismi Christus non inquit, Baptisate in Deum, cuius est una essentia & tres personæ.
units.tr: In the words of Baptism Christ does not say, "Baptize into God, whose essence is one and whose persons are three."

units.la: Ergo non est Deus talis.
units.tr: Therefore God is not such.

units.la: R. Eodem pertinet hæc argumentatio. Nam res sunt eadem. Quem enim Deum Christus ibi distinctis personis nominat, Ecclesia dicit esse unū Deum, seu unam essentiam, quæ quidem essentia sit Pater, Filius, & Spiritus sanctus. Debebant igitur isti Ariani probare euidenter, loquutionem Ecclesiæ, à rebus & à doctrina Christi dissentire. Hoc est πρωτόμενον [?]. Nam verborum variatio non semper mutat rem ipsam. Imò ipsimet alijs verbis utuntur, quàm in sacris literis extant, ut suam opinionem declarent.
units.tr: R. This argument belongs to the same category, for the things are the same. For the God whom Christ there names with distinct persons, the Church says is one God, or one essence, which essence is indeed the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. The Arians therefore ought to prove plainly that the Church's way of speaking dissents from the things and the doctrine of Christ. This is begging the question. For a variation of words does not always change the thing itself. Indeed, they themselves use other words than those found in Holy Scripture, in order to declare their opinion.

units.la: IIII.
units.tr: IIII.

units.la: 1.Corinth.8 .dicitur, Nobis unus est Deus Pater, ex quo omnia. Unus Dominus Iesus Christus per quem omnia. Unus Spiritus sanctus omnia sanctificans, Ephes.4. Unus Deus & Pater omnium.
units.tr: "1 Corinthians 8 says: 'For us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things; and one Holy Spirit, sanctifying all things.'" Ephesians 4: "One God and Father of all."

units.la: Ergo non recte dicitur, Pater, Filius & Spiritus sanctus, sunt unicus & verus Deus.
units.tr: Therefore it is not rightly said that the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are the one and true God.

units.la: R. Argumentum ex insciitia phrasis, vel ex crassa cæcitate oritur. Nam in hisce testimoniis non excluduntur Filius & Spiritus sanctus, quò minus & hæ personæ sint unus & verus Deus cum Patre. Nam Iohannes disertè inquit, Hi tres vnum sunt. Deinde non attendunt isti vertiginosi spiritus, vocabulum Dei, 1.Cor.8. primum generaliter poni, deinde per exegesin seu specialem enumerationem, personas subiicit: quae quidem phrasis saepius in scriptis Paulinis occurrit, praesertim vero in salutationibus, vt, Gratia vobis a Deo Patre nostro, & Domino Iesu Christo. Hic vocabulum Dei non tantum Patri, sed & Christo conuenit, sicut alia testimonia id luculenter probant. Tertio quando Christus vocatur Dominus, idem est, ac si Deus diceretur. Nam vocabulum Iehoua, quod soli Deo proprium est, Graeci verterunt per κύριος. Sicut igitur non excluditur Pater in hoc membro orationis, Vnus Dominus Iesus Christus, quo minus & ipse Pater sit Iehoua seu Dominus, sicut Filius: ita etiam in priori parte, Vnus est Deus Pater, non excluditur Filius, quo minus & ipse sit Vnicus ille & verus Deus, cum Patre & Spiritu sancto.
units.tr: R. The argument arises from ignorance of the idiom, or from gross blindness. For in these testimonies the Son and the Holy Spirit are not excluded, so that these persons may not be the one and true God together with the Father. For John plainly says, "These three are one." Next, these giddy spirits do not notice that the word God in 1 Cor. 8 is first put in general terms, and then, by exegesis or a specific enumeration, the persons are added. This idiom occurs often in Paul's writings, especially in the salutations, as in "Grace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ." Here the word God belongs not only to the Father but also to Christ, as other testimonies clearly prove. Thirdly, when Christ is called Lord, it is the same as if he were called God. For the word Iehoua, which belongs to God alone, the Greeks rendered by [κύριος]. Just as, therefore, the Father is not excluded in this clause, "One Lord Jesus Christ," so that the Father himself may not be Iehoua or Lord as the Son is, so also in the earlier part, "One God the Father," the Son is not excluded, so that he may not be that one and true God together with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Esa.44. dicitur: Ego sum primus & nouissimus, & praeter me non est Deus. Iohannes de Christo ista profert, Ego sum primus & nouissimus, A & Ω, principium & finis. Si quis hinc inferret, Ergo solus Filius Dei est vnicus Deus, non Pater, non Spiritus sanctus, nonne iudicaretur insanire? Cum igitur scriptura dicat, Filium esse primum & nouissimum, hoc est, vnicum Deum. Item dicat de Patre, eum esse vnicum Deum. Insuper dicat etiam de Spiritu sancto, eum esse vnicu Deum. Ergo manifestu est, Patrem, Filium, & Spiritum sanctum, esse vnicum & verum Deum, no Patrem solum, & phrasim, Audi Israel, Dominus Deus tuus, synecdochice de Patre, Filio, & Spiritu sancto, accipiendam esse. Sic & hanc, Vnus Deus & Pater omnium.
units.tr: Isaiah 44 says: "I am the first and the last, and beside me there is no God." John says these things of Christ: "I am the first and the last, the A and the Ω, the beginning and the end." If someone were to infer from this, "Therefore the Son of God alone is the one God, and not the Father or the Holy Spirit," would he not be judged to be mad? Since, therefore, Scripture says that the Son is the first and the last, that is, the one God, and likewise says of the Father that he is the one God, and moreover says of the Holy Spirit also that he is the one God, it is manifest that the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are the one and true God, and not the Father alone. The phrase "Hear, O Israel, the Lord thy God" is to be taken synecdochically of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. So also with this one: "One God and Father of all." V.

units.la: Philippus non cupiebat nosse essentiam vel trinum, sed Deum Patrem.
units.tr: Philip did not desire to know an essence or a Trinity, but God the Father.

units.la: Ergo Filius & Spiritus sanctus, non sunt vnicus Deus cum Patre. Sed Pater est vnicus & verus Deus duntaxat.
units.tr: Therefore the Son and the Holy Spirit are not the one God with the Father. But the Father alone is the one and true God.

units.la: R. Quis non affectatam maliciam in hac argumentatione deprehendit? Verba Essentiae & Trinitatis in ea historia non exprimuntur. Ergo de rebus illis non fit in hisce Philippi verbis mentio. Qualis haec quaeso est consequentia? An non duo de eadem re, verbis dissimilibus loqui possunt? Deinde non somnium Patris, sed verum & existentem Patrem Christi oculis carnalibus intueri cupiebat Philippus, Ergo essentiam Patris cernere desiderabat. Porro si non existit, si non est essentia Pater caelestis, Ergo NIHIL est. Deinde non cupiebat Philippus alium Deum videre, quam eum, quem postea Christus in verbis Baptismi nominat, nempe qui est Pater, Filius, & Spiritus sanctus, licet tantum Patrem exoptabat sibi monstrari. Atqui Pater, Filius & Spiritus sanEius[?] sunt tres, etiam istorum Arianorum confessione. Ergo illum Deum volebat intueri Philippus, qui esset trinus in personis, sicut tres distinctas & unas res Christus sæpe nominat.
units.tr: R. Who does not detect deliberate malice in this argument? The words essence and Trinity are not expressed in that story. Therefore no mention of those things is made in these words of Philip. What kind of inference is this, pray? Can two different words not speak of the same thing? Next, Philip did not desire to see a dream of the Father, but the true and existing Father of Christ with carnal eyes; therefore he longed to behold the essence of the Father. Further, if the heavenly Father does not exist, if the Father is not an essence, then he is NOTHING. Next, Philip did not desire to see another God than the one whom Christ afterwards names in the words of Baptism, namely the one who is Father, Son and Holy Spirit, although he only desired to have the Father shown to him. And yet the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are three, even by the confession of these Arians. Therefore Philip wanted to behold that God who is three in persons, just as Christ often names three distinct and yet one things.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: In Symbolo dicitur, Credo in Deū Patrem, & in IESVM CHRISTVM, & in Spiritum sanctum.
units.tr: In the Creed it is said, "I believe in God the Father, and in JESUS CHRIST, and in the Holy Spirit."

units.la: Ergo Pater est unicus DEVS, non Filius, non Spiritus sanctus. Nam vocabulum, Deus, tantùm Patri apponitur.
units.tr: Therefore the Father alone is the one GOD, not the Son, not the Holy Spirit. For the word God is applied only to the Father.

units.la: R. Nomen Dei, in huius professionis initio, collectiuè, morè Scripturæ sacræ vsurpatur. Deinde subiicitur enolutio[?] seu enumeratio specierum. Ac sacrilegium est infandum & intolerandum, Filium & Spiritum sanctum, in Symbolo priuare isthoc epitheto, quasi ipsis quoque non conueniat nomen Dei.
units.tr: R. The name of God, at the beginning of this profession, is used collectively, after the manner of holy Scripture. Then follows the unfolding, or enumeration, of the persons. And it is an unspeakable and intolerable sacrilege to strip the Son and the Holy Spirit of this epithet in the Creed, as if the name of God did not belong to them too.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Hæc est vita æterna, vt cognoscant te solum verum Deum, & quem misisti Iesum Christum.
units.tr: This is eternal life, that they may know you the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.

units.la: Ergo solus Pater est solus Deus, Iesus Christus autè non est ille solus Deus cum Patre & Spiritu sancto.
units.tr: Therefore the Father alone is the only God, but Jesus Christ is not that only God together with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

units.la: R. Hoc ipso dicto Ariani veteres istorum recentium patres, ad suam rabiem abusi sunt, vt ostenderent Filium Dei non esse Deum. Est autem mera calumnia & depravatio dicti Christi. Est enim diabolus mendax, & veracissimi Christi verba impudentissimè corrumpit atque detorquet. Nam Christus clarissimè inquit, ad æternam vitam consequendam pertinere, vt homines vtrumque cognoscant, tam Filium quam Patrem. Ergo in opere hoc, quod soli Deo competit, nempe in donatione vitæ æternæ, copulantur Pater & Filius. Hinc argumentum texitur,
units.tr: R. By this very saying the ancient Arians, the fathers of these recent men, abused it in their frenzy to show that the Son of God is not God. But this is pure calumny and a distortion of Christ's words. For the devil is a liar, and most shamelessly corrupts and twists the most truthful words of Christ. Christ says most clearly that it pertains to attaining eternal life that human beings know both, the Son as well as the Father. Therefore in this work, which belongs to God alone, namely in the bestowing of eternal life, the Father and the Son are joined together. From this the argument is woven:

units.la: Solius Dei est vitam æternam dare.
units.tr: To give eternal life belongs to God alone.

units.la: Sed Pater & Filius largiuntur vitam æternam notitia sui, seu fide in vtrunque fixa & collocata, teste Christo.
units.tr: But the Father and the Son bestow eternal life by the knowledge of themselves, or by faith fixed and placed in both, as Christ testifies.

units.la: Ergo Pater & Filius sunt solus ille, seu vnicus & verus Deus. Non autem excluditur Spiritus sanctus: nam sacræ literæ sæpe tantùm Patris & Filij meminerunt.
units.tr: Therefore the Father and the Son are that alone, or the one and true God. Yet the Holy Spirit is not excluded, for the sacred letters often mention only the Father and the Son.

units.la: Deinde luculenter coniunguntur in hoc dicto, Pater & Filius per coniunctionem ET, quæ quidem coniunctio clarissimè docet, tum Patrem, tum Filium esse SOLVM illum Deum verum, qui est agnoscêdus & colèndus. Non enim hìc dicit Christus, Vt te Patrem cognoscant solum esse verum & vnicum Deum, Filium vero tuum non. Neque inquit, Iesum Christum esse inferiorem Deum, ac nō pertinere ad unitatem Deitatis. Sed verba plana sunt, ut TE & IESUM CHRISTUM, quē misisti, cognoscāt SOLUM DEUM VERUM. Prudentissimè igitur Sapientia Dei ista verba protulit. Verba enim TE & QUEM misisti Iesum Christū, sunt subiecta in hac propositione siue oratione, SOLUM Deum verum, sunt praedicata de utroque subiecto: id quod reliqua scriptura declarat. Primum enim disertissimè Filium tam appellat Deum, quàm Patrem. Deinde generalia dicta unitatem Dei adstruunt, non excludentia, sed includentia potius Patrem, Filium & Spiritum sanctum.
units.tr: Next, the Father and the Son are clearly joined in this saying by the conjunction AND, which conjunction most plainly teaches that both the Father and the Son are the ONLY true God, who is to be known and worshipped. For Christ does not here say, "that they may know that you the Father are the only and one true God, but your Son is not." Nor does he say that Jesus Christ is an inferior god, and does not belong to the unity of the Deity. But the words are plain: that they may know YOU and JESUS CHRIST, whom you have sent, as the ONLY true GOD. Wisely, therefore, did the Wisdom of God utter these words. For the words YOU and JESUS CHRIST, whom you have sent, are the subjects in this proposition or sentence, and ONLY true God is the predicate applied to each subject, as the rest of Scripture declares. For first, it calls the Son as plainly God as the Father. Then, its general statements affirm the unity of God, not excluding but rather including the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

units.la: In hac expositione libenter sequor Augustinum, qui hac ratione istam orationem intelligit atque distribuit, quanquam non ignorem, alios nonnullos existimare, Augustini syntaxin nimis esse coactam, praecipuè propter articulum τοῦ. Verum explanatio Augustini sacris literis est consentanea. Cum autem verba Augustini hanc doctrinam illustrent, non pigeat ea legere. Sic inquit: Ordo verborum est, Ut te & quem misisti Iesum Christum, cognoscant solum verum Deum. Consequenter enim & Spiritus sanctus intelligitur, quia Spiritus est Patris & Filij, tanquā charitas substantialis & cosubstantialis amborum, quoniam non duo Dij Pater & Filius, nec tres Dij, Pater, & Filius & Spiritus sanctus: sed ipsa Trinitas unus solus verus Deus: nec idem tamen Pater qui Filius, nec idem Filius qui Pater, nec idem Spiritus sanctus, qui Pater & Filius, quoniam tres sunt Pater & Filius & Spiritus sanctus, sed ipsa Trinitas unus est Deus. Usitata & haec responsio est, Ista vocabula, solum verum Deum, opponi Ethnicis & commentitiis Diis, qui tantum sunt hominum figmenta, nec sunt unicus & verus Deus. Neque illam expositionem plane reiicimus, si dextrè accipiatur, Ut te Patrem cognoscant solum verum Deum, hoc est, non esse numen fictitium, ut Ethnicorum dij sunt, & quem misisti, ESSE Iesum Christum, hoc est, verum Messiam. Neque enim hoc pacto Filius Dei à Deitate excluditur. Nam mentio officij non tollit ipsam substantiam, ut omnes sani intelligunt.
units.tr: In this exposition I gladly follow Augustine, who understands and divides this sentence in this way, although I am not unaware that some others think Augustine's syntax is too forced, especially on account of the article [τοῦ]. But Augustine's explanation agrees with the sacred letters. Since Augustine's words illustrate this doctrine, let us not be reluctant to read them. He says: "The order of the words is, that they may know you and Jesus Christ whom you have sent, the only true God. For by consequence the Holy Spirit is also understood, because the Spirit is of the Father and the Son, as the substantial and co-substantial charity of both; since the Father and the Son are not two gods, nor are the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit three gods, but the Trinity itself is the one, only, true God. Yet the Father is not the same as the Son, nor the Son the same as the Father, nor the Holy Spirit the same as the Father and the Son, since the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit are three, but the Trinity itself is one God." This is also the usual answer: these words, only true God, are set against the heathen and the fictitious gods, which are merely the figments of men and are not the one and true God. Nor do we entirely reject that exposition, if it is rightly understood: that they may know you the Father as the only true God, that is, that you are not a fictitious deity, as the gods of the heathen are; and whom you have sent, that is, Jesus Christ, is the true Messiah. For in this way the Son of God is not excluded from the Deity. For mention of an office does not take away the substance itself, as all sound people understand.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: Gratia & pax à Deo Patre & Domino Iesu Christo.
units.tr: Grace and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

units.la: Ergo solus Pater est Deus, Filius autem nō est unicus ille & verus Deus, licet & ipse Deus sit, utpote Filius Dei.
units.tr: Therefore the Father alone is God, but the Son is not that one and true God, although he too is God, inasmuch as he is the Son of God.

units.la: R. Est calumnia sententiae Paulinae, & nota vertiginosi & maledici Spiritus. Nam sacra Scriptura, pro synonymis usurpat ista duo vocabula, Deus & Dominus. Imò Dominus est ipsa vox Iehova. Sed Iehovae appellatio soli Deo in sacris literis adscribitur. Ergo ita vocat Paulus Jesum Christum Deum, quàm Patrem, & quidem illum ipsum Deum, qui est unicus & solus, scilicet juxta declarationem sacræ scripturæ.
units.tr: R. This is a calumny against the words of Paul, and the mark of a giddy and slanderous spirit. For holy Scripture uses the two words God and Lord as synonyms. Indeed, Lord is the very word Iehova. But the name Iehova is ascribed in the sacred letters to God alone. Therefore Paul calls Jesus Christ God no less than the Father, and indeed that very God who is one and alone, namely according to the declaration of holy Scripture.

units.la: Argumenta, quæ ex ratiocinationibus qui-busdam extruuntur.
units.tr: Arguments that are built from certain lines of reasoning.

units.la: IX.
units.tr: IX.

units.la: Qui non genuit, nec genitus est, nec procedit, non est verus Deus.
units.tr: He who has not begotten, nor been begotten, nor proceeds, is not the true God.

units.la: Sed unus Deus in essentia, nec genuit, nec genitus est, nec procedit.
units.tr: But the one God in essence neither begot, nor was begotten, nor proceeds.

units.la: Ergo ille unus Deus in essentia, non est verus Deus.
units.tr: Therefore that one God in essence is not the true God.

units.la: Minorem probant: Quia Sententiarij dicunt, essentiam non generare.
units.tr: They prove the minor premise because the Sententiarii say that essence does not beget.

units.la: R. Minor est calumnia. Nam ita unitas essentiæ asseritur, ut non separe-tur, neque excludatur personarum distinctio. Nam illa unitas non est alius Deus, non aliud quiddam, quàm Pater, Filius, & Spiritus sanctus. Extra has tres personas nulla unitas essentiæ imaginanda est, & extra hanc unitatem, nullæ tres personæ divinitatis imaginandæ sunt. Causa eius rei est, Quòd utra-que in verbo Dei sunt manifestata, nempe quòd unicus Deus existat, & quòd nihilominus sint tres, Pater nimirum, Filius & Spiritus sanctus. Indistinctus est Deus, si unitatem spectes. Distincti sunt Pater Filius, & Spiritus sanctus, si personas spectes. Imò ipsemet Ariani noui eadem proferunt, licet postea more hæreticorum, semetipsos rursus destruant. Nam tres inquiunt, esse unius naturæ divinæ: Natura autem divina & essentia divina, idem sunt: Er-go idem dicunt quod nos. Nam æquipollet ista: Tres sunt, & isti tres sunt unius naturæ divinæ. Ac deinde nostra loquutio, Tres sunt personæ, & una essentia divina. Hæc ideo credimus & profitemur, quia scriptura ea docet, licet ratio hu-mana explicare hoc mysterium nequeat, quomodo Deus sit unus, & tamen-ille unicus Deus sint tres, Pater nempe, Filius & Spiritus sanctus. Ille unus Deus nullus est, si non est Pater, Filius & Spiritus sanctus. Sic Pater, Filius & Spiritus sanctus non sunt, si non sunt unus ille & verus Deus. Mentiuntur igitur Ariani isti, quòd talis à nobis constituatur essentiæ divinæ unitas, à qua personarum distinctio sit penitus explosa.
units.tr: Reply: The minor premise is a calumny. For the unity of essence is so asserted that the distinction of persons is neither separated nor excluded. That unity is not another God, nor some other thing, than the Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Outside these three persons no unity of essence is to be imagined, and outside this unity no three persons of the divinity are to be imagined. The reason is that both are manifested in the Word of God: that God is one, and that nevertheless there are three, namely the Father, Son and Holy Spirit. God is undivided if you look at the unity; the Father, Son and Holy Spirit are distinct if you look at the persons. Indeed the Arians themselves, though afterwards, in the manner of heretics, they again destroy themselves, bring forward the same things. For they say that the three are of one divine nature; but divine nature and divine essence are the same. Therefore they say what we say. For this is equivalent: "There are three, and these three are of one divine nature," and our statement: "There are three persons, and one divine essence." We believe and profess these things because Scripture teaches them, although human reason cannot explain this mystery, how God is one and yet that one unique God is three, namely Father, Son and Holy Spirit. That one God does not exist if he is not Father, Son and Holy Spirit; so the Father, Son and Holy Spirit do not exist if they are not that one and true God. The Arians therefore lie when they claim that we set up such a unity of the divine essence from which the distinction of persons is utterly banished.

units.la: Probatio Minoris non ex perspicuo verbo Dei, sed ex Sententiarius sumi-tur. Cùm autem hoc sit mysterium quoddam, ideò variant sententiæ. Nam aliqui vocem Essentiæ absolutè, aliqui relatiuè accipiunt. Certù autem ex verbo Dei est, Patrem genuisse Filium, & Filium esse genitum, & Spiritum sanctum à Patre & Filio procedere. Quomodo autem id factum sit vel fiat, ratio-nis captum excedit, eámque ob causam ea in parte sententiæ non congruunt.
units.tr: The proof of the minor premise is taken not from the plain Word of God but from the Sententiarii. Since this is a certain mystery, opinions vary: some take the word essence absolutely, others relatively. But it is certain from the Word of God that the Father begot the Son, that the Son was begotten, and that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. How this has happened or happens, however, exceeds the grasp of reason, and for that reason opinions do not agree on this point.

units.la: Quando autem pii dicunt, Essentiam generare, respiciunt personarum distin-ctionem. Nam hoc argumentum planum est.
units.tr: When the godly say that essence begets, however, they have regard to the distinction of persons. For this argument is plain:

units.la: Filius Dei est genitus.
units.tr: The Son of God is begotten.

units.la: Filius Dei est essentia, est res viva, non est somnium aut phantasma. Item est Deus. Ista duæ propositiones ex verbo Dei sunt manifestæ.
units.tr: The Son of God is essence, is a living thing, is not a dream or a phantasm. Likewise he is God. These two propositions are manifest from the Word of God.

units.la: Ergo essentia etiam generat.
units.tr: Therefore essence also begets.

units.la: Spinositates[?] quas ratio humana infert, & scrutatur istius mysterij modum, repudiamus: quia scriptum est, Mulier, id est, ratio caca in Ecclesia taceat. Revelatis in Ecclesia Dei simus contenti. Item, Qui scrutatur Maiestatem, opprimetur à gloria. Et sicut Augustinus inquit, Cælo tonante, rana taceant.
units.tr: We reject the speculations that human reason brings in, and that scrutinize the manner of this mystery, because it is written: "Woman," that is, blind reason, "keep silent in the Church." Let us be content with what is revealed in the Church of God. Likewise: "He who searches out the Majesty will be overwhelmed by glory." And as Augustine says, "When heaven thunders, let the frogs be silent."

units.la: Quando autem alij defendunt istam sententiam, Essentiam non generare, respiciunt communionem & unitatem Deitatis seu naturæ: neque tamen eùt[?] inficias, Patrem Filium generasse, Filium esse natum, & Spiritum sanctum procedere ab utroque, & hosce tres unius esse naturæ divinæ, seu unicum & verum Deum. Utrum sententia iam in hac disputatione Scholasticorum, an essentia generet, sit planior, & minus reprehensioni obnoxia, candidi Lectores non difficile iudicant.
units.tr: When others defend the opposite opinion, that essence does not beget, they have regard to the communion and unity of the Deity or nature. Yet they do not deny that the Father begot the Son, that the Son was begotten, that the Holy Spirit proceeds from both, and that these three are of one divine nature, or the one and true God. Which opinion is clearer and less open to reproach in this scholastic dispute, whether essence begets, honest readers do not find hard to judge.

units.la: Improbè autem faciunt Ariani, quòd ob loquutionem de modo generandi, ipsam doctrinam de unitate Dei & tribus personis cõuellunt. Nam Ecclesiæ nostræ utrumque ex sacris literis palàm asserunt & profitentur, unicū esse Deum, & non plures, Et tres esse personas, quæ sunt ille unicus Deus, & non alius. Non excluditur unitas à personis, neque persona ab unitate. Sicut enim rectè dicitur, Hi tres unum sunt: ita etiam rectè dicitur, Unus Deus est Pater, Filius & Spiritus sanctus. Ad hanc doctrinam ipsa ratio hominis allidit: sed verbo Dei firma fide acquiescendum est. Hæc de speciosissimo nouorum Arianorum argumento dicta sufficiant.
units.tr: The Arians act wickedly, however, when, on account of a manner of speaking about the mode of begetting, they tear apart the very doctrine of the unity of God and of the three persons. For our Church openly asserts and professes from the sacred letters both things: that God is one and not several, and that there are three persons who are that one God, and not another. Unity is not excluded from the persons, nor person from unity. For just as it is rightly said, "These three are one," so too it is rightly said, "The one God is Father, Son and Holy Spirit." Human reason dashes itself against this doctrine, but one must rest with firm faith in the Word of God. Let these things said about the most showy argument of the new Arians suffice.

units.la: X.
units.tr: X.

units.la: Qui non genuit, nec genitus est, non est Pater Christi, nec Filius Patris, nec Mediator.
units.tr: He who has not begotten, nor been begotten, is not the Father of Christ, nor the Son of the Father, nor the Mediator.

units.la: Sed unus Deus in essentia, non genuit, nec genitus est.
units.tr: But the one God in essence has not begotten, nor been begotten.

units.la: Ergo ille unus Deus in essentia, nō est Pater Christi, nec Filius Patris, nec Mediator.
units.tr: Therefore that one God in essence is not the Father of Christ, nor the Son of the Father, nor the Mediator.

units.la: Minor iterum incumbit isti fundamento, quia Scholastici dicant, Essentiam non generare.
units.tr: Again the minor premise rests on that foundation, because the Scholastics say that essence does not beget.

units.la: R. Est idem argumentum cum præcedente, & procedit tantum ex malitiosa exagitatione loquutionis, quâ usi sunt Scholastici in explicatione generationis divinæ, cuius quidem rei modum nemo hominum explicare poterit. Sicut præclarè inquit Ambrosius, Licèt scire quòd natus sit, non licet discu-tere, quomodo natus sit. Illud mihi negare non licet, hoc quærere meum est.
units.tr: Reply: It is the same argument as the preceding, and it proceeds only from a malicious harassing of the manner of speaking that the Scholastics used in explaining divine generation, a mode which no man can explain. As Ambrose rightly says: "It is allowed to know that he was begotten; it is not allowed to examine how he was begotten. It is not mine to deny the former; it is mine to seek the latter."

units.la: Est igitur Minor mera calumnia: quia non asseritur talis Vnitas, seu talis vnus DEVS qui sit alius, quàm Pater, Filius, & Spiritus sanctus. Sed profitemur Patrem, & Filium, & Spiritum sanctum, esse Vnicum & verum Deum, qui se certo verbo & patefactionibus declarauit, nec esse aliū. Iohan. 10. Christus inquit, Ego & Pater vnum sumus. Ait se vnum esse cum Patre, verùm non exclusa Patris & Filij distinctione. Et perspicuè Ioannes inquit, Hi tres vnum sunt. Tres audis esse, & tamen hi tres vnum sunt. Non est vnitas absque tribus, & non sunt tres absque vnitate. Hæc non docet Arithmetica, non ratio in capite istorum Arianorum: sed verbum Dei, cui omnes tenentur acquiescere, & non scrutari, quomodo hæc sint possibilia. Nam rationi tuæ cæcæ nunquam erunt possibilia, fidei verò innitenti verbo divino, certa & immobilia sunt. Simul etiam accuratè observetur, quod & suprà monui, vocabulum Essentiæ vsurpari aliàs absolutè, hoc est pro natura seu diuinitate: aliàs verò relatiuè, quando personæ considerantur. Has diuersas significationes isti noui Ariani, résque ipsas simul nefariè & petulanter confundunt.
units.tr: The minor premise is therefore sheer calumny, because no such unity is asserted, nor such a one God who is other than the Father, Son and Holy Spirit. But we profess that the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are the one and true God, who has declared himself by his certain Word and manifestations, and that there is no other. John 10. Christ says: "I and the Father are one." He says that he is one with the Father, yet without excluding the distinction of Father and Son. And John plainly says: "These three are one." You hear that there are three, and yet these three are one. There is no unity without the three, and the three are not without unity. Arithmetic does not teach this, nor reason in the head of these Arians, but the Word of God, to which all are bound to assent and not to search how these things are possible. For to your blind reason they will never be possible, but to faith resting on the divine Word they are certain and unshakeable. At the same time let it be carefully observed, as I have warned above, that the word essence is sometimes used absolutely, that is, for nature or divinity, and sometimes relatively, when the persons are considered. These different senses the new Arians wickedly and wantonly confuse, and the things themselves along with them.

units.la: XI.
units.tr: XI.

units.la: Qui vnum essentia, trinum personis profitentur Deum, nullum Deum profitentur.
units.tr: Those who profess God as one in essence and three in persons profess no God.

units.la: Sed hoc vos facitis.
units.tr: But you do this.

units.la: Ergo nullum Deum profitemini.
units.tr: Therefore you profess no God.

units.la: Ratio Maioris est, quia vnum fingitis Deum, qui non sit tres, & tres, qui non sint illa vnica essentia.
units.tr: The reason for the major premise is that you feign one God who is not three, and three who are not that one essence.

units.la: R. Maior nullam habet connexionem firmam. Imò mendacium est. Nam sacræ literæ docent, vnum esse Deum, & tamen esse tres, Patrem, Filium & Spiritum sanctum. Ideo iuxta verbum Dei, verum Deum docemus, invocamus, & profitemur. Si verò Ariani isti iudicant, verba quibus vtitur Ecclesia, à rebus quas tradit sacra Scriptura dissidere, monstrent discrepantiam, & doceant meliores loquutiones.
units.tr: Reply: The major premise has no firm connection; indeed it is a lie. For the sacred letters teach that there is one God, and yet that there are three, Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Therefore, according to the Word of God, we teach, invoke and profess the true God. But if these Arians judge that the words the Church uses differ from the things that Holy Scripture delivers, let them show the discrepancy and teach better expressions.

units.la: XII.
units.tr: XII.

units.la: Quos Scriptura non appellat Deos, non sunt appellandi Dij.
units.tr: Those whom Scripture does not call gods are not to be called gods.

units.la: Istos tres, Patrem nempe, Filium & Spiritum sanctum, scriptura nusquam appellat tres Deos.
units.tr: Scripture nowhere calls these three, namely the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, three gods.

units.la: Ergo hi tres non sunt vnus Deus.
units.tr: Therefore these three are not one God.

units.la: R. Plus in conclusionem ingeritur, quàm præmissis inest. Hoc sequitur, Ergo nõ sunt tres Dij: idque verum est. Atqui istos tres non esse vnicum illum & verum Deum, ex præmissis nõ sequitur. Nam scriptura sacra cuilibet personæ attribuit istud genus, quòd sit Deus: non tamen tres esse Deos docet, sed vnicum duntaxat Deum, qui est Pater, Filius & Spiritus sanctus.
units.tr: R. More is put into the conclusion than is contained in the premises. What follows is "Therefore they are not three Gods," and that is true. But that these three are not the one and true God does not follow from the premises. For holy Scripture ascribes the name of God to each person, yet it teaches not that there are three Gods, but only one God, who is the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

units.la: XIII.
units.tr: XIII.

units.la: Vbi non est doctrina, quòd vnus sit Deus Pater, qui per Filium à peccatis nos redemit, ibi non est doctrina de misericordia & iustitia Dei.
units.tr: Where there is no teaching that the one God is the Father, who through the Son redeemed us from sins, there is no teaching about the mercy and justice of God.

units.la: Sed qui docent, Deum vnum essentia esse, non habent hanc veram de Deo doctrinam.
units.tr: But those who teach that God is one in essence do not hold this true doctrine of God.

units.la: Ergo & hi de misericordia & iustitia Dei non possunt docere.
units.tr: Therefore they too cannot teach about the mercy and justice of God.

units.la: Minorem probant, quia nescitur, an ista essentia sit Pater vel mater.
units.tr: They prove the minor premise because it is not known whether that essence is Father or mother.

units.la: R. Confundat os blasphemum Dominus. Minor est tetra calumnia: quia non docemus essentiam Dei, si vox Essentiæ absolutè accipiatur, pro Natura seu Diuinitate, in qua non sit Trinitas seu tres distinctæ personæ. Vel, vt loquitur Scriptura, Docemus vnicum esse Deum, qui sit Pater Filius & Spiritus sanctus, & non alius. Itaque vnicus ille Deus, quem Vetus ac Nouum Testamentum, omnesque orthodoxi docent & profitentur, est ille ipse Pater, qui genuit Filium: & est Filius, qui genitus est à Patre: & est Spiritus sanctus, qui à Patre & Filio procedit.
units.tr: R. May the Lord confound the blasphemous mouth. The minor is a foul calumny: we do not teach the essence of God if the word "essence" is taken absolutely, for Nature or Deity, in which there is no Trinity or three distinct persons. Or, as Scripture speaks, we teach that there is one God, who is Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and no other. Therefore that one God, whom the Old and New Testaments and all the orthodox teach and profess, is that very Father who begot the Son; and is the Son, who was begotten of the Father; and is the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Father and the Son.

units.la: Si verò argumetum ad Iudæos & Turcas accommodaueris, locum sanè habebit. Nam etsi illi quoque vnum Deum profitentur, tamen pernegant eum vnicum esse Deum, qui sit Pater, Filius, & Spiritus sanctus. Ideo de Vnitate Dei non rectè sentiunt.
units.tr: But if you apply the argument to Jews and Turks, it will certainly have force. For although they too profess one God, they utterly deny that he is the one God who is Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Therefore they do not think rightly about the unity of God.

units.la: XIIII.
units.tr: XIIII.

units.la: Si Deus vnus essentia non genuit, vana est redemptio, fides, inuocatio.
units.tr: If God one in essence did not beget, redemption, faith and invocation are vain.

units.la: Sed vos Deum Vnum essentia, dicitis non genuisse.
units.tr: But you say that God one in essence did not beget.

units.la: Ergo non est redemptio, fides, inuocatio.
units.tr: Therefore there is no redemption, faith or invocation.
