Ego Filium esse natum confiteor, quod reliquum est impietatis horresco. scriptum enim est in Esaia, Ante me non fuit Deus, & post me non erit. Quis ergo hoc dicit? Paterne an Filius? Si Filius ante me non fuit, alius Deus, inquit, Si Pater post me nō erit, hic priorem, ille posteriorem non habet. Invicem in se, & Pater in Filio, & Filius in Patre cognoscitur. Quum Patrem nominas Deum, Filium designasti, quia nemo est ipse sibi Pater. Quum Filium nominas, etiam Patrem fateris, quia nemo sibi ipsi Filius est. Itaque nec Filius sine Patre, nec Pater esse potest sine Filio. semper ergo Pater, & semper Filius est, & uterque semper unus sunt Deus. Quod autem dicis Patrem esse Filij essentiatorem, insidiose & impie dicitur. Etsi enim Pater gignit Filium, non tamen gignit essentiam, sed personam, neque est origo, neque principium, neque causa, neque essentiator essentiæ Filij, sed personæ. Alioqui ipse sibi esset essentiator, quia eadem est essentia in Patre, & Filio, & Spiritu sancto, & tota in tribus & singulis personis.
units.tr: I recognise the argument of Arius: If God the Father begot the Son God, then he begot either himself God or another God, not himself God. But nothing begets itself; therefore another God. I answer with Ambrose: Tell me, heretic, was there a time when the almighty Father was God and was not Father, and afterwards became Father, so that he was changed by the addition of generation? I confess that the Son was born, and I shudder at the rest of the impiety. For it is written in Isaiah: "Before me there was no God, and after me there shall be none." Who then says this, the Father or the Son? If the Son says, "Before me there was no God," he is speaking of another God; if the Father says, "After me there shall be none," then the one has no predecessor and the other has no successor. Thus in each other the Father is known in the Son, and the Son in the Father. When you name the Father God, you designate the Son, because no one is his own Father. When you name the Son, you also confess the Father, because no one is his own Son. Therefore the Son cannot exist without the Father, nor the Father without the Son. Always, then, the Father is Father, and always the Son is Son, and both are always one God. But when you say that the Father is the essentiator of the Son, you speak insidiously and impiously. For although the Father begets the Son, he does not beget the essence but the person; he is not the origin, nor the principle, nor the cause, nor the essentiator of the essence of the Son, but of the person. Otherwise he would be the essentiator of himself, since the essence is the same in the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and whole in each of the three persons.

units.la: Ut enim Hilarius lib. 7. De Trinitate ait: Quod etiam ex vivo vivum natum est, habet nativitatis perfectü sine nouitate naturæ. In Deo enim totum quod est vivit, Deus enim vita est, & ex vita non potest esse nisi vivum: neque ex derivatione, sed ex virtute nativitas est, ac si totum quod est, vivit, & quum totum quod ex eo nascitur virtus est, habet nativitatem Filius, non derivationem aut demutationem.
units.tr: For as Hilary says in the seventh book of On the Trinity: "What is born living from the living has the perfection of birth without any novelty of nature. For in God whatever he is, he lives; God is life, and from life there can be nothing but the living. The birth is not by derivation but by power, as if whatever he is, he lives; and since all that is born from him is power, the Son has birth, not derivation or alteration."

units.la: Patrem, inquit Hilarius libro 4. De Trinitate, in Filio, & Filium in Patre esse, plenitudo in utroque divinitatis perfecta est, quia plenitudo divinitatis in Filio, quod in Patre est, hoc & Filio est, quod in ingenito est, hoc & genito, alter ab altero, & uterque unum, is scilicet qui est nihil habens quod non sit in eo etiam, a quo est, non duo unus, sed alius in alio, quia non aliud in utroque, ut unum sint in fide nostra, utque non unus, nec eundē utrunq;,nec aliud cōfitemur,quia Deū ex Deo natū, nec eundē natiui-tas,nec aliud esse permittit.Eandē ergo in utroque,& virtutis similitudinē & deitatis plenitudinē cōfitemur:quia veritas dicit, Ego in Patre,& Pater in me est. Omnia enim Filius accepit à Patre.Nam si partē eiusdem qui genuit ac-cepit, Neuter ergo perfectus est. Deest enim ei unde decessit, nec plenitudo in eo erit, qui ex portione constiterit. Neuter ergo perfectus est si plenitudi-nem suam,& qui genuit amittit, nec qui natus est consequitur. Fateamur i-gitur quòd Pater est in Filio,& Filius in Patre,& Deus in Deo,non per du-plicem conuenientiam,generum conuenientiam,nec per insititiam[?] capacioris substantiæ naturam,sed per naturæ veritatem, similitudinem per natiuitatem viuentis,ex viuente natura,dum res non differtur,dum naturam Dei non de-generat natiuitas,dum non aliud aliquid ex Deo quàm Deus nascitur.
units.tr: Hilary says in the fourth book of On the Trinity: "That the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, the fullness of divinity is perfect in each. For the fullness of divinity that is in the Father is in the Son too; what is in the unbegotten is in the begotten also; the one is from the other, and each is one: that is, he who has nothing that is not also in him from whom he is. They are not two, one; but one in another, because the one is not other in each, so that they may be one in our faith. Nor do we confess that the two are the same, nor that they are different, since birth permits neither that the same God born from God be the same, nor that he be different. We therefore confess the same in each, both the likeness of power and the fullness of deity, because truth says: 'I am in the Father, and the Father is in me.' For the Son has received all things from the Father. For if he received a part of what the begetter has, then neither is perfect: the one lacks what he has given away, and the fullness will not be in him who consists of a portion. Neither, then, is perfect if the begetter loses his fullness, and the one who is born does not attain it. Let us confess, therefore, that the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, and God in God, not by a double agreement, nor by an agreement of kind, nor by the grafting of a nature of greater substance, but by the truth of nature, by likeness through the birth of a living being from a living nature, since the thing is not distinguished, since birth does not degrade the nature of God, since nothing other than God is born from God."

units.la: LXX.
units.tr: LXX.

units.la: Ad dictum Mosis, Audi Israel, Dominus Deus noster Dominus unus est. & dictum Malachiæ : Nunquid non unus Pater omnium nostrum? respondet Augustinus: Non potest dici trinitas Pater, nisi forsan transfitiuè[?] ad creaturam ratione creationis. Quod enim scriptum est: Audi Israel,Dominus Deus tuus, Deus unus est,non utique excepto Filio,& Spiritu sancto oportet intelligi,quia rectè Dominum Deum nostrum dicimus etiam Patrem nostrum per gratiam,& regenerationem.
units.tr: To the saying of Moses, "Hear, Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one," and the saying of Malachi, "Has not one Father of us all?" Augustine answers: The Trinity cannot be called the Father, unless perhaps transitively to the creature, by reason of creation. For what is written, "Hear, Israel, the Lord your God is one God," must be understood not excluding the Son and the Holy Spirit; for we rightly call the Lord our God also our Father, by grace and regeneration.

units.la: LXXI.
units.tr: LXXI.

units.la: Ad sententiam Apostoli, Nobis autem unus est Deus Pater ille à quo omnia, nihil opus est responsione,quia continuò sequitur, Et unus Dominus Iesus Christus per quem omnia,& nos per illum.ex quo sequitur,Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum unum esse cum Patre Deū,à quo nos sumus conditi.
units.tr: To the saying of the Apostle, "But for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things," no answer is needed, because it immediately follows: "And one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him." From this it follows that our Lord Jesus Christ is one God with the Father, by whom we were created.

units.la: LXXII.
units.tr: LXXII.

units.la: Ex alio loco Pauli: Vnus Deus & unus mediator hominum homo Iesus Christus, unus Dominus, una fides, unum baptisma, unus Deus & Pater omnium:manifestè colligitur, personam Fili discerni à persona Patris, propter incarnationem: cæterum esse eundem cum eo Deum, quandoquidem unum est baptisma quo baptizamur in nomine Patris & Filii & Spiritus sancti, & confitemur nos credere in unum Deum Patrem & Filium & Spiritum sanctum. Ad illa quæ profers ex Ignatio & Tertulliano, supra responsum est. Sed illud ad finem taxandum putaui, Christum ideo dici Deum, quòd sit ex immensa Dei substantia,à qua nihil quod extat separari potest, ac ne dæmones quidem,nisi quantum ad voluntatem. Hæc enim vox non Christiani hominus mihi videtur ac memini Seruetum docere, Christum esse naturam filium Dei, quòd Deus ex sua substantia guttas quasdam roridas demiserit in ute-rum virginis, ut contendat, Deum esse corporeum, sicut Mahometus. Quod si ex eius es schola, & ita sentis, sicut scribis, nihil quod extat separari posse ab immensa Dei substantia, ac ne daemones quidem, Et Filium ideo verum dici Deum, quia est de substantia Dei infinita, ex qua sunt omnes creaturae, deterior es Ario, & indignus cui a Christianis respondeatur, & simpliciter tibi dicendum: Increpet te Sathan Dominus, qui ante non es veritus dicere, quòd Filius Dei in Beelzebub principe daemoniorum eiiceret daemones, & eius diuinitatem ambiuisti ante conditum mundum, & primos homines ambire fecisti, & ab eo petiuisti ut te adoraret, pollicitus regna mundi, quæ idololatris, qui te pro Filio Dei adorant, partiris.
units.tr: From another passage of Paul: "There is one God and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus; one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all," it is plainly gathered that the person of the Son is distinguished from the person of the Father on account of the incarnation, but that he is the same God with him, since there is one baptism in which we are baptised in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and we confess that we believe in one God, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. As for what you produce from Ignatius and Tertullian, I have answered above. But I thought this point should be touched upon at the end: that Christ is called God because he is of the immense substance of God, from which nothing that exists can be separated, not even demons, except as to will. For this phrase does not seem to me to be the language of a Christian, and I remember that Servetus taught that Christ is the natural Son of God because God let some dewy drops of his own substance fall into the womb of the virgin, so that he might contend that God is corporeal, as Muhammad did. But if you belong to his school and think as you write, that nothing that exists can be separated from the immense substance of God, not even demons, and that the Son is therefore truly called God because he is of the infinite substance of God, from which all creatures come, then you are worse than Arius, and unworthy of being answered by Christians; and I must simply say to you: "May the Lord rebuke you, Satan." You who earlier did not hesitate to say that the Son of God cast out demons by Beelzebub, the prince of demons, and who sought his divinity before the world was made, and made the first men seek it, and asked him to worship you, promising the kingdoms of the world, which you share with idolaters who worship you as the Son of God.

units.la: LXXIII.
units.tr: LXXIII.

units.la: Sed scripturæ & sancti patres longè aliter de substantia Dei docent, & definiunt: Deum esse essentiam spiritualem, æternam, simplicissimam, incommunicabilem, cui nihil creatum admixtum est, infinitæ potentiæ, sapientiæ, & bonitatis. Patrem æternum, qui ab æterno genuit sibi Filium coæternum ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης καὶ χαρακτῆρα [?] τῆς ὑποστάσεως αὐτοῦ. Et Spiritum sanctum paracletum, ut ante in expositione Symboli ex Cypriano ostendi.
units.tr: But the Scriptures and the holy Fathers teach and define the substance of God quite differently: God is a spiritual essence, eternal, most simple, incommunicable, to which nothing created is mixed, of infinite power, wisdom and goodness; the eternal Father, who from eternity begot for himself a co-eternal Son, "the brightness of his glory and the express image of his person" [ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης καὶ χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως αὐτοῦ]; and the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, as I showed earlier in the exposition of the Creed from Cyprian.

units.la: LXXIIII.
units.tr: LXXIIII.

units.la: Tu conaris hanc collectionem eludere, Pater est Deus, Filius est Deus, Spiritus sanctus est Deus, & non sunt tres Dij. Igitur sunt unus Deus, quandoquidem scriptura dicit, Tres sunt qui testimonium dant in coelo, Pater, Verbum & Spiritus sanctus. Sic inquâ conaris hæc eludere. Rectè inquis scriptura dicit, Ii tres unum sunt, non unus, quia tres substantiali numero sine contradictione in adiecto, unus numero dici non possunt. Quod si Pater, Filius & Spiritus sanctus unus simpliciter non sunt, nec dicuntur unus: similiter quoque cum adiuncto non sunt nec dicuntur unus Deus. Imo inquit Ambrosius libro De trinitate: Quod unius est substantiæ separari non potest, etsi non sit singularitatis sed unitatis Deus. Unus enim quum dicitur, nequaquam Deitas trinitatem excludit. Non est diuersa, vel singularis æqualitas, nec iuxta Sabellianos Patrem Filiumque confundens, nec iuxta Arianos, Patrem Filiumque secernens: Pater enim & Filius distinctionem habent, separationem non habent. Pater & Filius diuinitate sunt unum, nec est ibi substantiæ differentia, nec ulla diuersitas, alioqui quomodo unum Deum dicimus?
units.tr: You try to evade this conclusion by saying: the Father is God, the Son is God, the Holy Spirit is God, and yet they are not three Gods. Therefore they are one God, since Scripture says: "There are three that bear record in heaven: the Father, the Word and the Holy Spirit." This, I say, is how you try to evade it. You rightly say that Scripture says "these three are one" and not "one," because three in substantial number, without contradiction in the adjective, cannot be called one in number. But if the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are not simply one, and are not called one, then likewise with the addition they are not and are not called one God. Indeed, Ambrose says in his book On the Trinity: "What is of one substance cannot be separated, although God is not of singularity but of unity. For when he is called one, the Godhead by no means excludes the Trinity. It is not a different or singular equality, nor, as the Sabellians hold, does it confuse Father and Son, nor, as the Arians hold, does it separate Father and Son. For Father and Son have distinction but not separation. Father and Son are one in divinity, and there is no difference of substance nor any diversity. Otherwise, how do we say one God?"

units.la: LXXV.
units.tr: LXXV.

units.la: Hoc testimonio Ambrosii, quem Ecclesia catholica pro vero interprete scripturæ agnoscit, tota tua sophistica refutatur, & confirmatur vera Symboli expositio.
units.tr: By this testimony of Ambrose, whom the catholic Church acknowledges as the true interpreter of Scripture, your whole sophistry is refuted, and the true exposition of the Creed is confirmed.

units.la: LXXVI.
units.tr: LXXVI.

units.la: Te quoque mentiri, quū ais inter Arium & Sabellium media via incede-re, demonstrat Hieronymus, & ostendit quæ via sit, qua inter hæresiarchas medius tutissimus ibis, scribens ad Alypium & Augustinum catholicæ fidei columnas: Non enim, inquit, prorsus aliquis est in trinitate gradus, nihilque quod inferius, superiusque dici possit: sed tota diuinitas sui perfectione æqualis est, ut exceptis vocabulis, quæ proprietatem indicant personarum, quicquid de una persona dicitur, de tribus possit dignissimè intelligi. Atqui ut confutantes Arium unam eandemque trinitatis essentiam vel substantiam, & Deum unum in tribus personis fatemur: ita etiam impietatem Sabellij declinantes tres personas expressas, sub proprietate distinguimus, non ipsum sibi Patrem, non ipsum sibi Filium, non ipsum sibi Spiritum sanctum esse dicentes, aliam Patris, aliam Filii aliam Spiritus sancti esse personam. Non enim nomina tantummodo, sed etiam nominum proprietates, id est, personas, vel, ut Græci exprimunt ὑποστάσεις[?], subsistentiásque confitemur. Nec Pater Filii, vel Spiritus sancti personam aliquando excludit, nec Filius vel Spiritus sanctus Pa-tris nomen, personámque recipit: sed Pater semper Pater, & Filius semper Filius, & Spiritus sanctus semper Spiritus sanctus. Itaque substantia unum sunt, sed personis & nominibus distinguuntur. Hæc Hieronymus.
units.tr: That you also lie when you say you walk a middle way between Arius and Sabellius is shown by Jerome, who also indicates which way it is by which you would go most safely between the heresiarchs. Writing to Alypius and Augustine, pillars of the catholic faith, he says: "There is, indeed, no degree at all in the Trinity, and nothing that can be called lower or higher; but the whole divinity is equal in its perfection, so that, apart from the words that indicate the property of the persons, whatever is said of one person can most worthily be understood of all three. Accordingly, while refuting Arius, we confess one and the same essence or substance of the Trinity, and one God in three persons; and so, avoiding the impiety of Sabellius, we distinguish the three persons, expressed under their properties, not saying that the Father is himself his own Father, nor the Son his own Son, nor the Holy Spirit his own Holy Spirit, but that the person of the Father is one, of the Son another, and of the Holy Spirit another. For we confess not only the names, but also the properties of the names, that is, the persons, or, as the Greeks express it, the subsistences [ὑποστάσεις]. Nor does the Father at any time exclude the person of the Son or of the Holy Spirit, nor does the Son or the Holy Spirit receive the name or person of the Father; but the Father is always Father, the Son always Son, and the Holy Spirit always Holy Spirit. Thus they are one in substance, but are distinguished by persons and names." These are Jerome's words.

units.la: Hæc visum est hoc tempore ita proponere, ut distincta capitibus certius co-gnosci, & de his consuetudine Academiæ nostræ disputari posset, quo æter-na Veritas patefacta verbo Dei & declarata scriptis sacrarum literarum, ma-gis & illustrius emineret. Undique enim huic vel insidiæ struuntur, vel ma-nifesta bella inferuntur, dum ab aliis veteres hæreses renouando ventilantur, ab aliis detecti errores decernendo stabiliuntur. Sed pro illa pïs & religiosis multò acriùs quam pro aris & focis, ut dicitur, propugnandum est. Hac enim labefactata cætera ruunt omnia. Atque oportebat sanè accedere ad doctrinæ puræ & syncerae integritatem, vitæ quoque & morum sanctitatem, & disciplinam eam, quam doctrina illa requirit. Cuius rei necessariæ inprimis negli-gentia animaduersionem scilicet Dei commouet, permittentis nos tam graviter tentari, & punientis obliuionem maximorum beneficiorum, quæ in nos clementissimè contulit. Restat igitur ut unusquisque non sit tantū verbis & oratione, sed efficacitatem quoque & studio Christianus, ne temere & falso tam gloriosum nomen vsurpetur: sed vt omnibus consiliis factisque & dictis nostris æternum PatER Domini & saluatoris nostri ISSV CHRISTI Filii vnigeniti, vnà cum sancto Spiritu, trinitas hæc vna Deitas, id est, vt Gregorius Nassansenus caute est loquutus, ἐν ἐν τοῖς τρισί, καὶ τρία ἕν [?], id est persona tres, Deus vnus, solus, verus, sanctus, fortis, immortalis, iustus, misericors, celebretur & glorificetur in secula seculorum. Amen.
units.tr: It has seemed good at this time to set these things out in this way, under distinct headings, so that they may be more surely known and may be debated in the customary manner of our Academy, so that the eternal Truth, revealed in the Word of God and declared in the writings of holy Scripture, may shine forth the more clearly and brilliantly. For on all sides either snares are laid against it, or open wars are waged against it: on the one hand old heresies are stirred up again and revived, on the other errors once detected are firmly established by decrees. But for that pure and religious faith we must fight much more keenly than, as the saying goes, for altars and hearths. For once this is overthrown, all the rest collapses. And it was certainly fitting to add to the purity and sincerity of doctrine the integrity of life and the holiness of conduct, and that discipline which this doctrine requires. The neglect of this necessary matter especially stirs up the displeasure of God, who permits us to be so grievously tempted, and punishes our forgetfulness of the very great benefits which he has most mercifully bestowed upon us. It remains, therefore, that each of us be a Christian not only in words and speech, but also in effectiveness and zeal, lest so glorious a name be taken up rashly and falsely; but that in all our counsels, deeds and words, the eternal Father of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, his only-begotten Son, together with the Holy Spirit, this Trinity, one Godhead, that is, as Gregory of Nyssa carefully spoke, one in the three and three in one [ἐν ἐν τοῖς τρισί, καὶ τρία ἕν], that is, three persons, one God, alone, true, holy, strong, immortal, just and merciful, may be celebrated and glorified for ever and ever. Amen.

units.la: DE VNITATE ESSENTIA DIVINA, & tribus in ea subsistentibus personis, aduersus Arianos ὁμοιοσίως.
units.tr: On the Unity of the Divine Essence, and the Three Persons Subsisting in It, against the Arians, ὁμοιοσίως.

units.la: Ministrorum Geneuensium Epistola.
units.tr: Letter of the Ministers of Geneva.

units.la: ILLVSTRISSIMO PRINCIPI NICOLAO RADZVVILO, DEI GRATIA IN OLIIKA ET Niessvvesch Duci, D.in Kleczko & Grodeck, Palatino Vilnensi, Magni Ducatus Lithuaniæ supremo Marschalco & Archicancellario Brestensi, Cauionensi, Borissouiensi, Schmolensi-Capitaneo generali.
units.tr: To the most illustrious prince Nicholas Radziwiłł, by the grace of God duke of Olyka and Nieśwież, of Kleczko and Grodeck, Palatine of Vilnius, supreme Marshal and Archchancellor of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, captain-general of Brest, Kowno, Borisov and Smolensk.

units.la: Illustrissime Princeps, binas à Celsitudine tua literas vno tempore accepimus, vnas D.I.Caluino, beatæ memoriæ viro, alteras nobis inscriptas, vtrasque copiosè & eleganter scriptas: quibus quòd tam sero respondeamus, rogamus C.T. vt neque negligentiæ, neque vlli alii rei tribuat, quàm tabellariorum à nobis Tubingam, vnde missæ sunt ad nos literæ, commeantium penuriæ. Quòd vero in re tam graui, tamque seria, adeo paucis respondeamus, hæ sunt causæ.
units.tr: Most illustrious Prince, we received two letters from your Highness at the same time, one addressed to Master Calvin, of blessed memory, and the other to us, both written at length and elegantly. That we reply so late, we ask your Highness to attribute neither to negligence nor to anything else but the shortage of couriers travelling from Tübingen, whence the letters were sent to us. That we reply so briefly to a matter so grave and serious has the following causes.

units.la: Legimus, idque non sine horrore, quæ Gregorius Paulus Casanonius, & alii nonnulli à Blandrata & Gentile fascinati, tres personas, siue ὑποστάσεις in tres numero οὐσίας siue essentias transformantes, variis libellis scripserunt: in quibus tam multa tum ambigua tum etiam ἀσυστασία [?] comperimus, vt de eorum dogmatibus & argumentis ne nunc quidem penè nobis liqueat.
units.tr: We have read, not without horror, the various little books which Gregorio Paolo Casanonio and some others, bewitched by Blandrata and Gentile, have written, transforming the three persons, or hypostases, into three essences [ἀσυστασία]. In them we have found so many things that are ambiguous and even inconsistent [ἀσυστασία] that we are scarcely clear, even now, about their doctrines and arguments.

units.la: Literæ vero tuæ, quanuis multò clariùs perscriptæ, tamen nostræ ruditati, vt ingenuè cum T.C.loquamur, non per omnia satisfaciunt, præsertim in tertia illius conciliatoriæ sententiæ explicatione: quam si rectè intelligimus, putamus ab illa ab illa siue Gentilitia, siue Gregoriana parum admodum dissidere.
units.tr: Your letter, although written much more clearly, does not fully satisfy our slowness, to speak frankly with your Highness, especially in the explanation of the third point of that conciliatory opinion. If we understand it rightly, we think it differs very little from that view, whether Gentile's or Gregorio's.

units.la: Itaque quum de rebus ipsis, ac multò minus etiam de aduersariorum argumentis nondum ita nobis constet, quin merito vereamur ne videri posimus vel de rebus non controuersis frustra laborare, vel non satis appositè aduersariorum sententiam oppugnare, quæres posset istas infelices contentiones potius accendere quàm extinguere: ac præterea etiam quum res ipsa ostendat, scribendis vltro citróque tam multis, crescere potius altercationes, quàm imminui, dum vnusquisque quod semel scripsit non patitur reprehendi: idcirco priusquam iustum ad singula responsum edamus, hoc à T.C. pro Christi nomine flagitamus, vt istos quibus non placet hæc propositio, PATER, FILIVS, SPIRITVS SANCTVS SVNT VNVS ET IDEM DEVS, huc adigas, vt totū suū dogma tū de essentia, tū de hypostasibus, sigillatim, clarè, & distinctè, certis & perspicuis thesibus perscribant: deinde suas etiā rationes tū ex Dei verbo, tum ex patrum Græcorum & Latinorum scriptis descriptas adiiciant, atque etiam, si libebit, nostrorum argumentorū, quæ non ignorāt, refutationes.
units.tr: Since we are not yet so clear about the matters themselves, and even less about the arguments of our opponents, we rightly fear that we may seem either to labour in vain over matters not in dispute, or to attack the opponents' view not closely enough; and someone might ask whether we would rather kindle these unhappy quarrels than extinguish them. Moreover, the thing itself shows that, when so many things are written back and forth, the disputes grow rather than diminish, since each person does not allow what he has once written to be criticised. Therefore, before we give a proper answer to each point, we ask your Highness, in the name of Christ, to bring those who dislike this proposition, THE FATHER, THE SON, AND THE HOLY SPIRIT ARE ONE AND THE SAME GOD, to set out their whole doctrine, both of the essence and of the hypostases, point by point, clearly and distinctly, in certain and plain theses; then to add their own reasons, drawn both from the Word of God and from the writings of the Greek and Latin Fathers, and also, if they wish, refutations of our arguments, which they are not unaware of.

units.la: Nam ita demum fiet, vt & plenius & certius respondeamus: quod quum etiam si T.C. à nobis pro suo in patriam atque adeò in totam Ecclesiam studio non petiisset, vltro facturi essemus: multò nunc etiam à T.C. interpellati, libentius ac diligentius pro modulo gratiæ nobis à Deo Opt. Max. concessæ facere omnino decreuimus.
units.tr: For only in this way will we be able to answer both more fully and more certainly. Even if your Highness had not asked us for this, out of your zeal for your country and indeed for the whole Church, we would have done it of our own accord. Now, since your Highness has urged us so strongly, we have quite decided to do it more willingly and carefully, as far as the measure of grace granted to us by God Most Good and Most High allows.

units.la: Interea verò ne nos arbitrentur nonnulli vel tergiuersatione, vel aliquo responsum differre, palàm testamur apud C.T. Illustrissime Princeps, nos per Dei gratiam in vera & orthodoxa sententia de Patre, Filio, & Spiritu sancto, tribus quidem numero & reipsa distinctis personis, & vno nihilominus ac eodem secundum essentiam Deo, non modò perseuerare, sed etiam magnopere perlectis istorum commentis fuisse confirmatos.
units.tr: Meanwhile, lest some people think that we are delaying the answer through evasion or some pretext, we openly testify before your Highness, most illustrious Prince, that by the grace of God we not only persevere in the true and orthodox view concerning the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, who are indeed three in number and really distinct persons, and yet one and the same God according to essence, but have also been greatly confirmed by reading through the inventions of those men.

units.la: Quid enim ineptius, imò verò quid magis impium, quàm simplicissimam infinitatem numero multiplicare?
units.tr: For what is more foolish, or rather what is more impious, than to multiply in number the most simple infinity?

units.la: Itaque est quidē horrenda Iudæorū cæcitas, qui indistincta οὐσίαν statuunt, & execrāda Sabellii impudētia, qui personas sic agnoscit, vt verbo tenus nō re distinguat, & horrēda Arianorū blasphemia, quorū alii ἑτεροούσιον, alii ὁμοιούσιον Christum constituūt: quod idē Macedoniani de Spiritu sancto docuerunt.
units.tr: There is indeed the dreadful blindness of the Jews, who posit an undistinguished essence; and the accursed impudence of Sabellius, who recognises the persons in such a way that he distinguishes them in name only and not in reality; and the dreadful blasphemy of the Arians, some of whom make Christ of a different essence [ἑτεροούσιον], others of a like essence [ὁμοιούσιον]; which the Macedonians also taught concerning the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Sed omnes istos quantumuis detestabiles, minus tamen absurdè, quàm olim Seuerianos, & nunc istos de quibus agimus, loquutos fuisse arbitramur.
units.tr: But we think that all these, however detestable, spoke less absurdly than the Severians of old, and than those of whom we are now speaking.

units.la: Retinent enim illi hoc fundamentū, vnicum esse Deum sicut vnica est eius essentia, cuius realem in tres personas, absque essentiæ diuisione, distinctionem quum solum Dei verbum declaret, ex eo autem sapere illi recusarint, non mirum est eos istam personarum distinctionem non tenuisse.
units.tr: For those men hold this foundation, that God is one, just as his essence is one; and since they have refused to learn from it, but only from the word of God, which declares a real distinction of three persons without division of the essence, it is no wonder that they have not held this distinction of persons.

units.la: Isti vero quid tandem discerpta in tres deos divina essentia, integrum in Religionis fundamento relinquent?
units.tr: But what, pray, will those people leave intact in the foundation of religion, when they have torn the divine essence into three gods?

units.la: Libenter tamen nobis persuaserint sese multitudinem deorum vitare, si dixerint, Pater, Filius, & Spiritus sanctus sunt unum, id est, una divina natura, sive essentia. Quasi vero etiamsi (exempli causa) Petrus, Ioannes, & Iacobus dicantur unum esse specie, idcirco tres homines non statuantur.
units.tr: Yet they would gladly persuade us that they avoid a multitude of gods if they say, The Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are one, that is, one divine nature or essence. As if, for example, Peter, John and James, even if they are said to be one in species, were therefore not held to be three men!

units.la: Quid igitur attinet tergiversari, & cur nō potius libere & ingenuē proferunt quod ex eorum dogmate prorsus consequitur, nimirum unā quidē esse divinitatem, sed tres deos, & quidem inter se impares, quum maius sit esse a seipso, quam habere suum esse ab alio, sive precario Deum esse?
units.tr: Why, then, do they evade the question, and why do they not rather freely and openly state what follows entirely from their doctrine, namely that there is indeed one divinity, but three gods, and unequal among themselves, since it is greater to be from oneself than to have one's being from another, or to be God by favour?

units.la: Certè vel unicū numero Deū constituat oportet, vel plures. Si unicū, qua de re digladiatur? Sin plures (deriuata videlicet Filii essētia à Patris essentia, vt sint duæ numero essentiæ) qua fronte audebunt negare se plures numero deos statuere?
units.tr: Surely they must posit either one God in number or several. If one, why do they wrangle about it? But if several (namely, the essence of the Son being derived from the essence of the Father, so that there are two essences in number), with what face will they dare to deny that they posit several gods in number?

units.la: Itaque si istis credimus, nō erant simpliciter accusandi veteres illi idololatræ, quòd multos deos colerent, sed quòd plures tribus, & quidē falsos deos colerent.
units.tr: Thus, if we believe them, those ancient idolaters were not to be simply accused for worshipping many gods, but for worshipping more than three gods, and indeed false ones.

units.la: Iam verò ista essentiæ diuinæ multiplicatio sive in duos (audimus enim iā etiam Spiritum sanctū à quibusdā illorū expungi) sive in tres deos, quomodo cū altero ipsorum dogmate conuenit, quæcunque videlicet de vno & solo Deo in Scripturis dicuntur, nec de Filio, nec de Spiritu sancto esse intelligenda?
units.tr: Moreover, how does this multiplication of the divine essence, whether into two (for we hear that some of them are already striking out the Holy Spirit), or into three gods, agree with another of their doctrines, namely that whatever is said in the Scriptures about the one and only God is not to be understood of the Son or of the Holy Spirit?

units.la: Nā si vnus & solus Pater est Deus, consequitur Filium vel Deū non esse, vel alio genere diuinitatis Deū esse, quàm Patrē: qui est Arianorū error: sicut si nato Abele, solus & vnº[?] Adā erat homo, Abel filius eius vel homo nō erat, vel alia humana natura, quàm pater ipsius præditus, ac proinde specie differēs.
units.tr: For if the Father alone is the one and only God, it follows that the Son either is not God, or is God in another kind of divinity than the Father, which is the error of the Arians. It is as if, Abel being born, Adam alone was man, and Abel his son either was not a man, or had a human nature other than that of his father, and so differed in species.

units.la: Quod enim respondent, solum Patrem esse αὐτόθεον, id est, vt interpretantur, à seipso suum esse habere, ac proinde solum Deum dici, quàm inepte dicitur?
units.tr: For what of their reply, that the Father alone is self-God [αὐτόθεον], that is, as they interpret it, has his being from himself, and therefore alone is called God? How foolishly this is said!

units.la: Nam à se vel ab alio esse aliā naturæ speciem non constituit: ac proinde Pater ob illam causam solus & vnicus Deus esse dici non potest nec debet, sed solus & vnicus Pater, sicut solus & vnicus Filius, quia vnigenitus.
units.tr: For having being from oneself or from another does not constitute a different species of nature. Therefore the Father cannot and ought not to be called the only and single God for that reason, but only and single Father, just as the Son is the only and single Son, because he is the only-begotten.

units.la: Nec tale quidquam quale isti comminiscuntur Apostolo in mentem venit, quum vnum solum Deum Patrem, & vnum ac solum Dominum Iesum Christum vocaret: sicut copiosius aliquando, fauente Deo, declarabimus.
units.tr: Nor did anything like what they invent come into the mind of the Apostle, when he called the Father the one God, and Jesus Christ the one and only Lord; as we shall, God willing, declare more fully at some other time.

units.la: Quod porrò nos vt Sabellianos accusant, quo tandē iure faciūt? Sabellio Essentiæ & Personæ nomina confundenti, Pater, Filius, & Spiritus sanctus erat vnus, qui nobis tres sunt, suis incommunicabilibus proprietatibus vere & reipsa distincti. distincti. Quæ igitur inter illum & nos affinitas? nempe quæ inter tenebras & lucem.
units.tr: As to their accusing us of being Sabellians, with what right do they do so? For in Sabellius, who confused the names of essence and person, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit were one, whereas to us they are three, truly and really distinct by their incommunicable properties. What affinity, then, is there between him and us? Surely that between darkness and light.

units.la: Nec enim hæ duæ enuntiationes, PATER, FILIVS, ET SPIRI-TVS SANCTVS SVNT VNVS, & PATER, FILIVS ET SPI-RITVS SANCTVS SVNT VNVS DEVS, idem declarant. Illa enim personas confundit, quod est Sabellianum: ista vero docet sic distingui per-sonas, vt singulæ in vna eademque divina essentia subsistant: ac proinde singu-læ sint non tantum vna divinitas, sed etiam vnus & idem numero Deus, cuius in vno Deo triplicis subsistentiæ ordo à Patre incipit, & in Spiritum S. desinit.
units.tr: For these two statements, THE FATHER, THE SON, AND THE HOLY SPIRIT ARE ONE, and THE FATHER, THE SON AND THE HOLY SPIRIT ARE ONE GOD, do not mean the same thing. The first confuses the persons, which is Sabellian; but the second teaches that the persons are so distinguished that each subsists in the one and the same divine essence, and so each is not only one divinity but also one and the same God in number, in whose one God the order of the threefold subsistence begins with the Father and ends in the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Itaque quum nos irridentisti quasi contradictoria loquentes, quum tres u-num esse dicimus, vix responsionem merentur. Neque enim dicimus tres per-sonas esse vnam cum Sabellio, sed hypostases in vna essentia ex verbo Dei di-stinguimus proprietatibus & numero.
units.tr: Since they mock us as speaking self-contradictions when we say that three are one, they hardly deserve an answer. For we do not say, with Sabellius, that the three persons are one. Rather, following the Word of God, we distinguish the hypostases within one essence by their properties and by number.

units.la: At enim, inquiunt, non dicitis VNVM, sed VNVS: Imo vero non dicimus simpliciter VNVS, sed cum adiectione, VNVS DEVS, respectu videlicet vnius eiusdemque essentiæ, in qua tres illi sic subsistunt, vt nec divisi sint, nec confuncti, siue συγχύσεως[?]: sed ita suis proprietatibus incommunicabilibus reipsa distincti, vt quilibet tritu[?] alius sit secundi[?] hypostasin, quam reliqui duo: & tamen quia in tota eadem essentia subsistit, ideo sit vn°[?] & idem Deo atque reliqui duo.
units.tr: "But," they say, "you do not say UNUM, you say UNUS." Indeed we do not say simply UNUS, but add the words UNUS DEUS, with reference to the one and the same essence in which those three subsist, so that they are neither divided nor confused [συγχύσεως]. Yet they are so distinguished in reality by their incommunicable properties that each is a hypostasis different from the other two; and yet, because each subsists in the whole of the same essence, each is one and the same God as the other two.

units.la: Nec aliud intellexit Nicenum Concilium, licet ambigua loquutione, quum scriberet DEVM DE DEO, non vt duos deos constitueret, siue aliquam deitatem ex deitate deduceret: sed simpliciter vt essentiæ identitatem in duabus personis aduersus Arium assereret.
units.tr: The Nicene Council meant nothing else, although its language was ambiguous, when it wrote God from God. It did not mean to set up two gods, or to derive some deity from deity. It simply meant to assert, against Arius, the identity of essence in the two persons.

units.la: Sic Ioannes, Verbum quod Deus erat apud Deum, in principio fuisse scribit, non duas numero essentias, sed duas in vna & eadem essentia subsistentes personas declarans.
units.tr: So John writes that the Word, who was God, was in the beginning with God. He is declaring not two numerically distinct essences, but two persons subsisting in one and the same essence.

units.la: Nec alio sensu Hilarius (quem vnum isti authorem laudant) illud, VNVS EX VNO, TOTVS EX TOTO, PERFECTVS EX PERFECTO, sic inculcat, vt tamen non modo duplicem diuinitatem, sed etiam duos numero deos esse neget: quoniam videlicet sic Filius est alius a Patre, atque adeo secundus ordine, quatenus est genitus, vt tamen quia totus in vna eademque essentia subsistit, sit vnus & idem atque Pater, quatenus est Deus.
units.tr: Nor does Hilary, whom they alone praise as their authority, press the words ONE FROM ONE, WHOLE FROM WHOLE, PERFECT FROM PERFECT in a different sense. He does not thereby deny merely a double divinity; he also denies that there are two numerically distinct gods. The Son is other than the Father, and so second in order inasmuch as he is begotten; yet, because he subsists wholly in one and the same essence, he is one and the same as the Father inasmuch as he is God.

units.la: Qua ratione vero in speciebus creatis similiter nō eueniat, sic etiā T.C. accipiat. Species creatæ, vt homo, etsi secundum formam diuidi non possunt, tamen quoniam in diuiduis quantitatis (vt ita loquar) substernuntur[?]: idcirco secundum quantitatē reipsa diuiduntur. Itaque (quod dictu sit exempli causa) Petrus, Ioannes, Iacobus, quaŭis forma illa universali & specifica unum sint, tamen non unus homo, sed tres homines dicuntur: reipsa nimirum, non tantum suis proprietatibus incommunicabilibus distincti, sed etiam sua quantitate divisi. Sic Gabrielem, Raphaelē, & Michaelē nō modo tres distinctas unius Angelicæ naturæ hypostases, sed etiā tres spiritus esse dicimus: quia etsi non quantitate corporea, substantiæ tamē proprietate finiti, reipsa inter se secernuntur. At in divina essentia omnibꝰ modis simplicissima, & actu infinitissima, nec divisioni nec cōpositioni locus esse potest, sed soli distinctioni, quam nobis nec caro nec sanguis, sed Filius ipse patefecit.
units.tr: Let T.C. also consider why this does not happen in the same way with created species. Created species, such as man, cannot be divided according to form; yet, since they are underlain by divisible quantity, so to speak, they are for that very reason really divided according to quantity. So, to give an example, Peter, John and James are one by that universal and specific form, yet they are not called one man but three men. They are really distinct, not only by their incommunicable properties, but also divided by their quantity. Likewise we say that Gabriel, Raphael and Michael are not merely three distinct hypostases of one angelic nature but also three spirits. For although they are not separated from one another by bodily quantity, they are really distinguished from one another by the property of their finite substance. But in the divine essence, which is in every respect most simple and in act most infinite, there can be no place for division or composition, but only for distinction. This distinction was revealed to us not by flesh and blood, but by the Son himself.

units.la: Quæ autem est ipsius naturæ, eadem quoque est eorum ratio, quæ absolutè de ea prædicatur: ac proinde singulæ personæ sunt unus & idem æternus, immensus, infinitus, & omnipotens Deus.
units.tr: Whatever belongs to the nature itself belongs also to the account of what is predicated of it absolutely. Therefore each person is the one and the same eternal, immense, infinite and almighty God.

units.la: Itaque quum apud illum & re & nomine Gentile in illo adversus Athanasium libello plures æternos & omnipotentes legeremus, agnouimus in illo impletum esse quod fore prædixit Apostolus, nempe ut eiusmodi homines in reprobam, sive in omnis sensus ac iudicii expertem mentem traderentur.
units.tr: Therefore, when we read in that book of his against Athanasius, both in fact and in name, of several eternals and omnipotents, we recognised fulfilled in him what the Apostle foretold: that such men would be given over to a reprobate mind, or to a mind void of all sense and judgment.

units.la: De iis autem quæ per relationem prædicantur, & eam quidem eiusmodi, ὡς ὑφισταμένων ὑποστάσεις[?] describant, aliter sentiendum: quoniam, ut adversus Praxeam rectè declarat Tertullianus, hæc est relativorum natura, ut neque eadem, neque alterum absque altero esse possit.
units.tr: But those things that are predicated by relation, and which they describe as the subsistences of subsisting things [ὡς ὑφισταμένων ὑποστάσεις], must be understood differently. As Tertullian rightly declares against Praxeas, this is the nature of relatives: neither can be the same without the other, nor can one exist without the other.

units.la: Quaternitatem denique qua tandem fronte nobis imputant? Somniant enim (quod libro 4. satis tamē obscurè arguit Hilarius) nos per οὐσίαν[?] nescio quid seorsim Patre, Filio ac Spiritu sancto anterius significare quod sit in se De꤀ꝰ, ut sit hoc modo quartus quidam communis Deus, ad quem tres illæ personæ adiungantur, ut sic quatuor euadant: aut certè tres illæ personæ tanquam totius partes illud commune constituant.
units.tr: Finally, with what face do they charge us with a quaternity? They dream (which Hilary, though rather obscurely, argues in book 4) that by "substance" we signify something prior to and separate from Father, Son and Holy Spirit, namely what is God in himself. In this way there would be a fourth, common God, to whom those three persons are added, so that they become four. Or else those three persons, as parts of a whole, would constitute that common thing.

units.la: Illud autem commentum quàm sit insipidum, vel ipse sensus communis in rebus naturalibus docet. Neque enim per se universalia quæ vocant, existunt, sed hypostases in ipsis subsistunt. Nisi forte isti humanam naturam extra sua individua tanquam unum quidpiam numerent: ita ut ad individua accedens eorum numerum augeat.
units.tr: How foolish that invention is, even common sense in natural things teaches. Universals, as they call them, do not exist in themselves; hypostases subsist in them. Unless perhaps these men count human nature, apart from its individuals, as some single thing, so that by joining the individuals it increases their number.

units.la: Itaque sciat illi nos, quũ essentiam divinam nominamus, nō commune aliquem seu aggregatiuum Deum, sed id in quo toto & eodē singulæ illæ personæ subsistunt suis substātialibus proprietatibus, ut ante diximus, distinctæ, animo concipere: & ita quidē ut Trinitatis nomine non unū cōmunem Deū seorsim, sed tres in una essentia subsistētes personas intelligamus: quia sicut rectè scripsit Gregorius ille Naziãzenus, nec vnā essentiā extra illas tres personas, nec tres personas extra totam illam eandem & vnam essentiam animo concipere possumus. Hinc etiam factum, vt rectè parens ille noster beatæ memoriæ D. Ioannes Caluinus, verus huius veritatis assertor, precationem illam, Sancta Trinitas vnus Deus, scripserit barbariem sapere: quoniam nimirum nisi dextra interpretatione molliatur, quiddam extra tres personas subsistens, aut ipsas tres personas componēs innuere videtur, ad illud vniuersale (quod tamen per se non subsistit, sed in quo potius tria illa subsistunt) innuocationem[?] dirigens.
units.tr: Let them therefore know that when we name the divine essence we do not conceive some common or aggregate God. We conceive that in which, as a whole and the same, those single persons subsist, distinguished by their substantial properties, as we said before. We understand by the name of Trinity not one common God apart from them, but three persons subsisting in one essence. For, as that Gregory of Nazianzus rightly wrote, we can conceive neither one essence apart from those three persons, nor three persons apart from the whole of that same and one essence. Hence it also came about that our father of blessed memory, Master John Calvin, the true asserter of this truth, rightly wrote that the prayer "Holy Trinity, one God" smacks of barbarism. Unless it is softened by a proper interpretation, it seems to hint at something subsisting apart from the three persons, or to compose the three persons, and to direct the invocation to that universal, which does not subsist in itself but rather is that in which the three subsist.

units.la: Quanquam aliud sensisse non dubitamus, qui sic primi sunt loquuti. Hoc autem qui sic arripuerũt, vt T.C.scribit, magnam optimo viro iniuriam faciũt, & suam impudentiam aperte produnt.
units.tr: Yet we do not doubt that those who first spoke this way meant otherwise. But those who have seized on it in the way T.C. writes do great wrong to an excellent man, and openly betray their own impudence.

units.la: Sed iam nobis videntur illi postulare, vt non rationibus, quas humanas vocant, sed ex verbo Dei pugnemus. Quasi vero tres personas, vnica numero manente ipsarum essentia, constituere, philosophicum sit commentum.
units.tr: But now they seem to demand that we fight not with what they call human reasons but from the Word of God. As if constituting three persons, while the essence itself remains numerically one, were a philosophical invention!

units.la: Cæterum dum plenum illud à T.C. responsum expectamus, vt singula verbi Dei testimonia accuratius explicemus, semel istis opponimus quæcũque pro vno Deo aduersus deorum multitudinem in Scripturis dicuntur.
units.tr: Meanwhile, while we await T.C.'s full reply, so that we may explain each testimony of God's Word more carefully, we once and for all set against them whatever the Scriptures say for one God against a multitude of gods.

units.la: Et quoniam Filium & Spiritum sanctum non secus quàm Patrem adoramus, qui tamen vnum Deum iubemur adorare: idcirco Patrem, à quo tamen, vt principio, manat personarum distinctio, Filium & Spiritum sanctum singillatim vnicum illum esse Deum credimus ac profitemur, qui solus est adorandus.
units.tr: Since we adore the Son and the Holy Spirit no less than the Father, although we are commanded to adore one God, we therefore believe and profess that the Father, from whom the distinction of persons flows as from a beginning, and the Son and the Holy Spirit each singly, is that one God who alone is to be adored.

units.la: Solum Iehouam fuisse Israelis ducem testatur in cantico suo Moses: hunc autem aperte nominat Christum Paulus. Itaque non duos, sed vnum numero Iehouam esse fateantur necesse est, qui solus dux fuisse dicatur: quanuis alia sit Patris, alia magni ipsius Angeli persona.
units.tr: Moses testifies in his canticle that Jehovah alone was the leader of Israel, and Paul clearly names this leader as Christ. Therefore they must confess that it is not two but one numerical Jehovah who is said to have been the sole leader, although the person of the Father is other than that of the great Angel himself.

units.la: Sed de his aliâs plura, vbi quod à T.C. petimus præstiterint. Nunc ad T.C. redeamus. Precamur Illustris. Princeps, vt istos hùc adigas, vt quam blasphemiam de pluribus numero diis iampridem in animo habent, aperte tandem eloquantur.
units.tr: But more on these matters elsewhere, when they have done what we ask of T.C. Now let us return to T.C. We beg you, most illustrious Prince, to drive them to this: that they openly declare at last the blasphemy about many gods, which they have long had in mind.

units.la: Oportet, inquam, eos vel vnum eundémque Deum nobiscum fateri, vel plures ex vno deducere: ac proinde vni vero Deo, & omnibus eius sanctis execrabiles fieri.
units.tr: They must, I say, either confess with us one and the same God, or deduce several gods from one; and by doing so they become accursed to the one true God and to all his saints.

units.la: Age igitur, probent aperte suum dogma, quod ex Philopono, Seuero, Damiano, & cæteris infelicis memoriæ monstris hauserunt, idque si possunt vel rationibus, vel ex Scripturis, vel Patrum veterisque Ecclesiæ consensu confirment. Nos vicissim eandem conditionem accipimus: & nisi tam manifeste ipsorum blasphemiam patefecerimus quàm clarus est meridies, tum demum, Illustriss. Princeps, pro pseudoprophetis haberi ac traduci minimè recusamus.
units.tr: Come then, let them plainly prove their dogma, which they drew from Philoponus, Severus, Damian and the other monsters of unhappy memory. Let them confirm it, if they can, either by reasons, or from the Scriptures, or by the consensus of the Fathers and the ancient Church. We in turn accept the same condition. Unless we expose their blasphemy as clearly as midday is bright, then at last, most illustrious Prince, we do not refuse to be held and denounced as false prophets.

units.la: Hilarium unum prae caeteris laudant, nempe quoniam nihil eo durius nec obscurius esse potest: quod tamen nulla ipsius iniuria dictum velimus.
units.tr: They praise Hilary above all the others, namely because nothing can be harsher or more obscure than he is; yet I would not want this said to his injury.

units.la: Augustinum autem sine controversia optimum ac doctissimum scriptorem, atque adeo Hilarij σύγχρονον[?], cur tandem non admittunt? nempe quoniam illis est sophista: adeo ut Augustinianum quendam deum per ludibrium iactent. Atqui vel unica ista vox, Illustriss. Princeps, sic mentes piorum omnium vulnerauit (ac merito quidem) ut minimè miremur pios omnes qui nunc istic su-persunt, ab istis non minus, quàm ab ipso diabolo refugere. Quis enim sano homini persuaserit aliter docuisse Augustinum de Trinitate, quàm Aphricanas Ecclesias? & istas rursus aliter, quàm catholicus consensus ferret sensisse?
units.tr: Augustine, beyond dispute an excellent and most learned writer, and indeed Hilary's contemporary [σύγχρονον?], why on earth do they not accept him? Because to them he is a sophist, so much so that they mock him as some "Augustinian god." And yet that one word, Most Illustrious Prince, has wounded the minds of all the godly, and rightly so, so that we are not at all surprised that all the pious who still survive there flee from these men no less than from the devil himself. For who could persuade a sound man that Augustine taught about the Trinity otherwise than the African Churches did? And who could believe that those Churches in turn thought otherwise than the catholic consensus holds?

units.la: Sunt quidem, fateor, sui in Patribus naevi (quis enim hoc neger[?]?) sed tales ut fundamentum divinitatis salvum retineant: quo sublato, quàm fuisse illorum fidem, & quàm Ecclesiam arbitrabimur?
units.tr: I admit that there are indeed blemishes in the Fathers (for who would deny it?), but of such a kind that they leave the foundation of the divinity intact. If that is removed, what would we think of their faith, or of their Church?

units.la: Itaque Illustriss. Princeps, dissimulare apud C. T. nec possumus nec debemus, inexcusabiles esse quicunque istiusmodi hominibus aditum istuc patefecerunt: quum praesertim & quis homo sit Blandrata, & quae infamis ac periu-ri illius Gentilis impuritas publicis etiam scriptis mature ac vere simul simus testati.
units.tr: Therefore, Most Illustrious Prince, we can and must not conceal from Your Highness that all who have opened the door there to men of this kind are inexcusable, especially since we have both promptly and truthfully borne witness, in public writings also, to what sort of man Blandrata is and to the infamous and perjured impurity of that Gentile.

units.la: Deinde etsi grauis & ardua imprimis est ista quaestio, tamen est ex earum genere, de quibus post innumera illa contra haereticos certamina, nō magis fas sit quaerere, quàm an sit aliquod numen, & aeterna vita ambigere.
units.tr: Next, although this question is indeed grave and especially difficult, it is nevertheless of the kind which, after those countless struggles against heretics, may no more rightly be asked than whether there is some deity, or whether there is eternal life.

units.la: Quòd igitur nunc adeò miserè non modò impeditur praeclarum illud Domini opus, sed etiam universum Poloniae regnum tristissimis dissidiis laceratur, do-lemus certè ex animo, & assiduis cum lachrymis deploramus. Interea tamen iustum Dei iudicium, sic quorundam quos minimè oportuit (quod sine convitio dictum sit) curiositatem ac vanitatem iusta excaecatione vindicantis, agnoscere & adorare cogimur.
units.tr: That this excellent work of the Lord is now so wretchedly hindered, and that the whole kingdom of Poland is torn apart by the most grievous dissensions, we grieve from our hearts and lament with constant tears. Meanwhile, however, we are compelled to acknowledge and adore God's just judgment, which punishes the curiosity and vanity of some who ought least of all to have them (let this be said without reproach) with a just blindness.

units.la: Ipsius autem Regiae maiestatis pium ac prudens consilium de blasphemis istis ex ditione sua semel quaqua ratione tollendis non aliter, quàm sancta illa Ezechiae, Iosiae, Azae, & piorum aliquot Regum Iudah edicta laudamus ac praedicamus: modò ne hoc praetextu vera religio astutia quorundam damnetur, & qui ab istis fascinati in errorem abducti sunt, ab ipsis blasphemiarum authoribus ac defensoribus, sicuti par est, discernantur.
units.tr: As for the pious and prudent counsel of His Royal Majesty to remove these blasphemies from his dominions, by any means once and for all, we praise and proclaim it no differently than the holy edicts of Hezekiah, Josiah, Asa and some other pious kings of Judah. Only let not true religion be condemned under this pretext by the cunning of certain men, and let those who have been bewitched by them and led into error be distinguished, as is fitting, from the very authors and defenders of the blasphemies.

units.la: Priuatos autem fratres, ac imprimis orthodoxos Ecclesiarum Pastores hortamur in Domino, vt seditiones ac tumultus ab indiscreto zelo proficiscentes pro viribus impediant: & memores non sibi, sed Magistratui gladium esse concessum. Spiritu oris Dei, fide, patientia, precibus aduersus istos animarum subuersores indefatigabili labore decertent.
units.tr: We exhort in the Lord the private brethren, and above all the orthodox ministers of the Churches, that they prevent by all their strength the seditions and tumults arising from indiscreet zeal, and remember that the sword has been granted not to them but to the magistrate. Let them contend against these destroyers of souls with the Spirit of the mouth of God, with faith, patience and prayers, and with tireless labour.

units.la: Quod enim nonnulli quædam D.Caluini verba ex posteriore ipsius ad fratres Polonos Epistola detorserunt, quasi ad mutuas cædes eos hortaretur, est intolerabilis impudentiæ calumnia.
units.tr: For the claim that some have twisted certain words of Master Calvin from his later Epistle to the Polish brethren, as though he urged them to mutual slaughter, is a calumny of intolerable impudence.

units.la: Denique fortissimam illam Polonicam Nobilitatem, ac T. imprimis C. Illustrissime Princeps, quem audimus pietate ac dignitate in Polonico regno excellere, per ipsum Patrem, Filium, ac Spiritum sanctum vnum Deum nostrum obtestamur, vt sibi ac patriæ ab istis vastatoribus multo etiam studiosius ac fortius, quàm ab vllis Tartaris ac Moscouitis caueat: quod si fiat, tunc optima & maxima quæque florentissimo Poloniæ regno ominamur: quoniam scriptum est fore, vt Deus honoret à quibus honoratur. Sin minus (quod Dominus pro sua bonitate auertat) prospicimus maximo cum animi nostri dolore futurum, vt quibus olim cladibus cœlestis ille Pater horrendas Arÿ[?] præsertim, Nestorÿ, Eutychetis, & aliorum eiusmodi, blasphemias vltus est, iisdem quoque non dissimiliter peccantes inuoluat.
units.tr: Finally, we beseech that most valiant Polish nobility, and above all Your Highness, whom we hear to excel in piety and dignity in the kingdom of Poland, by the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, our one God, to guard themselves and their country against these devastators far more diligently and bravely than against any Tatars or Muscovites. If this is done, we foresee the best and greatest things for the flourishing kingdom of Poland, since it is written that God will honour those who honour Him. But if not (which the Lord in His goodness turn away), we foresee, to our great grief of mind, that those who sin in much the same way will be caught up in the same disasters with which that heavenly Father once punished the horrible blasphemies of Arius especially, and of Nestorius, Eutyches and others of that kind.

units.la: His autem malis impediendis libenter non tantùm operam nostram: sed etiam vitam, Dei gratia freti impendemus.
units.tr: To prevent these evils we will gladly spend not only our labour but also our lives, relying on the grace of God.

units.la: Quod superest, Illustrissime Princeps, Dominum ac Deum nostrum precamur, vt afflictæ Ecclesiæ suæ misertus, Satanæ furores compescat, omnes Ecclesias, ac Polonicas imprimis, in vero sanæ religionis consensu stabiliat ac confirmet, tuámque C. magis ac magis omnibus donis ad tanti regni pacem ac tranquillitatem necessariis pergat exornare. Geneuæ 14. Calend. Aprilis,
units.tr: For the rest, Most Illustrious Prince, we beseech our Lord and God that, having pity on His afflicted Church, He restrain the rage of Satan, establish and confirm all the Churches, and above all the Polish ones, in the true consensus of sound religion, and that He continue to adorn Your Highness more and more with every gift necessary for the peace and tranquillity of so great a kingdom. Geneva, 14 days before the Kalends of April,

units.la: M. D. LXV.
V. C. addictissimi Geneuensis Ecclesiæ Pastores, ac Professores.
units.tr: Your most devoted pastors and professors of the Church of Geneva.

units.la: 1. Vera invocationis Dei praecipua pars, est vera de Deo scientia: quia rite non possumus adorare quod nescimus.
units.tr: 1. The chief part of the true invocation of God is true knowledge of God, because we cannot properly worship what we do not know.

units.la: 2. Vera Dei cognitio ex ipsius verbo petenda est, quoniam plenè in eo necalibi usquam sese nobis patefecit ad salutem, adeò ut qui de Deo extra verbum ipsius sapit, nihil ad salutem sapiat.
units.tr: 2. True knowledge of God must be sought from His Word, since He has not revealed Himself to us fully for salvation in any other place, so that whoever thinks rightly of God apart from His Word thinks nothing rightly towards salvation.

units.la: 3. Quum Deus in scriptis Prophetarum & Apostolorum, non tantùm verissimè, sed etiam maximè proprie vocabulis & sententiis appositissimis seipsum mundo patefecerit: danda nobis est opera, ut non modò quod ad rem ipsam attinet intra Scripturae fines maneamus, sed etiam formulas Scripturae usitatas mordicus retineamus.
units.tr: 3. Since God has revealed Himself to the world in the writings of the Prophets and Apostles, not only most truly but also most properly, with words and expressions most fitting, we must take care not only to remain within the limits of Scripture as regards the matter itself, but also to hold fast to the formulas customary in Scripture.

units.la: 4. Fecit tamen haereticorum importunitas, ut vitandis eorum cavillis, aliqua interdum vocabula excogitanda fuerint: quod tamen temerè à sanctis Patribus non factū est, sed summa potius religione, ita ut de Scripturarum sententia nihil prorsus imminueretur, nec quicquam in verbo Dei novaretur.
units.tr: 4. Yet the importunity of heretics has meant that, in order to avoid their cavils, some words have sometimes had to be devised; but this was not done rashly by the holy Fathers. It was done rather with the greatest reverence, so that nothing at all was taken away from the sense of Scripture and nothing new was introduced into the Word of God.

units.la: 5. Haec causa fuit, cur olim adversus Sabellium Afrum, qui personas cum essentia confundebat, & Samosatenum Anthiochenum, qui Filii divinam naturam tollebat, usurpata sint Graeca nomina οὐσίας[?] καὶ ὑποστάσεως[?]: quorum tamen posteriore usus etiam est author epistolae ad Hebraeos, cap.1.à quorum vocabulorum explicatione fere pendet tota de his rebus controversia.
units.tr: 5. This was the reason why, long ago, the Greek terms ousia and hypostasis [οὐσίας καὶ ὑποστάσεως] were employed against Sabellius of Africa, who confused the persons with the essence, and against Paul of Samosata of Antioch, who denied the divine nature of the Son. Of these words the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 1, also made use; and on the explanation of these words almost the whole controversy about these matters depends.

units.la: 6. Sciendum igitur Patres de divinis mysteriis loquentes, haec vocabula à rebus naturalibus esse mutuatos, non quòd res tam diversis putarent iisdem vocabulis proprie exponi posse: sed ut imparium rerum aliqua collatione, res divinas quodammodo nostris oculis subiicerent, & eos suis armis iugularent, qui Theologiam in philosophicas argutias transformabant.
units.tr: 6. We must therefore understand that the Fathers, when speaking of the divine mysteries, borrowed these terms from natural things, not because they thought that such different things could properly be explained by the same words, but so that, by some comparison of unequal things, they might set the divine things somehow before our eyes, and slay with their own weapons those who turned theology into philosophical quibbles.

units.la: 7. Dicemus ergo, quid sit οὐσία, & quid ὑπόστασις in rebus naturalibus, quantum quidem feret praesens argumentum, & postea quo respectu haec eadem vocabula ad divina mysteria transferantur.
units.tr: 7. We shall say, then, what ousia and hypostasis are in natural things, as far as the present argument allows, and afterwards in what respect these same words are transferred to the divine mysteries.

units.la: 8. Quaedam nomina sunt universalis & indeterminatae cuiusdam significationis, quae pari ratione multis numero differentibus tribuuntur, in quibus commune quiddam contemplamur, quod inest quidem pluribus illis rebus de quibus pari ratione dicitur, sed tamen extra illas non subsistit, sicut etiam illae non nisi in illo communi subsistant: ut quum hominem dico, nihil concipio proprie subsistens per se, sed communem quandam naturam absque peculiari vlla de-terminatione mente cõplector, in qua pari ratione Petrus, Paulus, Timotheus, & similia reliqua singularia subsistunt. Homo igitur est vocabulum significans οὐσίαν, quæ hominis nomine declaratur.
units.tr: 8. Some names are universal and of an indeterminate meaning, which are attributed in the same way to many things differing in number, in which we contemplate something common that indeed is present in those many things of which it is said in the same way, but does not subsist outside them, just as those things too subsist only in that common thing. When I say "man," I conceive nothing properly subsisting by itself, but in my mind I grasp a certain common nature without any particular determination, in which Peter, Paul, Timothy and the other similar individuals subsist in the same way. Man, therefore, is a word signifying the ousia that is declared by the name man.

units.la: Quoniam autem cogitatio ab illa vniuersalitate, postea ad singularia & propria quaedam delabitur, per quæ illæ res secernuntur, in quibus communis illa notio antea concipiebatur, quaeque istis proprietatibus circunscriptæ subsistunt: idcirco inuenta sunt etiam nomina istis significandis accommodata, vt, Petrus, Paulus, Timotheus: quæ dicuntur nomina τῶν ὑποστάσεων, siue, τῶν ὑφισταμένων, id est, rerum suis proprietatibus definitarum, & in illa sua communi οὐσία subsistentium.
units.tr: Since, however, thought descends from that universality afterwards to singular and particular things, through which those things are distinguished, in which that common notion was previously conceived, and which subsist circumscribed by these proprieties, therefore names have also been found suited to signifying these, such as Peter, Paul, Timothy; these are called names of the hypostases [τῶν ὑποστάσεων], or of the things that subsist [τῶν ὑφισταμένων], that is, of things defined by their own properties and subsisting in that their common ousia.

units.la: Hoc nomen Deus, declarat essentiam infinitam, æternam, sua ipsius vi ni-tentem, omnipotentem, creatricem & conseruatricem rerum omnium conditarum, atque adeo in qua omnis perfectio residet: & quū Deum nomino, essentiam illam intelligo indeterminatē, quæ communi ratione dicitur de suis hypostasibus in ea subsistentibus.
units.tr: The name God declares an infinite and eternal essence, resting on its own power, almighty, the creator and preserver of all things made, and so the essence in which all perfection resides. When I name God, I understand that essence indefinitely, which is predicated in a common way of its hypostases subsisting in it.

units.la: Hæ res istis nominibus significatæ, Pater, Filius, Spiritus sanctus, sunt ὑπο-στάσεις, id est, proprietatibus distinctæ, & in illa communi æternaque essentia ab æterno subsistentes, quia proprietatibus suis distinguuntur. Pater enim est ingenitus, Filium gignens: Filius ex Patre genitus: Spiritus sanctus nec gignens nec genitus, sed à Patre & Filio procedens.
units.tr: These things signified by these names, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, are hypostases [ὑποστάσεις], that is, distinguished by their properties, and subsisting from eternity in that common and eternal essence, because they are distinguished by their own properties. For the Father is unbegotten, begetting the Son; the Son is begotten of the Father; the Holy Spirit neither begets nor is begotten, but proceeds from the Father and the Son.

units.la: De procedendi & gignendi subtiliore differentia non laboro: & certè qui de hac re litigarunt, inscitè torserunt Scripturæ locos, qui nihil ad eam rem faciunt. Nam quod alicubi dicitur Spiritus sanctus procedere à Patre & Filio, ad manifestationem & dona refertur. Sufficiat communem esse Spiritum Patris & Filij, ac proinde ad vtrumque referri.
units.tr: I do not labour over the subtler difference between proceeding and begetting. Certainly those who have quarrelled over this matter have twisted the passages of Scripture, which have nothing to do with the question, in an unlearned way. For where it is said somewhere that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, this is referred to manifestation and gifts. It is enough that the Spirit is common to the Father and the Son, and therefore is referred to both.

units.la: Quoniam res creatæ finitam habet essentiam, idcirco necessariò finitæ sunt, ac proinde non tantum suis proprietatibus distinctæ, sed etiam re ipsa separatæ sunt earum ὑποστάσεις. Itaque Petrus, Paulus, Timotheus, quanuis communi ratione dicantur homines: tamen re ipsa nõ sunt vnus homo, sed tres homines, ipsius etiam humanitatis respectu. Quoniam enim Patres non possunt totam suam essentiam cum filiis communicare, sed aliquid duntaxat, quod seminis rationem habet, ex ipsis excernitur, vnde manat filiorum essentia: ideo filij non habent eandem illam singularem humanitatem quæ est in Patribus, sed similem duntaxat, quæ ex illa effluxit, ideóque singularis humanitas, vt pote finita, in diuersis subiectis esse non potest. Idcirco, inquam, omnibus modis tres sunt, Petrus, Paulus, Timotheus, non vnus.
units.tr: Since created things have a finite essence, they are necessarily finite, and therefore their hypostases are not only distinguished by their properties but are also really separated from one another. Thus Peter, Paul, and Timothy, although they are called men in a common sense, are nevertheless in fact not one man but three men, even with respect to humanity itself. For since fathers cannot communicate their whole essence to their children, but only something that has the nature of seed is secreted from them, from which the essence of the children flows, the children do not have that same singular humanity which is in the fathers, but only a similar humanity which has flowed from it. Therefore singular humanity, being finite, cannot exist in different subjects. For this reason, I say, in every way Peter, Paul, and Timothy are three, not one.

units.la: Sed in diuinis longè aliud est. Quoniâ enim diuina essentia infinita est, & simplicissima & æterna, idcirco tres ὑποστάσεις in ea subsistentes, etsi verè sunt tres numero, quoniam singulæ suis incommunicabilibus proprietatibus distinguuntur, tamen non sunt nec dicuntur tres dij, sicut tres homines: quoniam nec Filius genitus est à Patre, nec Spiritus sanctus procedit à Patre & Filio, aliqua partis resectione, id est, κατὰ μερισμὸν, vt quum res quæpiam in tria frusta diuiditur: neque fluxu quodam, hoc est, ἀπορροίᾳ, qualis est liberorum procreatio ex patrerno semine: neque productione, id est, προβολῇ, vt est propago in vitibus: sed ineffabili totius essentiæ communicatione ab æterno, in qua nullum dari punctum potest nec principij, nec medij, nec finis.
units.tr: But in the divine things it is quite otherwise. Since the divine essence is infinite, most simple, and eternal, the three hypostases subsisting in it, although they are truly three in number, since each is distinguished by its incommunicable properties, nevertheless are not and are not called three gods, as three men are. For the Son is not begotten of the Father, nor does the Holy Spirit proceed from the Father and the Son, by any cutting off of a part, that is, by division [κατὰ μερισμόν], as when some thing is divided into three pieces; nor by any flowing out, that is, by emanation [ἀπορροίᾳ], such as the procreation of children from the paternal seed; nor by production, that is, by projection [προβολῇ], as a shoot is on vines; but by an ineffable communication of the whole essence from eternity, in which no point can be given, neither of beginning, nor of middle, nor of end.

units.la: Vna igitur & prorsus eadem est essentia gignentis, geniti, & procedentis, quanuis nec Pater qui gignit, sit Filius genitus, aut Spiritus procedens: nec Filius sit Pater gignens, aut Spiritus procedens: nec Spiritus Pater gignens, aut Filius genitus. Nec Deus ipse est trinomius, quum re ipsa, non autem nomine tenus subsistant tres personæ in vna essentia: nec triformis, quoniam proprietates personarum non sunt imaginaria accidentia, quæ adesse vel abesse possint, aut re ipsa, aut cogitatione, sed verè insunt personis, & illas distinguunt: nec etiam aggregatiuus, idque duabus de causis, quoniam hæ tres personæ ita sunt distinctæ, vt non sint separatæ: deinde quia in qualibet persona non est aliqua Dei essentiæ pars, sed tota essentia, eaque insecabilis, quia infinita.
units.tr: Therefore the essence of the one who begets, of the begotten, and of the one who proceeds is one and altogether the same, although the Father who begets is not the Son who is begotten, or the Spirit who proceeds; nor is the Son the Father who begets, or the Spirit who proceeds; nor is the Spirit the Father who begets, or the Son who is begotten. Nor is God himself three-named, since the three persons subsist in one essence in reality and not merely in name; nor is he three-formed, since the properties of the persons are not imaginary accidents, which may be present or absent either in reality or in thought, but truly inhere in the persons and distinguish them; nor is he an aggregate, and this for two reasons: first, because these three persons are so distinct that they are not separated; second, because in each person there is not some part of the divine essence, but the whole essence, and that indivisible, because it is infinite.

units.la: Quod de vnitate & identitate essentiæ dixi, necessariò etiam intelligitur de communibus eius attributis, vt sicut vnus Deus est, sic etiam vnus sit infinitus, æternus, omnipotens, &c.
units.tr: What I have said about the unity and identity of the essence is necessarily understood also of its common attributes, so that just as God is one, so also his attributes are one: infinite, eternal, almighty, and so on.

units.la: Ὁμοούσια, siue ὁμοιούσια, in rebus naturalibus dicitur indiuidua, quæ in eadem essentia seu specie conueniunt, vt homo cum homine, brutum cum bruto, stirps cum stirpe. Estque hoc vocabulum diuinis rebus accommodatum ad confutandos Arianos, qui Filium dicebant à Patre, non ex Patris substantia genitum, sed ex nihilo factum, atque adeò participatione virtutis, nō natura Deum. Aduersus istos igitur constitutum est Filium esse ὁμοούσιον, siue ὁμοιούσιον Patri: quo tamen nomine similem esse essentiam Patris essentiæ Filij, non simpliciter voluerunt dicere, sicut in rebus naturalibus (ita enim duæ numero essentiæ constituerentur, ac proinde duo numero dij, quod nefas est) sed potius duo exprimere voluerunt. Vnum, essentia nō differre Filii à Patre, quoniam non ex nihilo, sed ex ipso Patre est genitus, idque ab æterno: quod alio nomine συνουσίαν[?] signi-ficarunt. ficarūt. Alterum, ita esse ex Patre, quatenus est Filius, vt sit vnū cum Patre quatenus est Deus, id est, essentia Filij non esse secundaria quanda essentia, quae ab altera primaria ortū sui habuerit, quod vocarunt haeretici ex traduce, & hodie quidam essentiationis nomine efferunt: sed eam ipsam essentiam totam, qua Pater Deus est, esse, Filium gignendo, à Patre cum illo communicatam, vt Pater & Filius quatenus in vna eademque essentia subsistunt, siue vnius eiusdem numero essentiae respectu, sint vnus idemque Deus, quum tamen Pater non sit Filius.
units.tr: Homoousia, or homoiousia [ὁμοούσια, ὁμοιούσια], is said in natural things of individuals which agree in the same essence or species, as man with man, beast with beast, stock with stock. This word has been adapted to divine things in order to refute the Arians, who said that the Son was begotten from the Father, not from the substance of the Father, but made out of nothing, and so God by participation of power, not by nature. Against them it was therefore established that the Son is homoousios, or homoiousios, with the Father; by this word, however, they did not wish to say simply that the essence of the Son is like the essence of the Father, as in natural things (for in that way two essences in number would be posited, and therefore two gods in number, which is impious), but rather they wished to express two things. First, that the essence of the Son does not differ from that of the Father, since he was begotten not out of nothing but from the Father himself, and this from eternity; this they signified by another word, the same essence [συνουσίαν]. Second, that the Son is from the Father in such a way, as he is Son, that he is one with the Father as he is God; that is, the essence of the Son is not some secondary essence which has derived its origin from another primary one (which the heretics called "from transmission," and today some express by the word "essentiation"), but that very whole essence by which the Father is God is communicated to the Son by the Father in begetting him, so that the Father and the Son, insofar as they subsist in one and the same essence, or with respect to the one essence identical in number, are one and the same God, although the Father is not the Son.

units.la: Merito igitur damnati sunt qui Filium vocabant ὁμοιούσιον, id est similis essentiae, vt qui duas numero essentias instituerent: itemque Ariani reliqui qui ἑτερούσιον, id est alterius essentiae Filium esse dicebant: & vt vitaretur eorum fraus qui ex ὁμοουσίου vnica literula interiecta ὁμοιούσιον faciebant, coeperunt patres ὁμοούσιον per Crasin dicere, eadem manente sententia.
units.tr: Those who called the Son homoiousios, that is, of like essence, were rightly condemned, since they would posit two essences in number. Likewise the rest of the Arians who said that the Son is of another essence, heterousios, were condemned.
