And so that the trickery of those who made homoiousios out of homoousios by inserting a single letter might be avoided, the Fathers began to say homoousios by contraction [per crasin], the meaning remaining the same.

units.la: Itaque quum Filium dicimus esse vnius essentiae cum Patre, personas non autem essentiam distinguimus: estque hoc dicendi genus de communibus essentiae attributis potius quam de ipsa essentia accipiendum: & maximè proprie loquimur, quum Patrem, Filium & Spiritum sanctum vnum esse essentia dicimus, siue vnam esse Patris, Filii, & Spiritus sancti essentiam.
units.tr: Therefore when we say that the Son is of one essence with the Father, we distinguish the persons but not the essence; and this way of speaking is to be understood of the common attributes of the essence rather than of the essence itself. And we speak most properly when we say that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one in essence, or that the essence of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one.

units.la: Veteres his formulis vsi sunt, non vt pluralitatem essentiarum inuehérent, sed vt in relatione personarum, identitatem essentiae ostenderent aduersus eos, qui Christum factum dicebant ex nihilo, & quidem in tempore. Huc enim spectabant istae eorum Arianorum sententiae ἦν ὅτε οὐκ ἦν, & ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων ἐποίησεν [?], id est, ex non existentibus conditus est. Patres igitur addiderunt Symbolo, Deum verum de Deo vero, vt ostenderent Deum a quo est Deus, id est Patrem: & Deum qui est a Deo, id est Filium, ratione essentiae vnum esse Deum.
units.tr: The ancients used these formulas not to introduce a plurality of essences, but to show, in relation to the persons, the identity of the essence, against those who said that Christ was made out of nothing, and indeed in time. For to this aim pointed those Arian opinions of theirs, "there was when he was not," and "he made him out of non-existent things," that is, he was created out of things that did not exist. The Fathers therefore added to the creed "true God from true God," to show that God from whom is God, that is the Father, and God who is from God, that is the Son, are by reason of their essence one God.

units.la: Quum aliqua sit homonymia inter εἶναι & ὑφίστασθαι, id est, esse & subsi-stere: itemque inter οὐσίαν & ὑπόστασιν, id est, essentiam & substantiam, adeò vt confusis istis nominibus, à quorum distinctione pendet huius controuersiae explicatio, magnos errores consequi necesse sit, quod veterum multorum, & quidem imprimis Hilarij & Hieronymi scripta declarat: idcirco Latini Per-sona nomen pro hypostasi vsurparunt, quod & Græcis similiter placuit.
units.tr: Since there is some homonymy between einai and hyphistasthai, that is, to be and to subsist, and likewise between ousia and hypostasis, that is, essence and substance, so that, if these names are confused, on whose distinction the explanation of this controversy depends, great errors must necessarily follow; this is shown by the writings of many of the ancients, and especially of Hilary and Jerome. Therefore the Latins have used the name persona for hypostasis, which also pleased the Greeks in a similar way.

units.la: MAgna est virtus, de Deo, rebusque Diuinis verecunde loqui. Quum enim Deus sit natura incomprehensibilis, potentia infinitus, nomine inenarrabilis: nullum ingenium capere hanc vim infinitam, nulla acies ad tantam lucem penetrare, lingua nulla eloqui potest: ideoque è philosophis qui fuere saniores, parce eam disputationem persecuti sunt. Laudatur in hac re Platonis modestia, qui mundi conditorem Deum non erubescit dicere: φιλάνθρωπον item, & rerum omnium prouidum curatorem: quia sit σοφώτατος, quia operis à se sapienter facti, non sit negligens aut contemptor. Interea fatetur oculos mortalium non posse diuina satis perspicere.
units.tr: It is a great virtue to speak of God and divine things with reverence. Since God is incomprehensible in nature, infinite in power and unspeakable in name, no mind can grasp this infinite power, no sight can penetrate so great a light, and no tongue can express it. For this reason the more sober of the philosophers treated the subject sparingly. Plato's modesty is praised in this matter, for he does not hesitate to call God the maker of the world, and likewise loving toward mankind and the provident guardian of all things, because he is most wise and does not neglect or despise the work he has wisely made. Yet he admits that the eyes of mortals cannot see the divine clearly enough.

units.la: Aristoteli satis est, ἕν τι constituere τὸ πρῶτον κινοῦν[?] per æthera. Quid de Deo dicat, non habet. Aliis placuit hanc quæstionem in totum intermittere: qua de re notum est Simonidis iudicium, qui Hieroni de Deo scisciitanti, dies aliquoties deliberando auxit: tandem vero respondit; Quanto diutius cogito, tanto res mihi videtur obscurior. Ita sane hæc Dei maiestas ingenia præstantissima extra ecclesiam exercuit, ac defatigauit, vt tandem homines coacti sint fateri numinis illius supremi maiestatem. Contra etiam in natura humana didicere eam esse caliginem, & virium imbecillitate, vt ad eam puritatem sese non possit attollere, sine peculiari numinis dispensatione.
units.tr: For Aristotle it is enough to posit a certain first mover [ἕν τι τὸ πρῶτον κινοῦν] beyond the heavens. What God is, he does not say. Others have chosen to drop this question altogether. Of this there is the well-known judgement of Simonides, who, when Hiero asked him about God, asked for a delay several times; at last he replied: "The longer I think about it, the more obscure the matter seems to me." Thus indeed this majesty of God has exercised and worn out the most outstanding minds outside the Church, until people were at last compelled to acknowledge the majesty of that supreme divinity. On the other hand, they have also learned that there is in human nature such darkness and such weakness of powers that it cannot raise itself to that purity without a special dispensation of the divinity.

units.la: In Ecclesia autem hæc doctrina de Deo, semper purior & magis perspicua mansit. Interea tamen & ipsi pij bonam sapientiæ partem iudicarunt, agnoscere in hac re suam imbecillitatem: ideoque eo con-tenti, quod de se Deus illis patefecerat, altiora non sunt perscrutati. Hinc illa in invocatione vox, Deus Abraham, Deus Isaac, Deus Ia-cob, Deus patrum nostrorum, &c. Et Iacob quum de nomine angeli curiosius inquireret, repulsus radijs Diuinæ maiestatis, audiuit, Cur sic interrogas de nomine meo? Moses etiam de nomine Dei mittentis interrogas, non aliud accepit, quā SVM qui SVM. Ité, Dic, Qui EST, misit me ad vos. ideoque meminisse nos decet etiam in hac re, quod monet Apostolus, μὴ ὑπερφρονεῖν παρ' ὃ δεῖ φρονεῖν, ἀλλὰ φρονεῖν εἰς τὸ σωφρονεῖν. Est enim verissimum, intellectum nostrum in rebus divi-nis non minus, imò magis cæcutire, quàm noctua in luce meridiana. Porrò quum nihilominus docendi sint homines de Deo, eáque doctri-na propria sit ecclesiæ, vtile est retinere formulam loquendi ex Pro-phetieis & Euangelicis scriptis: quia hæc ecclesia habet, dictante Deo, vnde & θεόπνευστος dicitur γραφή ab Apostolo, & eam etiam pu-ram retinuit & simplicem, donec homines ambitiosi emersere, qui vi-gore ingenij non repressò, abusi scripturæ simplicitate, nouas cœpere affingere interpretationes. Hos vt intra metas retinerent pij, & sen-tentiam illorum pugnare docerent cum scriptura, necessum fuit aliis verbis res limitare: ideóque quum verba verbis, phrases aliis formu-lis essent explicandæ, ad scripturas se se suáque retulere. Nemo enim est qui de Deo melius, quàm is ipse loqui possit. Quare de ipso loquu-turi, prius ipsum de se loquentem consulere debemus. Porrò vt impium est scripturæ formas loquendi negare: sic malitiosum est, vsu receptas damnare, quas tamen nulla ratio conuincat quicquam alienum à scri-pturis tueri. Huius rei multa extat exempla in historijs ecclesiæ, & synodicis actionibus, quæ non est necessum huc afferre. Vnum nostra hæc ætas vidit in Valentino Getile: qui vt essentiæ diuinæ vnitatem tolleret in explicadis tribus personis, voces receptas damnauit prius, quales sunt οὐσία, ὑπόστασις personarum. Nam iis in usu durantibus, vidit non posse stabiliri tres essentia & gradu distinctos spiritus. De hac doctrina quid statuerit consensus Ecclesiae, & unde orta sit illa corruptela, hic libellus hic indicat. Caeterum ad vos eam historiam mitto, viri clarissimi, quod in hac causa examinanda praesides fueritis, & doctrinae verae corruptelam magno saepe dolore induci audieritis. Et quum visa esset profutura multis, non tam mea privata, quam publica vestra in publicum prodire debuit voluntate. Dominus Iesus Christus vos suo Spiritu regat, ut ad sanae doctrinae defensionem, & patriae utilitatem, in his honoribus quam diutissime & felicissime vivatis. Amen. M. D. LXVII. Cal. Iunij.
units.tr: In the Church, however, this doctrine of God has always remained purer and clearer. Yet even the godly themselves have judged it a good part of wisdom to acknowledge their own weakness in this matter, and therefore, content with what God had revealed of himself to them, they did not search out higher things. Hence that form of invocation: "God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob, God of our fathers," and so on. And when Jacob inquired too curiously about the name of the angel, he was repulsed by the rays of the divine majesty and heard: "Why do you ask about my name in this way?" Moses too, when he asked the name of the God who sent him, received no other answer than "I AM WHO I AM," and: "Say, 'He who is' has sent me to you." Therefore we ought to remember in this matter also what the Apostle warns: "not to think more highly than we ought to think, but to think so as to think soberly" [μὴ ὑπερφρονεῖν παρ' ὃ δεῖ φρονεῖν, ἀλλὰ φρονεῖν εἰς τὸ σωφρονεῖν]. For it is most true that our understanding in divine matters is no less, indeed rather more, blind than an owl in the noonday light. Moreover, since men nevertheless must be taught about God, and this doctrine is proper to the Church, it is useful to retain the form of speaking taken from the prophetic and evangelical writings, because this Church has them by the dictation of God, whence Scripture is called "God-breathed" [θεόπνευστος γραφή] by the Apostle; and the Church has kept them pure and simple, until ambitious men arose who, their intellectual vigour unchecked, abused the simplicity of Scripture and began to fasten on new interpretations. To keep these men within bounds, so that the godly might show that their opinion fights against Scripture, it was necessary to limit matters in other words; and so, since words had to be explained by words and phrases by other formulas, they referred themselves and their cause to the Scriptures. For no one can speak of God better than he himself can. Therefore, when we are going to speak of him, we ought first to consult him speaking of himself. But just as it is impious to deny the forms of speech of Scripture, so it is malicious to condemn expressions received in use, which no reason can prove to defend anything foreign to the Scriptures. Many examples of this exist in the histories of the Church and in the acts of synods, which it is not necessary to bring forward here. Our own age has seen one such case in Valentine Gentilis: in order to remove the unity of the divine essence in explaining the three persons, he first condemned the received words, such as ousia and hypostasis [οὐσία, ὑπόστασις] of the persons. For while these were in use, he saw that three spirits distinct in essence and rank could not be established. What the consensus of the Church has decided on this doctrine, and whence that corruption arose, this little book shows. Moreover, I send this account to you, most distinguished men, because you were presidents in examining this cause, and you have often heard with great grief that the corruption of true doctrine was being introduced. And since it seemed likely to be of use to many, it ought to come forth to the public not so much by my private will as by your public will. May the Lord Jesus Christ govern you by his Spirit, so that you may live as long and as happily as possible in these honours, for the defence of sound doctrine and the benefit of the fatherland. Amen. 1567, Kalends of June.

units.tr: Most devoted, B. Aretius.

units.la: 1 Qua occasione in noua dogmata sit prolapsus: ubi item, & quanto cum damno ea sparserit.
units.tr: 1 By what occasion he fell into new doctrines; where, likewise, and with how great harm he spread them.

units.la: 2 Quare Bernam sit perductus.
units.tr: 2 Why he was brought to Berne.

units.la: 3 De scriptis illius, & capitibus accusationis.
units.tr: 3 His writings, and the heads of the accusation.

units.la: 4 An tanquam actor debuerit audiri.
units.tr: 4 Whether, as the accuser, he ought to have been heard.

units.la: 5 Propositiones ex illius scriptis excerptæ, quas falsas iudicamus.
units.tr: 5 Propositions excerpted from his writings, which we judge to be false.

units.la: 6 Declaratio errorum in negotio Trinitatis.
units.tr: 6 Exposure of the errors in the matter of the Trinity.

units.la: 7 De vocibus illis, Trinitas, οὐσία, ὑπόστασις [?] quid significent.
units.tr: 7 What the words Trinity, ousia [οὐσία] and hypostasis [ὑπόστασις] signify.

units.la: 8 Quæ fuerit Arij sententia, & quid cum illa commune habeat Gentilis.
units.tr: 8 What the opinion of Arius was, and what Gentile has in common with it.

units.tr: 9 On the generation of the Son of God, and how gennēton [γέννητον] should be understood.

units.tr: 10 Whether it is the peculiar property of the Father to be called the one and only God.

units.tr: 11 The judgment of Scripture, and the agreement of opinion on this matter.

units.tr: 12 Gentile's criticism of the writings of the Fathers.

units.tr: 16 On the other Fathers, especially Augustine.

units.tr: 17 On the communication of idioms.

units.tr: 18 The manifest blasphemies of the same Gentile.

units.tr: 20 Impostures.

units.tr: Valentine Gentile, a Calabrian, a short history of his execution at Bern and an orthodox defence of the article on the holy Trinity against his blasphemies

units.la: Qua occasione in nova dogmata sit prolapsus, ubi item, & quanto cum damno ea sparserit. I.
units.tr: How he came to fall into new doctrines, where he afterwards spread them, and at what cost. I.

units.la: VALENTINUS Gentilis Campanus, post relictam patriam Cosentiam, peragrata Neapo-li, Sicilia, & Italia, tandem Genevam pervenit. Aderant tum in Italica Ecclesia homines permulti ex tota Italia, qui alii alias ob causas eò sese contulerant: in primis verò, qui pietatis nomine extorres, è patria illuc profugerat. Inter hos erat quidam καινῶν δογμάτων ἀρετή[?]. Georg. enim Blandrata, professione medicus, negotium Trinitatis recenter coeperat convellere: agebatur tamen id adhuc privatim, & familiari scriptione ultro, citróque. Lis erat de vocibus receptis, ut est οὐσία[?], ὑπόστασις[?], Trinitas, ὁμοούσιον &c. Voluebant interea idem saxum M. Gribaldus Iurisconsultus celebris, & Ioann. Paulus Alciatus quidam Mediola-nensis.Hanc concertatione quum intelligeret novus hospes Gentilis, coepit acumen ingenii in eodem argumento exercere. Ac in eo, brevi cum aliis ita profecit, ut non dubitarent affirmare, Ecclesias Evangelicas adhuc graviter errare una cum Papistis, quibus in articulo Trinitatis adhuc parerent.
units.tr: Valentine Gentile of Campania, having left his native Cosenza and travelled through Naples, Sicily and Italy, at last came to Geneva. At that time many people were present in the Italian church there, from all over Italy, who had gone thither for various reasons; above all, those who had fled their homeland as exiles for the sake of piety. Among them was a certain man of novel doctrines [καινῶν δογμάτων ἀρετή]. For Giorgio Biandrata, a physician by profession, had recently begun to unsettle the doctrine of the Trinity; but this was still being done privately, through familiar letters passing back and forth. The dispute concerned the accepted terms, such as οὐσία, ὑπόστασις, Trinity, ὁμοούσιον, and so on. Meanwhile the famous jurist M. Gribaldi and a certain Giovanni Paolo Alciati of Milan were turning over the same stone. When the newcomer Gentile learned of this controversy, he began to exercise the keenness of his wit on the same subject. In this he soon made such progress with the others that they did not hesitate to assert that the Evangelical churches were still gravely in error, together with the Papists, since they still agreed with them on the article of the Trinity.

units.la: Nam illas cum Papatu tueri non Trinitatē, sed Quaternitatem potius. Veram Trinitatē habere tres Æternos, & distinctos Spiritus, non tam personali quàm essentiali numero differentes. Hæc tum omnium communis & uniformis erat sententia, à qua mox alii aliis diverticulis abeuntes, in opiniones pugnantes & monstrosas sunt prolapsi. Requisiti etiam Genevæ ob eam sententiam, alii aliis modis elapsi sunt, quæ non attinet hic commemorare: siquidem de Gentili solùm perstringemus brevem historiam. Is quum eandem sententiam cum Blandrata, Gribaldo, & Alciato tuendam suscepisset: paulò post tamen palinodiam cecinit, ac publicè non sine raro pœnitentiæ exemplo noua illa dogmata abiurauit. Acta sunt illa anno 1558. in cuius rei fidem historia publicè extat.
units.tr: For they maintained, together with the Papacy, not a Trinity but rather a Quaternity. The true Trinity, they said, consists of three eternal and distinct spirits, differing not so much in personal as in essential number. This was then the common and uniform opinion of all; from it others soon departed by various byways and fell into conflicting and monstrous opinions. Some, summoned to Geneva on account of this view, escaped in various ways, which it is not relevant to recall here; for we shall touch only briefly on the history of Gentile. He, having undertaken to defend the same view together with Biandrata, Gribaldi and Alciati, shortly afterwards sang a palinode, and publicly, not without a rare example of repentance, abjured those new doctrines. This was done in the year 1558, and the record of it survives publicly as proof.

units.la: Cæterùm, quia metu mortis potiùs, quàm quòd ferió ita sentiret, doctrinam suam damnasset, & animus ad eam tuendam superesset: mox spreta iurisiurandi religione, periurio se maculans, Geneua est egressus.
units.tr: Yet because, through fear of death rather than because he really thought so, he had condemned his doctrine, and because his mind still remained set on defending it, he soon, scorning the sanctity of his oath and staining himself with perjury, left Geneva.

units.la: Erat in confinio pagus Fargiarum, ubi habitabat M.Gribaldus. ad hunc igitur se contulit. Aderant ibidem Alciatus & alius quidam pædagogus filiorum Gribaldi, inter quos negotium hoc, post aduentum Gentilis, crebris disputationibus est excussum. quibus confirmatio redditus, inde discedens, Lugdunum petiit. Lugdunì copia librorum adiutus per Baptistam quendam Lucensem, subsidia collegit ex patribus ad roborandum dogma suum. Et quia vidit Latinos & Græcos uno ore à nostris citari, ipse ad antiquissimos quosque conatus est refugere.
units.tr: On the border there was a village, Fargiae, where M. Gribaldi lived. To him, then, he went. Alciati and another man, a tutor of Gribaldi's sons, were also there; and after Gentile's arrival this business was thrashed out among them in frequent disputations. Having been strengthened in his views, he left there and made for Lyons. At Lyons, aided by a supply of books and through a certain Baptista of Lucca, he gathered support from the Fathers to strengthen his doctrine. And because he saw that the Latins and Greeks were cited with one voice by our men, he himself tried to take refuge with the most ancient of them all.

units.la: Collegit igitur mutila quædam testimonia ex Ignatij epistolis, ex Iustino Martyre, ex Hilario, Tertulliano, nec puduit eum ex Alcorano subsidia petere. Reliquos scriptores fermè omnes pleno ore cœpit damnare, Augustinum, Hieronymum, Basilium, Chrysostomum, Damascenum, & si qui alij Trinitatis negotium contra ipsius mentè apertiùs explicaret. In Iustino martyre, & Tertulliano cœpit etiam quosdam libros damnare, alios in dubium vocare.
units.tr: He therefore gathered some mutilated testimonies from the letters of Ignatius, from Justin Martyr, from Hilary and Tertullian; nor was he ashamed to seek support from the Koran. He began to condemn almost all the other writers with full voice: Augustine, Jerome, Basil, Chrysostom, Damascene, and any others who explained the matter of the Trinity more plainly against his own mind. Against Justin Martyr and Tertullian he began to condemn certain books too, and to call others into doubt.

units.la: Porrò, quia tanta res indigebat scriptione, animum ad scribendum appulit. Ac mox libellum composuit Antidotorum titulo, in quo conatur se contra Geneuates purgare, & diluere quæ in suo scripto Ministri Italicæ Ecclesiæ attulerant contra sententiam ipsius, qui libellus editus non est, sed scriptus apud eum, & à nobis recens repertus. Ita instructus nouis argumentis & rationibus, Gratianopolin petiit. docebat enim illic publicè M. Gribaldus amicus & familiaris illius. Præterea inciderat in morbum, ut quærendus esset idoneus etiam locus, & hospitium tutum curandæ valetudinis homini per se egenti.
units.tr: Moreover, because so great a matter required writing, he turned his mind to writing. Soon he composed a little book entitled Antidotes, in which he tries to clear himself before the Genevans and to refute what the ministers of the Italian church had brought against his opinion in their writing. This little book was never published, but was written by him, and has been recently found by us. Thus equipped with new arguments and reasons, he made for Grenoble, for his friend and close associate M. Gribaldi was teaching there publicly. Besides, he had fallen ill, so that a suitable place had to be sought, and a safe lodging for a man who was himself without means for the care of his health.

units.la: Dum curatur valetudo, simul cœpit innotescere dogma illius: ideóque ab ordinario Magistratu petitur confessio. eam ita potuit attemperare, vt à Papistis admitteretur, solùm Euangelicas ecclesias, & nominatim Caluinum perstringens, caput verò rei & controuersiæ non attingens.
units.tr: While his health was being cared for, his doctrine at the same time began to become known; therefore a confession was demanded of him by the ordinary magistrate. He was able to shape it so that it was accepted by the Papists, attacking only the Evangelical churches and by name Calvin, but not touching the heart of the matter and the controversy.

units.la: Cameracum inde vicinum oppidum adiit, sed ne hîc quidem tutus Fargias rediit. Interea res percrebescere coepit. Etenim vici-na Geneua plenum dabat huic negotio testimonium. Ipse etiam Lugduni, Cameraci, Gratianopoli, & in Delphinatu hinc inde peregrinando innotuerat.
units.tr: From there he went to the neighbouring town of Cambrai, but not even there did he return to Fargiae in safety. Meanwhile the matter began to grow in notoriety. For neighbouring Geneva gave full testimony to this affair. He himself had also become known here and there at Lyons, Cambrai, Grenoble and in Dauphiné through his wanderings.

units.la: Est Fargiarum pagus in praefectura Gaiensi, ditionis magnificorum dominorum Bernensium: ideóque praefectus loci illius admonitus de hoc homine, missis idoneis ministris, Gaium perduci curauit, ac carceribus mancipauit. Post dies aliquot dimissus est ea conditione, vt deinceps tranquillè & pacificè viueret. Quæ quum ad dogmata sua negaret pertinere, nihilo segnius pergit sua spargere.
units.tr: The village of Fargiae is in the prefecture of Gex, under the jurisdiction of the magnificent lords of Bern. Therefore the prefect of that place, having been warned about this man, sent suitable officers and had him brought to Gex and consigned to prison. After some days he was released on condition that from then on he would live quietly and peaceably. Though he denied that this touched his doctrines, he nonetheless went on spreading them no less eagerly.

units.la: Accessit hic noua fraus. Confessionem enim, quam praefectus ab eo petierat, vt eam examinandam Ministris exhiberet, ac Bernam transmitteret, typis tradidit excudendam, quasi à praefecto sic iussus.eidem adiicit protheses quasdam, & criminationes in Athanasium. nec eo fuit contentus, sed abusus etiam nomine & authoritate praefecti, libellum eidem dedicauit: quam iniuriam grauissimè tulit praefectus, vt si in manus illius incidisset, statim ad carceres fuerit retrahendus.
units.tr: Here he committed a further fraud. For the confession which the prefect had demanded from him, so that he might present it to the ministers for examination and send it on to Bern, he handed over to the printers to be printed, as if ordered to do so by the prefect. To this he added certain prefaces and accusations against Athanasius. Not content with this, he also abused the name and authority of the prefect and dedicated the book to him. The prefect took this injury very badly, so that if Gentile had fallen into his hands he would at once have been dragged back to prison.

units.la: Abiit inde Lugdunum, vbi ab vrbis praefecto, ob eandem doctrinam fuit incarceratus ad dies 50. vnde tamen simili stratagemate euasit. Nam libellum antidotorum, & confessionem sic potuit attemperare, vt iudicaretur solum Caluinum impugnare, non ipsam Trinitatem: ideóque solutus carceribus, dimissus est.
units.tr: From there he went to Lyons, where he was thrown into prison by the prefect of the city for the same doctrine, for fifty days. Yet he escaped from there by a similar trick. For he was able to shape the Antidotes and the confession so that he was judged to attack only Calvin, not the Trinity itself; and so, released from prison, he was let go.

units.la: Sequenti æstate Poloniam petiit, euocatus à Blandrata & Al-ciato, quibus idoneus miles videbatur ad res innouandas per Ec-clesias Polonicas. Mansit illic amplius biénio, magno Ecclesiarum & regni Polonici malo. Ac maiora intulissent religioni vulnera, ni diuinitus incitati ipsi inter sese mox coepissent dissidere. Nam Blandrata palàm Arianus est factus, vt & Gentilis: Alciatus verò Ma-hometista: alii in alia monstra desciuere. Sic quum ab aliis Ec-clesiis omnibus dissiderent, inter sese etiâ malè concordes coeperunt esse. Rem ita habere testatur præsens Poloniæ status. Etenim Blandratæ discipuli eò processerunt, vt palàm nomen & doctrinam Arii tueantur. Damnant de nouo Nicenum concilium, & symbolum illius. Voces illas, ὑσία[?],ὑπόςασις,ὁμοούσιον explodūt. Alii accedunt, qui incarnatione Filii Dei negant: alii immortalitatem animarum impugnant. Quidam Christum habuisse principium ex Maria virgine: nonnulli polygamiam concedunt: nec desunt qui Mahumetanam insaniam tueantur. Sed hi sunt fructus spirituum erroris, quibus senescentem mundum dementat Satan iusto Dei iudicio. Et quantæ sint ex tot erroribus illic enatæ perturbationes, argumento est edictum Serenissimi Regis, quo extremam adhibiturus manum omnes peregrinos noui dogmatis auctores, iubet Polonia excedere, quo cum aliis etiam eiectus est Gentilis.
units.tr: In the following summer he made for Poland, summoned by Biandrata and Alciati, to whom he seemed a suitable soldier for stirring up affairs through the Polish churches. He stayed there for more than two years, to the great harm of the churches and the kingdom of Poland. And they would have inflicted greater wounds on religion, had they not, divinely stirred, soon begun to quarrel among themselves. For Biandrata openly became an Arian, and so did Gentile; Alciati became a Mahometan; others deserted to other monstrosities. Thus, while they disagreed with all the other churches, they also began to be ill-concordant among themselves. The present state of Poland bears witness that this is so. For the disciples of Biandrata have gone so far as to defend openly the name and doctrine of Arius. They condemn anew the Nicene council and its creed. They explode those terms, οὐσία, ὑπόστασις, ὁμοούσιον. Others come forward who deny the incarnation of the Son of God; others attack the immortality of souls. Some hold that Christ had his beginning from the Virgin Mary; some concede polygamy; nor are there lacking those who defend Mahometan madness. But these are the fruits of the spirits of error, by which Satan, by the just judgement of God, drives the ageing world mad. And how great the disturbances arising in that land from so many errors are, is shown by the edict of the most serene King, by which he, about to put the final hand to the matter, orders all foreign authors of the new doctrine to leave Poland; and with the others Gentile too was expelled.

units.la: Itaque Polonia eiectus, Moraviam adiit, vbi cum Anabaptistis multa contulit. Hinc in Austriam, Viennam accesit, vbique sua spargens εὑρήματα[?].
units.tr: Thus expelled from Poland, he went to Moravia, where he had much to do with the Anabaptists. From there he came to Vienna in Austria, everywhere spreading his inventions [εὑρήματα].

units.la: Cæterum quum nullibi posset consistere, de reditu in Sabaudiam cœpit cogitare. Dixit enim se has Ecclesias pacatiores & sinceriores iudicasse. Præterea existimabat superesse Gribaldum, & alios, quorum amicitia iuuari posset. Obierat etiam D. Caluinus, quem in hac tota causa acerrimum fuerat expertus antagonistam. Quare in has terras sese recepit, tanquam ex vasto peregrinationum mari, ad tranquilliorem portum. Ibi demum iusta Dei opt. maximi prouidentia ipsum excæcante, vt sese vltrò in iustas pœnas præcipitem daret, Gaium ipsum accedens, cui idem adhuc præfectus, prorogata forte ipsi extra ordinem eius prouinciæ administratione præerat, ab eo petit publicam disputationem. Respondit ille, Fiat quod iustum est: & ad carceres duci iusit. Hoc pacto tandem homo vafer, & multis Ecclesiis intolerabilis, in eas deuenit angustias, è quibus non potuit amplius emergere.
units.tr: But since he could settle nowhere, he began to think of returning to Savoy. For he said that he had judged these churches more peaceable and more sincere. Besides, he thought that Gribaldi and others were still alive, whose friendship might help him. Calvin, whom he had found the most bitter antagonist in this whole affair, had also died. So he betook himself back to these lands, as from the vast sea of his wanderings to a calmer harbour. There, at last, by the just providence of God, who blinded him so that he would of his own accord rush headlong into just punishments, he came to Gex itself, where the same prefect was still in charge, his term having perhaps been extended beyond the ordinary course of that province's administration; and he asked him for a public disputation. The prefect answered, "Let what is just be done," and ordered him led to prison. In this way at last this crafty man, intolerable to many churches, came into those straits from which he could no longer emerge.

units.la: Ista fuerunt hic statim ab initio copiosius narranda, vt constaret qua occasione in ista absurda dogmata fuerit prolapsus, vbi illa hinc inde sparserit: quantum mali attulerit Ecclesiis, quoties in periculum etiam ob illa venerit, semper autem calliditate quadam emerserit: demū vero iusto Dei iudicio in manus vltrices inciderit.
units.tr: These matters had to be related here at the outset, at some length, so that it would be clear on what occasion he fell into these absurd doctrines, where and how widely he spread them, how much harm he did to the Churches, how often he came into danger on their account yet always escaped by some trick, and at last fell into the avenging hands of the law by God's just judgment.

units.la: Quare Bernam fit perductus. II.
units.tr: Why he was brought to Berne. II.

units.la: QUum 11. Iunii anno Domini 1566. esset Gaii carceri-bus traditus, res mox amplissimo Senatui Bernensi est patefacta : Qui quum intelligeret eum errores docere semel abiuratos : periurio etiam graui sese com-maculasse: nostras Ecclesias damnare, quasi Papatui adhuc seruientes, quum interim ipse inter papistas constitutus, posset confessionibus editis elabi : conuelli etiam reipsa negotium Trinitatis funditus : mirum in modum per eum suosque cōplices turbatam Poloniam : & tamen ipsos doctores in dies magis magisque dissentire, alium Arianum, alium Mahometanum dici, qui idem dogma olim essent professi : adde quod palam damnaretur illorum per Germaniam doctrina, in Ecclesiis carpi illorum errores, in scholis, disputationibus publicis editis etiā libellis proscindi & eliminari dogma-ta : iussit magnificus Senatus hominem deduci Bernam. Accessit alia etiam ratio. Nam de editione libelli sub nomine praefecti Gaie-sis illi erat respondendum domino praefecto, qui de hac fraude & iniuria grauiter est coquestus. Sed & ipse Gentilis quum offensum aduerteret praefectum ea dedicatione, coepit ipse ad Senatum Ber-nam provocare, quo perductus est 19. Iulii.
units.tr: When, on 11 June in the year of the Lord 1566, Gentilis had been handed over to the prison of Geneva, the matter was soon laid before the most illustrious Senate of Berne. The Senate learned that he was teaching errors he had once abjured, that he had also stained himself with grave perjury, and that he condemned our Churches as still in thrall to Popery, while he himself, placed among the Papists, could slip away from the confessions he had published. It also learned that the doctrine of the Trinity was being overturned from its foundations in fact, that Poland had been thrown into a remarkable turmoil through him and his accomplices, and that the teachers themselves were disagreeing more and more every day: one was called an Arian, another a Mohammedan, though all had once professed the same dogma. Add that his doctrine was openly condemned throughout Germany, that his errors were attacked in the Churches, and that his dogmas were refuted in the schools, in public disputations and even in published books. The magnificent Senate therefore ordered the man to be brought to Berne. There was another reason as well. The prefect of Gex had to answer for the publication of a book under his name, and he complained bitterly of this fraud and injury. Gentilis himself, noticing that the prefect was offended by that dedication, began to appeal to the Senate of Berne, and he was brought there on 19 July.

units.la: De scriptis illius, & capitibus actionis. III.
units.tr: On his writings, and the heads of the charges. III.

units.la: Ita igitur Bernam perductus, diebus aliquot mansit in vinculis, ut nihil cum eo fit actum. post modum iubente amplissimo Senatu, inspecta sunt illius scripta, quae penes ipsum reperta sunt.
units.tr: So, having been brought to Berne, he remained in chains for some days, and nothing was done with him. Afterwards, at the command of the most illustrious Senate, his writings that had been found in his possession were examined.

units.la: Librum propria manu scriptum dedicauerat Serenissimo Polo-niae regi Sigismundo, chartarum 29. sol. 195. In hoc libro universa ipsius doctrina est comprehensa, quanvis diceret locupletiorem haberi descriptum à Blandrata.
units.tr: He had dedicated to the most serene King Sigismund of Poland a book written in his own hand, of 29 leaves, 195 pages. In this book his whole doctrine is contained, although he said a fuller copy was held by Blandrata.

units.la: Ad regem prolixa vtitur praefatione, vt sibi & causae suae propi-tium efficiat. Mox repetit suas confessiones Geneuae exhibitas an-tequam reuocasset: ex quibus confessionibus quum vltima esset confutata à Geneuensibus, subiecit ipse cofutationi huic libellum Antidotorum, quem Lugduni pridem composuerat. Inde refutat cap.13.lib.1. Institutionum Caluini, quo loco negotium Trinitatis, vt hactenus in omnibus Ecclesiis traditum est, in solidum da-mnat. His subiicit pthefes [?] ex Augustino, praesertim ex quindecim libris de Trinitate: quas vna cum authore optimo reiicit, ac ca-lumniose traducit. Adiecit noua collectanea ex Scriptura, patribus & Alcorano pro sua stabilienda sententia. Demum annotationes suas in Athanasium ad calcem libri addidit.
units.tr: To the king he uses a long preface, in order to make him favourable to himself and to his cause. Next he repeats the confessions he had submitted at Geneva before he recanted. When the last of these confessions had been refuted by the Genevans, he added to that refutation a little book of Antidotes, which he had composed earlier at Lyons. He then refutes chapter 13 of book 1 of Calvin's Institutes, where the doctrine of the Trinity, as it has hitherto been taught in all the Churches, is wholly condemned. To this he adds passages from Augustine, above all from the fifteen books On the Trinity, which he rejects along with that excellent author and distorts with slander. He added new collections from Scripture, the Fathers and the Koran to support his own opinion. Finally, he added to the end of the book his notes on Athanasius.

units.la: Reperta sunt carmina ipsius manu scripta de Trinitate, quibus Trinomius Deus perstringitur & eius cultores.
units.tr: Poems in his own hand about the Trinity were also found, in which the Trinitarian God and his worshippers are attacked.

units.la: Libellus Italicus, & similis Latinè compositus de Christi incarnatione.
units.tr: A little book in Italian, and a similar one composed in Latin, on the incarnation of Christ.

units.la: Libellus impressus, quem praefecto Gaiensi dedicauit ficto nomine, & praeliminari epistola Typographi ad filios Ecclesiae, qui quum Lugduni sit impressus, mentitur Antuerpiam.
units.tr: A printed little book, which he dedicated under a false name to the prefect of Gex, with a preliminary letter from the printer to the sons of the Church. Although it was printed at Lyons, it falsely claims to have been printed at Antwerp.

units.la: Ex his igitur scriptis collecti sunt articuli, & capita actionis, quae illi proponerentur. Fuerunt autem illa quadruplicia.
units.tr: From these writings the articles and heads of the charge that were to be put to him were gathered. They were in fourfold form.

units.la: Primum enim in doctrina de Trinitate a nobis & Orthodoxis differt.
units.tr: First, in the doctrine of the Trinity he differs from us and from the Orthodox.

units.la: Calumniis inauditis nostras Ecclesias onerat, ac haereseos nomine traducit.
units.tr: He burdens our Churches with unheard-of calumnies and slanders them with the name of heresy.

units.la: Insunt eius scriptis blasphemiae nefandae, quibus Trinitatem aspergit inter disputandum, a quibus nec inter agendum abstinuit.
units.tr: His writings contain abominable blasphemies, with which he defiles the Trinity in disputation, and from which he did not refrain even in his dealings with others.

units.la: Impofturae constant, quibus tum sua fucatè palliauit,tum astu pericula semper euasit, ac etiam alios capitalibus periculis obiicere est conatus:de quibus suo dicemus loco.
units.tr: There are deceptions by which he both disguised his views and, by cunning, always escaped danger, and he also tried to expose others to capital danger. These we shall discuss in their proper place.

units.la: Hæc dum illi proponerentur, primum videlicet ipsum in my-sterio Trinitatis errores intolerandos concepisse: deinde falso nobis imponere multa, quae nemo inter nos tueretur, imo nec ferret alium sic vel sentientem vel loquentem:
units.tr: When these charges were put to him, he was first to be asked whether he had indeed conceived intolerable errors about the mystery of the Trinity; secondly, whether he falsely attributed to us many things that no one among us would defend, nor would tolerate in another who thought or spoke in such a way.

units.la: Adde quod scripta eius passim habeant voces blasphemas, quae redundarent, non in docentium personas, sed in ipsum sacrofan-ctum negotium, de quo ageretur: demum quoniam malitiose causam obscuret agens saepius de eo, de quo non fit controuersia, vt videatur data opera latibula quaerere, petitur vt candidè, & ingenuè ad singula responderet, quae illi proponerentur.
units.tr: Add that his writings everywhere contain blasphemous expressions, which reflect not on the persons of the teachers but on the very holy matter under discussion. Lastly, since in pleading his case he often and maliciously obscures the question by dwelling on what is not in dispute, as if he were deliberately seeking hiding places, he was asked to answer each of the charges put to him frankly and openly.

units.la: Hic Gentilis multa praefatus de corporis debilitate, capitis do-loribus
units.tr: Here Gentilis, after a long preface about the weakness of his body and the pains in his head,

units.la: An tanquam actor debuerit audiri. IIII.
units.tr: Whether he ought to be heard as the plaintiff. IV.

units.la: Hæc exceptio primùm refutanda fuit. Cogitent autem pii homines, quid sibi voluerit iste λόγος [illegible, ~9 letters] φικός. Callidè præscribere voluit modum actionis, sibi idoneum, vt vel nullos, vel certè paucos haberet accusatores, ipse præsideret sententias dicturus in alios.
units.tr: This plea had first to be refuted. Let pious people consider what he meant by his logos [illegible] phikos. He cleverly tried to prescribe a mode of proceeding suited to himself, so that he would have either no accusers or certainly few, and so that he himself would preside and pass sentence on others.

units.la: Ac vt res ab omnibus rectiùs intelligatur, non pigebit rationes illius commemorare. Primùm aiebat se sponte huc accessisse, vt ageret negotium hoc apud Magnificos Dominos Bernates. Deinde se patronum esse eminentiæ Patris, & assertorem Euangelicæ veritatis contra Sophistas. Præterea se nondum esse coniunctum vllius erroris, nec scire se, quos hic aduersarios esset habiturus. Ista copiosè & diffusè egit, vt persuaderet dominis actionem sibi competere.
units.tr: So that the matter may be understood more clearly by all, it will not be tedious to recall his arguments. First he said that he had come here of his own accord, to conduct this business before the magnificent Lords of Berne. Next, that he was the defender of the honour of the Father and the champion of evangelical truth against the Sophists. Moreover, that he was not yet bound to any error, and did not know whom he would have as opponents here. He set this out at length and in detail, so as to persuade the lords that the role of plaintiff belonged to him.

units.la: Verùm responsum est considerandum esse ipsi qua sit in præsentia conditione, expenderet se esse in vinculis & carceribus pii magistratus: quæ conditio non sit actoris, sed rei.
units.tr: But it was answered that he must consider in what condition he now stood: he was in chains and in the prisons of a pious magistrate. That condition belongs not to the plaintiff but to the accused.

units.la: Deinde iustum esse, vt tanquam captiuus audiat prius causas incarcerationis, quas diluat honestis rationibus, siquidem velit è vinculis liberari. Nec enim morem esse, vt actor causam dicat è vinculis contra reos.
units.tr: Next, it was right that, as a prisoner, he should first hear the grounds of his imprisonment, which he might refute with honest reasons, if he wished to be freed from his chains. For it is not the custom for a plaintiff to plead from chains against the accused.

units.la: Quod verò afferat sponte se accessisse, id non iuuare causam ipsius, quum diuino iudicio id sæpe accidat reis, vt sponte petant illa loca, è quibus nunquam emergant. Verùm quidem esse quòd Gaium vltro accesserit, sed illic certis de causis custodiæ traditum, & huc captiuum perductum esse.
units.tr: As for his claim that he came of his own accord, this does not help his case, since by divine judgment it often happens to the accused that they voluntarily seek those places from which they never emerge. It is true that he went of his own will to Gex, but there, for certain reasons, he was handed over to custody, and so was brought here as a prisoner.

units.la: Deinde quòd constituat se patronum eminentiæ Patris, & veritatis assertorem contra Sophistas, frustrà dici. Nos enim nondum esse confirmatos de ipsius vocatione, necdum approbare illos horrores & motus, quibus diceret sese bis fuisse concussum inter orandum Geneuæ, & admonitū tacita Spiritus suggestione, vt diceret illos tueri Quaternitatem.
units.tr: Next, his claim that he is the defender of the honour of the Father and the champion of truth against the Sophists is said in vain. For we are not yet convinced of his calling, nor do we approve those terrors and agitations, by which he says he was twice shaken while praying at Geneva, and warned by a silent prompting of the Spirit to defend the Quaternity.

units.la: Et quòd attinet ad errores, putare nos illum satis conuictum esse, quum totam hanc doctrinam ipsemet Geneuæ reuocasset, & idcirco publicam egisset poenitentiam, de qua extant hæc verba in criminali sententia:
units.tr: As for his errors, we think he has been sufficiently convicted, since he himself recanted this whole doctrine at Geneva and therefore performed public repentance. The words of the criminal sentence on this point are as follows:

units.la: Te Valentinum Gentilem adiudicamus huic poenæ, vt exutus vsque ad camisiam, pedibus nudis, & capite discooperto, facem accensam manu tenens, genibus flexis in terram, veniam à nobis & iustitia deprecéris, fatendo te impiè & scelerate sparsisse falsam & hæreticam doctrinam, & scripta tua in eius defensionem detesteris, eaque propriis manibus tuis in ignem hic accensum coniicias, donec in cinerem redigantur, tanquam blasphemis mendaciis referta. Et quò amplior sit reparatio, Vt ad clangorem tubæ deducaris per omnia vrbis compita hoc habitu, cum inhibitione egrediendi ex vrbe, &c.
units.tr: We adjudge you, Valentinus Gentilis, to this punishment: that stripped to your shirt, with bare feet and bare head, holding a lighted torch in your hand, on bended knees on the ground, you beg pardon and justice from us, confessing that you wickedly and impiously spread a false and heretical doctrine, and that you repudiate your writings written in its defence, and that with your own hands you cast them into the fire lit here, until they are reduced to ashes, as writings full of blasphemous lies. And so that the reparation may be fuller, you shall be led through all the crossroads of the city to the sound of a trumpet, in this attire, with a prohibition on leaving the city, etc.

units.la: Hanc igitur doctrinam tam raro poenitentiæ exemplo damnatam, quæ nunc postliminio reuocatur, non debere tam malæ fidei habere actorem: præterea satis illum nosse, quòd se periurio macularit, quum sine venia non debuerit Geneuam egredi præstito iu-reiurando: quod sine causa negligens Geneua aufugerit: ad quod periurii crimè nihil aliud respondere potuerit, quàm se de eo dolere.
units.tr: Therefore, this doctrine, condemned by so rare an example of repentance and now restored by a kind of postliminy, ought not to have as its advocate a man of such bad faith. Besides, he knows well enough that he has stained himself with perjury, since, having sworn an oath, he should not have left Geneva without permission. He fled from Geneva without cause, and to this charge of perjury he could answer nothing except that he was sorry for it.

units.la: Quod si nescit quos habeat aduersarios, daturos nos quos hactenus habuit Geneuæ, vbi palinodiam cecinit: deinde etiam eos qui ipsum vna cum aliis peregrinis, & noui dogmatis authoribus, è Polonia eiecerunt. His etiam accedere Ecclesias per Germaniam sparsas, quæ doctrinam istam, vt Arianam publicè damnarunt: demum scholarum iudicia, in quibus eadem doctrina exploditur, & nominatim Valentinus Gentilis hæreseos damnatur, ex quorum numero est Alesius in schola Lipsiaca. Mirum autem esse, quòd quum tot tantósque habeat accusatores, secure tamen simulet se ignorare quos habeat aduersarios.
units.tr: If he does not know who his opponents are, we will name those he has had at Geneva, where he sang his palinode, and then those who, together with other foreigners and authors of a new doctrine, drove him out of Poland. To these may be added the churches scattered throughout Germany, which publicly condemned this doctrine as Arian, and finally the judgments of the schools, in which this doctrine is rejected and Valentinus Gentilis is named and condemned as a heretic, among them Alesius in the school at Leipzig. It is remarkable that, having so many and such weighty accusers, he nevertheless pretends with confidence not to know who his opponents are.

units.la: Hæc omnia quum ita vera sint, vt nulla impudentia negari possint, non posse, nec debere tanquam actorem admitti. Rationes sunt, quia hanc doctrinam semel damnauit: quia periurio in hac ipsa causa se polluit: quia certos & infinitos aduersarios habet: quia convellit articulū primariū, qui in papatu etiā mansit salvus: quia denique ipsi doctores huius dogmatis inter se dissidét. Blandratam enim dicebat Arianū factum: Alciatum autem Mahometistā: nec item cum Gribaldo sentiebat. Nam quum illi offerretur confessio nostra, cui olim subscripserat Gribaldus, damnarat eam, & Gribaldum graviter peccasse dixerat, quòd subscripsisset.
units.tr: All these facts are so true that they cannot be denied with any shamelessness, and for these reasons he cannot and should not be admitted as a plaintiff. The reasons are these: he has already condemned this doctrine once; he has defiled himself with perjury in this very cause; he has certain and countless opponents; he overturns the chief article, which survived even under the papacy; and finally, the teachers of this doctrine disagree among themselves. For he said that Blandrata had become an Arian, and Alciati a Mohammedan, and he did not agree with Gribaldi either. For when our confession, which Gribaldi had once signed, was offered to him, he condemned it and said that Gribaldi had sinned gravely in signing it.

units.la: His rationibus ab actione est exclusus, quas bonis viris æstiman-das relinquo: & iussus ad proposita accusationis capita sigillatim respondere.
units.tr: On these grounds he has been excluded from the action, and I leave it to good men to weigh these reasons. He was ordered to answer the articles of the accusation one by one.

units.la: Propositiones ex illius scriptis excerptæ de Trinitate, quas falsas iudicamus. V.
units.tr: Propositions excerpted from his writings concerning the Trinity, which we judge to be false. V.

units.la: Iudicent Ecclesiæ Christi, & pia posteritas quid senti-endum sit de illis sententiis, in quibus vel sycophantice ludit, ut nos calumniis oneret, aut certè blasphemus & impius est.
units.tr: Let the churches of Christ and pious posterity judge what is to be thought of those statements in which he either plays the sycophant to burden us with calumnies, or is plainly blasphemous and impious.

units.la: 1 Trinitas est merum humanum commentum, catholicis symbolis incognitum, cum Euangelica veritate ex diametro pugnans.
units.tr: 1. The Trinity is a mere human invention, unknown to the catholic creeds, and wholly at odds with the Gospel truth.

units.la: 2 Solus Pater unus ille Deus est, qui in scripturis unus & solus Deus dicitur.
units.tr: 2. The Father alone is that one God, who in the Scriptures is called the one and only God.

units.la: 3 Filius à seipso non est, sed à Patre, cui ut essentiatori subordi-natus est.
units.tr: 3. The Son is not from himself but from the Father, to whom he is subordinate as to the one who gives essence [essentiator].

units.la: 4 Pater,Filius,& Spiritus sanctus non solùm quod ad personas attinet,sed etiam quo ad οὐσίαν[?] diuisi sunt.
units.tr: 4. The Father, Son and Holy Spirit are divided not only as regards the persons but also as regards essence [οὐσία].

units.la: 5 Filius à Patre genitus est secundum οὐσίαν[?], ut subordinatus Spiritus differens à Patre.
units.tr: 5. The Son is begotten of the Father according to essence [οὐσία], as one subordinate; the Spirit differs from the Father.

units.la: 6 Tres sunt æterni Spiritus, quorum quilibet per se Deus est.
units.tr: 6. There are three eternal Spirits, each of whom is God in himself.

units.la: 7 Hos tres Spiritus distinctos esse ordine, gradu, & proprietate οὐσίας[?].
units.tr: 7. These three Spirits are distinct in order, degree and the property of essence [οὐσία].

units.la: Declaratio errorum in negotio Trinitatis. VI.
units.tr: Declaration of errors in the matter of the Trinity. VI.

units.la: I[?]n[?] omnibus suis scriptis de mysterio Trinitatis disserit: quod argumentum ita tractat, ut ab annis octo nihil aliud cogitasse, vel scripsisse videri queat.
units.tr: In all his writings he discusses the mystery of the Trinity, and treats this subject so persistently that he could seem for the past eight years to have thought or written about nothing else.

units.la: In primis vero in eam inducit distinctionem essen-tiæ, ut tres æternos numeret, & gradu distinctos constituat spiritus. Et quum nos dicimus, Pater Domini Jesu Christi est persona in una individua Trinitate: Gentilis falsam hanc esse contendit,& dicendum esse, Pater Domini Jesu Christi unus est ille Deus: item quum dicitur, Pater, Filius, & Spiritus sanctus nunc sunt Deus aeternus: ipse de haeresi nos accusat,& inquit,Solus Pater est αὐτόθεος, ἀγέννητος,& essentiator:Filius autem essentiatus,& quidem Deus,sed non αὐτόθεος: sic etiam Spiritus sanctus. ideóque non unus,sed tres aeterni.
units.tr: Above all, he introduces into it a distinction of essence, so that he counts three eternal beings and sets up spirits distinct in rank. When we say that the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ is a person in the one undivided Trinity, Gentilis contends that this is false and that it must be said instead that the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ is that one God. Likewise, when it is said that Father, Son and Holy Spirit are now the eternal God, he accuses us of heresy and says: the Father alone is autotheos [αὐτόθεος], unbegotten, and the essentiator; the Son is essentiated, and indeed God, but not autotheos; so too the Holy Spirit. Therefore they are not one, but three eternal beings.

units.la: Item, quòd dicimus unum Deum in Trinitate, & Trinitatem in unitate venerandam esse, hanc piam & simplicem sententiam dicit esse sophisticam,& tres Spiritus realiter subsistentes affirmat. Sic loquitur Antid.3.sol.27. Tres igitur sunt, quia tres aeterni Spiritus,& folio 70.sese aperit. Tres, inquit, aeterni Spiritus congruo ordine & gradu distincti. Et quanquam concedat Patrem,Filium,& Spiritum sanctum tres esse personas eiusdem naturae, tamen addit distinctos esse ordine,gradu,& proprietate:quae dum illi explicanda sunt, ait, Proprium Patris esse ut appelletur unus & solus Deus: qua explicatione manifeste excluditur Filius & Spiritus sanctus ab unitate deitatis. Fingit autem quandam αὐτουσίαν, quae in solo Patre consistat,ac Filij non sit: hinc Patrem αὐτόθεον nominat, ut per excellentiam vere & proprie Deus sit. Filius autem non αὐτόθεος,sed ἑτε-ρόθεος, aut ἑτερόθεος[?]. Hinc illud,Filius a seipso non est,sed a Patre Deo, qui est αὐτόθεος, sol.341.item sol.161. quod Pater in scripturis dicitur unus & solus Deus invisibilis,altissimus, & Deus Christi,sive verbi incarnati. Item sol.82. Filius subordinatus est essentiatori. Sic Patrem constituit essentiatorem: Filium autem essentiatum ab illo, ut Pater proprie Deus sit,Filius autem subordinatus Deus.
units.tr: Likewise, when we say that one God is to be worshipped in the Trinity and the Trinity in unity, he calls this pious and simple opinion sophistical, and affirms that three Spirits really subsist. He speaks thus in Antidote 3, sol. 27: "There are therefore three, because there are three eternal Spirits," and at folio 70 he reveals himself: "Three eternal Spirits, distinct in fitting order and rank." And although he grants that the Father, Son and Holy Spirit are three persons of the same nature, he still adds that they are distinct in order, rank and property. When he is asked to explain these, he says: "It is proper to the Father to be called the one and only God." By this explanation the Son and the Holy Spirit are manifestly excluded from the unity of the deity. He also invents a certain autousia [αὐτουσία], which resides in the Father alone and is not the Son's; hence he names the Father autotheos, so that by pre-eminence he is truly and properly God, whereas the Son is not autotheos but heterotheos [ἑτερόθεος]. Hence that saying: "The Son is not from himself, but from the Father God, who is autotheos," sol. 341; likewise sol. 161, that the Father is called in the Scriptures the one and only invisible God, most high, and the God of Christ, that is, of the incarnate Word. Likewise sol. 82: "The Son is subordinate to the essentiator." So he makes the Father the essentiator and the Son essentiated by him, so that the Father is properly God, while the Son is a subordinate God.

units.la: Nos contra in diuinitate nullos admittimus gradus, ac Dei essentia unam esse contendimus,non subordinatam. Verum ut huic succurrat, ait, Quum dico,Pater unus &solus Deus est,non ad substantialem numerum, sed ad solam ipsius Patris αὐτουσίαν hoc est referendum. Caeterum,quis non videt laboranti causae, non esse ita satis cautum? Nam manet absurditas illa, αὐτουσία igitur ad Filium non pertinet. Manet & repugnantia illa,Filius cum Patre unus est Deus,& solus Pater unus ille Deus est. Et illa quoque,ἰδία[?] diuinitatis communis est tribus personis per se, & αὐτουσία proprie ad Patrem solum referenda est. Porrò quum dicimus, Et tamen non tres dij, sed vnus est Deus, clamat, sententiam esse falsam, quia propositio hæc VNVS DEVS de solo Patre fit intelligenda, exclusò Filio. Hinc contendit Antid.5.non vnus Deus, sed vnum dici oportere, quia tres sunt vnius deitatis,non autem tres, vnus Deus. Mox addit, Solus pater est vnus Deus: ideóque indicat sol.50. dictionem VNVS, non ad οὐσίας singularitatem pertinere, sed ad Patris αὐτουσίαν[?]. Et mox colligit sol.59. Christum non esse αὐτόθεον, ac nobis exprobrat sol.73.quòd dictione (vnus) propriam,ad singularitatem οὐσίας personarum detorqueamus,contendens dici oportere,Pater,Filius, Spiritus sanctus sunt vnum: non autem, sunt vnus Deus. Quare quum dicimus, Et tamen non tres æterni, sed vnus æternus, Gentilis inquit falsum hoc esse, quia tres sunt æterni spiritus, qui vnus esse non possint. Iam recesui breuiter & perspicuè doctrinam eius ex ipsius scriptis, quam sæpius etiam ore est confessus ad hunc modum & tueri conatus est.
units.tr: We, on the contrary, admit no degrees in the Godhead, and we contend that the essence of God is one and not subordinate. But to help his case, he says: "When I say that the Father is the one and only God, this is to be referred not to the substantial number but to the autousia of the Father alone." But who does not see that this is not cautious enough for a cause in such difficulty? For that absurdity remains: therefore autousia does not belong to the Son. That contradiction remains too: the Son is one God with the Father, and yet the Father alone is that one God. And also that the property [ἰδία] of deity is common to the three persons in themselves, while autousia is to be referred properly to the Father alone. Further, when we say, "And yet not three gods, but there is one God," he cries out that the statement is false, because the proposition ONE GOD must be understood of the Father alone, with the Son excluded. Hence he contends in Antidote 5 that it should not be said "one God" but "one thing," because the three are of one deity, not three, one God. Next he adds: "The Father alone is the one God." Therefore he indicates at sol. 50 that the word ONE pertains not to the singularity of the essence but to the autousia of the Father. Soon afterwards he concludes at sol. 59 that Christ is not autotheos, and at sol. 73 he reproaches us for twisting the word "one," which is proper to the singularity of the essence, to the persons, contending that it should be said that Father, Son and Holy Spirit are one thing, not that they are one God. Therefore when we say, "And yet not three eternal, but one eternal," Gentilis says this is false, because there are three eternal Spirits, which cannot be one. I have now briefly and clearly set out his teaching from his own writings, which he has often also professed in speech in this way and tried to defend.

units.la: Summa in eo consistit, alium esse Deum Patrem, alium Filium Deum, alium Spiritum sanctum Deum, quoniam vnum quidem sint:at nō vnus Deus, sed tres subordinati spiritus. VNVS DEVS, de solo Patre dici,qui solus sit à seipso,& iure αὐτόθεος.
units.tr: The sum of it consists in this: the Father is one God, the Son is another God, the Holy Spirit is another God, since they are indeed one, yet not one God, but three subordinate spirits. "ONE GOD" is to be said of the Father alone, who alone is from himself and rightly self-God.

units.la: Sed nobis obseruandum est,quum dicitur VNVS DEVS,hanc sententiam dupliciter intelligi posse: primum οὐσίᾳ, deinde ὁμοφωνία. Priorem modum excludit, alioquin non posset tueri, tres distinctas οὐσίας intelligentes: posteriorem admittit, quam speciosè & magnificis verbis exornat, Vnum esse tres illos spiritus, consensu, voluntate,natura,plenitudine,potestate,imperio,operationibus &c. & huc trahit, quicquid scriptura de Vnitate dicit. Verùm consensus Ecclesiæ aliud docet, nimirum Deum vnum dici οὐσίᾳ, Trinum autem respectu personarum. Ita symbolum apostolicum intellexit hactenus Ecclesia. Credo in Deum, quem Deum? Patrem,Filium & Spiritum sanctum. Sic Nicenum symbolum vocem ὁμοούσιον adiecit, contra Arii blasphemiam, vt exprimeret ταυτότητα τῆς οὐσίας. Et Athanasij symbolum manifestè non tres, sed vnum Deum, Patrem, Filium, & Spiritum sanctum appellat, non confundendo ὑποστάσεις, nec separando οὐσίαν. Et in hac trinitate, inquit, nihil prius, nec posterius: nihil maius, nec minus: sed totæ tres personæ coæternae sibi sunt & coaequales, ita vt per omnia & trinitas in vnitate, & vnitas in trinitate veneranda sit. Haec omnia quum neget Valentinus, errores intolerabiles in Ecclesiam Christi inducit.
units.tr: But we must observe that when it is said "ONE GOD," this statement can be understood in two ways: first according to essence [οὐσίᾳ], and second according to agreement [ὁμοφωνία]. He excludes the first way, otherwise he could not maintain three distinct essences; the second he admits, which he adorns splendidly and with grand words: that those three Spirits are one by consent, will, nature, fullness, power, rule, operations, and so on; and he draws to this whatever Scripture says of unity. But the consensus of the Church teaches otherwise, namely that God is called one according to essence [οὐσίᾳ] and three with respect to the persons. So the Church has hitherto understood the Apostles' Creed: "I believe in God." What God? The Father, Son and Holy Spirit. So the Nicene Creed added the word homoousios [ὁμοούσιον] against the blasphemy of Arius, to express the identity of essence [ταυτότητα τῆς οὐσίας]. And the Athanasian Creed plainly calls God not three but one, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, neither confusing the subsistences [ὑποστάσεις] nor separating the essence [οὐσίαν]. "And in this Trinity," it says, "there is nothing first or last, nothing greater or less, but the three whole persons are coeternal and coequal with one another, so that in all things both the Trinity in unity and the unity in Trinity is to be worshipped." Since Valentinus denies all these things, he introduces intolerable errors into the Church of Christ.

units.la: De vocibus illis, Trinitas, οὐσία, ὑπόστασις, quid significent. VII.
units.tr: On the words Trinity, οὐσία and ὑπόστασις: what they mean. VII.

units.la: Via Trinitatis vocem, vt nobis est in vsu, insectatur: οὐσίαν vero cum ὑποστάσει vbique confundit, (perinde enim illi est Vsiam, substantiam, essentiam, personam dicere, siue ὑπόστασιν [?]) idcirco eas hic breuiter explicabimus. Sunt enim aptissimae ad fallendum artes, a cosueta vocum significatione recedere. ac verum quidem est, non oportere nos esse difficiles in vocum vsu, modo de re constet. Sed quae est temeritas, velle innouare voces, & sine causa receptas explodere? vtamur ergo moribus vetustis, & receptis vocibus. Trinitas in hac quaestione nō significat abstractum numerum, quemadmodum ternionem, quaternionem considerant geometrae, sed denotat ὑπαρξιν [?]. Hinc appellarunt τριάδα, ὑπερἀριθμον ὑπαρξιν [?]. Sic de Trinitate loquuntur Theologi Graeci, Gregorius Nazianzenus, Basilius, Damascenus, sic Latini etiam.
units.tr: Valentinus attacks the word Trinity as we use it, and he confuses οὐσία with ὑπόστασις everywhere. (For him it makes no difference whether one says ousia, substance, essence or person, or says hypostasis [?].) I shall therefore explain these terms briefly here. Changing the customary meaning of words is a most effective trick for deceiving people. It is true that we should not be fussy about how words are used, provided the thing itself is agreed. But what rashness it is to want to reshape words and reject without cause those that have long been accepted! Let us therefore keep the old customs and the received terms. In this question the word Trinity does not signify an abstract number, as geometers consider a threefold or fourfold number, but denotes a real existence [ὕπαρξιν?]. Hence they called it a Trinity, a supernumerary existence [ὑπερἀριθμον ὕπαρξιν?]. Thus the Greek theologians speak of the Trinity, Gregory Nazianzen, Basil, Damascene, and the Latins likewise.

units.la: Fallitur itaque Gentilis, dum colligit, Pater est Deus, Filius est Deus, Spiritus sanctus est Deus, & Trinitas est Deus. Ergo quatuor sunt personae Diuinitatis, vt vos non Trinitatem, sed Quaternitatem tuemini.
units.tr: Gentilis is therefore mistaken when he concludes: the Father is God, the Son is God, the Holy Spirit is God, and the Trinity is God. Therefore there are four persons of the Godhead, so that you defend not a Trinity but a Quaternity.

units.la: Negamus consequens. Nemo dicit Trinitatem extra personas, Patris, Filii, & Spiritus sancti, Deum esse. Quod enim Trinitas est, id in his personis est, extra quas nulla est nec Deitas, nec Diuinitatis essentia.
units.tr: We deny the consequence. No one says that the Trinity, apart from the persons of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, is God. For what the Trinity is, that is in these persons, outside of whom there is neither Deity nor the essence of the Godhead.

units.la: Manet igitur firma collectio & inconcussa, Pater est Deus, Filius, & Spiritus sanctus, & hi tres vnum sunt. Ergo vnus est Deus trinus, neque hic vllum fingimus Idolum.
units.tr: The inference therefore stands firm and unshaken: the Father is God, the Son and the Holy Spirit are God, and these three are one. Therefore there is one God, triune, and here we do not invent any idol.

units.la: Inducta est autem illa vox in ecclesiam magno consilio. Nam Episcopi cum Athanasio congregati in Alexandria, vt testis est So-zomenus lib. 6. cap. 20. Trip. historiae, vt confirmarent synodum Nicenam de consubstantialitate Patris, Filii, & Spiritus sancti, con-tra Atra Arianorum motus, τριάδα appellarunt, exprimentes ea voce, tres personas consubstantiales,non distrahentes οὐσίαν[?], nec confun-dētes personas. Et hac voce deinceps orthodoxa concilia usa sunt, similiter & patres Græci, & Latini. Sed & scriptura ita loquitur, Ioan.1.cap.5.Tres sunt in cælo,Pater,λόγος & Spiritus sanctus,& hi tres vnum sunt. Sic in baptismo Christi tres personæ patefiunt. Marci 1.Matth.3,& in institutione baptismi,Matth.28.
units.tr: That word, however, was introduced into the Church by a great council. For the bishops gathered with Athanasius at Alexandria, as Sozomen testifies in book 6, chapter 20 of the Tripartite History, in order to confirm the Nicene Synod concerning the consubstantiality of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, against the attacks of the Arians, called them a Trinity [τριάδα], expressing by that word three consubstantial persons, neither dividing the ousia nor confusing the persons. From then on the orthodox councils used this word, and likewise the Greek and Latin Fathers. Scripture too speaks thus, 1 John 5: "There are three in heaven, the Father, the Word [λόγος] and the Holy Spirit, and these three are one." So also at the baptism of Christ the three persons are revealed: Mark 1, Matthew 3; and in the institution of baptism, Matthew 28.

units.la: Impudens igitur est illa & nimium effrons temeritas, affirmare Trinitatem esse merum humanum commentum Catholicis Symbolis incognitum. Orthodoxa sunt Symbola Nicenum, Alexandrinum,Ephesinum,& illa agnoscunt hanc vocem. Impudens ergo mendacium est,quod nobis obtruditur hac censoria nota. Sed excipit, Deum Trinitatem illis incognitum fuisse. Ego vero miror, quem Deum Trinitatem nobis hic obtrudat. Si quartam quandam personam intelligit, de suo illam affert: ideoque merito explodimus illum cum suo figmento,& ipse merito impius dicetur, qui in re seria ad cauilla descendit: sin loquatur de Deo trino & uno, mendacii conuincitur.Nam cōcilia in hac significatione de Trinitate loquuntur,& vetus fuit illis Deus Trinus & Vnus.
units.tr: It is therefore shameless and far too brazen a rashness to assert that the Trinity is a mere human invention, unknown to the Catholic creeds. The orthodox creeds, the Nicene, the Alexandrian and the Ephesine, acknowledge this word. It is therefore a shameless lie that is thrust upon us with this censorious label. But he objects that the Trinity was unknown to them. I, however, wonder what Trinity-God he is thrusting upon us here. If he means some fourth person, he brings that in from his own imagination, and so we rightly reject him together with his fiction; and he himself will rightly be called impious, who in a serious matter descends to trifling. But if he means the triune and one God, he is convicted of lying, for the councils speak of the Trinity in this sense, and for them God was from of old Triune and One.

units.la: Verùm astutus artifex hoc nobis imponit, quasi affirmemus Deum Trinitatem,sine Patre, Filio, & Spiritu sancto. Sed fallitur: & absit tanta impietas ab Ecclesiis Christi. Neque vero necesse hic est operosius Trinitatem persequi.Satis est monstrasse Trinitatem significare ὑπαρξιν[?], quicquid nugetur Valentinus,& vocem esse cognitam Symbolis catholicis.
units.tr: But the crafty artificer imposes on us the claim as if we affirmed a Trinity of God without the Father, Son and Holy Spirit. But he is mistaken, and God forbid such impiety from the Churches of Christ. Nor is it necessary here to pursue the doctrine of the Trinity at greater length. It is enough to have shown that Trinity signifies a real existence [ὕπαρξιν?], whatever Valentinus trifles, and that the word is known from the Catholic creeds.

units.la: Pari improbitate lusit in vocibus,οὐσία,& ὑπόστασις,quas sæpe nugas appellare solet. Meminisse autem oportet non esse postremam in docendo virtutem, vocibus appositè res distinguere. Malitiosi autem animi cognitionem confusione vocum inuoluere, præsertim in re tam graui & mystica, quæ nulla humana acie explicari satis possit. Etenim quicquid de Deo dicimus,insufficiens est, & minus pro tata maiestate, vt recte dixerint veteres: rectius quid non sit,quàm quid sit Deus, explicari. Et memorabilis est in hac re Iustini Martyris sententia, θεὸν νοῆσαι μὲν χαλεπὸν· φράσαι δ' ἀδύνατον· τὸ δὲ νοῆσαι δύνατον[?]. Ideòque pie dixit Euagrius, vt refert Socrates lib.6. Trip. cap.21. Trinitatem ineffabilem adorandam potius silentio, quàm circunscribendam.Ita Deum dicimus quidem οὐσίαν, qui ne proprie quidem ita dici possit: fi quidem οὐσία definiri potest, Deus autem ἀπερίγραπτος est, & definiri nullis potest limitibus. Religiose igitur, ac reuerenter haec tractanda sunt, & vocibus, quoad fieri potest, vsitatis & appositis vtendum.
units.tr: With equal wickedness he plays with the words οὐσία and ὑπόστασις, which he is often wont to call trifles. But we must remember that it is no small skill in teaching to distinguish things precisely by words, whereas it is the mark of a malicious mind to entangle knowledge in a confusion of words, especially in a matter so weighty and mystical, which no human insight can sufficiently explain. For whatever we say about God is inadequate and falls short of his full majesty, so that the ancients rightly said that it is better to explain what God is not than what he is. A notable saying on this point is that of Justin Martyr: "To conceive God is difficult, to express him impossible, but to conceive him is possible" [θεὸν νοῆσαι μὲν χαλεπὸν· φράσαι δ' ἀδύνατον· τὸ δὲ νοῆσαι δύνατον]. Hence Evagrius piously said, as Socrates reports in book 6, chapter 21 of the Tripartite History, that the ineffable Trinity is to be adored in silence rather than circumscribed. Thus we do indeed call God ousia, though strictly speaking it cannot even be said so, since ousia can be defined, whereas God is incircumscribable and cannot be defined by any limits. Therefore these matters must be treated religiously and reverently, and we must use words that are customary and fitting, as far as possible.

units.la: Quia in scriptura Deus dicitur ὁ ὢν, vt apud Hebr. יהוה[?] ab היה[?], hinc in pari significatione ab ὢν dixerunt οὐσίαν, quemadmodum a Deo dicitur Deitas, & per οὐσίαν Deitatem significarunt.
units.tr: Because in Scripture God is called "He who is" [ὁ ὢν], as in Hebrew [יהוה] from [היה], from this in the same sense they called ousia from "being" [ὢν], just as Deity is named from God, and they signified the Deity by ousia.

units.la: Alioqui Graeci οὐσίαν appellant ὑπάρχοντα[?], vt δόσμοι τὸ μέρος τῆς οὐ-σίας. sed & quicquid accidens non est, οὐσίαν philosophi dixerunt.
units.tr: Otherwise the Greeks call ousia what exists [ὑπάρχοντα], as in the phrase "the part of the ousia" [δόσμοι τὸ μέρος τῆς οὐσίας]. The philosophers also called ousia whatever is not an accident.

units.la: Theologi vero in hac disputatione, essentiam diuinam οὐσίαν appellarunt. Et dubitatum est diu, rectiusne per essentiam, an vero per substantiam verteretur a Latinis. Sed apud plerosque obtinuit vsus, vt essentia dicatur οὐσία, qua exprimitur communis natura diuinitatis in Trinitate.
units.tr: The theologians, however, in this dispute called the divine essence ousia. And for a long time it was debated whether it ought to be rendered by the Latins as essentia or as substantia. But among most writers usage has prevailed that ousia is rendered essentia, by which the common nature of the Godhead in the Trinity is expressed.

units.la: Augustini sententia etiam est, rectius dici essentiam. Sed tamen, inquit, siue essentia dicatur, quod proprie dicitur, siue substantia, quod abusiue: vtrumque ad se dicitur, non relatiue ad aliquid. Sic lib.5. de Trinitate cap.8. Essentiam dico, quae οὐσία Graecis dicitur. Et mox, μίαν οὐσίαν, τρεῖς ὑποστάσεις, quod est Latine, vnam essentiam, tres substantias. Et eodem libro, cap.2. Est tamen sine dubitatione substantia, vel si melius haec appellatur, essentia, quam Graeci οὐσίαν vocant. Hieronymus alias vocabulum vsiae retinet, vt aduersus Luciferu: alias substantia vertit, vt ad Damas. Sufficiet, inquit, nobis dicere vnam substantiam, tres personas subsistentes, perfectas, aequales, coaeternas. Ibidem essentia vocat, vt, Deus essentiae nomen vere tenet. Item, nomen Essentiae sibi vendicat proprie Deus.
units.tr: Augustine also holds that essentia is the more correct term. Yet, he says, whether it is called essentia, which is what is properly meant, or substantia, which is a looser use, both are said of itself and not relatively to something else. So in book 5 of On the Trinity, chapter 8: "I say essence, which the Greeks call ousia." And soon after: one ousia, three hypostases, which in Latin is one essence, three substances. And in the same book, chapter 2: "It is nevertheless without doubt substance, or, if this is better called essence, which the Greeks call ousia." Jerome at one time keeps the word ousia, as against Lucifer; at another he translates it substantia, as in his letter to Damasus: "It will be enough for us to say one substance, three persons subsisting, perfect, equal, coeternal." In the same place he calls it essence: "God truly holds the name of essence." Likewise: "God alone properly claims for himself the name of Essence."

units.la: Hypostasis vero profanis scriptoribus significabat οὐσίαν, vt testatur Hieron. in epistola ad Damasum. Et Socrates in hist. Tripart. lib.6. cap.21. refert ex Ireneo grammatico, philosophos posteros pro οὐσίᾳ dixisse ὑπόστασιν, quae significatio manifest aliquando inter Theologos. Sic loquitur Socrates sol. 176, μὴ εἶναι ἐξ ἑτέρας τε ὑποστάσεως, οὐσίας, ἀλλ' ἐκ τῆς αὐτῆς[?] ἀρχῆς. Sed personam tum dixerunt ὑπαρξιν, vt est apud eundem Socrat. lib.1.cap.23. Alias ὑπαρξιν & ὑπόστασιν pro eodem sumpserunt, vt in illo Socratis ibidem, ἐνυπόστατον τε καὶ ἐνυπάρχοντα τὸν υἱὸν εἶναι τῷ Θεῷ, ἑνα τε Θεὸν ἐν τρισὶν ὑποστάσεσιν εἶναι ὁμολογοῦντες[?]. Tandem graui ratione adducti ὑπόστασιν solùm pro persona acceperè, vt sit idem ὑπόστασις quod πρόσωπον, Latinis persona & subsi-stentia. vt dixerunt ὑπόστασιν οὐσίαν μετὰ ἰδιωμάτων.
units.tr: Hypostasis, however, among profane writers signified ousia, as Jerome testifies in his letter to Damasus. And Socrates in the Tripartite History, book 6, chapter 21, reports from the grammarian Irenaeus that later philosophers used hypostasis for ousia; this sense is also clearly found at times among theologians. Socrates speaks thus in section 176: "not to be from another hypostasis or ousia, but from the same principle" [μὴ εἶναι ἐξ ἑτέρας τε ὑποστάσεως, οὐσίας, ἀλλ' ἐκ τῆς αὐτῆς ἀρχῆς]. But they once called person hypar-xis [ὕπαρξιν], as is found in the same Socrates, book 1, chapter 23. At other times they took hypar-xis and hypostasis in the same sense, as in that passage of Socrates in the same place: "confessing that the Son is in God subsisting and existing, and that God is one in three hypostases" [ἐνυπόστατον τε καὶ ἐνυπάρχοντα τὸν υἱὸν εἶναι τῷ Θεῷ, ἕνα τε Θεὸν ἐν τρισὶν ὑποστάσεσιν εἶναι ὁμολογοῦντες]. At last, led by weighty reason, they took hypostasis only for person, so that hypostasis is the same as prosopon, which the Latins render persona and subsistentia, as they said: "hypostasis, ousia with its properties."

units.la: Tempore Hieronymi adhuc controuersia fuit de voce, vnde nō uellā appellat, & alios ὑπόστασιν dixisse οὐσίαν: alios tres ὑποστάσεις, hoc est tres personas, ac de eo consulit Damasum. Non timebo, inquit, tres ὑποστάσεις dicere, si iubeas.
units.tr: In Jerome's time there was still controversy over the word, since some said that Basil of Ancyra [?] called it ousia, and others called three hypostases, that is three persons; and on this matter he consulted Damasus. "I shall not be afraid," he says, "to say three hypostases, if you bid me."

units.la: Cæterum historia Tripart. indicat sobrie has quæstiones à patribus tractatas, nec nisi vltima necessitate.
units.tr: Moreover, the Tripartite History shows that these questions were treated by the Fathers soberly, and only under the last necessity.

units.la: Quare Episcopi cum Athanasio cōgregati in Alexandria, quæstionem de οὐσία & ὑπόστασις consultò reliquerunt, vt illis vocibus contra Sabellium vterentur solum, ne vocum inopia idem nunc putaretur substantia οὐσία, & subsistentia ὑπόστασις. Idem refert Rufinus lib.10.cap.29.
