units.tr: Hence the bishops gathered with Athanasius at Alexandria deliberately left aside the question about ousia and hypostasis, and used those words only against Sabellius, lest, for want of words, the same thing should now be thought to be substance (ousia) and subsistence (hypostasis). Rufinus reports the same in book 10, chapter 29.

units.la: Hodie quidam οὐσίαν substantiam, ὑπόστασιν subsistentiam vertūt: alii expressius ὑπόστασιν personam malunt dicere, οὐσίαν autem essentiam. Nam vt Græcis οὐσία παρὰ τὸ εἶναι, sic Latinis ab esse essentia dicitur. Sed parum refert modò sensus idem sit.
units.tr: Today some translate οὐσία as "substance" and ὑπόστασις as "subsistence", while others prefer to say ὑπόστασις "person" and οὐσία "essence". For just as the Greeks derive οὐσία from εἶναι, so the Latins derive essentia from esse. But it matters little, provided the meaning is the same.

units.la: Communis natura diuinitatis οὐσία est, & secundùm hanc Deus vnus dicitur.personæ autem dicuntur ὑποστάσεις, vel πρόσωπα. Sic tres dicuntur ὑποστάσεις, hoc est subsistentiæ, siue tres sunt personæ,hoc est,vt Græci dicunt τρεῖς ὑποστάσεις ἐν τῇ μιᾷ οὐσίᾳ. Iustinus Martyr & alii vocant tres ὑπάρξεις,& tria ὑφιστάμενα.
units.tr: The common nature of the divinity is the οὐσία, and according to this God is said to be one. The persons, however, are called ὑποστάσεις or πρόσωπα. Thus three are called ὑποστάσεις, that is, subsistences, or three persons; as the Greeks put it, τρεῖς ὑποστάσεις ἐν τῇ μιᾷ οὐσίᾳ [three hypostases in the one substance]. Justin Martyr and others call them three ὑπάρξεις and three ὑφιστάμενα [three existences and three subsistents].

units.la: Gentilis verò Trinitatem explicans, non solùm confundit οὐσίαν cum ὑποστάσει, sed etiam supergressus, discrimen trium hypostaseon constituit ἐν τῇ οὐσίᾳ. Hoc quum diceremus contra scripturam fieri, & consensum vetustatis: respondit οὐσίας vocabulum non esse in scripturis expressum. in quo sanè Arii spiritū prodidit. Nam Hieronymus contra Lucif.indicat hoc ipsum fuisse Valentis & sequen-tium illius argumentum, qui simili arte vocem οὐσίας conati sunt e-liminare ex Ecclesia, & simul Nicenæ Synodi fidem damnare. Sed nos indicauimus qua ratione vox illa recepta sit contra Sabellium. Et quanquam cupiat iste medius incedere inter Arium & Sabel-lium, Arii tamen castra sequitur.
units.tr: Gentilis, in explaining the Trinity, not only confuses essence [οὐσίαν] with hypostasis [ὑποστάσει], but goes further and establishes a distinction among the three hypostases within the essence [ἐν τῇ οὐσίᾳ]. When we said this was contrary to Scripture and to the consensus of antiquity, he replied that the word essence [οὐσίας] is not expressed in Scripture. In this he indeed revealed the spirit of Arius. For Jerome, in his work against Lucifer, points out that this very argument was used by Valens and his followers, who by a similar device tried to remove the word essence [οὐσίας] from the Church and at the same time to condemn the faith of the Nicene Synod. But we have shown by what reasoning that word was received against Sabellius. And although this man wishes to walk a middle way between Arius and Sabellius, he nevertheless follows the camp of Arius.

units.la: Quae fuerit Arij sententia, & quid Gentilis cum illa commune habeat. VIII.
units.tr: What the opinion of Arius was, and what Gentilis has in common with it. VIII.

units.la: ET quia de Arii sententia etiam multi dubitare videntur, operæpretium fuerit eam hic paucis aperire. Res enim eò est progressa, vt palàm dicant non obid damnatum, quòd solum Deum agnosceret Patrem: sed quia Filium Dei creaturam faceret.
units.tr: Because many also seem to doubt what the opinion of Arius was, it will be worth while to set it out here briefly. For matters have advanced to the point that people openly say he was not condemned on the ground that he acknowledged only God the Father, but because he made the Son of God a creature.

units.la: Duo hic sunt: Filium Dei esse creaturam (dicit hoc Arius, non dicit Gentilis) alterum, Patrem solum esse illum vnum Deum altissimum, qui habitat lucem inaccessam. Hoc affirmat Gentilis, nō videtur idem dixisse Arius. & interea ne quid sibi cum Ario commune sit, vtrinque causam separat. Verum, si est vera Gentilis sententia, & proprium Patris est, vt dicatur vnus & solus Deus, non video, cur ab eo separandus sit Arius. Verum enim secundum Gentilem dixisset, quemadmodum idem non reprehensus fuit à patribus, quòd Christum diceret Filium Dei: verum enim id erat, & illi cum orthodoxis commune.
units.tr: There are two points here: that the Son of God is a creature (Arius says this, Gentilis does not), and the other, that the Father alone is that one most high God who dwells in unapproachable light. Gentilis affirms this, but Arius does not seem to have said the same. Yet meanwhile Gentilis separates his cause from Arius's on both points, so that nothing is held in common with Arius. But if Gentilis's view is true, and it is proper to the Father that he alone is called the one and only God, I do not see why Arius should be separated from him. For Arius would have spoken truly on Gentilis's view, just as he was not rebuked by the Fathers for calling Christ the Son of God; for that was true, and held in common with the orthodox.

units.la: Sin autem phrasi discrepant, re idem dicunt, palam est intercedere communionem sententiarum: quod vt intelligatur, expendamus quomodo Arii sententia posteritati sit tradita.
units.tr: But if they differ in wording while saying the same thing, it is plain that there is a community of opinion between them. To see this, let us consider how the view of Arius was handed down to posterity.

units.la: Apud Theodor. lib. 1. cap. 4. conqueritur Alexander Episcopus Alexandrinus, quòd Arius & Achilles Diuinitatem Christi negent. Verba eius sunt, τὴν[?] θεότητα τε σωτῆρος ἡμῶν ἀρνούμενοι, καὶ τοῖς πᾶσιν ἴσον εἶναι κηρύσσοντες. Et mox, Attribuunt, inquit, illi temporale principium. Sic enim loquitur Arius, ἦν ποτέ, ὅτε οὐκ ἦν ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ, καὶ γέγονεν ὕστερον, ὁ πρότερον μὴ ὑπάρχων, τοιοῦτος γενόμενος, ὁ τε ἦν ποτε γέγονεν, οἷον καὶ πᾶσιν εἶναι πέφυκεν ἀνθρώποις. πάντα γὰρ, φασὶν, ὁ θεὸς ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων ἐποίησεν, συναναλαμβάνοντες τὴν τῶν ἀπάντων λογικῶν τε καὶ ἀλόγων κτίσει, καὶ τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ θεοῦ[?].
units.tr: In Theodoret, book 1, chapter 4, Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, complains that Arius and Achilles deny the divinity of Christ. His words are: denying the divinity of our Saviour and proclaiming that he is equal to all things [τὴν θεότητα τε σωτῆρος ἡμῶν ἀρνούμενοι, καὶ τοῖς πᾶσιν ἴσον εἶναι κηρύσσοντες]. And soon after: "They attribute," he says, "a temporal beginning to him." For Arius speaks thus: there was once when the Son of God was not; and he came into being later, who previously did not exist; having become such, what once came to be is such as all men are by nature [ἦν ποτέ, ὅτε οὐκ ἦν ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ, καὶ γέγονεν ὕστερον, ὁ πρότερον μὴ ὑπάρχων, τοιοῦτος γενόμενος, ὁ τε ἦν ποτε γέγονεν, οἷον καὶ πᾶσιν εἶναι πέφυκεν ἀνθρώποις]. "For," they say, "God made all things out of things that were not," including in the creation of all rational and irrational beings also the Son of God [πάντα γὰρ, φασὶν, ὁ θεὸς ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων ἐποίησεν, συναναλαμβάνοντες τὴν τῶν ἀπάντων λογικῶν τε καὶ ἀλόγων κτίσει, καὶ τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ θεοῦ].

units.la: Ad eandem formam refertur eius sententia in hist. Trip. lib. 1. cap. 13. Non semper (inquiunt) Deus Pater fuit, non semper fuit Dei Verbum: sed fuit quando Deus, Pater non fuit. Dei autem Verbum ex non existentibus factum est, &c.
units.tr: His view is reported in the same form in the Tripartite History, book 1, chapter 13: "God the Father was not always; the Word of God was not always; but there was when God was not yet Father. The Word of God, however, was made out of things that did not exist," and so on.

units.la: Niceph. quoque lib. 8. cap. 8. Non semper Deus Pater erat, sed erat quum Deus Pater non erat. Non semper igitur Dei Verbum erat, sed ex non existentibus factum est. Qui enim erat Deus, eum qui non erat,ex non existente fecit,&c. plura vide etiam eodem li-bro cap.18. Ex quibus verbis perspici potest, Arium primum sepa-rasse effentia,aliam Patris,aliam Filii constituendo. Deinde Filio as-signasse temporale principium originis, ideoque ὁμοούσιον tantope-re damnasse,vt obtineret substantiæ separationem: & coæternum esse Patri negasse, vt constaret temporale principium. Hinc maio-ra sequebantur absurda, Filium Dei esse nudam creaturam. Item genitum ἐκ μὴ ὄντων. Videbant enim naturā Dei esse simplicissimam & perfectissimam, quæ nullam admitteret diuisionem secundum maius aut minus,ideoque λόγον separabant.
units.tr: Nicephorus also, book 8, chapter 8: "God the Father was not always, but there was when God the Father was not. Therefore the Word of God was not always, but was made out of things that did not exist. For he who was God made him who was not out of what did not exist," and so on. See more in the same book, chapter 18. From these words it can be seen that Arius first separated the essence, making one essence of the Father and another of the Son. Then he assigned to the Son a temporal beginning of origin, and therefore condemned ὁμοούσιον so strongly that he might secure a separation of substance; and he denied that the Son is coeternal with the Father, so that a temporal beginning might stand. From this there followed greater absurdities: that the Son of God is a bare creature, and likewise that he was begotten ἐκ μὴ ὄντων [out of nothing]. For they saw that the nature of God is most simple and most perfect, admitting no division by more or less; therefore they separated the Word.

units.la: Quid autè huic cōmune sit cum Gentili, facile est videre. Arius aiebat aliam Patris, aliam Filij esse οὐσίαν. Gentilis Patrem à Filio disiungit non solùm κατὰ τὴν ὑπόστασιν[?], sed etiam κατὰ τὴν οὐσίαν. Nec obstat quod affert, λόγον de substantia Patris genitum,& eidem consubstantialem: in quo sanè ab Ario differt. Sed tamen separatio-nem substantiæ inducit. Arius igitur ait ἐκ μὴ ὄντων, hic non ἐκ μὴ ὄντων, sed de substantia Patris Filium extitisse. Itaque inter se con-sentiunt in eo, quòd secundum essentiam Filium à Patre numero differre vterque sentit.
units.tr: It is easy to see what this has in common with Gentilis. Arius said that the essence of the Father is one, and that of the Son another. Gentilis separates the Father from the Son not only κατὰ τὴν ὑπόστασιν [according to the hypostasis], but also κατὰ τὴν οὐσίαν [according to the essence]. Nor does it count against this that he brings forward the Word as begotten of the substance of the Father and consubstantial with him; in that point he certainly differs from Arius. Yet he still introduces a separation of substance. Arius therefore says ἐκ μὴ ὄντων [out of nothing]; here it is not ἐκ μὴ ὄντων, but the Son has come forth from the substance of the Father. So they agree in this, that both hold the Son to differ from the Father in number according to essence.

units.la: Refert Nicephorus lib.18.cap.47.48.Philoponum nobilem phi-losophum hoc idem argumentum agitasse. Nam diuinam illam & indiuisibilem naturam in plures personas discernens, eam singu-latim indiuiduis tribuebat, & tribus illis supersubstantialis naturæ subfiftentiis dispertiebatur. Fuit item Monophysitorum dux, qui propter vnam in Christo hypostasin, vnam etiam φύσιν ex duabus conflatam dicebant: vt contrà Nestorius propter duas naturas, duas etiam ὑποστάσεις asseruit.
units.tr: Nicephorus, book 18, chapters 47 and 48, relates that the noted philosopher Philoponus took up this same argument. For, distinguishing that divine and indivisible nature into several persons, he assigned it to each individually, and it was divided among those three subsistences of a supersubstantial nature. There was also the leader of the Monophysites, who, because of one hypostasis in Christ, said there was also one nature compounded of two; whereas, on the contrary, Nestorius, because of two natures, also asserted two hypostases.

units.la: Deinde Arius solum Patrem principio carere dixit, λόγον autem principium habuisse, quod & Philoponus & Themistius philosophi defenderunt, vt est apud Niceph.lib.18.cap.50.
units.tr: Next, Arius said that only the Father lacks a beginning, but the Word had a beginning; and the philosophers Philoponus and Themistius defended this, as is reported in Nicephorus, book 18, chapter 50.

units.la: Gentilis autem genitum dicit Filium, & actum generandi præ-cessisse: quod si verum est, generatio posterior fuit tempore. Nec erubescit afferre testimonium Tertullian. non ideo Pater & iudex semper,quia Deus semper.Nam nec Pater potuit esse ante Filium, nec iudex ante delictum. Fuit autem tempus quum ei delictum & Filius non fuit.Quam sententiam approbans cum Tertulliano,in castra Arij transit. Nec vero refert Tertullianusne, an alius hoc scribat,& sentiat,quum hanc mentem Arij fuisse constet.
units.tr: Gentilis, however, says that the Son is begotten, and that the act of begetting came first; if that is true, the generation was posterior in time. Nor is he ashamed to bring forward a testimony from Tertullian: "not therefore is he Father and Judge always, because he is God always. For the Father could not be before the Son, nor the Judge before the offence. But there was a time when for him there was no offence and no Son." In approving this view along with Tertullian, he passes over into the camp of Arius. Nor does it matter whether Tertullian or someone else wrote and held this, since it is clear that this was the mind of Arius.

units.la: Duo igitur illi cum Ario communia sunt, primum quod diui-sionem in ὑπόστασιν Diuinitatis inducit:alterum,quod actum generan-di priore facit tempore,in quo locum habet illud Arij, ἦν ὅτε οὐκ ἦν.
units.tr: Therefore there are two points which he has in common with Arius: first, that he introduces a division of the hypostases of the Divinity; second, that he makes the act of begetting prior in time, in which the saying of Arius, there was when he was not [ἦν ὅτε οὐκ ἦν], applies.

units.la: De generatione Filij Dei, & quomodo intelligi debeat γεννητὸν & ἀγέννητον.
units.tr: On the generation of the Son of God, and how γεννητὸν and ἀγέννητον [gennēton, agennēton] should be understood.

units.la: Sed ad scripturas hic provocat Gentilis, in quibus generatio Filij Dei nobis proponitur. Ioan. 1. Vidimus gloriam eius, gloriam veluti vnigeniti à Patre. & Psal. 2.Filius meus es tu, hodie genui te: quem locum Paulus citat Act.13.& Apostolus ad Hebr.1.& 5. Pergit deinceps colligere, Genitum ab ingenito differt, eo quod illud quidem habet principium, hoc autem caret principio. Item, Patrem ingenitum dici, quia causam originis non habet, omnia vero ab ipso descendunt:Filium autem genitum,quia principium à Patre habet:illum essentiatorem, hunc essentiatum Spiritum. Opinor hic quemuis facile observare argumentum Arij. Nam qui legerunt Nicephorum, Theodor.aliosque scriptores Ecclesiasticos, sciunt hoc argumento vsos fuisse Arianos. At nos non solum agnoscimus generationem Filij Dei, & quod Pater fit ἀγέννητος, Filius autem γεννητός: verum insuper addimus generatione hanc carere temporis principio, & talem esse quae superet omnem omnium mortalium captum. Erat enim Verbum in principio, & omnia per ipsum facta sunt, quod postea Filius vnigenitus ibidem dicitur: de quo etiam dicit propheta, Ab vtero, ab aurora tibi ros natiuitatis tuae: quem locum ipsi Iudaei de aeterna Meschiae natiuitate interpretantur. Non igitur concluditur quod vult Gentilis. Inexplicabilis enim est illa γέννησις, & temporis principio caret. Igitur in ea nihil est posterius,nihil prius,sed tota est coaeternitas.
units.tr: But Gentilis appeals here to Scripture, in which the generation of the Son of God is set before us. John 1: "We saw his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father." And Psalm 2: "You are my Son; today I have begotten you," a passage which Paul cites in Acts 13, and which the Apostle cites in Hebrews 1 and 5. He then goes on to argue that the begotten differs from the unbegotten, in that the one has a beginning and the other has none. Likewise, the Father is called unbegotten because he has no cause of origin, while all things descend from him; the Son is called begotten because he has his beginning from the Father, the one being the giver of essence and the other the one who receives it. I think anyone can easily recognise here the argument of Arius. For those who have read Nicephorus, Theodoret and other ecclesiastical writers know that the Arians used this argument. But we not only acknowledge the generation of the Son of God, and that the Father is ἀγέννητος [agennētos] while the Son is γεννητός [gennētos]; we also add that this generation has no beginning in time, and that it is of a kind that surpasses the grasp of every mortal. For "the Word was in the beginning, and all things were made by him," and the same passage calls the Son the only begotten. Of him the prophet also says: "From the womb, from the dawn, the dew of your birth is yours" (Ps. 110.3); the Jews themselves interpret this passage of the eternal birth of the Messiah. Therefore what Gentilis wants does not follow. For that generation is inexplicable and has no beginning in time. Hence in it there is nothing later and nothing earlier, but the whole is co-eternity.

units.la: Ac miranda est humani ingenij temeritas, tantam rerum diui-narum maiestate & lucem absconditam conatis ingredi & enunciare. Si auris non audiuit, oculus non vidit, nec ingressa sunt in cor hominis, quae praeparauit Deus diligentibus se: quanto magis illud æterni Filij Dei mysterium,& æterna illa generatio adoranda potius erat,quàm perscrutanda ? Sed videamus quomodo hic sint loquuti veteres. Theod.lib.1.cap.4. ἐ χρονικῶς, ἐδ᾽ ἐκ διαςημάλος γεννη-σας τὸν μονογενῆ υἱόν, ibidem dicitur, υἱότης ἀμεταπλωτος. Item Filius Dei genitus, sed ἀρρήτως καὶ ἀνεκδιηγήτως, ἀκαταλαμπτως ἀπεριγραπτως. quibus verbis expresserunt modum imperscrutabilé. Idem vt indicarent hunc modum principio temporis carere, vocarunt γέννησιν ἀναρχον, vt est videre apud Damascenum & Theodoretum citato loco.
units.tr: How marvellous is the rashness of the human mind, which tries to enter into and declare a light so hidden from the majesty of divine things! "If the ear has not heard, nor the eye seen, nor has it entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him" (1 Cor. 2.9): how much more should the mystery of the eternal Son of God, and that eternal generation, have been adored rather than searched into? But let us see how the ancients spoke here. Theodoret, book 1, chapter 4: the Father begot the only-begotten Son not temporally, nor by any division [οὐ χρονικῶς, οὐδὲ ἐκ διασπάσεως] and there it is said that the sonship is unchangeable [υἱότης ἀμετάπτωτος]. Likewise, the Son of God is begotten ineffably and indescribably, incomprehensibly, uncircumscribably [ἀρρήτως καὶ ἀνεκδιηγήτως, ἀκαταλήπτως, ἀπεριγράπτως]. By these words they expressed the inscrutable manner. And to indicate that this manner has no beginning in time, they called the generation ἀναρχος [anarchos], without beginning, as may be seen in Damascene and Theodoret in the passage cited.

units.la: Socrates lib.1.cap.8. τῆ τρόπου τῆς γεννήσεως ἀνεκφράςου, καὶ ἀνεπιλο-γίςου πάσῃ γεννητῇ φύσει τυγχάνοντος. Statuamus ergo modum generationis Filij Dei hunc esse verum, ἄρρητον videlicet, ἀκαταληπτον, ἀπεριφράςον. Ex quo efficitur λόγον genitum sine tempore,& ante omne tempus, Filium semper cum Patre fuisse: nunquam etiam fuisse Deum,quo Pater non fuerit:nec fuisse aliquando, quo Filius non fuerit.
units.tr: Socrates, book 1, chapter 8: the manner of the generation is inexpressible and unreasonable, as belongs to every begotten nature [τῷ τρόπῳ τῆς γεννήσεως ἀνεκφράστου καὶ ἀνεπιλογίστου πάσῃ γεννητῇ φύσει τυγχάνοντος]. Let us therefore hold that the manner of the generation of the Son of God is this: that it is ineffable, incomprehensible and indescribable. From this it follows that the Word was begotten without time, before all time, that the Son has always been with the Father; nor was there ever a time when God was God and the Father was not Father, nor a time when the Son was not.

units.la: Reliquos modos repudiauit Ecclesia, & antiquissimi scriptores Christiani,vt Iustinus Martyr,Irenęus & alij,quos paucis perstrin-gemus.
units.tr: The Church rejected other modes, as did the most ancient Christian writers, such as Justin Martyr, Irenaeus and others, whom we will briefly touch upon.

units.la: Quidam dicebant Filium Dei à Patre descendere κατὰ μερισμὸν, qualis sententia videtur Philoponi fuisse, qui naturam Diuinam particulatim in personas distribuebat, quemadmodum fiunt ex eadem auri massa,duo,vel tria rameta,sic ἐν dicitur δισπρμένον εἰς δύο.
units.tr: Some said that the Son of God descends from the Father by division [κατὰ μερισμόν]. This seems to have been the opinion of Philoponus, who distributed the divine nature piece by piece among the persons, just as two or three branches are made from the same mass of gold; so the Word is said to be divided into two.

units.la: Alij κατὰ προβολὴν,hoc est,per germinationem,quemadmodum videmus ex radicibus surculos prodire.
units.tr: Others said by projection [κατὰ προβολήν], that is, by germination, just as we see shoots coming forth from roots.

units.la: Nonnulli κατὰ ῥεῦσιν, hoc est per defluxum, vt liberi à parenti-bus suis naturaliter nascuntur.
units.tr: Some said by flowing forth [κατὰ ῥεῦσιν], that is, by an outflow, just as children are naturally born from their parents.

units.la: Quidam etiam κατὰ ἐρυγῶ, hoc est per eructationem,vt est vide-re in epistola Arij,apud Theod.lib.1.cap.6.
units.tr: Some also said by belching forth [κατ᾽ ἐρυγήν], that is, by eructation, as may be seen in the letter of Arius, cited in Theodoret, book 1, chapter 6.

units.la: Nec defuerunt qui dicerent κατ᾽ ἀλλοίωσιν, hoc est per alteratio-nem substantiæ,vt est apud Socratem lib.1.cap.8.
units.tr: Nor were there lacking those who said by alteration [κατ᾽ ἀλλοίωσιν], that is, by an alteration of substance, as is found in Socrates, book 1, chapter 8.

units.la: Hos modos repudiauit antiquitas,&Ariani quoq;:sed alio fine, nempe vt ὁμοούσιον exploderent.de quo vide Niceph.lib.8.cap.18.
units.tr: Antiquity rejected these modes, and the Arians too, but for another purpose, namely to explode the term ὁμοούσιος [homoousios]. On this see Nicephorus, book 8, chapter 18.

units.la: Sic enim colligebant,Filius Dei non est natus à Patre κατὰ μερισ-μὸν, nō κατὰ προβολὴν,non κατὰ ῥεῦσιν non κατ᾽ ἐρυγῶ, non etiā κατ᾽ ἀλ-λοίωσιν.Ergo non est ὁμοούσιος dicendus,quia quod tale est,his modis tale esse dicitur.
units.tr: For they inferred thus: the Son of God is not begotten from the Father by division, nor by projection, nor by flowing forth, nor by belching forth, nor even by alteration. Therefore he is not to be called consubstantial, because what is of one substance is said to be so by these modes.

units.la: Respondemus, superesse alium modum, quem illi praetereunt, & quem unum approbavit Ecclesia, nempe κατὰ μονὴν [?], hoc est, per immanentiam, seu immansionem, aut κατὰ κοινωνίαν [?], qua tota natura communicatur: ideóque ὁμοούσιος est, & ut constaret de coaeternitate, ἀῤῥήτον [?] eundem & ἀκαταλήπτον [?] appellarunt.
units.tr: We answer that there remains another mode, which they pass over, and which the Church alone approved: namely, by abiding [κατὰ μονήν], that is, by immanence or indwelling, or by communion [κατὰ κοινωνίαν], by which the whole nature is communicated. Therefore he is ὁμοούσιος, and so that his co-eternity might be clear, they called him ineffable and incomprehensible [ἀῤῥήτον and ἀκαταλήπτον].

units.la: Caeterum has phrases antiquissimas fuisse, ex eo colligi potest, quòd apud Iustinum martyrem quoque reperiuntur. Is enim refutat aliquoties illud, κατ' ἀπόλομιν [?], κατὰ τομὴν [?], ἀπολομὴ ὡς ἀπομερίζομένης τῆς πατρικῆς οὐσίας [?]. Hunc modum posteri dixerunt κατὰ μερισμόν. Idem damnat eos qui dicebant, κατὰ διάστασιν aut κατ' ἀπόῤῥοιαν, Filium genitum. διάστασις videtur aliis fuisse προβολὴ. Nam ἀπόῤῥοια & ῥεῦσις idem declarant. Haec de modo generationis libuit repetere, vt constaret quomodo veteres sint locuti, & quàm temerè hodie res tanta & imperscrutabilis tractetur.
units.tr: Moreover, that these phrases are very ancient can be gathered from the fact that they are also found in Justin Martyr. For he repeatedly refutes the notion of generation by cutting off [κατ᾽ ἀπόλυσιν], by section [κατὰ τομήν], or by separation, as if the paternal substance were being parted off. Later writers called this mode "by division." The same Justin condemns those who said that the Son was begotten by separation [κατὰ διάστασιν] or by effusion [κατ᾽ ἀπόῤῥοιαν]. Separation seems to have been the same to others as projection, for effusion and flowing forth declare the same thing. I have thought it worth repeating these points about the mode of generation, so that it is clear how the ancients spoke, and how rashly so great and inscrutable a matter is handled today.

units.la: Quemadmodum autem non sequitur, Alius est generas, & alius genitus: ergo alia est οὐσία Patris, & alia τὸ λόγου [?]. ita non est consequens, alius est generans, & alius genitus: ergo λόγος genitus tempore posterior est generante. Nam hic ambiguitate vocis luditur, quod olim etiam Ariani factitarunt. ἀγέννητον ergo Patris esse proprium, & γέννητον Filij proprium esse concedimus, sed sano intellectu.
units.tr: Just as it does not follow that because one is the begetter and another the begotten, therefore the substance of the Father is one thing and the Word another, so it is not a consequence that because one is the begetter and another the begotten, therefore the begotten Word is later in time than the begetter. For here the ambiguity of the word is played upon, as the Arians once also did. We therefore concede that ἀγέννητον [agennēton] is proper to the Father and γεννητόν [gennēton] proper to the Son, but in a sound sense.

units.la: Primum enim ἀγέννητος dicitur, qui originè nullo modo habet, γεννητὸς autem qui à Patre est genitus. Sic Pater in se dicitur & solus ἀγέννητος, quia nulla est res, à qua origine trahat: Filius autem γεννητός, quia à Patre ἀῤῥήτως [?] genitus. Hoc sensu nihil absurdi habent voces illae: Sed potest tam Pater, quàm Spiritus sanctus dici ἀγέννητος, quatenus vterq; nullo patre ortus est: Filius autem solus γεννητὸς, ὡς ἐκ τῆς Πατρὸς γεννηθείς [?]. Deinde ἀγέννητος vel potius ἀγένητος significat etiam ἀγένη-τον [?], id est, quod non est factum. Sic Philosophi dixerunt elementa ingenita ἀγένητα [?], quia nulla his priora essent principia. ita Creator à creaturis separatur, vt ille ἀγέννητος, hæ autem γεννητὰ appellentur: qua significatione facile est videre, Christum non dici γεννητόν, sed ἀγένητον [?], cuiusmodi i est tota Diuinitas indiuisibilis.
units.tr: For he is called ἀγέννητος who in no way has origin, while he is γεννητός who has been begotten by the Father. In this sense the Father alone is called ἀγέννητος in himself, because there is no thing from which he draws origin; the Son is γεννητός because he is begotten by the Father ineffably. In this sense those terms have nothing absurd. But the Holy Spirit as well as the Father can be called ἀγέννητος, insofar as each is born of no father; the Son alone is γεννητός, as begotten of the Father. Further, ἀγέννητος, or rather ἀγένητος, also signifies ἀγένητον [agēneton], that is, what has not been made. Thus the philosophers called the elements ingenerate [ἀγένητα], because there were no principles prior to them. So the Creator is separated from creatures, so that he is called ἀγέννητος and they are called γεννητά. In this sense it is easy to see that Christ is not called γεννητός but ἀγένητος, as is the whole indivisible Divinity.

units.la: Demùm si opponatur ἀγέννητον τῷ γεννητῷ [?] temporis ratione, hoc est, quod nunquam esse coepit, sed fuit ab aeterno, ei quod illo posterius est, & coepit esse tempore aliquo: hoc pacto etiam omnes tres personae Diuinitatis sunt ingenitae, quia nullum habet temporis principium. Sed ante omne tempus fuere Ideóq; nō simpliciter admitti debet illa sententia, λόγος ἐστὶ γεννητὸς, & solus Pater est ἀγέννητος, quum suo modo etiam Filius sit ἀγέννητος.
units.tr: Finally, if ἀγέννητον is opposed to γεννητῷ in terms of time, that is, that what has never begun to be but has been from eternity, is opposed to what is later and began to be at some time, then in this way all three persons of the Godhead are unbegotten, because none of them has a beginning in time. For they existed before all time. Therefore that saying, "the Word is begotten, and the Father alone is unbegotten," must not be simply admitted, since in its own way the Son too is unbegotten.

units.la: An proprium Patris sit, vt appelletur vnus & solus Deus. X.
units.tr: Whether it is proper to the Father that he alone is called the one and only God. X.

units.la: Veniamus nunc ad eminentiā illam Dei Patris, cuius se patronū Gentilis cōstituit. Nam de se ita & scripsit, & loquutus est, quòd esset patronus summi Patris eminentiæ, & assertor gloriæ Patris. Nec dubitauit etiam dicere, Neminē adhuc, (quod ipse quidem sciret) pro gloria & eminentia Patris mortuum esse: Prophetas, Apostolos, piosque Martyres pro Filij gloria persecutiones, morte, & extrema quæq; passos esse: eminentiam autem Dei Patris, nullos adhuc Martyres habere.
units.tr: Let us now come to that pre-eminence of God the Father, of which Gentilis has made himself the champion. For he himself wrote and spoke thus, that he was the defender of the pre-eminence of the supreme Father and the upholder of the Father's glory. Nor did he hesitate to say that no one hitherto (so far as he himself knew) had died for the glory and pre-eminence of the Father: that the Prophets, Apostles and pious Martyrs had suffered persecutions, death and every extremity for the glory of the Son, but that the pre-eminence of God the Father had no Martyrs as yet.

units.la: Quæredum igitur, quænam hæc eminentia sit, quæ ad Patrem solum, ad Filium autem minimè pertinet. Respondet ille, Patrem esse vnum & solum Deum, quem nobis Scriptura proponat.
units.tr: We must ask, therefore, what this pre-eminence is, which pertains to the Father alone and not at all to the Son. He replies that the Father is the one and only God, whom Scripture sets before us.

units.la: Expendant hic boni viri, quàm sit illa sententia gloriæ Christi intolerabilis, vt quæ Patri Diuinitatè sic attribuit, vt eâdem Christum exuat & spoliet. De solo Patre intelligendum est, ait, quoties Scriptura vnius Dei, mentione facit. Christus igitur proprie Deus non est. Quæ enim vni & soli competunt proprie, alteri non possunt accommodari. quod si verum est, Christus non solùm ἰδία à Patre differet, sed ne Deus quidē dici poterit. Itaq; prius illud palàm audebat profiteri, differētes esse species, Patrem & Filium etiam secundùm essentiā: & in eo sic perfricuerat frontem, vt sine rubore differentiam illam vrgeret: posterius autem videbat apertiore habere blasphemiam, & inuidiam apud fideles. ideóq; dicebat Christum appellari etiam Deum communicatione Diuinitatis, sed ita vt alium induceret errorem, Christum videlicet tempore esse posteriorem Patre. Pater, inquiebat, ab æterno sine principio, Filius in tempore, & à principio. Pater per se Deus, Filius communicatione, quemadmodum in regni consortiū Rex admittit filium natū. Pater vnus Deus & solus Deus: Filius nō vnus, sed alius Deus, nec solus Deus.
units.tr: Let good men consider here how intolerable that statement is to the glory of Christ, which so attributes divinity to the Father that it strips and despoils Christ of the same. It must be understood of the Father alone, he says, whenever Scripture makes mention of the one God. Christ, therefore, is not properly God. For what belongs properly to the one and only is not able to be applied to another. And if this is true, Christ will not only differ from the Father in his own nature, but cannot even be called God. Thus he formerly dared to profess openly that the Father and the Son are different species, even according to essence; and in this he so hardened his forehead that he pressed that difference without blushing. But later he saw that this carried a more open blasphemy and hatred among the faithful. Therefore he said that Christ is called God also by communication of the Godhead, but in such a way as to introduce another error, namely that Christ is later in time than the Father. The Father, he said, is from eternity without beginning, the Son in time and from a beginning. The Father is God through himself, the Son by communication, just as a king admits a born son into partnership of the kingdom. The Father is the one God and the only God; the Son is not the one, but another God, and not the only God.

units.la: Cæterùm meminisse debemus Scriptura de Deo loqui interdū distinctè, id est, respectu certæ Diuinitatis personę, vt quū Ioan.dicit, λόγος erat apud Deum, manifestè Pater intelligitur. Sic Christus in cruce clamās, Deus meus, Deus meº, quare deseruisti me, ad Patrem inuocatione direxit, Matth.27. De Filio autem expresse dicit Ioan.Et λόγος[?] erat Deus. Sic Thomas de Filio ait, Dominus meus, & Deus meus. Joann.20. Act.5. Petrus ait Ananiam non hominibus mentitum, sed Deo, hoc est, Spiritui sancto.
units.tr: Moreover we must remember that Scripture sometimes speaks of God distinctly, that is, with respect to a certain person of the Godhead; as when John says that the Word was with God, it is clearly the Father who is understood. So Christ, crying on the cross, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me, directed his invocation to the Father (Matt. 27). But of the Son John says expressly, and the Word was God (John 1). So Thomas says of the Son, My Lord and my God (John 20). Peter says (Acts 5) that Ananias lied not to men but to God, that is, to the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Alias Scriptura de Deo loquitur absolutè, & secundum essentiam, ut intelligatur tota Divinitas, à qua nulla personarum excluditur, ut Joann. 4. Deus Spiritus est. Item Dei sumus cooperarij, Dei agricolatio, Dei ædificatio estis. 1.Cor.3.Sapientia mundi stultitia est apud Deum: apud quem Deum? Patremne ut excludatur Filius?minimè.sed essentialiter hic, ut alibi sæpius, ponitur vocabulum Dei, pertinens ad tres personas.
units.tr: At other times Scripture speaks of God absolutely and according to essence, so that the whole Godhead is understood, from which no person is excluded: as in John 4, God is Spirit. Likewise, we are God's fellow-workers, God's husbandry, God's building (1 Cor. 3). The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God: with which God? With the Father, so that the Son is excluded? By no means. But here, as elsewhere very often, the word God is used essentially, pertaining to the three persons.

units.la: Hæc quum negligat Gentilis, & contendat ubique Scripturam distinctè loqui de Deo, necessariò excludit Christum ab essentiæ unitate, & Divinitatis proprietate, ac demum tempore posteriorem facit. Accedit alia impietas & ambitiosa præsumptio, quòd separat genus martyrij. Illi enim vulgare iam est, & protritum pro gloria Christi patinouum[?] excogitauit, pro eminentia & gloria Patris mori. Grauis error est, Deum Patrem velle colere, & honorare extra Filium, grauius sine Filio, grauissimum cum Filii ignominia. Deus etiam colendus est, ut se patefacit: manifesta est patefactio Joan.5. Qui non honorat Filium, non honorat Patrem. & Joan.12. Pater cœlitus testatur se in Filio glorificari.
units.tr: Since Gentilis neglects these things, and contends that everywhere Scripture speaks of God in a distinct sense, he necessarily excludes Christ from unity of essence and from the proper attributes of the Godhead, and in the end makes him later in time. Another impiety and ambitious presumption is added, in that he separates the kind of martyrdom. For it is already commonplace and worn out for him to devise a kind of new martyrdom for the glory of Christ: to die for the pre-eminence and glory of the Father. It is a grave error to wish to worship and honour God the Father apart from the Son; graver still without the Son; gravest of all with dishonour to the Son. God must also be worshipped as he reveals himself; the revelation is plain in John 5: he who does not honour the Son does not honour the Father; and in John 12 the Father testifies from heaven that he is glorified in the Son.

units.la: Quare tenemus hanc certam & perpetuam formulam honorandi Patrem, ut illum in Filio honoremus, in quo unico & solo nobis placatus est, ut extra Filium nullus cultus Patri sit gratus. Sed astutus est Satan ad obruendam gloriam Christi speciosò prætextu abutens, quòd vindicet Patri suam eminentiam debitam, quem tamen à nullo Prophetarum, Apostolorum, vllisue piis requisiuit unquam. Verùm hæc via est ad contemptum Christi. Sic cum Judæis & Turcis facilè pacem fecisset Gentilis.
units.tr: Wherefore we hold this certain and perpetual formula of honouring the Father: that we honour him in the Son, in whom alone he is reconciled to us, so that no worship of the Father outside the Son is pleasing to him. But Satan is crafty, abusing a specious pretext in order to overthrow the glory of Christ, pretending to vindicate for the Father his due pre-eminence, which yet he never demanded from any of the Prophets, Apostles or pious people. Truly this way leads to the contempt of Christ. Thus Gentilis would have made an easy peace with the Jews and the Turks.

units.la: XI. Scripturæ judicium & consensus hac de re.
units.tr: XI. Scripture's judgment and consensus on this matter.

units.la: PErpetuus est scripturæ & veræ Ecclesiæ consensus, quo omnia illa dogmata damnantur. Hic veritatis consensus sic proponetur dilucidè & breviter:
units.tr: Perpetual is the agreement of Scripture and of the true Church, by which all those dogmas are condemned. This consensus of truth will be set out here clearly and briefly.

units.la: Essentia Divinitatis una est,in qua tres nobis hypo-stases ftafes[?] proponit scriptura, Patris videlicet, Filii, & Spiritus sancti, ita vt nec tres Deos, nec essentiæ distractionem agnoscamus. Filius & Spiritus sanctus ita sunt Patri consubstantiales, vt verus & vnus cum illo sint Deus æternus & infinitus.
units.tr: The essence of the Godhead is one, and in it Scripture presents to us three hypostases [ὑποστάσεις], namely of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, so that we acknowledge neither three Gods nor any division of the essence. The Son and the Holy Spirit are so consubstantial with the Father that, together with him, they are the one true, eternal and infinite God.

units.la: Vnus ille Deus & altissimus non solius Patris est appellatio, exclu-so Filio & Spiritu sancto.
units.tr: That one God, the Most High, is not the name of the Father alone, with the Son and the Holy Spirit excluded.

units.la: Consensum hunc esse dico scripturæ & Ecclesiæ veræ. Deus e-nim coli dicitur, vt sese patefecit, & sic coluit eum semper vera Ecclesia: patefecit autem se vnum, hoc est τῇ οὐσίᾳ rem esse vnam, per se subsistentem, æternam, intelligentem, bonam &c. personis autem, hoc est τῇ ὑποστάσει, patefecit se trinum.
units.tr: I say that this agreement belongs to Scripture and to the true Church. For God is said to be worshipped as he has revealed himself, and so the true Church has always worshipped him. He has revealed himself as one, that is, one thing in essence [τῇ οὐσίᾳ], subsisting through itself, eternal, intelligent, good, and so on; but in persons, that is in hypostasis [τῇ ὑποστάσει], he has revealed himself as three.

units.la: Quod οὐσία res sit vna, manifesta sunt testimonia, Deut. 6. Audi Israel, Dominus Deus tuus Deus v n v s est. 1.Cor.8.Scimus quod non sit Deus, nisi vnus. Ephef.4. Vnus est Deus. Deuter.4. יהוה[?] est Deus, & præter eum non est alius. Vnum ergo se patefecit. Quod autem personis trinum se patefecit Deus, testatur Marcus 1. Matt. 3. in baptismo Christi, Pater, Filius & Spiritus sanctus exprimuntur. Sic in baptismi institutione, Matth.28. Marc.16. Nec ferenda est illa elusio, qua ad solum consensum illa refert Gentilis. Non negamus consensum voluntatis, sed addimus vnitatem etiā essentiæ.
units.tr: That the essence [οὐσία] is one thing, the testimonies make plain. Deut. 6: "Hear, Israel, the Lord your God is one God." 1 Cor. 8: "We know that there is no God but one." Eph. 4: "There is one God." Deut. 4: YHWH [יהוה] is God, and there is no other besides him. He therefore revealed himself as one. That he revealed himself as three in persons, Mark 1 bears witness; in Matt. 3, at the baptism of Christ, Father, Son and Holy Spirit are named. So too in the institution of baptism, Matt. 28 and Mark 16. That evasion by which Gentilis refers these texts only to agreement of will is not to be borne. We do not deny agreement of will, but we add unity of essence as well.

units.la: Firma igitur manet, & Marpesia caute solidior, sententia illa. Deus patefecit se vnum essentia: Trinum autem in personis: ergo Trinitas in vnitate, & vnitas in Trinitate nobis est veneranda: atque hic verus & vnicus Dei cultus est.
units.tr: That saying therefore stands firm, and is more solid than any caution of Marpesia: God has revealed himself one in essence and three in persons. Therefore the Trinity in unity, and the unity in Trinity, is to be venerated by us; and this is the true and only worship of God.

units.la: Et ad hunc modum Ecclesia semper intellexit scriptura & symbolum Apostolicū, Credo in Deū videlicet essentia τῇ οὐσίᾳ VNVM. ac mox subiicitur enumeratione explicatio personarum, vt constet quis sit ille vnus Deus potens, videlicet Filius eius, & Spiritus sanctus.
units.tr: In this way the Church has always understood both Scripture and the Apostles' Creed, which says "I believe in God," namely one in essence [τῇ οὐσίᾳ]. Immediately afterwards comes the explanation of the persons, by enumeration, so that it is clear who that one powerful God is: namely his Son and the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Ac falsa est interpretatio Gentilis, qui hic distinguit ita: Credo in Deum Patrem: ac vocem, Deum, ad solum Patrem restringit. Sophistica (inquam) est interpretatio ex mala distinctione orta. Nec symbolum Nicenum, nec Athanasii, aut vllus recte sentientiū hoc pacto intellexit. Quare Filius & Spiritus sanctus, verus, & vnus cū Deo Patre, Deus sunt, & in scriptura nobis proponuntur, quoties de vno solo & vero Deo יהוה[?] Israelis loquitur. Marci cap.10, ait Christus adolescenti diviti, Nemo bonus nisi unus Deus. Quòd si hîc Valentini sententia dicitur locum habere, ita colligas necesse est:
units.tr: The interpretation of Gentilis is false, for he punctuates thus: "I believe in God the Father," and restricts the word "God" to the Father alone. It is a sophistical interpretation, I say, arising from a faulty punctuation. Neither the Nicene Creed, nor the Athanasian, nor anyone who thinks rightly has understood it in this way. Therefore the Son and the Holy Spirit, true and one with God the Father, are God, and are set before us in Scripture whenever it speaks of the one and only true God of Israel, YHWH [יהוה]. In Mark ch. 10 Christ says to the rich young man, "No one is good but one, God" [οὐδεὶς ἀγαθὸς εἰ μὴ εἷς ὁ θεός]. But if the opinion of Valentinus is said to hold here, you must necessarily infer the following:

units.la: Nemo bonus, nisi unus, nimirum Deus: At unus Deus solus est Pater: Ergo solus Pater bonus erit. Nam Christus exclusivè loquitur, Cur me bonû dicis? οὐδεὶς ἀγαθὸς, εἰ μὴ εἷς ὁ θεός[?]. Unus Deus est appellatio solius Patris: Ergo solius Patris est bonum esse.
units.tr: No one is good except the one, namely God; but the one God is the Father alone; therefore the Father alone will be good. For Christ speaks exclusively: "Why do you call me good?" "The one God" is the name of the Father alone; therefore it belongs to the Father alone to be good.

units.la: Nec potest se ex hoc labyrintho explicare, nisi quòd Christus communicatione bonus etiam dicatur, Pater autem proprie & primarie: quæ est intolerabilis blasphemia. Nam Christum separat à bonitate, ut etiam à Divinitate.
units.tr: Nor can he extricate himself from this labyrinth, except by saying that Christ is also called good by communication, while the Father is good properly and primarily. That is an intolerable blasphemy, for it separates Christ from goodness, and so also from Divinity.

units.la: Nos verò sic colligimus verè & piè: Qui proprie & per se bonus est, hunc oportet esse illum unum verum, & solum Deum ex ore Christi dicentis, Nemo bonus, nisi unus Deus: At Christus Filius Dei, & Spiritus sanctus per se, & proprie boni sunt: Ergo una cum Patre sunt ille unus, solus, & verus Deus, à quo omnia quæcunque bona sunt, suam bonitatem habent precatiam. Concidit hoc argumento, & evanescit tota illa subtilitas, Quòd Pater solus sit unus ille & solus Deus.
units.tr: But we conclude truly and piously as follows. He who is good properly and of himself must be that one true and only God, according to the words of Christ, "No one is good but one God." But Christ, the Son of God, and the Holy Spirit are good of themselves and properly; therefore together with the Father they are that one, only and true God, from whom all things that are good have their goodness as a gift. This argument overturns and dissolves that whole subtlety, that the Father alone is that one and only God.

units.la: Accedunt alia etiam testimonia, ut Esa.44. Unus ille Deus dicitur primus & novissimus: quod elogium de Patre intelligit Gentilis. Sed convincitur à Joann. qui Apocal. cap.1.21.22. idem Christo tribuit. Ex quo efficitur, Christum esse comprehensum in hoc titulo unius Dei. Nec admittimus quod affert, Christum dici primum & novissimum solo creaturarum respectu. Itè λόγος in novo testamento dicitur Deus non fictitius, sed verus. Joan. 1. At verus Deus tantùm unus est novi & veteris testamenti auctor. Ergo λόγος in eo titulo unius Dei est comprehensus, quia est testamenti auctor.
units.tr: There are other testimonies too. Isa. 44 calls that one God the first and the last, a title which Gentilis understands of the Father alone. But he is refuted by John, who in Apocal. 1.21.22 ascribes the same to Christ. From this it follows that Christ is comprised in this title of the one God. Nor do we accept what he adduces, that Christ is called first and last only with respect to creatures. Likewise the Word [λόγος] in the New Testament is called God, not as a fiction but truly (John 1). But the true God is the author of the old and new covenant alone. Therefore the Word is comprised in that title of the one God, because he is the author of the covenant.

units.la: Item unus ille & solus Deus, est verus & solus salvator. Esa.45. verf.11. At λόγος in novo testamento, nō est unus & solus ille Deus, si credimus Gentili. Liquet igitur λόγον non esse Salvatorem: quod non solum absurdum, sed etiam impium est. Joan.1. ait Andreas, Invenimus Messiam. Falsa igitur est minor, quam extruxit Getilis.
units.tr: Likewise that one and only God is the true and only Saviour (Isa. 45, v. 11). But the Word in the New Testament is not that one and only God, if we believe Gentilis. It is clear, then, that the Word is not the Saviour; which is not only absurd but impious. In John 1 Andrew says, "We have found the Messiah." Therefore the minor premise which Gentilis constructed is false.

units.la: Item præter illum unum & solum יהוה, non est alius אלהים Esa. 44. λόγος, ut ait Gentilis, non est unus ille & solus יהוה. Ergo λόγος non est verus אלהים, quod iterum absurdum. Falsum igitur Gentilis illud.
units.tr: Likewise, besides that one and only YHWH [יהוה] there is no other Elohim [אלהים] (Isa. 44). The Word, as Gentilis says, is not that one and only YHWH. Therefore the Word is not the true Elohim, which again is absurd. That claim of Gentilis is therefore false.

units.la: Præterea λόγος in novo testamento est creator, Coloss. 1. & Ioan. 1. quæ proprietas est solius & unius Dei. λόγος igitur ad unius & solius Dei nomen pertinet, &c.
units.tr: Moreover, the Word in the New Testament is creator (Col. 1 and John 1), and this property belongs to the one and only God. The Word therefore pertains to the name of the one and only God, and so on.

units.la: Ex his & similibus locis facile demonstrari poteit, quàm sit absurda & impia sententia, statuere, vnum & solum Deum Patrem tantùm dici, exclusò Filio: quum è contrario sentiat Ecclesia, Patre, Filium & Spiritum sanctū, esse vnum illum verum, & solum Deū patefactum in scripturis. Vnum, vt dicimus, propter οὐσίαν[?]: Trinum, quia his personis se patefacit. Neque hîc quæreda est illa οὐσίας[?] eminentia, quum Trinitas sit tota æqualitas, in qua nihil est maius, nec minus. Vnus & idem Deus Pater, & λόγος eius semper assistens humano generi, vt ait Irenæus lib.4.cap.47.
units.tr: From these and similar passages it can easily be shown how absurd and impious is the opinion that the one and only God is called the Father alone, with the Son excluded. On the contrary, the Church holds that Father, Son and Holy Spirit are that one true and only God revealed in the Scriptures: one, as we say, because of the essence [οὐσίαν], and three because he reveals himself in these persons. Nor is any eminence of essence to be sought here, since the Trinity is wholly equality, in which there is nothing greater or less. "One and the same God the Father, and his Word always present with the human race," as Irenaeus says in book 4, ch. 47.

units.la: Eminentia autem illa quam impugnamus, inducit nobis inæ- qualitatem, prius & posterius, maius & minus in Diuinitatis οὐσία[?]: ideoque exploditur. Interea tamen nō ignoramus, quomodo Christus humanitatis assumptę ratione, & officio mediationis minor sit Patre, & dicatur à scriptura. Sed id nihil ad rem. Nam inæqualitas, quam hîc confutamus, non in hypostasibus, sed in essentia Diuina locum quærit.
units.tr: But that eminence which we oppose introduces inequality into the essence [οὐσία] of the Godhead: before and after, greater and less. Therefore it is rejected. Meanwhile we are not unaware that Christ, by reason of the humanity he assumed and of the office of mediation, is less than the Father, and is so called in Scripture. But that is beside the point. For the inequality which we refute here has its place not in the hypostases but in the divine essence.

units.la: Censura Gentilis de patrum scriptis. XII.
units.tr: Gentile's criticism of the writings of the Fathers. XII.

units.la: DIximus sententiam nostram de Trinitate consentire cum scriptura, & cum Symbolis orthodoxis. Scripturam à Gentile in suas partes malè trahi, nouo genere interpretationis: sic etiam in Symboli expositione ludit. Et Apostolicum quidem non audet conuellere: tamen mala distinctione interpretatur. Reliqua symbola securius contemnit. Pari reuerentia tractat patres. Athanasiū probrosè insectatur, quasi corruptorem Symboli Niceni: Symbolum ipsius Athanasii nugas non erubescit dicere sol 30. Augustinum Magistrum imperiosum, alios aliis conuitiis repellit. At ne destitui videatur omni præsidio antiquitatis, ad omnes veteres confugit, quos nullo iure suos facit. Inprimis amplectitur Iustinum Martyrem, Ignatium, Tertullianum, Irenæū & Hilariū. Non tamè ita, quin interdum eos, si libeat, licere etiā sibi velit contemnere, vt huic malo domesticam esse dixeris [illegible, ~20 letters] Nos ex illis ipsis, quos ille admittit, nostram sen tentiū demonstrabimus. Nec erit interea difficile obseruatu, quàm astutè illorum authoritate & sententiis abutatur.
units.tr: We have said that our view of the Trinity agrees with Scripture and with the orthodox creeds. Gentile wrongly drags Scripture into his own camp by a new kind of interpretation, and he plays the same game in expounding the creed. He does not dare to overthrow the Apostles' Creed, but he interprets it with a bad distinction. The other creeds he despises more carelessly. He treats the Fathers with the same lack of reverence. He shamefully attacks Athanasius, as if he were a corrupter of the Nicene Creed, and he is not ashamed to call Athanasius's own creed trifles (p. 30). He calls Augustine an overbearing master and drives off others with abuse. But lest he seem to be left without any defence from antiquity, he flees to all the ancients, whom he claims as his own by no right. Above all he embraces Justin Martyr, Ignatius, Tertullian, Irenaeus and Hilary. Yet not so fully that he would not, whenever it pleased him, be willing to despise them as well, so that you might say this evil is native to him [illegible, about 20 letters]. We shall show our opinion from those very writers whom he admits, and meanwhile it will not be hard to see how cunningly he abuses their authority and their opinions.

units.la: Sententia Iustini Martyris & Philosophi. XIII.
units.tr: The opinion of Justin Martyr, philosopher. XIII.

units.la: Vstinus Martyr elegantissimus scriptor, & Apostolorū temporibus vicinus, rectè sentit de negotio Trinitatis, modò non malitiosè torqueatur ad nouam scripturæ interpretationem. Et obseruandum est, diuersam illi fuisse scribendi occasionem. Dum agit cum Tryphone Iudæo, illi probandum est contra Iudæos, præter Deum Patrem, quem Iudæi conditorem omnium agnoscūt, alium esse Dei Filium, qui sit quoque verus Deus. Nec interea discerpit [?]οσίαν, sed distinguit inter ὑποστάσεις. His sententiis abutitur iam Valentinus ad essentiæ separationem stabiliendam. Hanc autem mentem non fuisse Iustini, ex illis constat, quæ contra gentes scribit, vbi hoc vnicè vrget, non multos, sed vnum esse Deum. Hæc ita se habere, sciunt omnes, qui illum legerint diligentius.
units.tr: Justin Martyr, a most elegant writer and close to the times of the Apostles, judges the matter of the Trinity rightly, provided he is not maliciously twisted into a new interpretation of Scripture. It should be noted that he had a different occasion for writing. When he deals with the Jew Trypho, he has to prove against the Jews that, besides God the Father, whom the Jews acknowledge as maker of all things, there is another Son of God who is also true God. Nor does he divide the essence, but he distinguishes between the hypostases. Valentinus now abuses these statements to establish a separation of essence. That this was not Justin's mind is clear from what he writes against the Gentiles, where he presses this one point only: that God is not many but one. Everyone who has read him more carefully knows that this is so.

units.la: Duæ sunt igitur hæ propositiones Iustino propositæ. Vna contra gentes, Vnum esse Deum, nec plures, vt fabulose gentilitas credidit: altera, Hunc Deum vnum secundùm essentiam: Trinum autem numero personali, vel hypostatico.
units.tr: There are therefore two propositions put forward by Justin. The first, against the Gentiles: there is one God, and not several, as the Gentiles foolishly believed in their fables. The second: this God is one according to essence, but three according to personal or hypostatic number.

units.la: Quòd vnus sit Deus verus & æternus ex Poetis & Philosophis probat, quòd sacras literas gentes ignorarent. Vnde illud ex Orpheo citat, εἷς ἐξ' αὐτογενοῦς, ἑνὸς ἐκ [illegible, ~6 letters] πάντα τέτυκται. Et vt intelligamus ad societatem vnitatis pertinere etiam Filium, ex eiusdem Orphei ὄρφικος, affert illum versum: αὐδῶ ὀρκίζω σε, πατρὸς, τὸν φθέγξαλο πρῶτον. ac eleganter αὐδὴ interpretatur λόγον θεοῦ. Ex quo tandem efficit, illos veteres Poetas, voluisse nos διδάσκειν περὶ ἑνὸς καὶ μόνου θεοῦ. Iam tu colligi si εἷς καὶ μόνος θεὸς colligi potest ex Orpheo, non obstante quòd exprimit αὐτοξεύη καὶ αὐδῶ diuersas personas. Ergo ille αὐτοξεύης & αὐδὴ illius, vnus & solus Deus sunt.
units.tr: That there is one true and eternal God he proves from the poets and philosophers, since the Gentiles were ignorant of the sacred writings. Hence he cites from Orpheus the line: "One, from the self-begotten, from one all things were made" [εἷς ἐξ αὐτογενοῦς, ἑνὸς ἐκ ... πάντα τέτυκται]. And so that we may understand that the Son also belongs to the fellowship of unity, he quotes from the same Orpheus the verse: "I call upon you, the voice of the Father, who first spoke" [αὐδῶ ὀρκίζω σε, πατρὸς, τὸν φθέγξαλο πρῶτον], and he neatly interprets the voice as the Word of God. From this he finally concludes that those ancient poets meant to teach about one and only God. Now, if "one and only God" can be gathered from Orpheus, notwithstanding that he presents the self-begotten and the voice as different persons, then that self-begotten one and his voice are the one and only God.

units.la: Et vtvt se hic torqueat Valentinus, euidens[?] est id epitheton ad Filium etiam pertinere[?], vt scilicet εἷς, καὶ μόνος θεὸς appelletur. Nam, vt iam dixi, ex Orpheo αὐτοξεύη & αὐδῶ hac proprietate concludit.
units.tr: However Valentinus twists this, it is evident that this epithet also pertains to the Son, so that he too is called one and only God. For, as I have already said, from Orpheus he draws this very property for both the self-begotten and the voice.

units.la: Idem præterea manifestissimè de Filio affirmat, ὅτι αὐτὸς οὗτος μόνος καὶ ἄγιος καλούμενος καὶ θεὸς ὑπάρχων. qua sententia nihil manifestius stius de Filio Dei dici potest. Nō enim simpliciter, inquit, angelum appellari, & dominum esse: sed quòd hic ipse solus, & angelus dicatur, & Deus sit. Ubi est ergo proprietas illa Patris, qua unus & solus Deus dicitur? Habes hic τὸν λόγον εἶναι μόνον θεόν.
units.tr: Moreover, he affirms the same most plainly of the Son, that he alone is called angel and is God [ὅτι αὐτὸς οὗτος μόνος καὶ ἄγιος καλούμενος καὶ θεὸς ὑπάρχων]. Nothing plainer can be said of the Son of God than this statement. For he does not simply say that the angel is called and is Lord, but that this one alone is called angel and is God. Where, then, is that property of the Father by which he alone is called the one and only God? Here you have the Word being the only God.

units.la: Porrò quum Dominus inquit, ἐγὼ εἰμὶ ὁ ὤν, Iustinus reddit rationem, hoc illum dicere non respectu Filii, à quo ita se velit discernere, sed ἀντιδιαστέλλοντα ἑαυτὸν τοῖς μὴ οὖσιν. ex quo sequitur Filiū nō excludi in αὐτοθεουσίᾳ: sed hoc dictum esse, ut scirent homines se antea addictos fuisse non iis qui sunt, sed iis qui non sunt dii.
units.tr: Again, when the Lord says "I am who am", Justin gives the reason: he says this not with respect to the Son, from whom he wishes to distinguish himself, but setting himself over against those who are not [ἀντιδιαστέλλοντα ἑαυτὸν τοῖς μὴ οὖσιν]. From this it follows that the Son is not excluded from self-divinity; rather this was said so that men might know that they had formerly been bound not to those who are gods but to those who are not gods.

units.la: Et quod attinet ad vocem αὐτουσίας siue αὐτοθεουσίας, ait Iustinus, vocem αὐτὸς, de vero Deo intelligi debere. ἦ γὰρ[?], inquit, αὐτὸς, ἀντιτυπο-μία, τὸν ὄντως ὄντα σημαίνει θεόν. Itaque nihil hoc facit ad separationem Patris vel Filii. Nam mox λόγον θεοῦ ἀχώριστον appellat. Qua ergo te--meritate separaremus illum à Patris οὐσίᾳ, ut duæ sint numero οὐσίαι, & ita quidem ut hæc ab illa propagata sit? Magna profecto est præ-sumptio in tanto consensu, scrupulosius velle inquirere in res diui-nas, quæ δι᾽ ὧν διὰ πασῶν captum humani ingenii superant.
units.tr: As for the word "self-essence" or "self-divinity", Justin says that the word "self" must be understood of the true God, for "self", he says, signifies the God who truly is. So this does nothing for a separation of Father and Son. For soon afterwards he calls the Word of God inseparable. On what ground, then, should we separate him from the essence of the Father, so that there would be two essences in number, and indeed in such a way that the one is propagated from the other? Surely it is a great presumption, when there is such a consensus, to wish to inquire more scrupulously into divine things, which surpass the grasp of the human mind.

units.la: Præclarè igitur Iustinus, qui illa Mercurii sententia rem istam concludit: θεὸν νοῆσαι μὲν ἐστὶ χαλεπόν, φράσαι δὲ ἀδύνατον, ᾧ ἡ νοῆσαι δυνατόν.
units.tr: Justin therefore rightly concludes the matter with that saying of Mercury: to think God is difficult, but to express him is impossible [θεὸν νοῆσαι μὲν ἐστὶ χαλεπόν, φράσαι δὲ ἀδύνατον, ᾧ ἡ νοῆσαι δυνατόν].

units.la: Veniamus ad dialogum contra Tryphonem Iudæum, ut cōstet quàm appositè Gentilis suum δευτερώσιον inde probet: de quo cōstat ne somniasse quidem Iustinum. Illud igitur agit Tryphon Iudæus: Unum Deum creatorē cæli & terræ agnoscit, nō autē agnoscit Filiū Dei, nec Spiritum sanctū Deum. Quare Iustino probandū fuit, λόγον θεὸν quoque verum esse Deum, qui assumpserit hominem secundū Dei imaginē πλαστέν. Ideòque sæpe dicit, τὸν λόγον quoque esse verum Deum, qui homine assumpserit: ac proinde præter Patrem, alii quoque, nempe Filio competere Dei nomen, ut uterque sit unus Deus, quū plures non esse Deos ipse Tryphon affirmasset. Itaq; manifestè oppugnat Gentilitiū dogma Iustinus. nedū ut duas numero οὐσίας in Diuinis statuat, & ὁμοούσιον in ὁμοιούσιον transformet.
units.tr: Let us come to the dialogue against Trypho the Jew, so that it may be established how aptly Gentile proves his "second" point from it, a point of which it is certain Justin never even dreamed. Trypho the Jew does this: he acknowledges one God, creator of heaven and earth, but he does not acknowledge the Son of God or the Holy Spirit as God. Therefore Justin had to prove that the Word, who took on man according to the image of God, is also God and true God. So he often says that the Word is also the true God who took on man; and consequently, besides the Father, the name of God belongs also to another, namely the Son, so that each is one God, since Trypho himself had affirmed that there are not many gods. Thus Justin plainly opposes the Gentile dogma, far from establishing two essences in number in the divine nature and changing homoousios into homoiousios.

units.la: Eius verba hæc sunt, ἐστὶ ἡ λέγεται θεὸς καὶ κύριος ἕτερος ὑπὲρ τὸν ποιητὴν τῶν ὅλων, id est, alius præter illũ omnium cōditorem, est & dicitur Deus & Dominus. Item, ἔτος ὁ τῷ τε Αβραὰμ, ἡ τῷ Ιακὼβ, ἡ τῷ Μωσεῖ ὠφθαι λέγομενος ἡ γεγραμμένος θεός, ἕτερος ἐστὶ τῷ τὰ πάντα ποιήσαντος θεῷ, ἀριθμῷ λέγω ἀλλ᾽ ἡ γνώμῃ, id est, hic Deus qui dicitur & scribitur apparuisse Abrahamo, Iacobo, & Mosi, alius est quàm is Deus qui omnia fecit, numero dico, at nō sententia. Hæc ille, hypostases duas numero in vna οὐσίᾳ[?] constitues. Gentilem autem, vel Græcæ linguæ ignorātia, vel malitia fefellit, qui τὸν λόγον putarit à Iustino ἕτερον θεὸν vocari. Alibi aliquoties sese explicat, quum de Filio loquens θεὸς, φησὶ, καλεῖται, καὶ θεὸς ἐστι καὶ ἐστι[?]. Sed & αὐτόθεον non obscurè affirmat. Explicans enim locum Exod. 3. de Angelo Domini in rubo ardente, hunc Angelum ait fuisse λόγον Dei. & mox κύριον αὐτὸν ὄντα, καὶ θεὸν σημαί-νων, τὸν αὐτὸν λέγει. Ex quibus verbis non obscurè sequitur λόγον esse αὐτόθεον. Principio enim illum appellat Angelum Domini & ministrum Dei, mox eundem λόγον, κύριον αὐτὸν appellat, καὶ θεὸν αὐτόν. Ergo ille angelus Mosi visus, est αὐτόθεος secundum Iustinum.
units.tr: His words are these: "There is and is called God and Lord another beside the maker of all things" [ἔστι ... θεὸς καὶ κύριος ἕτερος ὑπὲρ τὸν ποιητὴν τῶν ὅλων], that is, another besides that creator of all is and is called God and Lord. Likewise: "This God who is said and written to have appeared to Abraham, Jacob and Moses is other than the God who made all things, other numerically I say, but not in judgement" [ἕτερος ἐστὶ τοῦ τὰ πάντα ποιήσαντος θεοῦ, ἀριθμῷ λέγω, ἀλλ᾽ οὐ γνώμῃ]. Here he sets up two hypostases numerically within one essence. Gentile, however, was misled either by ignorance of the Greek language or by malice, when he thought that Justin called the Word "another God". Elsewhere he explains himself several times, when speaking of the Son: he is called God, he says, and is God. But he also affirms the Son's self-divinity not obscurely. For in explaining the passage in Exodus 3 about the Angel of the Lord in the burning bush, he says this Angel was the Word of God, and then, showing that he is Lord and God himself, he calls him the same. From these words it follows, not obscurely, that the Word is self-God. For first he calls him the Angel of the Lord and minister of God, and then he calls the same Word "Lord himself" and "God himself". Therefore that angel who appeared to Moses is self-God according to Justin.

units.la: Videamus etiam modum generationis, quem Iustinus affert. Deus ab æterno genuit (inquit) δύναμιν quandam ἐξ ἑαυτοῦ λογικὴν, quæ & gloria Domini, Filius, Sapientia, Angelus, Deus, Dominus & λόγος dicitur. Non autem talis est ille λόγος, ait, qualem à nobis nasci videmus. Nos enim λόγον προβάλλοντες, λόγον γεννῶμεν, qui non est de substantia nostra, sed est ἑτερούσιος. Deus igitur λόγον genuit ὁμοούσιον. Sic postea, Verus est ille λόγος à Patre δυνάμει καὶ βουλῇ αὐτοῦ, sed non est verus, inquit, κατ' ἀποτομὴν, scilicet ὡς ἀπομερισζομένης τῆς τοῦ πατρὸς οὐσίας. Nam sic partita & secta non sunt τὰ αὐτὰ ἃ καὶ πρὶν τμηθῆναι, hoc est non sunt amplius id quod erant priusquam obsecarentur: ex quo manifestè colligi potest sententia Iustini, λόγον videlicet Dei τὸν αὐτὸν esse οὐσίᾳ cum generate. Idem quòd Filius fuerit cum Patre, indicat his verbis, τοῦτο τὸ γέννημα, πρὸ πάντων τῶν ποιημάτων συνὼν τῷ πα-τρί, καὶ τοῦτο ὁ πατὴρ προσωμίλει. Semper igitur Pater fuit, semper Filius fuit: & semper fuerunt, sunt, & erunt unus Deus.
units.tr: Let us also look at the mode of generation that Justin gives. God, he says, from eternity begat out of himself a certain rational power, which is also called the glory of the Lord, Son, Wisdom, Angel, God, Lord and Word. Yet that Word, he says, is not such as we see born from ourselves. For we, when we put forth a word, beget a word which is not of our substance but of another substance. God therefore begat a Word of the same essence (homoousios). So afterwards: the Word is true, from the Father, by his power and will; but he is not true, he says, by cutting off, that is, as if the substance of the Father were divided off. For things so divided and cut are not the same things they were before being cut, that is, they are no longer what they were before they were severed. From this one can clearly gather the opinion of Justin, namely that the Word of God is the same essence as the one who begat him. He indicates that the Son was with the Father by these words: "This offspring, existing with the Father before all creatures, and with him the Father conversed." Therefore the Father always was, the Son always was, and they always were, are and will be one God.

units.la: Alioquin, non rectè diceretur λόγος ἀτμητὸς καὶ ἀχώριστος τῷ πατρὸς, quemadmodū Solis φῶς ἀτμηλὸν ᾖ ἀχώρισ-τον ἐστι, τῇ ἡλίᾳ ἐν τῷ ἠέρᾳ ὄντος. Quoties igitur Iustinus λόγον appellat ἕτερον ἀριθμῷ, quum ait λόγος ἀ-ριθμῷ ἕτερον τί ἐστι. Et mox rursus τὸ γεννώμενον τῇ γεννῶντος ἀριθμῷ ἕτερον ἐστι[?], intelligi debet de numero hypostatico, nō autem de essentiali, quia duæ sunt personæ. Nisi enim de personis intelligamus, secū pu-gnantem faciemus Iustinū, qui toties urget unitate Patris & Filii. Deinde manifeste cum Ario faceret, qui hoc argumento est visus, ut probaret ἕτερόσιον inter Patre & Filiū, quomodo alius sit generas, alius genitus.Est igitur aliud τὸ γεννώμενον τῷ γεννῶντι, & quidē ἀριθμῷ aliud est, sed personali non substantiali: hoc est ὑποστάσει differunt, non autem οὐσίᾳ.
units.tr: Otherwise it would not be rightly said that the Word is indivisible and inseparable [ἀτμητὸς καὶ ἀχώριστος] from the Father, as the light of the sun is indivisible and inseparable from the sun while the sun is in the air. So whenever Justin calls the Word "other in number", as when he says "the Word is other in number [ἀριθμῷ ἕτερον] than what it is", and again soon after, "what is begotten is other in number than the one who begets it", this must be understood of hypostatic number, not essential number, because there are two persons. If we do not understand it of the persons, we will make Justin contradict himself, since he so often insists on the unity of Father and Son. Moreover, he would clearly be agreeing with Arius, who seemed to use this argument to prove a difference of essence between Father and Son, in that one is unbegotten and the other begotten. What is begotten is therefore other than the one who begets, and indeed other in number; but the difference is personal, not substantial. That is, they differ in hypostasis, not in essence.

units.la: Idem in priore apologia ad Senatu Romanu,ait, τὸν γὰρ ἀγέννητον καὶ ἀρρήτῳ θεῷ λόγον, μετὰ τὸν θεὸν προσκυνοῦμεν, ἀγαπῶμεν, ἐπὶ δὲ ἡμᾶς ἄνθρωπος γέγονεν, ὅπως ἡ τῶν παθῶν τῶν ἡμετέρων συμμέτοχος γενόμενος, ἡ ἔασιν ποιήσῃ [?]: quibus verbis distinguit inter personas Patris & Filii, & ostendit ad unum Filium spectare officium Mediatoris, incarnationis mysterium, & redemptionem humani generis, quae vera est ἰασις. Deinde indicat quis modus invocationis apud Christianos fit, quem Romani ignorabant: ea nimirum, qua Pater in Filii nomine invocatur, cuius merito ἰασιν acceperunt.
units.tr: In his earlier Apology to the Roman Senate, he says: "For we worship and love, after God, the Word from the unbegotten and ineffable God, who for our sake became man, so that by becoming a partaker of our sufferings he might also effect healing [ἴασις]." In these words he distinguishes between the persons of Father and Son, and shows that the office of Mediator, the mystery of the incarnation, and the redemption of the human race, which is the true healing, belong to the one Son. Then he indicates the manner of invocation that is practised among Christians, which the Romans did not know: namely, that by which the Father is invoked in the name of the Son, by whose merit they received healing.

units.la: Verum illa omnia Gentilis ad aliud propositu torquet. Ideoque etiā reliqua scripta Iustini reiicit. In primis autē ἔνθεσιν πίστεως, in quo fit aperte Triadis metio. Citas enim locu Eph.2. In quo & vos coaedificamini in habitaculu Dei in Spiritu, addit Iustinus χριστὸν θεὸν καὶ πνεῦμα τὴν μίαν θεότητα κατοικεῖν ἐν ἡμῖν καὶ ἐνέργειαν. Et mox, Σωτηρμένως ἡμῖν τὸ ἓν πρὸς [?] ἁγίῳ πνεύματος ἐν ὀνόματι παραδίδοται. Et rursum, τὸ τῆς οὐσίας ταυτὸν diserte appellat & probat. Item, In Triade (inquit) unitate intelligimus, & in unitate Triadem agnoscimus. Item, unius Deitatis tribus perfectis hypostasibus notitiam exposuimus, &c.
units.tr: But Gentilis twists all these things to another purpose, and therefore he rejects the rest of Justin's writings too, above all the Exhortation to Faith, in which the mention of the Trinity is plain. For Justin cites Ephesians 2: "In whom you also are built together into a dwelling place of God in the Spirit", and adds that Christ God and the Spirit, the one Godhead, dwells in us and works. And soon: the one is handed down to us in the name of the holy Spirit, who is saved for us. And again he expressly calls and proves that the Son is of the same substance [τὸ τῆς οὐσίας ταυτόν]. Likewise: "In the Trinity, he says, we understand unity, and in unity we acknowledge the Trinity." Likewise: "We have set out the knowledge of one Deity in three perfect hypostases", and so on.

units.la: Haec & similia, quia apertiora sunt, quam ut eludi potuerint, maluit Gentilis totam illam ἔνθεσιν πίστεως negare, quam sententia corrigere: ideoque non est opus plura inde proferre. satis enim cōstare arbitror ex iis quae diximus, quae sit hac de re Iustini Martyris, & Philosophi sententia.
units.tr: Since these and similar statements are too plain to be explained away, Gentilis preferred to deny that whole Exhortation to Faith rather than correct its meaning. So there is no need to bring forward more. I think it is sufficiently clear from what we have said what the opinion of Justin Martyr, the philosopher, is on this matter.

units.la: Ignatij Sententia. XIIII.
units.tr: The Opinion of Ignatius. XIIII.

units.la: Ignatius Polycarpi contemporaneus, & diui Ioannis fuit auditor, ut est apud Eusebium in Chronicis.
units.tr: Ignatius was a contemporary of Polycarp and a hearer of the divine John, as is recorded in Eusebius's Chronicle.

units.la: Hieronymus refert diuersas ab eo fuisse scriptas epi-stolas, ex quibus aliquot recenset. Apparet tamen sub illius nomine irrepsisse quaedam falso ei tributa. Verum de his nolo hic agere. Esto, sint ut vult Gentilis, omnia γνήσια. Videamus quantum ipsius sententiae patrocinetur.
units.tr: Jerome reports that several letters were written by him, and he lists some of them. Yet it appears that certain things falsely attributed to him have crept in under his name. But I do not wish to deal with these here. Granted, let them all be genuine, as Gentilis wishes. Let us see how far they support his opinion.

units.la: Conatur Getilis ex his epistolis probare, Filium essentia à Patre distinctū, seu vt ipse loquitur, duos esse æternos Spiritus essentiali numero differentes.
units.tr: Gentilis tries to prove from these letters that the Son is distinct from the Father in essence, or, as he himself puts it, that there are two eternal Spirits who differ in essential number.

units.la: Nos contrà affirmamus Ignatium tale nihil somniasse: sed docuisse λόγον esse cum Patre vnum & eundem Deum: ita tamen vt personaliter inter se differant. Epistola ad Magnesios, inquit λόγον non esse verbum prolatitium, sed substantiale: & quod ait mox, esse οὐσίαν γεννητὸν [?], id est, essentiam genitam, quauis dure sit dictum, tamen ex opposito satis intelligi potest eum nihil aliud ibi vocare οὐσίαν [?], quàm id quod reuera subsistit, id est, ὕπαρξιν [?], cui opponit prolatitium sonum statim euanescentem. In eadem epistola de Filio inquit: Vnum & solum Deum verum Patrem suum annuntiauit, loquens de doctrina Domini, quòd mundo verum Deum Patrem reuelauit.Sed quid hoc ad essentiæ separationem?
units.tr: We, on the contrary, affirm that Ignatius dreamed nothing of the kind, but taught that the Word is one and the same God with the Father, yet so that they differ personally. In the letter to the Magnesians he says that the Word is not an uttered word but a substantial one. What he says soon after, that there is a begotten essence [οὐσίαν γεννητὸν], that is, an essence that was begotten, though harshly put, can nevertheless be sufficiently understood from the contrast. He calls here "essence" nothing other than what truly subsists, that is, existence [ὕπαρξιν], and he opposes to it the uttered sound, which vanishes at once. In the same letter, speaking of the Son, he says that he revealed the one true God, his Father, teaching the doctrine of the Lord, and that he revealed to the world the true God the Father. But what has this to do with a separation of essence?

units.la: Epistola ad Tarsenses ait, λόγος non est ille, qui est super omnia Deus & Pater, sed Filius ipsius: quibus verbis nihil aliud dicit, quàm Filium non esse Patrem, quemadmodum Patripassiani personas confundebant.
units.tr: The letter to the Tarsians says that the Word is not that God and Father who is over all, but his Son. By these words he says nothing other than that the Son is not the Father, just as the Patripassians confused the persons.

units.la: Epistola ad Philippeses citat loc ūı.Cor.8. Vnus enim est omniū Deus.Et mox, Vnus est Deus & Pater,& nō duo vel tres, Vnus qui est,(& non est alius præter eum)solus verus. Et mox sese explicans subdit,Ergo nec tres sunt Patres,nec tres Filij,sed nec tres Paracleti:sed vnus Pater,&vnus Filius,&vnus Paracletus.Hanc Trinitatē confirmat baptismi institutione in nomine Patris, Filij, & Spiritus sancti, non in vnum quendam trinomium, neque in tres qui homines facti sint: sed in tres ὁμοΐμους [?], quoniam vnus est tantùm,qui homo factus est,non Pater,nec Paracletus,sed solus Filius:non putatiuè,neq; in phantasmate,sed certissima veritate. Verbum enim caro factū est,& habitauit in ea,&c. Apertus est igitur Ignatius Patripassianos oppugnās,& similes, nec huic dogmati patrocinatur.
units.tr: The letter to the Philippians cites 1 Corinthians 8: "For there is one God of all." And soon: "There is one God and Father, and not two or three; the one who is, and there is no other besides him, the only true one." Then, explaining himself, he adds: "Therefore there are neither three Fathers, nor three Sons, nor three Paracletes, but one Father, one Son, and one Paraclete." He confirms this Trinity by the institution of baptism in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, not in some one trinomial name, nor into three men who have been made, but into three [ὁμοίους]. Only one of them was made man, not the Father, nor the Paraclete, but the Son alone: not in appearance, nor in phantasm, but in most certain truth. For "the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us", and so on. Ignatius is therefore plainly opposing the Patripassians and their like, and does not favour this dogma.

units.la: In eadem epistola contra Patripassianos agens, sic scribit: Quomodo rursus non tibi videtur natus esse Christus ex Virgine, sed ille esse, qui est super omnia Deus, & omnipotens? Quis ergo est qui hunc misit? dicito, quisue huic dominetur, vel eius sententiæ subiectus fuit: aut cuius legem adimpleuit? tu, qui nullius sententiæ, vel potestati cedis, Christum separas à genitore, ingenitum constituis genitum esse, & cruci affixum illum, qui est sine principio:quæ disertè contra Patripassianos,siue Sabellianos disserit.
units.tr: In the same letter, arguing against the Patripassians, he writes thus: "How does it not seem to you that Christ was born of the Virgin, but that he is the God over all, and almighty? Who then sent him? Tell me, who rules over him, or to whose opinion was he subject, or whose law did he fulfil? You who yield to no opinion or power, you separate Christ from his begetter, you make the unbegotten to be begotten, and the one without beginning to be nailed to the cross." This plainly argues against the Patripassians, or Sabellians.

units.la: In eadem epistola inducit Christum loquentem contra Satanam.Scio enim(inquit)&novi unū solum,cui non denego servire, à quo tu apostata factus es.non enim sum ἀντίθεος[?], id est,contrarius Deo: sed confiteor eius eminentiam, & non recuso adorare eum, quem novi nativitatis meæ authorem & dominum, atque meæ perseverantiæ custodem.Ego enim vivo propter Patrem,&c.Hæc autem verba Christi sunt incarnati, qui secundum humanitatē se Patri inferiorem facit.Nam si de Divinitate intelligantur,quomodo Christus propter Patrem vivit,qui vitā à seipso habet, & ponit?
units.tr: In the same letter he introduces Christ speaking against Satan: "For I know, and recognize, only one, whom I do not refuse to serve, and by whom you were made an apostate. For I am not antitheos, that is, opposed to God; but I confess his eminence, and I do not refuse to adore him, whom I know to be the author of my birth and lord, and the guardian of my perseverance. For I live on account of the Father," and so on. These, however, are the words of Christ incarnate, who according to his humanity makes himself inferior to the Father. For if they are understood of the Divinity, how would Christ live on account of the Father, who has life from himself and gives it?

units.la: Epistola ad Philadelphios, ad unitatem hortatur, & sumit argumenta ab unitate carnis & sanguinis Christi,item mystici panis & calicis, itémque ab unitate Filij & Patris.
