Verba sunt: Quia & unus est ingenitus Pater: & unus unigenitus Filius, Deus verbum & homo: & unus Paracletus Spiritus veritatis,una etiā prædicatio, & una fides, & unū Baptisma,& una Ecclesia. Quibus verbis nihil aliud urget,quàm concordiā &unitatem in Ecclesia.Hinc illa conclusio: Hos ergo oportet,sicut populum sacerdotalem, & gentem sanctam in concordiam omnes consumari. Eodem faciunt quæ disputat in hac epistola contra Hebionem, qui Christum purum hominem dixit, ideóque ostendit Christum esse Deum genitum à Patre:quæ nihil habent absurdi,nisi torqueantur.
units.tr: The letter to the Philadelphians urges unity, and draws its arguments from the unity of Christ's flesh and blood, likewise from the mystical bread and cup, and likewise from the unity of Son and Father. The words are: "For there is one unbegotten Father, and one only-begotten Son, God the Word and man, and one Paraclete, the Spirit of truth; also one preaching, one faith, one baptism, and one Church." These words urge nothing other than concord and unity in the Church. Hence that conclusion: "All of you must be brought together into concord, as a priestly people and a holy nation." What he argues in this letter against Ebion, who said that Christ was a mere man, works to the same end, and therefore he shows that Christ is God begotten of the Father. These things contain nothing absurd, unless they are twisted.

units.la: Epistola ad Polycarpum, Hic (inquit) stadium est, illic corona, expecta Christum Filium Dei, intemporalem in tempore, quod est, ἀχρόνον ἐν χρόνῳ[?]. Sic Damascenus & alij λόγον ἀχρόνον appellarunt. Addit Ignatius,Impassibilem ut Deum: passibilem vero propter nos, & hominem. Quid contrà Gentilis? Christum ut Deum passum, & λόγον proprie carnem & sanguinem habere. Ignatius contrà aperte & sanctè distinguit duas naturas in una persona Christi: quarum Divina proprie, & per se impassibilis est: altera vero Humana, proprie passibilis.Has proprietates naturarum Gentilis confundit,& affirmat λόγον omnia in sese proprie habere.Christus proprie carnem & offahabet[?] & sanguinem,quia verè & proprie incarnatus est: sed λόγος in Christo, seu Divina illius natura, non habet illa in se proprie.
units.tr: In the letter to Polycarp: "Here is the stadium, there the crown; wait for Christ the Son of God, timeless in time [ἀχρόνον ἐν χρόνῳ]." So Damascene and others called the Word "timeless". Ignatius adds: "impassible as God, but passible for us, and as man." What does Gentilis say on the contrary? That Christ suffered as God, and that the Word properly has flesh and blood. Ignatius, on the contrary, clearly and soundly distinguishes two natures in the one person of Christ: of these the divine is properly and in itself impassible, while the human is properly passible. Gentilis confuses these properties of the natures and affirms that the Word properly has all things in himself. Christ properly has flesh, bones and blood, because he was truly and properly incarnate; but the Word in Christ, or his divine nature, does not properly have these in himself.

units.la: Epistola ad Antiochenos,Non oportet,inquit,Christum ad excusationem unius Dei negare. & adducit testimonia ex scriptura, Deut.6.Esa.44.Gen.1.& 17.quæ omnia loquuntur de uno Deo, & simul exprimunt diuersas personas, vt quod ait Moses, Pluit Do-minus à Domino,quum tamen alibi dicat vnum esse Deum: quæ vnitas non excludit Filium nec Spiritum sanctum, quos è contrario cum Patre in vnitate Diuinitatis includit,ita vt personarum Tri-nitas non intercipiat vnitatem essentiæ.
units.tr: Ignatius, in his Letter to the Antiochenes, says: "It is not right for Christ to be denied for the sake of defending the one God." He adduces testimonies from Scripture, Deut. 6, Isa. 44, and Gen. 1 and 17, all of which speak of one God and at the same time express diverse persons, as when Moses says, "The Lord rained from the Lord," though elsewhere he says that there is one God. This unity does not exclude the Son or the Holy Spirit, whom on the contrary he includes with the Father in the unity of the Godhead, so that the Trinity of persons does not destroy the unity of essence.

units.la: Idem ad finem illius epistolæ rectè distinguit personarum pro-prietates.Incolumes seruet vos ille (inquit) qui est solus ingenitus (quod de Patre dicitur)per illum qui ante secula genitus est, id est per Filium,cuius proprium est natum esse. Sed hîc excipit Gētilis, scilicet, vltimam hanc eiusdem epistolæ clausulam, Valete Deo & Christo. quasi verò hæc diuersa sint, & Pater solus dicatur Deus: Christus autem Dominus, ita vt à communione solius Dei excludatur.
units.tr: At the end of the same letter he rightly distinguishes the properties of the persons: "May he who alone is unbegotten (which is said of the Father) keep you safe, through him who was begotten before the ages, that is, through the Son, whose property it is to be begotten." But Gentilis takes exception here to the final clause of the same letter, "Farewell in God and Christ," as if these were different things, and the Father alone were called God, while Christ was called Lord, so that Christ is excluded from the communion of the one God.

units.la: Epistola ad Ephesios,illos laudat,quòd sint vnum corpus.& addit argumentum, Vnus enimDominus, vna fides, vnum baptisma, vnus Deus Pater omnium.Non est autem Ignatii sententia, quòd Pater solus vnus Deus sit, vt nec in illa sequete sententia, Medicus noster est solus verus Deus, Deus ingenitus. (nam ita Filius medicus noster non esset) sed distinguit personas suis proprietatibus. Mox enim Christum medicum nostrum appellat,& impassibilem in corpore passibili.
units.tr: Ignatius, in his Letter to the Ephesians, praises them because they are one body, and adds the argument: "For one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all." It is not Ignatius's opinion that the Father alone is the one God, nor is it so in the following sentence, "Our physician is the only true God, unbegotten God" (for in that case the Son would not be our physician). Rather, he distinguishes the persons by their properties. For soon afterwards he calls Christ our physician, and impassible in a passible body. ## Sententia Tertulliani. XV.

units.la: Sententia Tertulliani. XV.

TErtullianus extra controuersiam caute legendus est, quod & Gentilis fatetur: ideóque illi facilius est, eum quoties ipsi libuit præterire,& negare authoritatem illius, quam tamè rursus quum libet magnificè extollit.
units.tr: Tertullian is undoubtedly to be read with caution, as Gentilis himself admits. So it is easy for Gentilis, whenever it pleases him, to pass Tertullian over and deny his authority, though whenever it suits him again he extols that same authority magnificently.

units.la: Sed rectè loquitur aliâs Tertullianus,vt contra Praxeam expres-sè ait, Numerum sine diuisione patiuntur.Et posteà, Vbique teneo vnam substantiam in tribus cohærentibus. In his & similibus sententiis,ait Gentilis,lubricè fuisse loquutum, & Montani paracleto hæc tribuit,quæ tamen sunt orthodoxa.
units.tr: But elsewhere Tertullian speaks rightly, as when he says expressly against Praxeas, "They suffer number without division." And afterwards: "Everywhere I hold one substance in three cohering." In these and similar statements, says Gentilis, Tertullian spoke slipperily, and he attributes them to Montanus's Paraclete, though they are orthodox.

units.la: Nos contrà, dicimus Tertullianum aduersus Hermog. non solùm lubricè loquutum, sed etiam Arii phrasibus & verbis, quum ait,Fuit tempus, quando Filius non fuit:quæ sententia Gentili mirificè placet,vt qui Christum Patre posteriorem Diuinitatis gradu faciat.Sed est certè palàm Ariana sententia, ἦν ὅτε ἦν[?], de qua iam diximus ex Niceph.lib.8.cap.8.
units.tr: We, on the contrary, say that Tertullian, in his work against Hermogenes, not only spoke slipperily but even used Arian phrases and words when he said, "There was a time when the Son was not." This sentence pleases Gentilis wonderfully, since he makes Christ later than the Father in degree of Godhead. But it is plainly the Arian opinion, "there was when he was not" [ἦν ὅτε οὐκ ἦν], of which we have already spoken, from Nicephorus, book 8, chapter 8.

units.la: Tamen colligit se aliquoties Tertullianus, & recte nō solùm loqui, sed etiam sentire videtur, vt aduersus eundem Hermog. Diuinitas (inquit) gradum non habet, vt pote vnica.
units.tr: Nevertheless, Tertullian sometimes collects himself, and he seems not only to speak rightly but also to think rightly, as in the same work against Hermogenes: "The Godhead (he says) has no degree, being single."

units.la: Hæ & similes sententiæ satis indicant Tertullianum nullam in Diuinitate agnouisse separationem, nullam partitionem: interim numerum admisisse, quem ad personarum differentiam refert.
units.tr: These and similar statements sufficiently indicate that Tertullian recognised no separation or division in the Godhead; yet he admitted a number, which he referred to the difference of persons.

units.la: Hæc ex Iustino Martyre, Ignatio, & Tertulliano afferre libuit. Hos enim Gentilis ita suos facit, vt ipsos ex asse patronos suæ causæ constituat. de reliquis hic nolo esse prolixior. Nam Hilarii & Irenæi sententia notior est, quàm vt quisquam eos huic errori patrocinari merito suspicetur. Et quæ ex his citat Gentilis, ex ipsis authoribus refelluntur. Ex multis etiam Græcis & Latinis scriptoribus non affero in præsentia quicquam, quia illorum authoritatem contemnit Gentilis.
units.tr: I have thought it worth citing these from Justin Martyr, Ignatius and Tertullian. Gentilis so claims them for his own side that he makes them outright advocates of his cause. I do not want to be more long-winded about the others here. The view of Hilary and Irenaeus is too well known for anyone reasonably to suspect them of backing this error. And what Gentilis cites from them is refuted from the authors themselves. I also am not offering anything at present from the many Greek and Latin writers, because Gentilis holds their authority in contempt.

units.la: De reliquis patribus, præsertim Augustino. XVI.
units.tr: On the other Fathers, especially Augustine. XVI.

units.la: Reliquos igitur, tum Græcos, tum Latinos scriptores omnes, & sine discrimine Gentilis reiicit: in quo certè admiranda est hominis audacia. Nouus Aristarchus totam vetustatem in crimen vocat, nisi confiteatur tres æternos & differètes Spiritus in Diuina œconomia. Niceneæ Synodi patres 318, omnes cum hæreticis coniungit, quia vnum confessi sunt Deum æternum. Arium illis omnibus præfert, si vocem ὁμοού-σιος admisisset, ita quidem vt ipse explicat. Sed nolo ei homines, & humanam authoritatem obtrudere. Verbo Dei conuinci potest hæc blasphemia. Et pridem Arius, cuius spiritus in hoc monstro repullulat, damnatus & confutatus est, non humana authoritate, sed scripturis, & consensu Ecclesiæ. Tantum historiam texo, vt cohstet[?] nouam afferri ab isto homine interpretationem locorum scripturæ: quod vt liberius obtineat, sine rubore licenter debacchatur non solùm in omnes scriptores, sed etiam in orthodoxa concilia.
units.tr: So Gentilis rejects all the other writers, Greek and Latin alike, without distinction. In this his audacity is truly remarkable. This new Aristarchus accuses all antiquity of a crime, unless it confesses three eternal and differing Spirits in the divine economy. He lumps together all the fathers of the Nicene Synod, the 318, with the heretics, because they confessed the one eternal God. He would prefer Arius to all of them, if they had admitted the word "one in essence" [ὁμοούσιος], and that in the sense he himself explains. But I do not want to thrust men and human authority on him. This blasphemy can be refuted by the Word of God. Long ago Arius, whose spirit is sprouting again in this monster, was condemned and refuted, not by human authority but by the Scriptures and the consensus of the Church. I am only recounting history so that it may be clear that this man is introducing a new interpretation of the passages of Scripture. To make this stick more freely, he rages without shame and without restraint, not only against all the writers but also against the orthodox councils.

units.la: Oportebat autem probatos scriptores, & consensum vetustatis vel admittere, vel refutare aperto Dei verbo. Id non facit: sed loca citat, quibus nouam assuit interpretationem: quam dum illi negamus,afferentes Christi Ecclesiā ita non intellexisse illa loca,& provocamus ad probatos scriptores Latinos & Græcos: ille exclamat imperiosos nos esse magistros, & hæreticos, & transfugit ad Arij partes, & eos Episcopos qui Arium sequuti sunt, quasi tum apud illos melior fuerit scripturæ interpretatio, quàm apud Athanasiū, & eos,qui huius confessionem approbarunt. Augustinum quoque tractat probrosè & præter meritum optimi scriptoris. Obiicit illi, vti & nobis Quaternitatem, quam nunquam somniauit,ne per febrim quidem:magicum scriptorem & sophistam vocat, quibus cōuitiis hactenus caruit, etiam apud capitales suos hostes.Imaginariam appellat essentiam vnam & trinam, & Augustini deam, quæ impia est blasphemia. Nihilominus tamen astutus scriptor, vt sibi Augustinum placaret, & inuidiā apud pios declinaret, subito fundit oraculum.Non enim dubitat affirmare, quin si Augustinus vixeret, & superesset in hac Euangelii luce, libros suos de Trinitate scriptos ipsemet in ignem coniiceret. Faceret id scilicet Augustinus huius exemplo,& nimirum periurio sese, vt iste macularet. Ve-rum nunc ista missa facio.
units.tr: Yet he ought either to admit the approved writers and the consensus of antiquity, or to refute them by the plain Word of God. This he does not do; instead he cites passages to which he has attached a new interpretation. When we deny this, asserting that the Church of Christ did not understand those passages in that way, and appeal to the approved Latin and Greek writers, he cries out that we are domineering teachers and heretics. He deserts to the side of Arius, and to those bishops who followed Arius, as if the interpretation of Scripture were then better among them than among Athanasius and those who approved his confession. He also treats Augustine abusively and beyond the merit of that excellent writer. He objects to Augustine, as also to us, a Quaternity, which he never dreamed of, not even in a fever. He calls him a magical writer and a sophist, insults which Augustine has hitherto escaped even from his chief enemies. He calls the one and triune essence an imaginary thing, and Augustine's goddess, which is an impious blasphemy. Nevertheless, the crafty writer, in order to placate Augustine and avoid odium among the godly, suddenly pours forth an oracle. For he does not hesitate to affirm that if Augustine were alive and survived in this light of the Gospel, he would himself throw his books on the Trinity into the fire. Augustine, of course, would be doing that following this man's example, and no doubt so that he might stain himself with perjury, as this man does. But now I set these things aside.

units.la: De communicatione idiomatum. XVII.
units.tr: On the communication of idioms. XVII.

units.la: Scriptura de Filio Dei loquens, interdum vni naturæ tribuit quod est alterius, Ioann.3.Nemo ascendit in cælum,nisi Filius hominis,qui est in cælo.
units.tr: Scripture, speaking of the Son of God, sometimes attributes to one nature what belongs to the other: John 3: "No one has ascended into heaven, except the Son of man, who is in heaven."

units.la: Christus sane quatenus est Filius hominis,tunc non erat in cælo,quum illa diceret, nec carnem suam è cælo attulerat. Sed illa sunt diuinæ naturæ propria, ac de toto Christo recte dicuntur,propter personalem vnionem verbi cum homine.
units.tr: Christ, as he is the Son of man, was not in heaven when he said these words, and he had not brought his flesh down from heaven. But these things are proper to the divine nature, and they are rightly said of the whole Christ, on account of the personal union of the Word with the human nature.

units.la: Simili orationis genere dicimus,Deus pro nobis passus est,mortuus est: quæ sententiæ impropriæ sunt:quia mori & pati, de Deo proprie non possunt prædicari. Quare addi solet per explicationem,In carne assumpta.
units.tr: We speak in a similar way when we say, "God suffered for us, God died." These statements are improper, because dying and suffering cannot properly be predicated of God. For this reason it is customary to add by way of explanation, "in the assumed flesh."

units.la: Hanc loquendi formam communicationem idiomatum appellarunt veteres, alii ἀλλοίωσιν, Damascenus τρόπον ἀντιδόσεως [?] vocauit: quasi dicas mutuam largitionem, qua id quod diuinæ est naturæ, tribuitur humanæ,vt in cælo esse ante incarnationem:aut contrà, quod humanæ est,tribuitur diuinæ, vt mori,pati. Aut de tota persona dicitur, quod est unius naturæ: ut Christus mortuus est, rectè & proprie dicitur, quia humana natura in Christo proprie mortua est, diuina non item.
units.tr: The ancients called this manner of speaking the communication of idioms; others called it alteration [ἀλλοίωσιν], and Damascene called it a mode of exchange [τρόπον ἀντιδόσεως]. That is, as one might say, a mutual bestowal, by which what belongs to the divine nature is ascribed to the human, as being in heaven before the incarnation, or conversely, what belongs to the human nature is ascribed to the divine, as dying and suffering. Or else something proper to one nature is said of the whole person. Thus we say rightly and properly that Christ died, because the human nature in Christ truly died, while the divine nature did not.

units.la: Nec est absurda aut absona loquendi formula. Dicimus enim simili ratione de nobis mortalibus, Homo ille mortuus est, quum tamen id de toto homine proprie verû non fit. Homo enim corpore tantùm mortalis est: & anima post mortem, & in morte superstes manet, & immortalis. Quia tamen animæ & corporis unio hominem unum efficit, tribuitur toti homini, quod partis tantùm est proprium. Ita de Christo dicimus illum mortuû esse, passum esse: quæ proprie in diuinitatem non cadunt, sed Christi hominis sunt, qui idem simul Deus est, & unus idémque Christus.
units.tr: Nor is this form of speech absurd or unfitting. For we say in a similar way of us mortals, "That man died," although this is not strictly true of the whole man. For a man is mortal only in body; the soul survives after death and in death, and is immortal. Yet because the union of soul and body makes one man, what belongs only to a part is ascribed to the whole man. So we say of Christ that he died and suffered; these things do not properly apply to the divinity, but belong to Christ as man, who is at the same time God, and one and the same Christ.

units.la: Hîc vociferatur Gentilis, nos Christum scindere, & διάλυσιν[?] instituere: & tamen fatetur quædam non nisi Verbo, nondum carne vestito competere posse, quale est illud Ioann.3.Nemo ascendit in cœlum, nisi qui descendit de cœlo, Filius hominis, qui est in cœlo &c. & Ioann.8. Antequam Abraham esset ego sum. & Hebr.1.Per quem & condidit secula. Quæ si, ut concedit Gentilis, non nisi Verbo nondum carne vestito competere possunt, manifestum est eadem illa, de humana Christi natura improprie dici, & rectè à nobis per communicationem idiomatum explicari.
units.tr: Here Gentilis cries out that we divide Christ and introduce a division [διάλυσιν]. Yet he himself admits that some things can apply only to the Word before it was clothed with flesh, such as John 3: "No one has ascended into heaven, except him who descended from heaven, the Son of man, who is in heaven," etc.; and John 8: "Before Abraham was, I am"; and Heb. 1: "by whom also he made the worlds." If, as Gentilis concedes, these things can apply only to the Word not yet clothed with flesh, it is plain that these same things are said improperly of the human nature of Christ, and are rightly explained by us through the communication of idioms.

units.la: Et quòd à nobis non scindatur Christus, nec ullam hîc διάλυσιν[?] statuamus, aut defendamus, testatur doctrina nostrarum Ecclesia-rum, in qua manifestè duas in Christo naturas confitemur, eásque sine confusione naturarum, unione personali unum & eundem constituente Christum Filium Dei & Virginis. Naturas quoque suis proprietatibus distinguimus, nō scindimus, ac personæ Christi sua integra relinquimus officia.
units.tr: That we do not divide Christ, nor set up or defend any division here, is attested by the doctrine of our churches, in which we openly confess two natures in Christ, and these without confusion of the natures, with a personal union making one and the same Christ, the Son of God and of the Virgin. We also distinguish the natures by their own properties; we do not divide them, and we leave to the person of Christ his whole offices.

units.la: Humanæ naturæ dicimus proprium esse, flere, esurire, dormire, pati, mori, in loco esse, &c. Diuinæ autem, impatibilem esse, conde-re secula, apud Patrem ab æterno ante tempora Abrahæ fuisse &c. Christi officia dicimus, redimere genus humanum, intercedere, regere Ecclesiam suam, & quæcunque de Christi, Doctoris, Sacer-dotis & Regis officio dici possunt.
units.tr: We say that it is proper to the human nature to weep, to hunger, to sleep, to suffer, to die, to be in a place, etc. But it is proper to the divine nature to be impassible, to make the worlds, to have been with the Father from eternity, before the time of Abraham, etc. We say that the offices of Christ are to redeem the human race, to intercede, to rule his Church, and whatever can be said of the office of Christ as Teacher, Priest and King.

units.la: Quæ quum Gentilis negare non possit, certum est studio & ardore pugnæ, longius progressum nodum in scirpo quærere. Immerito certe doctrinam hanc orthodoxam nugas vocat ab Ecclesia Dei explodendas, quod non solum facit in praefatione ad serenifs. Poloniæ Regem, sed etiam Antidot.12.copiose & bibliose insectatur, sine iusta & firma ratione.
units.tr: Since Gentilis cannot deny these things, it is certain that, through zeal and ardour for the fight, he has gone too far and is seeking a knot in a bulrush. He has certainly been wrong to call this orthodox doctrine trifles to be cast out by the Church of God, and he does this not only in the preface to the most serene King of Poland, but also in Antidote 12, where he attacks it at length and with much citation of Scripture, without any just or firm reason.

units.la: Apparet tamen hic subesse aliud monstrum. Nam sæpius affirmat λόγον vere & proprie habere carnem & sanguinem, & λόγον vere & proprie pependisse in ligno crucis, & λόγον proprie passum: quæ si de Christo prædicaret, extra controversiam vera essent. Cæterum quum λόγος significet in Christo divinam naturam, quæ in persona Christi humanæ est vnita, necesse est, aut sentiat Spiritum habere proprie carnem & sanguinem, quod negat Christus: aut λόγον in carnem coaluisse, & vt aiebant Monophysitæ, vnam naturam ex duabus fuisse conflatam, nisi nobiscum fateatur, non esse proprium sermonem, quum dicimus, λόγος est passus & mortuus: sed divinæ tribui quod sit humanæ naturæ proprium, idque propter vnionem hypostaticam duarum in Christo naturarum, quæ ipsa est communicatio idiomatum.
units.tr: Yet there seems to lie hidden here another monster. For he often affirms that the Word truly and properly has flesh and blood, that the Word truly and properly hung on the cross, and that the Word properly suffered. If he were saying these things of Christ, they would be true beyond dispute. But since the Word signifies in Christ the divine nature, which is united with the human nature in the person of Christ, he must either hold that the Spirit properly has flesh and blood, which Christ denies, or that the Word has merged into the flesh, so that, as the Monophysites used to say, one nature was compounded out of two. Unless he agrees with us that it is not proper speech when we say that the Word suffered and died, but that what is proper to the human nature is ascribed to the divine, and this on account of the hypostatic union of the two natures in Christ, which is itself the communication of idioms.

units.la: Blasphemiæ eiusdem Gentilis manifestæ. XVIII.
units.tr: The Manifest Blasphemies of the Same Gentilis. XVIII.

units.la: Aliud impietatis caput est, quòd negotium hoc sacrosanctum, & adorandum potius mysterium, quàm excutiendum, probrosis vocibus incessit, & voces blasphemas eructat. Solet interdum etiam boni viri diffidere in rerum explicationibus, necnon in interpretandis interdum Scripturæ locis: sed hoc faciunt sine insectatione & convitiis. In primis vero a blasphemiis sibi temperat. Non est enim piæ mentis rem ipsam, de qua controversia est, insectari & proscindere. Verum in eo genere ita liber est Gentilis, vt ex Acherusia palude fœdiores non exhalent vapores: nec Anagyris commota ita possit esse molesta sano capiti.
units.tr: Another head of his impiety is that he assails this sacred mystery, which ought rather to be adored than examined, with abusive words and belches out blasphemous expressions. Good men sometimes distrust their explanations of things, and sometimes their interpretations of passages of Scripture, but they do so without invective and insults. Above all, they refrain from blasphemy. For it is not the mark of a pious mind to attack and tear apart the very matter in dispute. Gentilis, however, is so unrestrained in this kind of thing that no fouler vapours rise from the Acherusian marsh, and the stinking anagyris, once disturbed, could not be more troublesome to a healthy head.

units.la: Trinitatem sine discrimine nouum vocat Idolum, turrim Babel, nouum idolum supra Patrem, quod nos tuemur. Tripersona-tum Deum, sophisticum Deum, sol.30. Diabolicam personam & fictitiam, sol.6. Fictitiam proprietatem & personam sophisticam in nouo Deo, sol.7. Personam phantasticam, sol.8. Et sol.28. Trium horrendam confusionem, execrabilemque mixturam. Item nos nouum Deum Trinitatem ex cerebro confingere, sol.33. Item quartum idolum, in orcum detrudendum, sol.39. Item sol.44. appellat primam personam magicam in vno Deo, quae vere Larua & inane spectrum sit, & quae alteram personam imaginariam seu vanam relationem genuerit.
units.tr: He calls the Trinity, without distinction, a new idol, a tower of Babel, a new idol above the Father, which we uphold. He calls God a tripersonal God, a sophistical God (p. 30). A diabolical and fictitious person (p. 6). A fictitious property and a sophistical person in a new God (p. 7). A phantastic person (p. 8). And (p. 28) a horrible confusion of three and a detestable mixture. Likewise (p. 33) he says we invent a new God, the Trinity, out of our own brains. Likewise (p. 39) a fourth idol, to be thrust down into hell. Likewise (p. 44) he calls the first person a magical person in the one God, which is really a mask and an empty phantom, and which has begotten another person, an imaginary or vain relation.

units.la: Antid.3. Monstrosum nomen, Deum trinitatem,& sol.56. Magicas personas & proprietates, ibidem Magica proprietas in nouo Idolo. sol.34. Deum trinitatem, turrim Babel vocat, sol.94. Tres personas, tres magicas praestigias, & vnum Deum, quartum idolum ignotum.
units.tr: In the Antidote, p. 3, he speaks of a "monstrous name, God the Trinity," and at p. 56 of "magical persons and properties," and in the same place of "a magical property in a new idol." At p. 34 he calls God the Trinity a tower of Babel, and at p. 94 "three persons, three magical tricks, and one God, a fourth unknown idol."

units.la: In libello impresso,sol.6. Trinitatem Deum,humanu commentum cum Euangelica veritate ex diametro pugnans,fide de Trinitate,fidem sophistica,Deum trinomiu,quasi cum Sabellio luderet. Item sol.8. nouum Deum, indefinitum, triperfonatum, quem nemo ex Prophetis aut Patriarchis cognouit, nec Christus patefecit,nec Apostoli praedicarunt.
units.tr: In the printed booklet, p. 6, he calls the Trinity a human invention, fighting diametrically against the Gospel truth, a sophistical faith in the Trinity, a three-named God, as though he were playing with Sabellius. Likewise at p. 8 he calls it a new God, undefined, tripersonal, whom no one among the Prophets or Patriarchs knew, whom Christ did not reveal, and whom the Apostles did not preach.

units.la: Christum item Redemptorem nostrum tergeminu Christum nobis obtrudit,sol.14.impressi libelli,& in epistola ad filios Ecclesiae,Christum transformatum in eum qui Filius Dei non sit.
units.tr: Likewise he thrusts upon us Christ our Redeemer as a threefold Christ (p. 14 of the printed booklet), and in the letter to the sons of the Church he speaks of Christ transformed into one who is not the Son of God.

units.la: Item sol.15. Patris,hoc est, vanae relationis Filium, tripartitum & in alium transformatum, Deum Patrem, sterilem, otiosum, ignotum Deum. Et ne obiicias talia nobis obtrudi conuitia, non autem de reipsa dici: verum quidem est,Gentilem vbique illa nobis conari obtrudere, & falso criminari his titulis nostram doctrinam: negari tamen non potest infinitis locis sine exceptione eum sic profanum esse,ac vocem Trinitatis simpliciter damnare,quan-uis eadem ipse vtatur. Testis eius rei est praefatio ad Regem Polon. vbi sol. 6. conqueritur monstrosas & profanas voces in Ecclesiam Dei esse inuectas, vt sunt ὁμοούσιον[?], Persona, Essentia, Vnitas,Trinitas, quibus omnia Diuina mysteria peruerterunt, vt sempiternus ille Deus cum suo Filio,& Spiritu sancto prorsus ignoretur. Cuius rei habuit antesignanum, Gregorium Paulum, qui in suo libello Sathanae stratagemata appellat has phrases, Vna Dei essetia, Vnus Deus in tribus personis. Verum quum has phrases Ecclesia reti-nuerit, quas illi conantur impugnare: facile intelligi potest,quam ipsemet profanus sit, & Satanæ utatur stratagemate.
units.tr: Likewise at p. 15 he speaks of the Son of the Father, that is, of an empty relation, tripartite and transformed into another, and of God the Father as barren, idle, and an unknown God. And lest you object that such insults are not really aimed at us, that they are not truly said of us: it is true that Gentilis everywhere tries to foist these things on us and falsely charges our doctrine with these labels; yet it cannot be denied that in countless places, without exception, he is so profane that he simply condemns the word "Trinity," although he himself uses it. Witness to this is the preface to the King of Poland, where at p. 6 he complains that monstrous and profane words have been introduced into the Church of God, such as consubstantial [ὁμοούσιον], person, essence, unity, and trinity, by which they have perverted all the divine mysteries, so that the eternal God, with his Son and Holy Spirit, is utterly unknown. He had a forerunner in this, Gregory Paul, who in his little book calls these phrases Satan's stratagems: "one essence of God," "one God in three persons." But since the Church has retained these phrases, which they try to attack, it is easy to see how profane he himself is, and that he makes use of Satan's stratagem.

units.la: Atque hæc illa est pugna suprema & splendidissima, qua illis est depugnandum. Gentilis apud regem Sigismundum conqueritur, Lutherum, Zvvinglium, Bucerum, in oppugnando Antichristo solùm occupatos fuisse in caudæ oppugnatione, solúmque Philippum ex tot millibus unum fuisse, qui quasi aliud agens lethale vulnus ei potius minari, quàm infligere videatur. Idem facit Gregorius ille Paulus. Scribit Deum per Lutherum cœpisse Ecclesiam Antichristi à tecto demoliri, non à fundamento, ne domus putrida eum opprimeret. Scilicet quia negotium Trinitatis inconvulsum reliquerunt, ideo caudam & tectum tantùm oppugnarunt, non caput & fundamenta. Ita colludunt inter se belli homines.
units.tr: And this is that supreme and most splendid battle in which they must fight. Gentilis complains before King Sigismund that Luther, Zwingli and Bucer were occupied only in attacking Antichrist's tail, and that only Philip, out of so many thousands, was one who, as though doing something else, seems to threaten a deadly wound rather than to inflict one. Gregory Paul does the same. He writes that God began through Luther to pull down the Church of Antichrist from the roof, not from the foundation, lest the rotten house should crush him. Clearly, because they left the matter of the Trinity unshaken, they attacked only the tail and the roof, not the head and the foundations. Thus do these warriors collude with one another.

units.la: Certum est autem illos hoc unum quærere, ut possint emergere. Ideo non parcunt piissimis bonorum virorum laboribus. Deinde præsumptuosè omnia interpretantur: demum licenter omnia damnant, quæ ipsis adversantur. Hinc voces & phrases emendare conantur: quod quum sit supra ipsorum vires, horrendas voces, & diras insectationes euomunt, quas piæ & Christianæ aures non sine horrore audire possunt. His floribus & ornamentis scatet liber ad regem Poloniæ, nec illis caruit etiam sermo loquetis interdum, ut sibi ludere & laudem hinc captare sit visus.
units.tr: It is certain, however, that they seek this one thing, that they may emerge with credit. Therefore they spare not the most pious labours of good men. Then they interpret everything presumptuously; finally they freely condemn everything that stands against them. Hence they try to emend words and phrases, and since this is beyond their powers, they belch out horrible words and dire invectives, which pious and Christian ears cannot hear without horror. The book to the King of Poland is full of these flowers and ornaments, nor did his speech lack them when he sometimes spoke, so that he seemed to be playing and seeking praise from this.

units.la: Calumniæ quibus nostram doctrinam falsò onerat. XIX.
units.tr: Calumnies with which he falsely burdens our doctrine. XIX.

units.la: Pari facilitate erumpit in calumnias. Nam Ecclesiis nostris imponit immeritò, quæ nũquam probare potest. qualia sunt illa, Quòd Christum unius Dei Filium impudenter negemus.
units.tr: With equal ease he breaks out into calumnies. For he unjustly imputes to our churches things which he can never prove, such as that we shamelessly deny Christ, the one Son of God.

units.la: Quòd novũ Deũ in Christianā religione temerè invexerimus.
units.tr: That we have rashly introduced a new God into the Christian religion.

units.la: Quòd Deum non genuisse Filium ex propria substantia affirmemus. Id si fecit Nicolaus Cusanus Cardinalis, viderit ipse, non debet id crimen Euangelicis ecclesiis imponi.
units.tr: That we affirm God did not beget the Son from his own substance. If Cardinal Nicholas of Cusa did this, let him answer for it; that charge should not be laid on the Evangelical churches.

units.la: Quòd Deum Trinum confingamus contra omnium Scripturarum authoritatem.
units.tr: That we invent a Trinune God, contrary to the authority of all the Scriptures.

units.la: Plura huius farinæ habentur Antidoto. 24. sol. 86.quæ studiosè hîc prætereo. Quis enim feret talem nebulonem, ita petulanter rem Christianam evertentem?
units.tr: Many charges of this sort are found in the Antidote (p. 24, p. 86), which I deliberately pass over here. For who would tolerate such a scoundrel, so wantonly overturning the Christian faith?

units.la: Hinc illa ornamenta, quòd nos Antitheos, hæreticos Iudæis si-miles, Turcis pares appellat. Et his nominibus etiam Sabaudicas Ecclesias ornat: quas tamen non dubitat reliquis anteferre, tanquam puriores & synceriores.
units.tr: Hence those ornaments: he calls us Antitheists, heretics like the Jews, equal to the Turks. And with these names he also adorns the Savoyard churches, which nonetheless he does not hesitate to prefer to the rest as purer and more sincere.

units.la: Nos cum Iudæis & Turcis confert, quòd cum Mahomete negemus Deum genuisse Filium. Quis verò unquam talia inter nos audiuit, quòd nouum quendam Deum supra Christi Patrem nobis commentemur? Quis unquam nostrùm ita vel docuit, vel loquutus est?
units.tr: He compares us with Jews and Turks because we deny with Muhammad that God begot a Son. But who among us has ever heard such things, that we invent some new God above Christ's Father? Which of us has ever taught or said anything like this?

units.la: Hinc illa speciosa Quaternitas, quæ nunquam est in nostris Ec-clesiis nec visa, nec audita, ne dicam culta.
units.tr: Hence that showy "Quaternity," which has never been seen or heard in our churches, let alone worshipped.

units.la: Fides nostra illi sophistica est, & nos noui sophistæ: nec dum attulit rationes. Ita veterator scenicè ludit. Sed hinc illud est, quòd negemus illi tres æternos Spiritus, & dicamus cum Athanasio, V-nus æternus, & unus omnipotens: tres autem personas doceamus tria esse ὑφιστάμενα[?] vel tres ὑποστάσεις[?]. Quum igitur Deum dicimus trinum, exilit tanquam œstro correptus, clamitans, nos Trinitatem facere Deum quendam quartum, quasi nos extra Patrem, Filium & Spiritum sanctum, alium quendam Deum Trinitate con-stituamus. Certè nimis aperta est hæc calumnia. Trinitatem enim ad personas referimus, extra quas nec Deus, nec Trinitas est.
units.tr: Our faith is sophistical to him, and we are new sophists; yet he has not yet brought forward any arguments. So the old trickster plays his stage part. But hence it is that we deny him three eternal spirits, and say with Athanasius: one eternal, and one almighty; yet we teach that the three persons are three subsistences [ὑφιστάμενα], or three hypostases [ὑποστάσεις]. When therefore we say that God is triune, he leaps up as if stung by a gadfly, shouting that we make a fourth God through the Trinity, as though we set up some other God beside the Trinity, apart from the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Surely this calumny is far too obvious. For we refer the Trinity to the persons, outside of which there is neither God nor Trinity.

units.la: Similis calumnia est, quòd incognitû Deum supra Patrem Christi tueamur. Item quòd ex vno Christo tergeminum faciamus.
units.tr: Similar is the calumny that we uphold an unknown God above the Father of Christ, and likewise that from the one Christ we make a threefold one.

units.la: Tuemur Deum patribus notum & patefactum, nullum inco-gnitum nouimus. Christum vnum scimus, in quo duæ sunt natu-ræ confusæ, vnam personam constituentes: ideoque impium iudi-camus tergeminum Christum dicere.
units.tr: We uphold the God known and revealed to the fathers; we know no unknown God. We know one Christ, in whom are two natures, unconfused, constituting one person; therefore we judge it impious to speak of a threefold Christ.

units.la: Sceleratius etiam est quòd aspergit nobis, nos Christum discer-pere, & in alium Christum, qui non sit viuentis Dei Filius trans-formare. Ostendat nobis homo blasphemus, alium Christum præ-ter illum Dei Filium, & monstret vbi, & quomodo discerpatur à nobis.
units.tr: Even more wicked is his charge that we tear Christ apart and transform him into another Christ, who is not the Son of the living God. Let this blasphemous man show us another Christ besides that Son of God, and point out where and how he is torn apart by us.

units.la: Similes sunt præstigiæ quas nobis obiicit, quòd Christum nouæ relationis Filium præstigiemur, & præstigiosè credamus Dei Filiū.
units.tr: Similar are the sleights of hand with which he charges us: that we conjure Christ into a Son of some new relation, and believe in the Son of God by trickery.

units.la: Nos Christum Dei Filium secundum scripturas credimus, nul-las præstigias Gentilitias agnoscimus: & tres personas constanter asserimus in Diuinitate sine præstigiis, nec diuidimus substantiam, sed inter personas distinguimus. Cantilenam Sabellii nobis obgannitnos iustius illi Arii blasphemias occinimus. Doctrina nostrarū Ecclesiarum satis testatur, nobis cum Sabellio nihil esse commune, quum ille interdum non erubescat palàm Arium tueri, & patribus Niceni cõcilii præferre. Interea cautus homo medius inter Arium & Sabellium ingredi conatus, duabus, opinor, sellis male sedet.
units.tr: We believe Christ to be the Son of God according to the Scriptures; we recognise no Gentile tricks. We steadfastly assert three persons in the Godhead, without tricks, and we do not divide the substance but distinguish among the persons. He sings us the old tune of Sabellius; we more justly sing back to him the blasphemies of Arius. The doctrine of our churches sufficiently testifies that we have nothing in common with Sabellius, since he does not blush to openly defend Arius and to prefer him to the Fathers of the Council of Nicaea. Meanwhile this cautious fellow, trying to walk a middle path between Arius and Sabellius, I think sits badly on two stools.

units.la: Imposturæ, quibus fucum hominibus piis conatus est facere. XX.
units.tr: The impostures by which he tried to deceive pious men. XX.

units.la: Venio ad extremum caput, in quo explicabo quibus artibus Gentilis omnes fallere studuerit. Nam certè declarat hîc sese qualem Mercurium expressit poeta, de quo festiuè exclamat, ὡς ἀγαθὸν ἐς ἐπωνυμίας πολλὰς ἔχειν [?].
units.tr: I come now to the last chapter, in which I will explain by what arts Gentilis tried to deceive everyone. For here he certainly reveals himself as the sort of Mercury the poet described, of whom he jokingly exclaims, how good it is to have many names [?].

units.la: Confessioni à se editæ præfixit ementitam præfationem sub typographi Theophili nomine ad filios Ecclesiæ. Hanc ipse propria manu & composuit, & scripsit. Commendat autem magnificè Lectori maximos thesauros parui libelli, quem dignum pronunciat, quo omnes fruantur Ecclesiæ:&, vt vino non satis vendibili, suspendat hederam, fingit mirificè anhelantem typographum ad reliqua Gentilis scripta. Contemnit præ his Chrysippeos quosdam acervos, & longissimas Iliadas παραδόξων [?].
units.tr: Before the confession he published, he placed a made-up preface in the name of the printer Theophilus, addressed to the sons of the Church. He himself composed and wrote this preface with his own hand. In it he praises magnificently to the reader the great treasures of this little book, which he declares worthy for all of the Church to enjoy; and, as if to advertise wine that will not sell well, he hangs out the ivy bush, pretending that the printer is wonderfully eager for the rest of Gentilis's writings. He scorns beside these certain heaps of Chrysippus and very long Iliads of paradoxes [?].

units.la: Hæc sanè viri boni & ingenui nõ sunt, præsertim in re tâta. Christus, Prophetæ, & Apostoli nõ his artibus sua cõmendarunt posteritati. Rectè dixit Salomon, Laudet te alienus, & non os tuū. Nostri etiâ homines dicere solet, Malos esse vicinos iis qui sua prædicant. Sed metuebat nimirum quod res erat, defore nimirum præcones, nisi in aliena persona sibi triumphum præcineret.
units.tr: Such things are certainly not the marks of good and honest men, especially in a matter of such weight. Christ, the Prophets and the Apostles did not commend their words to posterity by such arts. Solomon rightly said, Let another praise you, and not your own mouth. Our people also commonly say that those who proclaim their own wares make bad neighbours. But he evidently feared what was the case: that there would be no heralds, unless he sang his own triumph through another's person.

units.la: Sed & locum editionis veritus est prodere. Nam Lugduni quū sit editus, ille Antuerpiam nobis præstigiis suis nominat. Hæc ciuilia illi sunt mendacia in ferenda tam perniciosa doctrina.
units.tr: But he was also afraid to reveal the place of publication. For although it was published at Lyon, he names Antwerp to us in his trickery. These are the lies of a citizen in bringing forth such a pernicious doctrine.

units.la: Confessionem pari fide orditur, Iussisti vir præstantissime, &c. Hanc fraudem vt intelligant boni viri, sciant rem ita gestam. Gentilis incarceratus, in vinculis iussus erat exhibere cõfessionem domino Gaiëfi præfecto, quam ministris prouinciæ daret examinandam. Interea intercedentibus amicis, Valentinus nõ satis notus li-beraberatur ex carcere,& nondum excussa confessione admonetur, vt deinceps pacificè & tranquillè viuat: nec suspicabatur præfectus exemplar illius confessionis illum penes se retinuisse.
units.tr: He begins the confession with equal faith: "You have ordered, most excellent sir, etc." So that good men may understand this fraud, let them know how the matter was done. Gentilis was imprisoned, and in chains he was ordered to hand over a confession to the lord Gaiëfi, the prefect, which he would give to the officials of the province for examination. Meanwhile, through the intercession of friends, Valentinus, not well known, was released from prison, and before the confession had been extracted he was warned to live peacefully and quietly from then on; nor did the prefect suspect that he had kept a copy of that confession for himself.

units.la: At iste liberatus, mox eandem sparsit in vulgus, quasi iubente & volente præfecto, id faceret. Iussus erat, vt homo suspectus, confessionem dare præfecto, non autem vt eandem tot blasphemiis refertam sub illius nomine diuenderet.
units.tr: But that man, once freed, soon spread the same document among the public, as if he did this by the prefect's command and with his consent. He had been ordered, as a suspect man, to give a confession to the prefect, not to sell it under the prefect's name, stuffed as it was with so many blasphemies.

units.la: Hanc calumniam & impostturam non aliter postea diluit, quàm quòd diceret præfectum quidem non iussisse vt ederet, sed tamen non prohibuisse. Verùm quomodo prohiberi poterat, quod eum vnquam facturum suspicio nulla erat?
units.tr: Afterwards he met this charge and imposture in no other way than by saying that the prefect had indeed not ordered him to publish it, but had not forbidden it either. But how could it be forbidden, when there was no suspicion at all that he would ever do it?

units.la: Cæterùm retulimus supra ex ipsiusmet ore, quod etiâ Gratiano-poli similiter, & Lugduni confessione ediderit de Trinitate, quam ferre potuere papistæ. Interea nos criminatur, quòd cum illis tueamur Quaternitate, & erremus grauiter cum magistris illis Græcis & Latinis in hoc negotio. Oportet igitur hominẽ hunc malitiosè agere hoc negotiũ, & data opera ambagibus ludere. Has ego verius præstigias, sophisticem, magiam, & si quid asperius est, dixerim.
units.tr: Moreover, we have already reported from his own mouth that he likewise published a confession on the Trinity at Gratianopolis and at Lyon, which the Papists were able to tolerate. Meanwhile he accuses us of holding a Quaternity with them, and of erring gravely in this matter together with those Greek and Latin masters. It must therefore be that this man acts maliciously in this business and deliberately plays with ambiguities. These tricks I would more truly call deceit, sophistry, magic, and, if something harsher is wanted, anything else.

units.la: Reuersus tandem ex Polonia, dom. præfecto Gaiensi formulam obtulit institutedæ disputationis, quam ex eius autographo huc ad verbum subscribam, vt videant cordati homines, quis in hac tota actione ipsum gubernarit spiritus. Ita igitur sub nomine præfecti publicari disputationem terminandam præscripsit,
units.tr: Returning at last from Poland, he offered to the lord prefect of Gex a plan for arranging the disputation, which I will here copy word for word from his own hand, so that thoughtful men may see what spirit guided him in this whole affair. He therefore ordered the disputation to be published under the prefect's name, with these terms:

units.la: Vniuersis & singulis Ecclesiarum pastoribus, doctoribus, diaconis & senioribus, qui passim in Gallia & Sabaudia Euãgelicam pietatem profitentur, has nostras literas inspecturis, lecturisve salutem & pacem in Domino.
units.tr: To all and each of the ministers, teachers, deacons and elders of the Churches who everywhere in France and Savoy profess evangelical piety, who shall look upon or read these our letters: greeting and peace in the Lord.

units.la: Lectis ac diligenter expensis supra scriptis inter se oppositis propositionibus: audita quoque Valentini Gentilis Itali perquam iusta petitione, nempe vt de re tanta iudicium fiat ex simplici Dei verbo: visum est magnifico domino Gaii præfecto vtriusque assertionis dogmata in varia Galliæ & Sabaudiæ loca, præsertim Geneuam & Lugdunum transmittere, vt si quis domini Caluini discipulus voluerit præceptoris sui sententiam tueri, possit intra hebdomadem Gaium accedere, ea cõditione cum Gentili congressurus, vt nisi quisque assertiones, quas tuendas susceperit, ex aperto Dei verbo veras esse demonstret, sit tanquam manifestus impostor, & falsae religionis assertor, capitis poenam luiturus. Quod si nemo ad praescriptum tempus comparuerit, magnificus dominus Praefectus, cum vniuerso Senatu Gaiensi, vti par est, clare pronunciabit, praefatum Gentilem de altissimo Deo, & Filio eius Iesu Christo pie & orthodoxe sentire, &c.
units.tr: Having read and carefully weighed the propositions set against each other above, and having also heard the very just petition of Valentinus Gentilis, an Italian, namely that judgment on so great a matter be made from the simple Word of God, the magnificent lord prefect of Gex has thought fit to send the doctrines of both assertions to various places in France and Savoy, especially Geneva and Lyon, so that if any disciple of Master Calvin wishes to defend his teacher's opinion, he may come to Gex within a week, on this condition: that he is to contend with Gentilis, and unless each one demonstrates from the plain Word of God that the assertions he has undertaken to defend are true, he shall be held as a manifest impostor and an advocate of false religion, and shall pay the penalty of death. But if no one appears at the appointed time, the magnificent lord Prefect, together with the whole Senate of Gex, as is fitting, will clearly declare that the said Gentilis thinks piously and orthodoxly about the Most High God and his Son Jesus Christ, etc.

units.la: In hac formula expendant pii homines ab aduersario componi modum sibi idoneum : pias & iustas iudicari propositiones Gentilis: deinde dari spatium dierum octo, intra quos aduolent disputaturi, quū vix tot diebus illuc mitti potuerint: in primis vero quòd sub capitis periculo tantùm admittuntur aduersarii ad disputationem. An non vero hoc firmum est argumentum spiritus improbi & seductoris? Hoc igitur quum illi obiiceretur, non aliter diluit, quàm id à se factum dicendo, vt pauciores haberet aduersarios. Sed prodit se spiritus sanguinarius caede & erroribus pietatem implicaturus, nisi Domini providentia factum esset, vt in hoc ipsum periculum incideret, quod aliis fuerat machinatus.
units.tr: In this formula let pious men weigh that the adversary has laid down a manner of proceeding suited to himself: that Gentilis's propositions are judged pious and just; then that a space of eight days is given, within which the disputants are to hurry there, though they could scarcely have been sent there in so many days; and above all that opponents are admitted to the disputation only under pain of death. Is this not a firm proof of a wicked and seducing spirit? When this was objected to him, he met it in no other way than by saying he had done it so that he would have fewer opponents. But the bloodthirsty spirit reveals itself, meaning to entangle piety in slaughter and error; had it not been for the providence of the Lord, he would have fallen into the very danger which he had devised for others.

units.la: Demum quū illi causa esset dicenda, & defendenda sua doctrina, singulari improbitatis exemplo ius actionis ad se conatus est rapere, vt audiretur tanquam actor, nec constitueretur reus. quod quum obtinere non posset, doctrinam suam lubricè proposuit, saepius rixas mouit de rebus extra controuersiam positis: vt an vnus sit altissimus Deus, Christum esse Filium Dei, & similia, quae nemo illi negauit vnquam. Verùm illud constanter illi pernegatum est, quòd Christus ab vnitate illius aeterni Dei esset excludendus, & quòd tres aeternos Spiritus essentiali numero differentes essent constituendi.
units.tr: Finally, when he had to state his case and defend his doctrine, with a unique example of wickedness he tried to seize for himself the right of action, so that he would be heard as the plaintiff and not placed as the defendant. When he could not obtain this, he proposed his doctrine in a slippery way and often stirred up quarrels over matters placed beyond controversy: whether there is only one Most High God, that Christ is the Son of God, and similar things, which no one ever denied to him. But this was constantly and flatly denied to him: that Christ must be excluded from the unity of that eternal God, and that three eternal Spirits, differing in essential number, must be posited.

units.la: Ex his iudicium facient pii religionis aestimatores, quid de huiusmodi blasphemiae spiritu sentiendum, & quàm iustis de causis poenas dederit, qui alios capitali poena propositâ, sit ausus ad disputationem prouocare.
units.tr: From these facts pious judges of religion will form a judgment about what ought to be thought of such a spirit of blasphemy, and for how just reasons he has paid the penalty, who, with a capital penalty set before him, dared to challenge others to dispute.

units.la: Caeterùm par est, vt tandem huic negotio colophonem impo-mus. Quum igitur à quinta Augusti mensis, vsque ad 9. Sena-ptembris, saepe diùque cum homine illo esset actû, semper autem in suis persisteret dogmatibus, morti tandem à magnifico Senatu est adiudicatus. Et quia auidum eius rei fore lectorem puto, non pigebit eius sententiam hic ad finem referre. Formula igitur talis fermè fuit.
units.tr: Moreover, it is fitting that we at last put a finishing touch on this business. Since, then, from the fifth of August until the ninth of September he was often and at length dealt with, but always persisted in his opinions, he was at last condemned to death by the magnificent Senate. And because I think the reader will be eager for this, I will not hesitate to set down here the sentence itself. The formula was, then, roughly as follows.

units.la: Valentinus hic Gentilis, ex Cosentio Neapolitani regni oriundus, postquam sibi ante annos octo proposuisset articulum Trinitatis impugnare, passim docere coepit, tres esse distinctos spiritus, essentiali numero differentes: inter quos Patrem solum agnoscit illum adorandum & infinitum Deum, non sine magna Filii Dei blasphemia. Huic dogmati alii etiam annexi sunt errores, ob quos pridem à magnifico magistratu Geneuensi comprehensus ad plenam errorum declarationem, palinodiam cecinit. Etenim & errores palàm agnouit & detestatus est, & abiurauit, ac insuper iureiurando sese astrinxit, urbem se illam, sine Senatus venia non egressurum. Verùm quia illa omnia non tanti apud ipsum fuere momenti, quin neglecta iuramenti religione, clàm inde profugeret, ac deinceps ad errores abiuratos postliminio rediret, maiorique deinceps conatu & disputando & scribendo contra aperta scripturæ testimonia, propugnarit: quibus inaudita accedunt maledicta, & horrendæ blasphemiæ in Dei Filium & Trinitatis mysterium. Demum quia iam etiam in vinculis magnifici Senatus ad plenam & sufficientem instructionem incurabilem sese præbet, pertinaciter in erroribus sui dogmatis persistendo: censuit magnificus Senatus huius Reipub. ad præcauenda dissidia, & eliminandos tam atroces errores, capite plectendum.
units.tr: Valentinus Gentilis here, a native of Cosenza in the kingdom of Naples, after he had proposed eight years ago to attack the article of the Trinity, began to teach everywhere that there are three distinct Spirits, differing in essential number, among whom he acknowledges only the Father as the adorable and infinite God, not without a great blasphemy against the Son of God. Other errors also were linked to this doctrine, on account of which he had earlier been seized by the magnificent magistracy of Geneva, and, for a full declaration of his errors, he sang a palinode. For he openly acknowledged and detested the errors, and abjured them, and moreover bound himself by oath not to leave that city without the Senate's permission. But since all these things were of so little weight with him that, disregarding the sanctity of the oath, he fled secretly from there and afterwards returned by right of return to the errors he had abjured, and with greater effort, both by disputing and by writing, defended them against the plain testimonies of Scripture; to these are added unheard-of curses and horrible blasphemies against the Son of God and the mystery of the Trinity. Finally, since even now, in the chains of the magnificent Senate, he shows himself incurable for a full and sufficient instruction, persisting obstinately in the errors of his doctrine, the magnificent Senate of this Commonwealth has judged, to prevent discord and to eliminate such atrocious errors, that he is to be punished by beheading.

units.la: Quum igitur ad supplicium educeretur, non desiit homo pertinacissimus, & ex sola indomita peruicacia gloriam quærens, (sicut Satanæ martyres solent) ingeminare se pro gloria altissimi Dei pati, nos omnes esse Sabellianos, & Deum habere trinomium: se verò nullũ Deum ἄθεον[?] agnoscere. cui quum vicissim respõderemus, falsa hæc esse, & calumniosa quæ nobis obiiceret, sophisticum autem esse quod de altissimo Deo prædicaret, & porrò impium quòd plures numero deos statueret: nihil tamen profecimus. Subinde enim ille sua repetebat, vsque dum videret nihil aliud superesse, quàm vt iugulum præberet. Tum verò coepit labascere, & se dicere nobiscum consentire, dummodo Christum esse Filium Dei crederemus: quod quum nunquam à nobis negatum exciperemus, (qualis enim alioqui fides nostra fuerit?) tum rursus manifeste patuit ipsius dolus, qui appellationem Dei ad solam Patris personam restringere consevisset: in qua tamen teterrima blasphemia vir pessimus perseverans, rogante Dominum tota quae adstabat Ecclesia, ut eius animum immutaret, & nobis hominem assidue ad resipiscentiam hortantibus, tandem justo Dei judicio caesus, blasphemare simul & viuere in hoc mundo desiit.
units.tr: When he was led out to execution, this most obstinate man, seeking glory from nothing but his unbroken stubbornness (as Satan's martyrs usually do), kept insisting that he suffered for the glory of the Most High God, that all of us were Sabellians, and that God had three names, while he himself acknowledged no God [ἄθεον]. When we answered in turn that what he objected to us was false and slanderous, that what he said about the Most High God was sophistry, and that his claim of many gods was impious, we achieved nothing. He kept repeating his own assertions until he saw that nothing remained but to offer his throat. Then he began to waver and said that he agreed with us, provided we believed that Christ is the Son of God. When we never denied this, since what else would our faith be, his trickery became plain again, for he had tried to restrict the name of God to the person of the Father alone. Persisting in this most wicked blasphemy, the man, though the whole Church standing by prayed to the Lord to change his heart and we repeatedly urged him to repent, was at last struck down by the just judgment of God and ceased to blaspheme and to live in this world.

units.la: Habes, pie lector, historiae diffusae breuem & veram explicationem. Tu nobiscum Deum æternum invoca, ut tanta scandala ab Ecclesia sua clementer avertat, populo suo largiatur vigilantes & idoneos ministros, qui serio ament διδασκαλίαν ὑγιαινούσαν, ἀντιλέγοντας [?] utiliter possint ἐλέγχειν: universum autem veritatis sermone norint ὀρθοτομεῖν ad nominis sui gloriam, & Ecclesiae utilitatem per Jesum Christum Filium eius unicum & coæternum, Amen.
units.tr: You have, pious reader, a brief and true account of this lengthy affair. Join with us in calling upon the eternal God, that he may mercifully turn such scandals away from his Church, and grant to his people watchful and fit ministers who earnestly love sound teaching [διδασκαλίαν ὑγιαινούσαν], who can usefully refute those who contradict [ἀντιλέγοντας] it, and who know how to handle the word of truth rightly [ὀρθοτομεῖν] to the glory of his name and the good of the Church, through Jesus Christ, his only and coeternal Son. Amen.

units.tr: When the ecclesiastical writers whom we call the Fathers lived and flourished.
