units.la: CENSURA CONCLUSIONUM, quòd Baptismus non successerit Circuncisioni, contra Paedobaptistas.
units.tr: CENSURE OF THE CONCLUSIONS, that Baptism did not succeed Circumcision, against the Paedobaptists.

units.la: ORNATISSIMO VIRO D. Christophoro Thretio Polono. S.P.
units.tr: To the most distinguished man, Mr. Christophorus Thretius, a Pole. Greetings.

units.la: Vidi, doctissime Christophore, conclusiones, quibus asseritur, quòd baptismus nō successerit circuncisioni, contra Paedobaptistas. In quibus quum multa possis merito requirere, in primis tamen καινότητα[?], hoc est, argumenti novitatem, & ἀνύστατον[?] genus probandi admiror. Posterius ei commune cum multis, prius illi proprium esse videtur. Nemo enim hactenus analogiam istam sacramentorum convellere est conatus, ne apud veteres quidem, & qui hodie apud nos Paedobaptismum impugnant, hac via non ingrediuntur. Apparet igitur à temporibus Apostolorum saluum hoc fuisse argumentum. Sed habet aliud etiam hæc argumenti novitas. Cœnæ Domini & paschatis analogiam nō obscurè conatur suspectam reddere, quum mannæ quodammodo respondisse ait. Quod si res succedat in priori, paratus est etiam in hac quæstione anagyrin commoucre. Dolendum sanè vehementer, nihil non in controversiam vocari hominum curiositate. Habuit philosophia dum floreret, & hodie apud eruditos retinet adhuc multa certa & firma: quæ quia ab omnibus admittebatur, dicta sunt ἀναμβισβήτητα[?]. Habuit sub Mose vera religio, & Patriarchis ac Prophetis, certa quædam de quibus non licebat quæstionem movere. Sed & Apostolis firma quædam fuere, & primæ ecclesiæ indubitata. Nostrum verò seculum eò est infelicius, quia nihil ita firmum & expressum habetur, quod in controversiam venire non soleat: in qua re exemplis non est opus, res ipsa loquitur. Effectum est ex hac licentia, alterum, quod huic commune diximus cum multis: [illegible, ~9 letters] enim oportet afferant multa, quae rem bene constitutam convellere primitus conantur: quod tamen vitium alij alijs accuratius tegunt. hic vero author sic illud palam prodit, ut a pueris in triuio facile deprehendi possit.
units.tr: I have seen your conclusions, most learned Christophorus, in which it is asserted that baptism did not succeed circumcision, against the Paedobaptists. There is much in them that you could rightly be asked to explain, but first of all I admire the novelty [καινότητα] of the argument and the unshakable [ἀνύστατον] kind of proof. The latter seems to be shared with many others; the former seems to be peculiar to you. For no one hitherto has tried to overturn this analogy between the sacraments, not even among the ancients, and those who today attack infant baptism among us do not take this road. It appears, then, that this argument has been safe since the times of the Apostles. But this novelty of argument has another feature as well. It openly tries to make the analogy between the Lord's Supper and the Passover suspect, when it says that the manna in some way corresponded to it. If the matter succeeds in the former case, you are ready to stir up the anagyrus in this question too. It is greatly to be lamented that, through human curiosity, nothing is left that is not called into dispute. Philosophy, while it flourished, had many things that were certain and firm, and even today it still keeps many such things among the learned; because these were accepted by everyone, they were called indisputable [ἀναμφισβήτητα]. True religion under Moses, and among the Patriarchs and Prophets, had certain matters about which it was not permitted to raise a question. The Apostles too had firm points, and the primitive Church had undoubted ones. But our own age is the more unhappy, because nothing is held so firmly and clearly that it does not usually come into controversy; examples are not needed in this matter, the thing speaks for itself. From this licence there has followed another feature, which I said is common to you and to many others: [illegible, ~9 letters], for they must bring forward many arguments which first try to overturn a matter well settled. Yet other men conceal this fault more carefully than others do; this author, however, displays it so openly that it could easily be detected by boys at the crossroads.

units.la: Caeterum has conclusiones cum censura qualicunque mea ad te remitto, mi Threti: primum quia in tua Polonia natae sunt, & tua opera ad nos perlatae, deinde quod te id cupere perspexi: demum ut esset etiam in hac re publicum veritatis testimonium. denique volui etiam ut extaret amoris erga te mei testimonium qualecunque. Si enim in amore debet esse ἀντιφίλησις, utique honestorum amor eam inprimis requirit. Et quia graviora te negotia in patriam hinc avocant, volo haec meo nomine apud te esse προπεμπτικά, hoc est, quae te honoris ergo deducant. Igitur mi Threti hanc meam censuram, tanquam animi mei ingenuam & veram effigiem accipe. Placet enim hoc Platonico concludere, Εἰκόνες ὄντως τῶν ψυχῶν εἰσιν οἱ λόγοι. Vale, Bernae Helvetiorum M. D. LXVII. 25. Iulij.
units.tr: Meanwhile I send these conclusions back to you, my Thretius, together with my censure, such as it is: first, because they were born in your Poland and brought to us through your work; second, because I have perceived that you desired this; and last, so that there might also be a public testimony to the truth in this matter. Finally, I wanted there also to be some testimony, such as it is, of my affection for you. For if there ought to be mutual love in friendship, then the love of good men above all requires it. And since more serious business calls you from here back to your homeland, I want these pages to be, on my behalf, parting gifts [προπεμπτικά] with you, that is, things to escort you with honour. Therefore, my Thretius, accept this my censure as a frank and true likeness of my mind. For I like to conclude with Plato: "Words are truly the images of souls [Εἰκόνες ὄντως τῶν ψυχῶν εἰσιν οἱ λόγοι]." Farewell. From Bern in Switzerland, 25 July 1567.

units.la: T. Bened. Aretius.
units.tr: Yours, Benedictus Aretius.

units.la: CENSVRA CONCLVSIO-num, quòd Baptismus non successerit Circuncisioni, contra Pædobaptistas.
units.tr: CONCLUSION OF THE JUDGMENT, that Baptism did not succeed Circumcision, against the Pædobaptists.

units.la: De successione Baptismi in locum Circuncisionis, breuis assertio, in qua etiam refutatur argumenta, quibus nonnulli Pædobaptismum conati sunt tollere.
units.tr: On the succession of Baptism in the place of Circumcision: a brief assertion, in which the arguments by which some have tried to overthrow infant baptism are also refuted.

units.la: QVI hactenus Pædobaptismum impugnarunt, eo maximè nitebantur argumento, quòd infantes prius instruendi essent in fide: deinde, quòd sine Baptismo decedentes vitam æternam consequi possent. Verùm quia his copiosè & sæpe responsum est, noui defensores dogmatis illius, ad noua sese contulerunt argumenta, & reperta sunt ingenia, quæ à fundamentis Baptismum conuellendum censerent: ad quam rem idoneum aditum habere se arbitrantur, si monstrent Baptismum in locum Circuncisionis non successisse, ideóq; hoc Sacramentum non esse tanti momenti, quanti homines Christiani hactenus credidêre. Quo sanè impetrato, Baptismus non solùm facilè eludetur, sed liberè contemnetur, imò in vniuersum ab Ecclesia Christi eliminabitur.
units.tr: Those who have hitherto attacked infant baptism relied chiefly on two arguments: that infants must first be instructed in the faith, and that those who die without Baptism can still attain eternal life. But since these points have been answered fully and often, new defenders of that doctrine have turned to new arguments, and clever minds have arisen who think Baptism must be overthrown from its foundations. They believe they will have a suitable opening for this if they can show that Baptism did not succeed Circumcision in its place, and that this sacrament is therefore not as important as Christians have hitherto believed. Once that is granted, Baptism will not only be easily evaded but freely despised, and indeed will be eliminated altogether from the Church of Christ.

units.la: Quare, vt illi homines solertes sunt in oppugnanda veritate: ita nos in eadem defendêda decet esse vigilantes. Illi noua in dies proferunt, & ἀθεμίτα ὥσπερ ἰὸς δηλητήρια ἐπιχειρήματα [?]: nos illis ex Scripturis noua ἀλεξητήρια καὶ ἀνίδοτους λόγους [?] proferamus, vt si illi sanabiles non sint, tamen veneni vim à nobis propellamus: vt illa δήγματα ἀλεξήρια [?] si non sanare, certè aperire videamur. medico enim quandoque satis est vim morbi patefecisse.
units.tr: Just as those clever men are skilled at attacking the truth, so we ought to be watchful in defending it. Daily they bring forward new arguments, unlawful and deadly like the poison of a viper [ἀθεμίτα ὥσπερ ἰὸς δηλητήρια ἐπιχειρήματα]. Let us in turn bring forward from the Scriptures new remedies and antidotes [ἀλεξητήρια καὶ ἀνίδοτους λόγους], so that, if those men cannot be cured, we may at least drive back the force of the poison from ourselves, and, if we cannot heal the bites [δήγματα ἀλεξήρια], at least appear to lay them open. For it is often enough for a physician to have revealed the force of the disease.

units.la: Indicabimus igitur, Baptismum Circuncisioni rectè esse substitutum. Deinde quàm infirmis rationibus hanc successionem nonnulli conentur tollere, aperiemus.
units.tr: We will therefore show that Baptism was rightly substituted for Circumcision. Then we will reveal how weak are the reasons by which some try to overthrow this succession.

units.la: Ac Baptismum Circuncisioni successisse, palàm est. orbis enim Christianus vbique, explosa Circuncisione, recepit pro illa Baptifmum,&id ita constanter,ut nemo in censu Christianorum haberi possit,qui vel utrunque simul,vel, hoc neglecto,illam amplecti velit. Iudæum & Turcam ex Circuncisione cognoscas:Christianum ex Baptismo : defectorem ex utroque. quare communis est tessera Christianismi, quam non erubescunt pro Circuncisione agnoscere.Ideoque quòd successerit,extra quaestionem est. Sed de iure hic quaeritur. Non enim quae publicam habent approbationem, mox vera sunt:quū errores etiam quandoque publico recipiantur consensu.
units.tr: That Baptism succeeded Circumcision is plain. For the Christian world everywhere, having cast Circumcision aside, has received Baptism in its place, and so constantly that no one can be counted among Christians who would wish to embrace both together, or, neglecting this, to embrace the other alone. You may know a Jew or a Turk by circumcision, a Christian by baptism, and an apostate by both. Therefore Baptism is the common badge of Christianity, which they are not ashamed to acknowledge in place of Circumcision. That it succeeded is thus beyond question. But the question here is one of right. For not all things that have public approval are at once true, since errors too are sometimes received by common consent.

units.la: Doceamus ergo Ecclesiam Christi recte,abolita Circuncisione, in illius locum recepisse Baptismum. Primum Ecclesia Christi recte dicitur,quae audit vocem illius. Ioan.10. Oues veri pastoris vocem norunt, & alienum non sequuntur. Christi autem veri pastoris, vox est, Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua & Spiritu, non potest introire in regnum Dei.Ioann.3.& Matth.28.Marci 16. Manifesta est institutio Baptismi a Christo mandata Ecclesiae: quo nouo Sacramento constituto, veterem Circuncisionem, ut umbram abo-levit. Recte igitur fecit Ecclesia Christi, quae audiendo vocem Pastoris sui, pro Circuncisione recepit Baptismum.
units.tr: Let us therefore teach that the Church of Christ, having abolished Circumcision, rightly received Baptism in its place. First, the Church of Christ is rightly so called when it hears his voice: John 10. "The sheep know the voice of the true shepherd, and do not follow a stranger." The voice of Christ, the true shepherd, is: "Unless a man is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God," John 3; also Matt. 28; Mark 16. The institution of Baptism commanded by Christ to the Church is plain. By establishing this new sacrament, he abolished the old Circumcision as a shadow. Rightly, therefore, the Church of Christ, hearing the voice of its shepherd, received Baptism in place of Circumcision.

units.la: Deinde Apostoli, sequentes summi Pastoris vestigia, eandem, substituto Baptismo,reiecerunt.Gal.5.Si circuncidimini,Christus nihil vobis proderit. Contrà de Baptismo habemus, Quicunque baptizati estis,Christum induistis, Gal.3. Iure igitur, explosa Circuncisione, Ecclesia recepit Baptismum.
units.tr: Next, the Apostles, following the footsteps of the chief Shepherd, rejected the one when Baptism was substituted for it. Gal. 5: "If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing." On the other hand, of Baptism we have: "As many of you as have been baptized have put on Christ," Gal. 3. Rightly, therefore, with Circumcision cast aside, the Church received Baptism.

units.la: Sed fortasse, ne sic quidem collimamus. Nam & Baptismum a Christo recte institutum esse, & explosam Circucisionem: non tamen ob id illum in huius locum succedere. Videamus igitur etiam hoc. Primum succedere sibi dicitur, vbi vno sublato alterum substituitur in locum illius:ut typi in veteri testamento sublati func[?],in quorum locum successerunt antitypa, hoc est,res per typos adumbratae. Hoc pacto, ni fallor, illi negant Baptismum successisse Circuncisioni. & quanuis ab illis iure postulandum fuerat, ut monstrarent alia analoga Sacramenta: tamen praesenti seruiemus causae, & ostendemus Baptismum hoc ipso fuisse in locum Circuncisionis substitutum, quia illa huius fuerit typus.
units.tr: But perhaps we do not hit the mark even so. For although Baptism was rightly instituted by Christ and Circumcision abolished, it does not follow that Baptism succeeds to its place. Let us consider this too. First, one thing is said to succeed another when, one being removed, the other is put in its place; as the types of the Old Testament were removed, and the antitypes, that is, the realities foreshadowed through the types, succeeded in their place. In this way, I think, they deny that Baptism succeeded Circumcision. And although they ought rightly to be required to show other analogous sacraments, yet we will serve the present cause and show that Baptism was substituted in the place of Circumcision precisely because Circumcision was its type.

units.la: Primum enim illa regenerationis fuit apud Iudaeos Sacramentum tum, quemadmodum Baptismus apud nos. & dabatur quidem in carne, sed cum dolore & sanguinis effusione. admonebat enim eos de poenitentia & interiori quadam cordis emendatione. Ideoque Scriptura alias expresse exigit non tam praeputij, quam cordis Circumcisionem. Deut. 10. Circuncidite praeputium cordis vestri. Deut. 30. Circumcidet Dominus Deus tuus cor tuum: & passim Prophetae emendationem cordis urgent, ut scopum externi istius Sacramenti patefacerent. Idem requirit Baptismus in nobis: unde Baptismus poenitentiae dicitur, Lucae 3. Mar. 1. & Lauacrum regenerationis, ad Titum 3. Qunm igitur Circucisio non sine Baptismo fit facta, & finis quoque idem sit, sequitur hunc in illius locum succedere.
units.tr: For first, among the Jews Circumcision was then the sacrament of regeneration, just as Baptism is among us. It was given in the flesh, but with pain and the shedding of blood. It admonished them concerning repentance and a certain inward amendment of the heart. Hence Scripture elsewhere expressly demands not so much circumcision of the foreskin as circumcision of the heart: Deut. 10: "Circumcise the foreskin of your heart." Deut. 30: "The Lord your God will circumcise your heart." Everywhere the prophets urge amendment of the heart, so as to reveal the aim of that external sacrament. Baptism requires the same in us; hence Baptism is called the baptism of repentance, Luke 3; Mark 1, and the washing of regeneration, Titus 3. Since therefore Circumcision was not made without Baptism, and the end is the same, it follows that Baptism succeeds to its place.

units.la: Sed requirūt expressam Scripturam. Si Iudaei essent, qui hoc faciunt, remitteremus illos ad Mosen & Prophetas, qui Messiae novum foedus & noua foederis symbola concedunt. Deinde a docto-ribus Rabinis discere poterant fideles matronas quae Circuncisio-nis capaces non erant, baptizatas transfuiisse ad consortium foede-ris. quod tradunt de Sara, Rebecca, Rachele & Lea. Sed quia Chri-stiani sunt, damus illis Paulum Col. 2. Per quem circuncisi estis circuncisione non manu facta in depositione corporis peccato-rum carnis, in circuncisione Christi, consepulti cum illo in Baptis-mo: quibus verbis Baptismus, Circuncisio Christi dicitur. Quare hic illi recte successit, alioqui non erat ratio cur haec duo conecteret.
units.tr: But they demand express Scripture. If they were Jews who did this, we would send them back to Moses and the Prophets, who grant to the Messiah a new covenant and new signs of the covenant. Moreover, from the learned rabbis they could learn that faithful matrons, who were not capable of circumcision, were admitted by baptism into fellowship of the covenant; they relate this of Sarah, Rebecca, Rachel and Leah. But since they are Christians, we give them Paul, Col. 2: "In whom you were circumcised with a circumcision not made by hands, in putting off the body of the sins of the flesh, in the circumcision of Christ; buried with him in Baptism." By these words Baptism is called the circumcision of Christ. Therefore it rightly succeeded here; otherwise there would be no reason why he joined these two together.

units.la: Hanc sententia confirmat consensus veterū scriptorum de qui-bus paucula haec testimonia addemus. Iustinus Martyr cōtra Try-phonem agens de hac re, ita scribit: Accepimus non illam secundum carnem Circuncisionem, sed spiritualem, quam Enoch & similes custodierunt, nos tamen per Baptismum accepimus. Et paulo superius externam Circuncisionem ait typum fuisse internae & ἀληθεινῆς περιτομῆς [?]: per quam ab erroribus & malitia sumus circuncisi per eum qui una Sabbathorum resurrexit a mortuis.
units.tr: The consent of the ancient writers confirms this view, and we will add a few testimonies. Justin Martyr, treating this matter against Trypho, writes thus: "We have received not that circumcision according to the flesh, but the spiritual one, which Enoch and like men kept; yet we have received it through Baptism." A little earlier he says that external Circumcision was a type of the internal and true circumcision [ἀληθεινῆς περιτομῆς], by which we are circumcised from errors and wickedness through him who rose from the dead on the first of the Sabbaths.

units.la: Athanasius quoque in hac sententia est, explicans illud Lucae 10. Omnia mihi tradita sunt a Patre. Circuncisio, inquit, figura erat exuviarum quae per Baptismum deponuntur. & mox, Abraham enim ubi Deo crediderat, Circuncisionem accepit pro nota, insignibusque eius regenerationis, quae per Baptismum coficitur. Quapropter ubi venerat res, quæ figura denotabatur: nota ipsa, figuraque intercidit, & conquieuit. Circuncifio enim nota erat: Lavacrum autem regenerationis idipsum est, quod denotabatur.
units.tr: Athanasius too is of this view, explaining Luke 10: "All things have been delivered to me by the Father." Circumcision, he says, was a figure of the cast-off garments which are put off through Baptism. And soon after: "For Abraham, when he had believed God, received Circumcision as a mark and token of that regeneration which is accomplished through Baptism. Therefore, when the thing signified by the figure had come, the mark and figure itself ceased and came to rest. For Circumcision was a mark; but the washing of regeneration is that very thing which was signified."

units.la: Epiphanius appellat Circuncifionem magnam, ipsum Baptismum: ut quum Epicureos cōfutat, ait, Illic fuit Circuncifio carnalis, quæ inseruiuit tempori, usque ad magnam Circuncifionem, hoc est, Baptismum, qui circuncidit nos à peccatis, & obsignat nos in nomen Dei. Idem contra Cerinthum agens scribit: Durauit Circuncifio tempori inseruiens, donec maior Circuncifio accessit, hoc est, Lavacrum regenerationis.
units.tr: Epiphanius calls Baptism itself the great Circumcision. When he refutes the Epicureans he says: "There was carnal Circumcision, which served the time, until the great Circumcision came, that is Baptism, which circumcises us from sins and seals us into the name of God." Writing the same against Cerinthus, he says: "Circumcision lasted, serving the time, until the greater Circumcision came, that is the washing of regeneration."

units.la: Augustinus epistola 108.affirmat Christum in Ecclesia sua dedisse, pro Circucisione carnis, Baptismum: & in epistola ad Dardanum, eiusdem naturæ esse testatur Circuncisione & Baptismum.
units.tr: Augustine, in Epistle 108, affirms that Christ gave Baptism in his Church in place of the circumcision of the flesh; and in his letter to Dardanus he testifies that Circumcision and Baptism are of the same nature.

units.la: Maneat igitur indubitata successio huius Sacramenti: quia Christus ita instituit, Apostoli sic docuerunt, sanèti[?] Patres non aliter intellexerūt, & pia Ecclesia rem ita accepit, servat, servabitque usque ad Domini Christi adventum.
units.tr: Let the succession of this sacrament therefore remain undoubted: because Christ so instituted it, the Apostles so taught, the holy Fathers understood it no otherwise, and the pious Church has received the matter in this way, keeps it, and will keep it until the coming of the Lord Christ.

units.la: Superest ut eorum audiamus rationes, quibus hoc novum do-gma stabilire conantur. Primum, aiunt, Circuncisio non nisi uni sexui mandata erat. Genef.17. contrà Baptismus utrique sexui convenit. Matth.28. Marci 16. Actor.8.16.
units.tr: It remains that we hear their reasons by which they try to establish this new doctrine. First, they say, Circumcision was commanded only to one sex: Gen. 17. On the other hand, Baptism belongs to both sexes: Matt. 28; Mark 16; Acts 8:16.

units.la: Infirmum est argumentum: quia ex consideratione unius circunstantiæ seu partis, generatim de re tota statuit. Non enim satis est causæ, tollere successionem ex eo, quòd illa solis masculis competebat: hic autem utrique sexui. Imò quid si ob idipsum debuerit succedere Baptismus tanquam perfectior? An verò admittemus successionem, si uni tantùm sexui applicetur Baptismus? Imò nec tum quidem succedet, si per omnia idem fiat Baptismus. Oportet enim res aliquas esse differentes, ut salua maneat successio. Nam quæ prorsus eadem sunt omnibus circûstantiis, successionem non admittunt. & ex una circunstatia aut duabus tollere successionem, magis ineptire est, quàm iustam adferre causam. Porrò quòd uni sexui solùm applicata fuit Circuncisio, sumit ex Genef.17. Quod tamen simpliciter verum non est. nam res Circuncisionis & substantia fœderis ad utrumque sexum spectat, secundum illud, Ero Deus tuus & seminis tui post te: & illud Ieremiæ 4. Circuncida-mini mini in Domino. Quod autè attinet ad carnis Circucisionem, vni tantùm sexui mandata fuit: quia alter sexus illius signi non erat capax.at baptismi capax est: nõ igitur prohibet quin succedat. Porrò Deus in applicatione signi magis respiciebat ad personâ cum qua foedus contrahebatur. Et quia cum Abrahamo,ex quo Christus erat nasciturus,foedus initur: masculinum sexum signo obligare voluit.Interea à re signi mulier non excludebatur,cuius rei perspicua adfertur ratione Rom. 4. quia Circuncisio non dabatur in iustitiâ, sed in signum iustitiæ, εἰς σημεῖον, οὐκ εἰς δικαιοσύνην: ideóque signacu-lũ appellatur:cuius iustitiæ quum particeps esset Sara,nõ referebat quo signo foedus confirmaretur inter Deum & Abrahamũ. Ideóque rectè hinc colligit Iustinus Martyr, Circuncisionem non esse opus iustitię,quum ad foeminas nõ pertineret:quandoquidẽ Deus iusta tam à mulieribus quàm viris præstari vult. quod si verum est, nulla erit causa, quo minus baptismus illi succedat: licet illa viris solùm, hæc autem fœminis etiam sit communis. Sed videtur hoc argumentum etiam Iudaismum sapere, quũ quærit tale correspondens sacramentum,quod etiam in nouo Testamento solis viris cõpetat.quo sanè non solùm baptismum conculcat, sed Iudaismo & Mahumetismo aperire fenestram nititur. Sed ad alterũ veniamus.
units.tr: The argument is weak, because it decides the whole matter from the consideration of one circumstance or part. It is not enough for the case to remove succession on the ground that Circumcision belonged only to males, whereas Baptism belongs to both sexes. Indeed, what if for that very reason Baptism ought to succeed, as more perfect? Or shall we admit succession only if Baptism were applied to one sex alone? Indeed, not even then would it succeed, if Baptism were in every respect the same. For some things must differ if succession is to remain. Things that are altogether the same in every circumstance do not admit succession; and to remove succession on one or two circumstances is more foolish than to bring a just cause. Moreover, that Circumcision was applied to one sex only he takes from Gen. 17, yet this is not simply true. For the matter of Circumcision and the substance of the covenant pertain to both sexes, according to that: "I will be your God and the God of your seed after you," and Jer. 4: "Circumcise yourselves to the Lord." As for the circumcision of the flesh, it was commanded to one sex only, because the other sex was not capable of that sign; but it is capable of Baptism, and therefore nothing prevents its succeeding. Moreover, in applying the sign God looked chiefly to the person with whom the covenant was made. Since the covenant was contracted with Abraham, from whom Christ was to be born, he willed that the male sex be bound by the sign. Meanwhile women were not excluded from the thing signified, of which a clear reason is given at Rom. 4: Circumcision was given not for righteousness but as a sign of righteousness [εἰς σημεῖον, οὐκ εἰς δικαιοσύνην]; therefore it is called a seal. Since Sarah too shared in that righteousness, it made no difference by what sign the covenant between God and Abraham was confirmed. Hence Justin Martyr rightly concludes that Circumcision was not a work of righteousness, since it did not pertain to women, when God wills righteousness to be performed by women as well as by men. If this is true, there will be no cause why Baptism should not succeed it, even though the one is common to men only and the other is common to women as well. But this argument seems also to savour of Judaism, when it seeks a corresponding sacrament that in the New Testament too belongs only to men; by this it not only tramples underfoot Baptism but strives to open a window for Judaism and Mahumetism. But let us come to the other argument.

units.la: Circuncisio non nisi octauo die fiebat: contrà baptismus nun-quàm non administratur, dumodo baptizandus crediderit. Act.8.
units.tr: Circumcision was performed only on the eighth day, whereas baptism is never withheld, provided the one to be baptized believes. Acts 8.

units.la: Mala est consequentia. nam à circunstantia temporis colligit ad totius subuersionem. Circuncisio octauo tantùm fiebat die:baptismus autem liber est, ut semper dari possit. ergo non succedit ille huic? perinde est ac si dicas, Pesach semel tantùm in anno celebrabatur: Coena autem Domini sæpius: ergo coena non succedit pa-schati. Quis non rideat tale argumentum?hoc quidem hinc infertur,ergo baptismus ratione temporis non succedit Circuncisioni, ut scilicet administretur solùm octauo die,quemadmodũ non succedit ut administretur solùm masculis. In his rectè concludit. Verùm ampliorem affectat prædam:totam enim successionem tollit. oportebat autem eum esse memorem, ne plus inferret in conclusione, quàm medium præmissarum admittit:quod quũ sit singulare, non aliud quàm de singulari circunstantia cõcludere debet. ut, Circuncisio solùm octauo die dabatur, baptismus nunquam non: ergo quod ad circunstantiam temporis attinet,non illi successit. liberior enim est baptismus. Sic pesach in primo solo mense celebrari debuit,coena nunquam non: ergo ratione temporis non successit, vt essct alligata ad eadem temporum moneta.Caeterum inferre,ergo simpliciter non successit, nugari potius est,quàm iustu adferre argumentum. Haec ad formam argumenti istius. Porrò idem sehic prodit spiritus,qui suprà. Primùm desiderat alia Sacramenta veteribus analoga, pertesus fortasis horum quae Ecclesia semper habuit.Deinde in omnibus circunstantiis noua veteribus cogit respondere. Sed ne tum quidem succedent, sed plane eadem erunt.
units.tr: The consequence is bad, for he infers from a circumstance of time to the overthrow of the whole matter. Circumcision was performed only on the eighth day, but baptism is free, so that it can always be given. Therefore, he says, baptism does not succeed circumcision? It is just as if you said that the Passover was celebrated only once a year, but the Lord's Supper more often, and therefore the Lord's Supper does not succeed the Passover. Who would not laugh at such an argument? Here is the inference: baptism therefore does not succeed circumcision in respect of time, namely in being administered only on the eighth day, just as it does not succeed in being administered only to males. In these points he concludes rightly. But he aims at a larger prey, for he removes the whole succession. He ought, however, to have been careful not to infer in the conclusion more than the middle term of his premises allows. Since that term is particular, it should yield a conclusion only about a particular circumstance. For example: circumcision was given only on the eighth day, baptism never not; therefore, as regards the circumstance of time, baptism did not succeed it, for baptism is freer. So too the Passover ought to have been celebrated only in the first month, the Supper never not; therefore in respect of time the Supper did not succeed it, in that it was not bound to the same times. But to infer, therefore simply it did not succeed, is trifling rather than a proper argument. So much for the form of that argument. Moreover, the same spirit appears here as above. First he desires other sacraments analogous to the old ones, perhaps weary of those which the Church has always had. Then, in every circumstance, he forces the new to answer to the old. But not even then will they succeed; they will be entirely the same.

units.la: Demum annectit particulam Anabaptistici spiritus. Dummodo baptizandus, inquit, crediderit. Ergone tibi non baptizabitur nisi credat,hoc est,fidem ore profiteri possit? exempli gratia de infantibus,quos dices non esse baptizandos,hoc ipso quia nondum possunt credere. quò facit locus citatus Actor.8. vbi Philippus in Samaria praedicat:cui quum credidissent de Christo euangelizati,baptizati sunt viri simul & mulieres. Idem de Eunucho dicitur,quòd sit baptizatus à Philippo postquam credidit. & Lydia credit, postea demù baptizatur.ita custos carceris, cum sua familia. Sed quid? eadémne ratio adultorum & paruulorum habenda erit? De adul-tis rectè dicas.Priùs fidem suam confiteri debent,antequàm ad baptismum admittantur. Nam adulti ne admittent quidem baptismum nisi instituantur,nec admittendi sunt,ni consentiant doctrinae, & promittant poenitentiam in nouo credentium caetu. Ideo Ioannes Baptista à doctrina est exorsus. Idem fecit Christus & Apostoli. Nam ecclesia Christi erat colligeda ex adultis, quorum authoritate postea adducerentur familiae integrae. Haec ratio cum in-fantibus seruari nō debuit, quemadmodum nec in Circuncisione.
units.tr: Finally he adds a touch of the Anabaptist spirit: "provided the one to be baptized believes." Then, he asks, will no one be baptized unless he believes, that is, unless he can profess faith with his mouth? Take infants, for example, whom you say are not to be baptized precisely because they cannot yet believe. The passage he cites, Acts 8, where Philip preaches in Samaria, is no help to him: when they had believed the good news about Christ, men and women alike were baptized. The same is said of the eunuch, that he was baptized by Philip after he believed. Lydia believes and only afterwards is baptized; so too the jailer, with his family. But what follows? Is the same reasoning to be applied to adults and little children? Of adults you may rightly say that they must first profess their faith before they are admitted to baptism. Adults are not even admitted to baptism unless they have been instructed, nor are they to be admitted unless they assent to the doctrine and promise repentance within the new assembly of believers. That is why John the Baptist began with teaching, and Christ and the apostles did the same. For the Church of Christ was to be gathered from adults, by whose authority whole families were afterwards brought in. This reasoning could not be kept with infants, just as it was not kept in circumcision.

units.la: Nam proselytus apud Iudaeos non circucidebatur, nisi priùs in Lege essetbene confirmatus: cui tamen non obstabat quò minus infantes sub Lege nati, circucciderentur. Ergo in baptismo valeat eadem ratio. Qui ex adultis accedunt ad fidem Christi, merito priùs instituendi sunt: sed qui nascuntur in Ecclesia, nihil impedit quo minus infantes baptizentur. Praeterea quū legamus totas familias baptizatas esse, vt Actor. 16, custos carceris cum omnibus domesticis. & 1.Corinth. 1, domus Stephanae: magna certe est audacia, familias sine infantibus cogitare. At leguntur tantum baptizati adulti. Respondeo, sed non omnes. ergone qui non leguntur baptizati, non baptizatos dices? Stolidum sane & infantile sit hoc dicere. Quod si iste urgeat τὸ ῥητὸν[?], dumodo baptizandus crediderit, ex in-stitutione Christi, Quicunq; crediderit & baptizatus fuerit: reponemus ei, si placet syllabas numerare, dictum Christi, Ioann.3.Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua & Spiritu, &c. Praecedit aqua, sequitur hic Spiritus. Concludo igitur infantes baptizandos esse, quia ad regnum coelorum pertinent.
units.tr: For among the Jews a proselyte was not circumcised unless he had first been well instructed in the Law; yet this did not prevent infants born under the Law from being circumcised. So in baptism the same reasoning should hold. Those who come to the faith of Christ from adulthood are rightly to be instructed first; but those who are born in the Church, nothing hinders infants from being baptized. Moreover, since we read that whole families were baptized, as in Acts 16, where the jailer was baptized with all his household, and 1 Cor. 1, the household of Stephanas, it is surely great audacity to imagine families without infants. But only adults are read of as baptized. I reply: not all of them. Will you then say that those who are not read of as baptized were not baptized? That is a foolish and childish thing to say. But if he presses the text [τὸ ῥητὸν], "provided the one to be baptized believes," from Christ's institution, "Whoever believes and is baptized...", we shall reply, if he likes counting syllables, with Christ's words in John 3: "Unless one is born again of water and the Spirit, etc." Water comes first; here the Spirit follows. I conclude, therefore, that infants are to be baptized, because they belong to the kingdom of heaven.

units.la: Sed & illud praesumptuosum est, quod infantibus fidem plane negat. Notum est, a multis fidem eis suo modo tribui, inter quos etiā est Augustinus. Sed esto, fidem non habeant, quandoquidem miraculosa ratione illis concedi fidem scriptura non exprimit: quanuis Deus id possit. Detur ergo infantes fidem non habere. habent tamen eam parentes: infantes eam paulo post habebūt. & infantes ipsi sunt sancti, 1.Corinth.7.& pertinent ad Ecclesiā Christi, & habent Spiritum sanctum, qui administrator est veri baptismi. quid ergo impediet quo minus baptizentur? An in liciores erunt infantibus Iudaeorum, quos infantia a signo foederis nō excludebat? An noster baptismus Circuncisione est inferior, ut non applicari possit infantiae? Ait, Respōdeant illi mihi, quomodo infantes sancti esse possint, Spiritum sanctum habere, ad vitam aeternam pertinere sine fide, quum quicquid ex fide non fit, peccatū fit. Possunt igitur infantes suo modo fideles dici, quū habeant fideles parentes, habeat Spiritum sanctum, & paulo post accessura sit externa professio. quemadmodū dicuntur habere rationem, ita habere fidem dici possunt, imò firmiori quadam ratione, quū sit Dei occulta & secreta electio. ideóque nostrum est bene de illis sperare. Sed reuertamur ad ipsum argumentum.
units.tr: But that too is presumptuous, which flatly denies faith to infants. It is well known that many attribute faith to them in their own way, among them Augustine. But grant that they have no faith, since Scripture does not say that faith is given to them by some miraculous means, although God can do it. Let it be granted, then, that infants have no faith. Yet their parents have it, and the infants will have it shortly afterwards. The infants themselves are holy, 1 Cor. 7, and belong to the Church of Christ, and have the Holy Spirit, who is the administrator of true baptism. What then will prevent them from being baptized? Or will they be less worthy than the infants of the Jews, whom infancy did not exclude from the sign of the covenant? Or is our baptism inferior to circumcision, so that it cannot be applied to infancy? He says: let them answer me how infants can be holy, have the Holy Spirit, and belong to eternal life without faith, since whatever is not of faith is sin. Infants, then, can be called faithful in their own way: they have faithful parents, they have the Holy Spirit, and an outward profession will follow shortly. Just as they are said to have reason, so they can be said to have faith, and indeed by a firmer reason, since it rests on God's hidden and secret election. Therefore it is our duty to hope well of them. But let us return to the argument itself.

units.la: Circuncisio solùm administratur octauo die: baptismus nun-quam non. ergo illa huic non succedit. Diximus falsam esse consequetiam, & quę in materia desideremus. Nūc & illud addamus, q[?] ex typo octaui diei veteres hanc successionem comprobarūt. Nam Christus octauo die resurrexit, in quo plenè est peccati abolitio & nos in eodem.Col.2.Sic de hac re loquitur Augustinus epistola 89. Et Iustinus Martyr contra Tryphonem. Cyprianus ad resurrectio-nem nouæ vitæ refert, quòd qui se Deo confecrassent vitæ inno-centia, post septimanâ huius vitæ, octauæ, hoc est, æternæ beatitu-dinis cōsortes fierent. Et Athanasius inquit, Exuimus eum qui se-xto die mortuus est, & renouamur dominico die.
units.tr: Circumcision is administered only on the eighth day; baptism is never not administered. Therefore baptism does not succeed circumcision. We have said that the consequence is false and that we want more in the matter. Now let us add this as well: the ancients proved this succession from the type of the eighth day. For Christ rose on the eighth day, in which there is the full abolition of sin, and we in the same, Col. 2. Augustine speaks in this way about this matter in Epistle 89, and Justin Martyr in his dialogue against Trypho. Cyprian refers the eighth day to the resurrection of the new life: those who had consecrated themselves to God by innocence of life, after the seventh day of this life, that is, the eighth, would become partners of eternal blessedness. And Athanasius says: "We put off him who died on the sixth day, and are renewed on the Lord's day."

units.la: Circuncisio etiam adultis citra vllam verborum administratur formam. Contrà baptismus sine illa forma, Ego te baptizo, &c.fieri nequit.
units.tr: Circumcision was administered even to adults without any form of words. By contrast, baptism cannot be performed without that form, "I baptize you," etc.

units.la: Forma argumenti vitiosa est, quemadmodum in superioribus: ideóque mittamus illam. Non enim sufficit quod adfert[?]: imò quia sunt diuersa symbola, debuit etiam diuersa forma administrandi esse. Ac de formula Circucisionis, scriptura solum ritum actionis indicat, Genes. 17. Iosuæ 5. tamē Iudæi hodie etiam certam verborum formulam habet: & credibile est Patriarchas & Iudæos in genere, Circuncisionis actionem non mutam habuisse. praesumptuosum igitur est rem dubiam & inconfessam tanquam confessam sumere.
units.tr: The form of the argument is faulty, as in the earlier cases, so let us drop it. For it is not enough that he brings it forward. Indeed, since the signs are different, the form of administering them ought to be different too. As for the formula of circumcision, Scripture indicates only the ritual of the action, Gen. 17, Josh. 5; yet the Jews today also have a fixed formula of words, and it is credible that the patriarchs and the Jews in general did not perform the action of circumcision without words. It is presumptuous, therefore, to take a doubtful and unconfessed matter as if it were confessed.

units.la: Quis enim spiritus huic patefecit, quòd Circuncisio citra vllam verborum formam administraretur? quid si negent hoc Iudæi? quid si hic id probare non possit? Si igitur (quod est probabile) Circuncisio cum certa verborum forma administrabatur, & in Baptismo idem fit: nonne consequens est vt Baptismus Circuncisioni successerit? Habuit enim illa suam formulam rei competentem: habet etiam Baptismus suam formam à Christo praescriptam. Huic argumeto nihil deest, nisi quòd probabiliter dicitur de Circuncisione, quod de Baptismo indubitatè verum est Matth.28. Marci 16. Sed mittamus ista. esto, illic nulla fuerit verborum forma, hic certa est: quid hoc ad successione? nisi ostendat ipse, formulam baptismi talem esse, quæ legitimam successionē excludat, aut rem sacramenti in Circucisione talem esse, ad quam formula baptismi non possit pertingere. quorum neutrum facit.
units.tr: For what spirit revealed to him that circumcision was administered without any form of words? What if the Jews deny it? What if he cannot prove it here? If therefore (which is probable) circumcision was administered with a fixed form of words, and the same is done in baptism, does it not follow that baptism succeeded circumcision? For circumcision had its own formula suited to the thing, and baptism too has its form prescribed by Christ. Nothing is lacking to this argument, except that what is said probably of circumcision is what is undoubtedly true of baptism, Matt. 28, Mark 16. But let us set those aside. Grant that there was no form of words there, and here there is a fixed one: what has this to do with succession? Unless he shows that the formula of baptism is such as to exclude lawful succession, or that the reality of the sacrament in circumcision is such that the formula of baptism cannot reach it. He does neither.

units.la: Baptismus nisi rite administretur, reiteratur. Actor.19. at Circu-cisio etiam à fœmina collata, nequaquam repetitur. Exod.4.
units.tr: Baptism, unless it is rightly administered, is repeated (Acts 19). But circumcision, even when it was performed by a woman, is never repeated (Exod. 4).

units.la: Circuncisio repeti non potest in vno & eodem homine, siquidem præputium tantum vnum est. Sed quid sibi vult, à fœmina administrari? ânne vt Baptismus quoque à mulieribus administretur? quod sane hæretici quidâ permisere: & Epiphanius hoc Martioni aperte obiicit.sed esto,illa de Circuncisione solùm dicat. Num sin-gularis casus Zipporæ in circuncidendo Ehazero filio, legem po-nèt, ut mulieribus liceat conferre inter Iudæos Circuncisionem? Sed ad prius veniamus. Baptismus nisi ritè administretur, reitera-tur. Anabaptistâ hîc agnoscas.Sed unde reiteratio probatur? Acto. 19. Paulus Ephesi, baptizatos Ioannis baptismate, rebaptizauit in nomine Iesu. Primùm verbis Lucæ fit iniuria.Non enim scribitur, & rebaptizati sunt: sed, His auditis baptizati sunt in nomine Domini Iesu. Deinde nondùm satis constat an baptismus hîc ad elemetum aquæ referri debeat,quum probabili ratione ad professionem doctrinæ possit referri, ut mens sit,initiati sunt in nouum doctrinæ genus: quam sententiā sequentia explicant, Et impositis manibus descendit super eos Spiritus sanctus. sed esto, sint hi duodecim viri baptizati à Paulo: tum prior, baptismus non fuit. Nam de Spiritu sancto nihil audiuerant,ideóque non iteratio, sed noui & veri baptismi erat collatio. Ita quidem Damascenus rem explicat. Augustinus alibi scribit, quosdam dixisse hos discipulos mentitos fuisse, quum dicerent se accepisse baptismum Ioannis, quem tamen non acceperint.Nam baptismus Ioannis referebatur ad Christum,non in ipsum Ioannem.Ideóque si in Ioannem baptizati fuerant, meritò irritus erat baptismus. D. Hyeronimus ait, imperfectum fuisse baptismū hunc, quia Spiritum sanctum non dedit, ideóque baptizandos fuisse.Cæterùm res ita est fortassis.Baptismus illorum multis modis erat vitiosus. primùm doctrina erat corrupta, de Spiritu sancto enim nihil nouerant.Deinde forma erat mala: non enim in nomine Patris, Filii, & Spiritus sancti erant baptizati. Tertiò, non seruatus erat finis à Ioanne præscriptus, ut remitterentur ad Christum,sed videntur simpliciter Ioanni consecrati fuisse: ideóque ne quidem Ioannis baptismus erat seruatus,alioquin Paulus in nomine Iesu non contulisset baptismum. Nam videmus eundem Apo-stolum 1.Cor.1.non iubere ut rebaptizetur Corinthii, sed ut corrigatur menda, hoc est, ne sectas instituerent ex doctorum nominibus,quum in cæteris baptismus rite esset seruatus.
units.tr: Circumcision cannot be repeated in one and the same man, since there is only one foreskin. But what does he mean by its being administered by a woman? Surely he does not mean that baptism too may be administered by women? Certain heretics did indeed allow this, and Epiphanius openly charges Marcion with it. But grant that he is speaking only of circumcision. Will the single case of Zipporah circumcising her son Eliezer establish a law that women may confer circumcision among the Jews? But let us come to the first point. Baptism, unless rightly administered, is repeated. Here you recognise an Anabaptist. But how is repetition proved? In Acts 19, Paul at Ephesus rebaptised those who had been baptised with John's baptism, in the name of Jesus. First, Luke's words are wronged, for it is not written "and they were rebaptised" but "when they heard this, they were baptised in the name of the Lord Jesus." Next, it is not yet sufficiently established whether the baptism here must be referred to the element of water, since with probable reason it can be referred to the profession of doctrine, so that the sense is that they were initiated into a new kind of doctrine. The following words explain this: "And when Paul had laid hands on them, the Holy Spirit came down upon them." But grant that these twelve men were baptised by Paul: then the earlier baptism was not a baptism at all. For they had heard nothing about the Holy Spirit, and so it was not a repetition but the conferring of a new and true baptism. This is how Damascene explains the matter. Augustine elsewhere writes that some have said these disciples were lying when they said they had received John's baptism, which in fact they had not received, since John's baptism was referred to Christ and not to John himself. So if they had been baptised into John, the baptism was rightly void. Jerome says that this baptism was imperfect because it did not give the Holy Spirit, and that therefore they had to be baptised. But the matter is perhaps as follows. Their baptism was faulty in many ways. First, the doctrine was corrupt, for they knew nothing of the Holy Spirit. Second, the form was bad, for they had not been baptised in the name of Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Third, the end prescribed by John was not kept, namely that they be referred to Christ; they seem simply to have been consecrated to John. So not even John's baptism was observed, for otherwise Paul would not have conferred baptism in the name of Jesus. For we see the same Apostle in 1 Cor. 1 not ordering the Corinthians to be rebaptised, but ordering that the fault be corrected, that is, that they not found sects from the names of their teachers, while in other respects baptism had been rightly observed.

units.la: Verùm illa omnia mittamus,demúsque nonnunquā repeti posse Baptismum.exempli gratia, si quis in idoli nomè sit baptizatus, & non in Trinitatem:aut in nomen alicuius sancti,puta Francisci, Ioannis,Pauli,ut constet illud,ὅτι[?] μὴ εἰς τὴν ἁγίαν τριάδα ἐβαπτίσθησαν, τότε δὲ ἀναβαπτίζεσθαι[?]. Quid tandem hinc concludetur? Baptismus aliquo casu repeti potest: Circuncifio autem non potest:ergo Baptismus illi non successit.Primùm illiberaliter nobiscum agit.Nam Baptismi corruptam formam cum integra Circuncifionis forma confert.Deinde falsum affumit. Prius hinc constat,quòd Zipporæ factum formam Circuncifionis seruauit: sed doctores illi, qui illos duodecim baptizarant, formam Baptismi non feruarant:ideóque non valet argumetum.Quòd autem falsum affumat,hinc constat, quòd Circuncifionis forma etiam corrumpi possit, vt fi non præputium,sed alia corporis pars circuncidatur. Quemadmodum igitur in aliquo casu Baptismus repeti potest, ita Circuncifio interdū repeti potuisset: quam similitudinē in collatis exemplis quum isti non obseruent,merito illis negamus totum argumentum.
units.tr: But let us set all those things aside and grant that baptism can sometimes be repeated: for example, if someone has been baptised into the name of an idol and not into the Trinity, or into the name of some saint, say Francis, John or Paul, so that it is established that "they were not baptised into the holy Trinity; then they are to be baptised again" [ὅτι μὴ εἰς τὴν ἁγίαν τριάδα ἐβαπτίσθησαν, τότε δὲ ἀναβαπτίζεσθαι]. What, then, will be concluded from this? Baptism can be repeated in some case; circumcision cannot; therefore baptism did not succeed to circumcision. First, he deals illiberally with us, for he compares a corrupt form of baptism with the whole form of circumcision. Second, he assumes something false. The first point is clear from this: Zipporah's act preserved the form of circumcision, but those teachers who had baptised those twelve men had not preserved the form of baptism; so the argument does not hold. That he assumes something false is clear from this: the form of circumcision can also be corrupted, as when not the foreskin but some other part of the body is circumcised. Therefore, just as in some case baptism can be repeated, so circumcision too might sometimes have been repeated. Since his opponents do not observe this similarity in the examples they compare, we rightly deny them the whole argument.

units.la: Cæterùm Ecclesia Christi semper reiterationem Baptismi studiose cauit. Cyprianus, qui tamen ab hæreticis baptizatos retingendos esse censebat, diserte scribit in Sermone De ablutione pedum, Baptismum repeti Ecclesiæ prohibent regulæ. Et Iuftinus Martyr quæstione 14.respondet, Baptismum non repeti, sed corrigi errores. Et in decretis expresse cauetur, ne rebaptizentur semel baptizati, vt est videre de consecrat.dift.4.cap.quanuis.& paulò infrà,rebaptizare hæreticũ. Augustinus quoque eandē rem persequitur lib.1.contra Donatistas, cap.19. Hùc facit quod de Athanafio refert Nicephorus, quòd per ludum ab eo baptizati pueri,nõ sint rebaptizati ab ordinario episcopo,sed Baptismus per iocũ collatus ratus habitus est. Vide lib.8.cap.44.qua de re tamẽ quęri posset.
units.tr: Moreover, the Church of Christ has always carefully guarded against the repetition of baptism. Cyprian, who nevertheless held that those baptised by heretics must be rebaptised, plainly writes in his sermon On the Washing of Feet that the rules of the Church forbid baptism to be repeated. Justin Martyr, in his fourteenth question, replies that baptism is not repeated but errors are corrected. And the decrees expressly provide that those once baptised are not to be rebaptised, as can be seen in De consecratione, dist. 4, cap. "Quamvis," and a little further on, "to rebaptise a heretic." Augustine too pursues the same matter in book 1 against the Donatists, chap. 19. What Nicephorus reports about Athanasius is relevant here: that boys baptised by him in play were not rebaptised by the ordinary bishop, but the baptism conferred in jest was held to be valid. See book 8, chap. 44, though this matter could be inquired into.

units.la: Circuncifio nemini ex Gentilismo conuerso dabatur, fi non illi manendum erat inter Israelitas: patet ex Naamano Syro ,Ietrone, Nebuchadnefare, &c. At Baptismus nemini mortalium non concedendus, fi modò credat. Respondemus iterum male conferri causam. Nam qui cõuertebantur ex Gentilismo, & mansuri erant in populo Dei, his tandem dabatur Circuncifio: qui autem nolent esse, neque censeri aut haberi de illo populo ,his minimè dabatur. Nunc maneas in collatione pari. Baptismus obfignatio est Ecclesiæ Christi omnibus volentibus in eadem manere. Quemadmodum igitur Circuncifio ei non dabatur, qui Iudæus esse nollet: ita Baptismus merito non datur ei, qui Christianus esse nolit. Et quod attinet ad exempla, satis constat Naamanū, etiamsi esset curatus à lepra, Iudæum tamen esse noluisse. ita socer Mosis, quanuis agnosceret præsentiam Dei in populo illo, tamen de numero illius haberi nolebat. Idem dici potest de Nebuchadnezar, qui Iudæus esse noluit: alioquin, deserto suo regno, integrum fuisset illi transire ad Iudæos. Similis plane ratio est de Baptismo. Nam Iudæus seu Turca, licet agnoscant Christum Dei Filium: si tamen nolint esse de numero Christianorum, utique Baptismum non accipient.
units.tr: Circumcision was given to no one from the Gentiles who had converted, unless he was to remain among the Israelites. This is clear from Naaman the Syrian, Jethro, Nebuchadnezzar, and so on. But baptism is not to be denied to any mortal, provided only that he believes. Again we reply that the case is badly compared. For those who were converted from Gentilism and were going to remain among the people of God were at last given circumcision; but those who were unwilling to be, or to be counted or regarded as, members of that people were in no way given it. Now keep to the comparison on equal terms. Baptism is the seal of the Church of Christ for all who are willing to remain in it. Just as circumcision was not given to one who was unwilling to be a Jew, so baptism is rightly not given to one who is unwilling to be a Christian. As for the examples, it is quite clear that Naaman, even though he was cured of leprosy, was unwilling to be a Jew; likewise Moses' father-in-law, although he acknowledged the presence of God among that people, nevertheless was unwilling to be counted in their number. The same can be said of Nebuchadnezzar, who was unwilling to be a Jew; otherwise, having abandoned his kingdom, he would have been free to pass over to the Jews. The reasoning about baptism is plainly similar. For a Jew or a Turk, although they acknowledge Christ as the Son of God, if they are nevertheless unwilling to be numbered among Christians, will certainly not receive baptism.

units.la: Si Circuncisio idem Sacramentum quod Baptismus fuit: ergo Circuncisionis figura erat diluuium, siquidem Baptismi fuit. 1. Pet.4.quod utique falsum est.
units.tr: If circumcision were the same sacrament as baptism, then the figure of circumcision would have been the flood, since the flood was a figure of baptism (1 Pet. 4), which is certainly false.

units.la: Primùm, non dicimus idem esse Circuncisione & Baptismum: sed hunc illi succeßisse. in qua re callidè iam nobis mutat verba. longè enim aliud est, idem esse, & succedere. Sed tamen demus idem esse Sacramentū, scilicet, quod ad rem ipsam & scopum attinet: interea, diuersa esse symbola utrinque, & alias circunstantias satis notum est, quæ tamen successionem non impediunt. Deinde typos male sibi accommodat. ita enim colligit, Circuncisio fuit figura Baptismi, diluuium quoque fuit figura Baptismi: ergo diluuium fuit figura Circuncisionis. quis non rideat puerile argumentum, vt quod in secunda figura affirmatiuè colligit? Sed ita poterat colligi: ergo Circuncisio & diluuium sunt figura Baptismi. nam vna res diuersos habet typos: qui inter se tamen non habent typicam rationem, vt Ænæus serpens typus fuit Christi: Ionas quoque typus fuit Christi: ergo Ænæus serpens typus fuit Ionæ? non sequitur. Sic diluuium fuit typus Baptismi, & transitus maris fuit typus Baptismi: ergo diluuium fuit typus marini transitus? Item, Nubes fuit typus Baptismi. 1. Corinth. 10. & Diluuium fuit typus Baptismi. 1. Pet. 3. ergo nubes fuit typus diluuii? Simile plane est, diluuium fuit typus Baptismi, Circuncisio fuit typus Baptismi: ergo diluuium fuit typus Circuncisionis? Opinor pueros in scho-lis ridere tam ineptum argumentatorem.
units.tr: First, we do not say that circumcision and baptism are the same, but that the latter succeeded the former. In this he has already cleverly altered our words, for it is one thing to be the same and quite another to succeed. But grant that they are the same sacrament, namely as regards the thing itself and its aim. Meanwhile it is well known that the signs on each side are different, and so are other circumstances, which nevertheless do not prevent succession. Next, he applies the types badly. For he infers thus: circumcision was a figure of baptism, the flood also was a figure of baptism; therefore the flood was a figure of circumcision. Who would not laugh at so childish an argument, since he is drawing an affirmative conclusion in the second figure? But it could be inferred thus: therefore circumcision and the flood are figures of baptism. For one thing may have several types which nevertheless have no typical relation to one another. The brazen serpent was a type of Christ, and Jonah too was a type of Christ; therefore the brazen serpent was a type of Jonah? It does not follow. So the flood was a type of baptism, and the passage through the sea was a type of baptism; therefore the flood was a type of the passage through the sea? Likewise, the cloud was a type of baptism (1 Cor. 10), and the flood was a type of baptism (1 Pet. 3); therefore the cloud was a type of the flood? The case is quite similar: the flood was a type of baptism, and circumcision was a type of baptism; therefore the flood was a type of circumcision? I suppose schoolboys would laugh at so inept an arguer.

units.la: Si Circuncisio idem est cum Baptismo: ergo Israelitis aut duæ Circuncisiones aut duo baptismi erant. 1.Corinth.10.
units.tr: If circumcision is the same as baptism, then the Israelites had either two circumcisions or two baptisms (1 Cor. 10).

units.la: Prius diximus longè aliud esse, duo idem esse, & vnum alteri succedere:ideóque vel hac distinctione cótenti poteramus esse. Nam thesibus suis hunc titulum praefixerunt, Coclusiones quòd baptismus non successerit Circuncisioni, contra Paedobaptistas. Iam verum Succedendi trasformat in Idem esse: & nobis quidem satis erat ostendere, quòd baptismus Circuncisioni successerit pro Paedo baptistis: tamen ostendimus suo modo etiam idem esse, quanuis symbola diuersa sint. Caeterum ut illa mittamus, quomodo probabis Israelitis duas fuisse Circuncisiones? Fortasse quia transitus per mare & Circuncisio carnis idem tibi sunt, quod probas in secunda figura affirmatiuè. Transitus per mare est typus baptismi. 1.Corin. 10, & Circuncisio est typus baptismi secundùm nos: ergo transitus per mare & Circuncisio idem sunt, secundùm te: quod falsum est. Sed ex falso concludamus verum. Quæ idem sunt, non constituunt duo sacramenta: transitus per mare & Circuncisio idem sunt, vt tu male concludis: ergo non constituunt duo Sacramenta, quod ve-rum est. Sed quod res est dicamus. Israelitis duae Circuncisiones fuere, quanuis hoc tibi absurdum videatur: alia in carne, alia cordis. Deut. 10. Circuncidamini praeputio cordis vestri. Ieremiae 4, Circuncidamini Domino, & auferte praeputium cordis vestri. Imò Iudaei quadruplicem agnoscunt, carnis, oris, aurium & cordis: & tibi absurdum videtur duas esse? De baptismo idem dici potest. duos habemus, vnum corporalem, alium cordis, regenerantem nos ad vitam æternam. Sed illud non vis, hoc fortasse, duas Circucisiones externas, aut duos baptismos externos: circuncisionem corporis & baptismum in mari & nube. Atqui idem dicis esse. nō ergo duo sunt, sed idem. quod si fine & substantia dicas idem, damus etiam hoc: sin symbola dicas eadem esse, negamus, & tibi noua ineunda est ratio, vt idem esse probes.
units.tr: Earlier we said that it is one thing for two things to be the same, and another for one to succeed the other; so we could have been content with this distinction alone. For in their theses they prefixed this title: "Conclusions that baptism did not succeed circumcision, against the Paedobaptists." Now he transforms "succeeding" into "being the same." For us it was enough to show that baptism succeeded circumcision, as the Paedobaptists maintain; yet we have shown, in his own way, that they are even the same, although their signs are different. But leaving those things aside, how will you prove that the Israelites had two circumcisions? Perhaps because the passage through the sea and the circumcision of the flesh are the same to you, which you prove by an affirmative conclusion in the second figure. The passage through the sea is a type of baptism (1 Cor. 10), and circumcision is a type of baptism according to us; therefore the passage through the sea and circumcision are the same, according to you, which is false. But let us draw a true conclusion from a false premise. Things that are the same do not constitute two sacraments. The passage through the sea and circumcision are the same, as you wrongly conclude; therefore they do not constitute two sacraments, which is true. But let us say how the matter stands. The Israelites had two circumcisions, although this may seem absurd to you: one in the flesh, the other of the heart (Deut. 10: "Circumcise the foreskin of your heart"; Jer. 4: "Circumcise yourselves to the Lord, and take away the foreskin of your heart"). Indeed, the Jews acknowledge four: of the flesh, of the lips, of the ears and of the heart; and does it seem absurd to you that there should be two? The same can be said of baptism: we have two, one bodily and the other of the heart, which regenerates us to eternal life. But you do not want that; perhaps you want two external circumcisions, or two external baptisms: circumcision of the body and baptism in the sea and the cloud. Yet you say they are the same. So they are not two but one. But if you say they are the same in end and substance, we grant that too; but if you say they are the same in signs, we deny it, and you must find a new argument to prove that they are the same.

units.la: Si Circuncisio idem est quod baptismus, ergo Christus, Aposto-li, & quotquot erant ex Circuncisione bis fuerunt tincti: quod est absurdum.
units.tr: If circumcision is the same as baptism, then Christ, the apostles, and all who came from circumcision were baptized twice, which is absurd.

units.la: Idem esse & succedere aliud est. quod autem infert, ergo Christus & Apostoli fuerunt bis tincti, negamus. Si enim idem sunt, quod ad rem Sacramenti attinet, non fuerunt bis tincti. Sed hoc sequitur firmiter, Christus est circuncisus, Lucæ.2. Et Christus est baptizatus, Matth.3. Baptismus autem & Circuncisio re & substātia idem sunt: ergo utroque symbolo Christus initiatus est in rem eandem. non autè sequitur, ergo bis tinctus est, quia externa symbola non sunt unum & idem. Apostolorum Circuncisionem & baptismum non legimus, credimus autem.
units.tr: To be the same and to succeed are different things. As for the inference that Christ and the apostles were therefore baptized twice, we deny it. For if the two are the same as far as the reality of the sacrament is concerned, they were not baptized twice. But this follows firmly: Christ was circumcised (Luke 2), and Christ was baptized (Matt. 3). Baptism and circumcision are the same in reality and substance, so by either sign Christ was initiated into the same thing. It does not follow that he was baptized twice, because the external signs are not one and the same. We do not read of the circumcision and baptism of the apostles, but we believe that they happened.

units.la: Manna quodammodo respondebat Coenæ Dominicæ:sed manna Israelitarum nōdum adulti liberi vescebantur, quum tamé Coe-na dominica eiusmodi infantibus non liceat uti,iuxta illud, Probet autem seipsum homo:nam non potest rationis expers seipsum probare. ergo non valet argumentum a Circuncisione sumptum.
units.tr: Manna in some way corresponded to the Lord's Supper. But the manna was eaten by Israelite children who were not yet adults, whereas the Lord's Supper is not permitted to infants of that kind, according to the saying, "Let a man examine himself" (1 Cor. 11), for one who lacks reason cannot examine himself. Therefore the argument taken from circumcision is not valid.

units.la: Argumentum hoc non pertinet ad negandam successionem Baptismi, quod initiò coeperat: sed ad subuertendum Paedobaptif-mum: hoc modo, Nos probamus ab analogia Paedobaptismum. Sub Mose circuncisi sunt infantes. ergo sub Christo baptizandi sunt infantes. quia Baptismus Circuncisioni successit. Contrà ille excipit id non consequi. quia Coena, Mannæ respondens, non datur infantibus, cùm tamen Manna infantes uterentur. Respondemus malam adferri Analogiam Mannæ & Coenæ.nam Manna non fuit ordinarium Sacramentum in populo Dei, quemadmodum nec coturnices in deserto, aut aqua de petra.Circuncisio autem & Pesach foederis fuerunt Sacramenta, quibus hæc nostra sunt analoga. Ac mirandum est cur placuerit illi, Coenam & Mannā conferre:quin potius Pascati coenā aptare poterat.sed vidit obstare illi, quòd ad esum agni Paschalis tota familia admittitur: & ob id etiam pueri, quorum Baptismum hic demolitur.Sed reuertamur ad institutum. Probādum erat negotium per aperta, quæ non essent in controuersia, alioquin obscura per magis obscura probantur: quæ species est petitionis principij. Probādum illi erat, pueros non esse baptizandos.Argumentum sumit:quia pueri non admittuntur ad Coenam: ergo non etiam ad Baptismum. utrunque perinde controuersum est.Sed esto,proba pueros non esse admittendos ad coenam. Adfert argumentum ab analogia, quia admittebantur ad Mannæ esum. Habes expressum argumetum à contrario. Ergo ad Coenam admitti non debent. Contrà si analoga sunt Manna & Coena, & illic admissi sunt infantes, ergo hic etiam debent admitti. Vides te laborare in tua analogia, & institutum euerti, si rectè ducatur argumentum.Nam hinc probabitur infantes esse admittendos ad Cœnam, & ex consequenti, infantes esse baptizandos. Hinc constat, non sine causa veteres hanc quæstionem agitasse, an infantibus danda esset Cœna. Certè temporibus Cypriani illis data est, & Augustini sæculo idem factum apparet ex epistola 23. & ex Sermone 8. explicàs verba Apostoli. 1. Timoth. 1. Fidelis sermo, & dignus quem omnibus modis suscipiamus, &c. Et in Hypognostico contra Pelagianos, lib. 5. sed esto, nos habere in hac re melius constitutas Ecclesias hodie: & quod verum est, melius negari infantibus Cœnam, quàm dari: an ob id negari debet etiam Baptismus? Quis apud Iudæos tulisset hoc cauillum: Circuncisio fœminis non datur: ergo Pesach etiam illis dari non debet? Ita minimè valet consequens: Cœna non datur infantibus: ergo illis etiam non debet dari Baptismus.
units.tr: This argument does not bear on denying the succession of baptism, which had begun at the outset. It is directed rather at overturning infant baptism, and it runs like this: we prove infant baptism from analogy. Under Moses infants were circumcised; therefore under Christ infants are to be baptized, because baptism succeeded circumcision. Against this he objects that it does not follow, because the Supper, which corresponds to manna, is not given to infants, although infants did eat manna. We reply that a bad analogy is being drawn between manna and the Supper. Manna was not an ordinary sacrament among the people of God, just as the quails in the desert were not, nor the water from the rock. But circumcision and the Passover were sacraments of the covenant, and our sacraments are analogous to these. It is strange why he chose to compare the Supper with manna; he could rather have fitted it to the Passover supper. But he saw that this stood in his way, because the whole family is admitted to eating the paschal lamb, and so too the children, whose baptism he here seeks to demolish. But let us return to the subject. The matter had to be proved by things that are clear and not in controversy; otherwise obscure things are proved by things more obscure, which is a form of begging the question. He had to prove that children are not to be baptized. He takes up an argument: because children are not admitted to the Supper, therefore not to baptism either. Each point is equally in dispute. But grant it: prove that children are not to be admitted to the Supper. He brings an argument from analogy, because they were admitted to eating manna. You have an express argument from the contrary: therefore they ought not to be admitted to the Supper. On the contrary, if manna and the Supper are analogous, and infants were admitted there, then they ought to be admitted here too. You see that you labour over your analogy, and your position is overturned if the argument is rightly drawn. For from this it will be proved that infants are to be admitted to the Supper and, as a consequence, that infants are to be baptized. From this it is clear that the ancients did not debate without reason whether infants should be given the Supper. Certainly in the time of Cyprian it was given to them, and in Augustine's century the same practice appears from letter 23 and from sermon 8, where he explains the words of the Apostle, 1 Tim. 1: "Faithful is the saying, and worthy of all acceptation," etc. Also in the Hypognosticon against the Pelagians, book 5. But grant that we today have churches better constituted in this matter, and that it is true that it is better to deny the Supper to infants than to give it. Should baptism therefore be denied as well? Who among the Jews would have tolerated this quibble: circumcision is not given to women, therefore the Passover should not be given to them either? The consequence is in no way valid: the Supper is not given to infants, therefore baptism should not be given to them either.

units.la: X. Baptismus datur in remissionem peccatorum, Lucæ 3. Actor. 2. 22. Contrà Circuncisio non nisi signaculum iustitiæ fidei erat, Rom. 4. Imò nihil valet. 1. Corinth. 7. Gal. 6.
units.tr: X. Baptism is given for the remission of sins (Luke 3; Acts 2:22). On the contrary, circumcision was only a seal of the righteousness of faith (Rom. 4), indeed it is worth nothing (1 Cor. 7; Gal. 6).

units.la: Seipsum euertit argumentum. Si enim Baptismus datur in remissionem peccatorum, vtique illius remissionis obsignatio est, quemadmodum Circuncisio obsignatio est iustitiæ. Ideoque Apostolus de Abrahamo ait, quòd in præputio placuerit Deo, & iustus sit pronunciatus: postea verò signaculum iustitiæ acceperit. Conueniunt igitur Baptismus & Circuncisio, quòd vtrunque sit obsignatio iustitiæ, seu remissionis peccatorum. & ob id rectè docemus, quòd Baptismus successerit Circuncisioni. Cæterum, postea se corrigit hæc propositio. Imò, inquit, nihil valet. Quomodo hæc se non euertunt, signaculum esse iustitiæ fidei, quod rectè probauit ex Rom. 4. & eandem nihil valere? quod non rectè huc accommodat ex 1. Corinth. 7. Galat. 6. Nam Apostolus non eodem pacto loquitur in his locis de Circuncisione. Ad Rom. commendat fidem Abrahæ, vt quæ sit confirmata speciosissimo illo signaculo, scilicet, Circuncisione: quam ibi non damnat, vt quæ recenter esset inducta. sed ad Corinthios, & ad Galatas loquitur de Circuncisione iam abolita, & sublata per Christi aduentum, quo tempore cœpit nihil valere, imò pernitiosa esse: & ob id ei rectè successit Baptismus.
units.tr: The argument overturns itself. For if baptism is given for the remission of sins, it is surely the seal of that remission, just as circumcision is the seal of righteousness. Hence the Apostle says of Abraham that he pleased God and was pronounced righteous while still uncircumcised, and afterwards received the sign of righteousness. Baptism and circumcision therefore agree in that both are seals of righteousness, or of the remission of sins, and for this reason we rightly teach that baptism succeeded circumcision. Otherwise, this proposition is corrected afterwards: "Indeed," he says, "it is worth nothing." How do these not contradict each other: that it is a sign of the righteousness of faith, which he rightly proved from Rom. 4, and that the same thing is worth nothing? He does not apply here rightly what he takes from 1 Cor. 7 and Gal. 6. For the Apostle does not speak of circumcision in the same way in these places. In Romans he commends the faith of Abraham, which was confirmed by that most splendid seal, namely circumcision, which there he does not condemn, as if it had only recently been introduced. But to the Corinthians and the Galatians he speaks of circumcision already abolished and taken away by the coming of Christ, from which time it began to be worth nothing, indeed to be harmful. For this reason baptism rightly succeeded it.

units.la: X I. Baptismus facit vt Christum induamus, Gal. 3. Contrà Circuncisio efficit vt nihil nobis Christus prosit, Galat. 5.
units.tr: XI. Baptism makes us put on Christ (Gal. 3). On the contrary, circumcision makes Christ of no advantage to us (Gal. 5).

units.la: Argumentum pro nobis facit. Circuncisio sublata est per aduentum Christi, ideóque nihil prodest, si qui illam retinere velint: iinò efficit vt etiā Christus illis reddatur inutilis: ergo merito abolita est, quia nullus illius vsus, sed abusus superest. Contrà Baptismus inserit nos Christo,& efficit vt Christum induamus. rectè igitur successit in illius locum.
units.tr: The argument works in our favour. Circumcision was abolished by the coming of Christ, and so it is of no benefit to those who wish to retain it; indeed it makes Christ himself useless to them. Therefore it was rightly abolished, since no use of it remains, only abuse. Baptism, on the contrary, ingrafts us into Christ and makes us put on Christ. Rightly, therefore, it succeeded circumcision in its place.

units.tr: END.
